visits.text: Milos is the quintessential volcanic island—more than 70 beaches, each different in the color of its sand and the shape of its cliffs. Kleftiko, on the southwest coast, is the highlight: ancient white limestone formations pierced by sea caves, accessible by sea. It was a hideout for Saracen pirates, as its name recalls (kleftiko = place of bandits). Today, boat excursions leave Adamas every morning. The caves can be reached by swimming from the boat—light filtering underwater creates captivating shades of blue and green. Dolphins, turtles and seals frequent the area.

Adamas, Milos's main port, sits on one of the Mediterranean's largest natural bays. The waterfront is lively and well supplied. From the port, boat excursions take you to Kleftiko, Sarakiniko (the lunar scenery of the north), and the syrmata—boat garages carved into the colorful shoreline rocks, a symbol of Milos.

activities.text: Snorkeling at Kleftiko: the sea caves can be reached by swimming from excursion boats. Bring a mask and fins. Don't go ashore from your sailboat, as access is regulated—daytime anchorage only.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The scent of pine accompanies you on the approach to the Temple of Aphaia. Its Doric columns overlook the sea from a hill on the island; the current sanctuary dates to around 500–490 BC and replaced a temple destroyed by fire. Plan to travel there by vehicle from Aegina and check opening hours before leaving the port.

You can stop at Agios Nektarios Monastery between the port of Aegina and the Temple of Aphaia. This pilgrimage site is one of the island’s well-visited sanctuaries, while Paleochora occupies the neighboring hill. Keep your shoulders and knees covered and give worshippers priority during services in the church.

Good shoes matter more than a packed schedule when visiting Paleochora. Nicknamed the “Mystras of Aegina,” this former medieval capital occupies the slopes above Agios Nektarios: you will be walking through an abandoned historic settlement, rather than an inhabited village. Stick to passable paths and bring water for this exposed walk.

activities.text: If you want to bring home more than a photo, try a pistachio tasting in Aegina town. The local pistachio has protected designation of origin status, and shops are clustered along Aphaias Street behind the waterfront. Compare the different preparations and check where the products come from before buying a bag.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses

visits.text: You’ll follow the walkway through Aggitis Cave upstream along the underground river. At Maaras, water accompanies your visit beneath the stalactites; in the Wheel Chamber, an eight-meter waterwheel recalls how this resource was used. Confirm access before coming, especially after heavy rain.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: Wood that imitates marble: the Panagia church in Agiasos reveals this detail to visitors who examine its iconostasis. The current church dates to 1815; the wooden upper section continues the marble decoration with a carefully crafted imitation. View the whole structure without approaching worshippers at prayer, and postpone your visit if a service begins.

activities.text: Carved wood and ceramics fill the storefronts of Agiasos, on the wooded slopes of Mount Olympus. Workshops carry on a local craft tradition that is still alive, while the cafés on the square offer a break between shops. Ask what is made in the village and arrange sturdy packaging for fragile pieces.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Since the 10th century, the Basilica of Agios Achilleios has stood beneath the skies over Lake Mikri Prespa. Its walls remain, but the roof that once covered them is gone: the view now extends through the building to the lake landscape. Take in the basilica’s overall form before its details, and stay on the accessible paths around the ruins.

Panagia Porphyra extends the walk to the south of Agios Achilleios Island, far from the footbridge. The monastery preserves 18th-century wall paintings, another chapter in religious history after the great ruined basilica. Check access to the interior on site; leave enough time to walk back to the parking lot on the shore.

activities.text: You will cross the floating footbridge to Agios Achilleios with the lake almost level with your shoes. It connects the shore to an inhabited island in Lake Mikri Prespa: there is no need to book a ferry to reach the village. Leave your car on the shore, then continue on foot; the wind can make this crossing chilly even in spring.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: The blue dome stands out against the houses of Agios Kirykos. Above the harbor, the church dedicated to Saint Kirykos serves as a landmark as you explore the narrow streets; on the breakwater, the metal sculpture Ikariada depicts Icarus and his wings. Save the walk for softer light, then return through the waterfront square; wait until any service has ended before entering the church.

From classrooms to display cases: the Archaeological Museum of Agios Kirykos has taken on a new role. Housed in a former neoclassical high school, built in 1925 with support from Ikarians in America, it now displays objects recovered from excavations on the island and from shipwrecks. The marble staircase reflects the building’s ambition. Check opening hours with the museum before visiting, especially if your first day falls on a weekend.

activities.text: Head to Therma to trade the narrow streets for a break by the water. The Spilaio thermal spa uses a natural cave near the small harbor; Apollon offers another option on the village square. Choose one establishment, then leave time for the bay. Check its opening hours and entry requirements before setting out, bring a swimsuit and towel, and follow the staff’s instructions.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 3 Days: Hot Springs, Beaches, and Villages
Ikaria in 3 Days: Hot Springs, Beaches, and Villages

visits.text: Start at Lake Voulismeni, the beating heart of Agios Nikolaos. This 64-meter-deep lake of karst origin was long thought to be bottomless—hence its local nickname—and ancient legend held that Athena and Artemis bathed here. Since 1870, a narrow canal has connected it to the harbor. The tavernas and cafés around it make this an ideal first stop. If you are here in September, do not miss the Cliff Diving Festival: divers from around the world leap from the cliffs overlooking the lake, an unexpected spectacle.

Don't skip the Archaeological Museum of Agios Nikolaos—it's the second most important in Crete after Heraklion. It traces the region's history from the Neolithic (around 5700 BC) through the Roman period. Its most famous treasure is the Goddess of Myrtos: a libation vessel shaped like a female figure with long outstretched arms, discovered at the Bronze Age settlement of Fournos Korifi and dating to approximately 2500 BC. Allow 60 to 90 minutes to see it properly.

On the road to Kritsa, stop 1 kilometer before the village: the Church of Panagia Kera sits tucked on the right side, guarded by an ancient olive tree with a hollow trunk. It's the best-preserved Byzantine monument on the entire island, and the frescoes covering every wall are the reason why. The central nave dates to the 13th century; the two lateral naves were added in the 14th—one bears the exact date of 1348 painted on the wall, along with a portrait of the donor Georgios Mazizanis, his wife, and child. The Palaeologan style, with its expressive figures, clean contours, and vivid colors, is rare for religious art of the period. Photos without flash are permitted.

Kritsa, perched at 300 meters elevation 9 kilometers from Agios Nikolaos, is one of Crete's largest villages and among its most picturesque, with stepped alleyways, stone houses, and weavers still working traditional looms. The local embroidery and textiles are renowned throughout the region—you'll find several artisans in the village center. In the evening, once the tour buses have left, the village becomes surprisingly quiet and authentic again.

From Kritsa, push on to the site of Lato, 3 kilometers away: a Dorian city founded in the 7th century BC, perched on two hills overlooking Mirabello Gulf. You'll find paved streets, monumental staircases, an agora, and temple foundations—and a view of the sea and mountains worth the trip alone. Allow 45 minutes to an hour for a leisurely visit. Bring water: there's no shade on the site.

activities.text: Stroll around Lake Voulismeni in the evening: that's when locals gather on the café terraces lining both shores, connected by a bridge. The buzz builds as night falls—there's real nightlife in the adjacent streets. If you're there early in the morning, the lake is strikingly calm and the reflections of the cliff in the water feel otherworldly.

Explore Kritsa for its craft workshops: weaving, embroidery, pottery, and local products (honey, oil, herbs) are sold directly by artisans in the alleyways. The village also has several modest museums, including the House of Kritsotopoula, a folklore museum housed in a traditional old dwelling, and the Rodanthi museum dedicated to Cretan medicinal plants and herbs.

If you're curious about the most ancient Cretan cuisine, order xinochondros at an Agios Nikolaos taverna: a fermented dried paste made from sheep's cheese and cracked wheat, a winter staple of the Cretan mountains, simmered into a soup with seasonal vegetables. It has a distinctly sour and salty taste—an acquired one, let's say. Pair it with a glass of Vilana white, the indigenous Cretan grape, light and fresh with citrus notes, ideal with fish from Mirabello Gulf.

Swim at Almyros Beach, about 2 kilometers south of Agios Nikolaos: a long stretch of fine sand with calm waters, well-equipped and less crowded than the town center beaches. Several beaches then dot the coast toward Istro and Pachia Ammos along Mirabello Bay—ideal for a late afternoon if you're returning from Lato or Kritsa.

visits.text: A broad expanse of water replaces the narrow bays in front of Agios Panteleimonas, on Lake Vegoritida. The village lies on the western shore, in a landscape of vineyards and mountains. Head to a public shore access point rather than following every road around the lake.

activities.text: A visit to Vegoritis Winery, on the slopes of Mount Voras descending toward the lake, may be the best complement to Lake Vegoritida. The estate welcomes visitors to introduce them to its vineyards, facilities, and wines in the Amyntaio area. Book before making the trip; this tasting remains optional, with a driver who refrains from drinking for the rest of the route.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: Folegandros is an island of character—lashed by the meltemi, with 300-meter cliffs plunging into intense blue sea, and a Chora perched on a vertiginous ledge that long served as a place of political exile (until 1969). The main village is entirely pedestrian: three beautiful squares lined up and shaded by plane trees, stone-paved lanes, an inhabited Venetian kastro, and the persistent feeling that time passes differently here. From Chora, the switchback trail (20-30 min) leads to the Panagia church on its promontory—the view over the Aegean and neighboring islands at sunset ranks among the Cyclades' most spectacular.

Agkali (or Angali) beach on the south coast is accessible by car or bus from Chora. Pebble bottom sheltered by a cliff, deep blue water, two tavernas under the tamarisks. No natural shade except at the cliff base—bring an umbrella. From there, a 30-minute coastal trail leads to the wild cove of Agios Nikolaos, a favorite among island regulars.

activities.text: Swimming and snorkeling at Agkali: the rocky seabed shelters varied marine life. The cove is sheltered enough to be pleasant even in moderate wind.
Sunset from anchorage or Panagia church—the golden light on Folegandros's white cliffs is a spectacle that regulars return for every summer.

visits.text: They may smell you before you see them: the ARCTUROS wolf and lynx sanctuary near Agrapidies houses rescued animals in an oak forest. Sightings are not guaranteed. Avoid Wednesdays; the advertised ticket covers all facilities, but confirm its validity if your visits fall on two different dates.

visits.text: To visit the archaeological site of Thermos, allow for a same-day round trip from Agrinio. It is one of this circuit's least-known destinations – and one of the most important for the history of Greek architecture. As the federal capital of the Aetolian League, the sanctuary was western Greece's equivalent of Delphi. Its temple of Apollo Thermos, dated to 630–610 BC, is one of the earliest known Doric temples – 38 m long, 12 m wide, with 15 columns along the long sides. The site reveals the evolution of Greek sacred architecture in visible layers: from the Mycenaean megaron (Megaron A, Mycenaean period) to the Archaic Doric temple. The painted terracotta metopes, among Greece's earliest, are displayed in the National Museum in Athens – the small local museum retains a few fragments.

Lake Trichonida, 6 km southeast of Agrinio, is Greece's largest natural lake at 98.6 km². A Natura 2000 site, it hosts nearly 200 bird species including grey herons, storks and pink flamingos during migration season. The road along its northern shore is pleasant, with tavernas serving freshwater fish right by the water. From Agrinio, it's 15 minutes' drive.

activities.text: Agrinio is the capital of Aetolia-Acarnania – a lively city with little tourist interest in itself, but a logical end to the circuit before heading to Aktion Airport (Preveza) for connections to the Ionian Islands, or taking the motorway back towards Athens. Have lunch on the shores of Lake Trichonida before choosing your direction.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

visits.text: Long before the conquests of Philip II, Aiani already had a history of its own: the Archaeological Museum of Aiani brings together evidence of that past. Its galleries display objects from Megali Rachi and the royal necropolis, combining everyday life with funerary rites. Visit in the morning and check the official opening hours before leaving Kozani.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

visits.text: Édipsos' thermal springs have risen from the depths of the earth for 20,000 years, welling up from 3,000 meters below. More than 80 springs dot the municipality—the largest concentration anywhere in Greece. The waters reach 70 to 84°C at the Damaria source, cooling to 40 to 50°C at the beach springs. The ancients knew these waters well: Plutarch, Aristotle, and Strabo all documented them as the "Springs of Heracles." Legend has it that after each of his Twelve Labors, Heracles himself soaked in these waters to recover. The Roman general Sulla, plagued by a mysterious skin condition, came here and departed healed—a victory that cemented Édipsos' reputation among the empire's elite.

Along the central beach, Roman bathing pools carved directly from the rock still feed from natural 38°C springs. You can dip your feet for free—search the rocky outcrops north of the waterfront for telltale steam rising from the stones. It's an extraordinary sensation: sulfur-tinged air, steam rising, the Aegean Sea just meters away. History hovers here too: Aristotle, whose family hailed from Chalcis, reportedly visited to study the region. Later arrivals included Winston Churchill, Greta Garbo, Maria Callas, and Omar Sharif, all seeking the waters' restorative magic.

Modern thermal facilities offer medically supervised treatments: thermal baths, hydrotherapy, mineral mud wraps, and programs for rheumatoid conditions. Recognized therapeutic applications include arthritis, sciatica, and circulatory disorders. If you're not taking a formal cure, you can access outdoor thermal pools on a day-visit basis—though advance booking is wise during peak season, as capacity is limited.

Édipsos' waterfront stretches several hundred meters along the North Euboean Gulf. Stroll it at late afternoon when the light rakes across the continental mountains across the strait—the panorama is particularly stunning at that golden hour. Tavernas, cafés, and small shops selling local produce line the promenade, where the pace slows to that of a quiet Greek seaside town.

activities.text: Thermal bathing or a structured cure: both are available. A medical cure lasting several days is recommended for rheumatism, arthritis, or sciatica—it requires a local doctor's prescription. For a shorter visit, stick to the outdoor pools or natural beach basins. Water temperatures of 28–34°C are considered optimal for therapeutic benefit.

Half-day excursion to northern Euboean villages: Istiaia and the small port of Oreoi, 20 km to the east. Istiaia is an animated market town; Oreoi has a picturesque jetty and waterfront tavernas beloved by locals. Plan roughly an hour's drive from Édipsos along the coast.

Taste kolokythokeftedes—herb-stuffed zucchini fritters fried golden in olive oil. It's the emblematic vegetarian mezze of the Greek summer, served everywhere along the waterfront. Pair them with local Savatiano, a crisp dry white produced on the island, which cuts beautifully through the richness of fried vegetables and grilled fish.

In the evening, order galaktoboureko: creamed semolina wrapped in crispy phyllo leaves, drenched in warm lemon syrup. It's the ultimate comfort dessert of this region—more tender than baklava, less aggressively sweet, often served still warm.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

places.name: Akrotiri

visits.text: Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes for the archaeological site of Akrotiri - it is Santorini's most impressive visit and one of the most important in Greece. Imagine an entire city buried under ash in 1600 BC and excavated only since 1967: it is the “Pompeii of the Aegean Sea”. Unlike Pompeii, no bodies were found there - the inhabitants had fled, probably alerted by preceding earthquakes. The city lies more than 10 metres deep beneath 40 metres of pumice and ash. A bioclimatic roof installed in 2012 keeps the temperature pleasant even in midsummer: it is one of the island's few comfortable visits in July and August. Arrive at 8:30 a.m. to get ahead of the groups.

On the suspended walkways above the ruins, you'll walk over paved streets, multi-storey homes, a complex drainage system and ceramic storage jars still in place - exactly where they sat 3,600 years ago. The city traded with the entire eastern Mediterranean and had a large port. The most spectacular frescoes (the 3.90m-long naval procession, the Young Boxers) were transferred to Athens' National Archaeological Museum, but Fira's Museum of Prehistoric Thera preserves several others. If you purchased the combined ticket on day one, your entry is already paid.

Make the detour to Akrotiri Lighthouse, built in 1892 on the island's southern cliffs - it's one of the Cyclades' oldest and best-preserved. The road leading there edges the caldeira for a few kilometres with views of Thirassia opposite. You'll be almost alone: tourists don't venture here, making it a remarkably restful break after the archaeological site's bustle.

Red Beach (Kokkini Paralia) sits 1.7 km from the archaeological site - allow twenty minutes on foot from the car park. Its ocre and red volcanic rock cliffs plunge into turquoise water: the colour contrast is striking and justifies the trip even if you don't swim. Arrive early: the beach is small, wind-exposed, and crowded in high season. Pebbles increasingly replace sand due to cliff erosion.

If you have late afternoon time, get lost in the lanes of Megalochori, one of Santorini's best-preserved inland villages. Its troglodytic caves carved from volcanic rock, intact Cycladic architecture and shaded main square with cafes give you the feel of an ordinary Greek village - a rarity on such a touristy island.

activities.text: Take your time at the Akrotiri site. Unlike museum displays, in situ objects - jars, staircases, shop fronts - restore the city's human scale. The short film shown at the tour's end contextualises the site well geologically and historically. Arrive at opening time (8:30am) to avoid groups.

White Beach (Lefki Paralia), a few minutes by boat from Red Beach, is even more spectacular but less accessible. It is visited mainly by small boats and organised excursions departing from the port of Akrotiri.

Hunt down a glass of Nykteri in a winery or taverna in the Akrotiri area. This Santorini white is produced by an old method: vintage happens at night (hence the name), then the wine undergoes slight controlled oxidation before bottling. It's rounder and more complex than classic dry Assyrtiko - if you've already tasted one, compare with the other to understand the island's vineyard range.

If you spot chlorotyri on a menu, order it without hesitation: it is a fresh goat's cheese from Santorini, slightly tangy and creamy, that you will hardly find anywhere off the island. It is served in a salad with tomato and capers, or simply drizzled with olive oil. Simple, local and far better than any imported cheese served in the tourist restaurants along the caldera.

visits.text: Three white flashes still punctuate the night at sea. The Alexandroupoli lighthouse has guided mariners since 1880, serving a purpose far beyond that of a photo landmark. Read the marble plaque at its base, then return after dark: the signal repeats every 15 seconds.

activities.text: You’ll return to the Alexandroupoli waterfront after the coastal loop, when the promenade comes alive again. The city developed around maritime trade and the railroad, rather than an ancient acropolis. Save this walk for the evening, after Makri and Mesimvria-Zone, to fit the archaeological site’s opening hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: The lighthouse of Alexandroupoli has been the city's emblem since 1880: 27 metres tall, six storeys of stone steps, and its light visible from 44 kilometres away. It's still listed under the city's former name, Dede-Agats, on nautical charts — the town was only renamed Alexandroupoli in 1920 during a visit by King Alexander of Greece, and definitively incorporated into Greece by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923. Grab a terrace seat facing the lighthouse for your morning coffee — it's the best introduction to the city.

The Ethnological Museum of Thrace occupies a Neoclassical house dating from 1899. Its collections of embroidered costumes, jewellery, craft tools and photographic archives offer a rich overview of the culture of Thrace — a region that was successively Bulgarian, Greek and Turkish in the 20th century before reaching its present configuration. Allow an hour: it's small but thoroughly documented.

In the village of Feres, east of Alexandroupoli, approximately 28 km from the town for this stage, a 25-minute drive, the monastery of Panagia Kosmosotira is worth the detour. Founded in 1152 by Isaac Komnenos, son of Emperor Alexios III, its structure resembles a smaller version of Hagia Sophia, with 12th-century frescoes of the Constantinopolitan school. Converted into a mosque in 1357, it was returned to Orthodox worship in 1920.

activities.text: Excursion to the Evros Delta, designated a national park in 2007 and a Ramsar wetland since 1974: 188 km² of wetlands on the Turkish border where 300 of Greece's 400 bird species pass through or nest. Dalmatian pelicans, white storks, purple herons and greater flamingos are regularly spotted. Start at the Traianoupoli Information Centre (village of Loutra) to obtain your military-zone entry permits and book a boat ride on the Drana Lagoon. The trip lasts about an hour and a half.

Evening walk along the Alexandroupoli seafront: the fish tavernas line up facing the Aegean and the illuminated lighthouse provides the backdrop. Order prawn saganaki — baked in a tomato sauce with melted feta and ouzo — it's the unmissable local speciality, far better here than in Athens because the prawns come straight from the gulf.

For your last meal, try kagianas: scrambled eggs with fresh tomato and feta, served on village bread. Technically a breakfast dish or an evening meze, though the tavernas in this region serve it at any hour. Simple, filling, and deeply rooted in everyday Thracian cooking.

days_plan.itin_title: Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi

visits.text: Gravity seems to lose the battle in Alistrati Cave. Among the stalactites and stalagmites, helictites grow in irregular directions, as though the rock were unsure which way to go. Bring a light layer for the visit and wear shoes with grippy soles.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: Patitiri, the port of Alonissos, takes its name (“wine press”) from the island's viticultural past. Rebuilt after the 1965 earthquake, it's a functional and endearing town with a paved waterfront, a few seafood tavernas, and above all the MOm Information Centre on the Mediterranean monk seal — a small educational centre with videos and infographics about the species and the challenges facing the marine park. Don't miss it if you have children or want to understand what you'll see on boat excursions.

The Chora — also known as Palia Alonissos or the Old Village — sits at 200 metres above sea level on a ridge overlooking the entire island. Abandoned after the 1965 earthquake that partly destroyed it, it was gradually restored from the 1970s onward by artists and lovers of authenticity. Today its cobbled lanes lined with whitewashed, blue-shuttered houses, cascading bougainvillea and 360° panoramas over the Aegean make it the most captivating spot on Alonissos. Come in the late afternoon for sunset from the taverna terraces — it's one of the quietest spectacles in all the Sporades.

The Alonissos National Marine Park, established in 1992, is Greece's first marine park and one of the largest in Europe, covering 251,440 hectares encompassing Alonissos, six smaller islands and 22 islets. It was created to protect the Mediterranean monk seal (Monachus monachus), the most endangered seal species on earth. The park's colony numbers between 50 and 60 individuals — roughly 10% of the 500 to 600 still alive worldwide. The core zone around the island of Piperi is strictly off-limits to visitors in order to safeguard breeding sites. The areas accessible on excursions, however, offer the chance to spot dolphins, sea turtles, and more than 300 fish species.

Kokkinokastro is a striking spot on the east coast of Alonissos: a pebble beach in shades of rust and ochre beneath cliffs of the same hue, coloured by oxidised iron in the rock. Remains of an ancient settlement and traces of Neolithic occupation have been found here. The colour of the soil makes a dramatic contrast against the blue of the sea — it's one of the most visually arresting sights on the island.

activities.text: The boat excursion through the marine park is the centrepiece of any visit to Alonissos. Departures are from Patitiri, with several options: a full-park trip (6 to 8 hours) taking in the islands of Kyra Panagia and Peristera, swimming stops in exceptionally clear water, and sometimes dolphin sightings. Spotting a monk seal remains rare and depends on luck — but even without one, the quality of the water and the beauty of the deserted islets make the trip more than worthwhile. Book ahead in July–August.

Since 2015, Alonissos has banned single-use plastic bags across the whole island - a pioneering decision in Greece that reflects the eco-minded identity of its people. If you want to find out more about this commitment and about the protection of the monk seal, drop into the information centre run by the organisation MOm in Patitiri: the team and volunteers explain the threats facing the species and the marine environment, and what can be done to help protect them.

Tyrokafteri is a dip of crushed feta blended with spicy red peppers and olive oil — creamy, punchy, with a hint of sweetness. On Alonissos it's served as a starter with slices of toasted bread to open every taverna meal. Order it with a glass of ice-cold tsipouro and olives marinated in the island's wild herbs for an aperitif that's thoroughly local.

days_plan.itin_title: Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos

visits.text: Sikinos is the least visited of the inhabited Cyclades—300 residents, little infrastructure, no hotel chains. Alopronia port is a peaceful fishing village with a small, calm sandy beach. Then take the road (or better, the paved mule path) climbing 4 km to the Kastro and Chora, perched at 280 meters—two quarters facing each other, the first lively with cafés and the town hall, the second a labyrinth of white lanes bordered by bougainvillea. Three windmills watch over both quarters from the cliff edge, facing the sea.

activities.text: Climb to Zoodochou Pigi monastery, built in 1690 atop the Kastro: panoramic view over the archipelago and beyond. The island's most astonishing monument, however, is Episkopi—a 3rd-century Roman mausoleum converted to a Christian temple in the 17th century, accessible via trail from the Kastro. The place radiates a particular energy.
Swimming on Alopronia beach below the port—fine sand, calm water, and tamarisks. It's the island's most accessible beach, perfect for a pause before continuing your journey.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The Lion of Amphipolis has stood beside the Strymon since its reconstruction in 1936 — a colossal 8-metre-tall statue (including its base) in Thasian marble, dated to the 4th century BC. Recent excavations suggest it crowned the Kasta burial mound. It is thought to have been erected in honour of Laomedon of Mytilene, one of Alexander the Great's generals. From the road, the lion's silhouette is clearly visible above the river — stop for the photo.

The Kasta tumulus, 4.5 km away, is the largest funerary monument ever discovered in Greece. Excavations since 2012 have revealed a 497-metre-long, 158-metre-diameter peribolos in Thasian marble, dated to the last quarter of the 4th century BC. In 2014, archaeologists uncovered inside a three-chambered Macedonian tomb with two sphinxes, two caryatids, a pebble mosaic depicting the abduction of Persephone by Hades and, in the third chamber, skeletal remains of at least five individuals. The identity of the deceased remains unknown. A protective building has been erected over the site — check opening times before visiting.

The Archaeological Museum of Amphipolis, in the village, displays finds from local excavations: marble reliefs, gold jewellery, vases, sculptures and liturgical objects testifying to the intense commercial activity of Amphipolis, founded by the Athenians in 437 BC on the Thracian site of Ennea Hodoi. The city was in turn Athenian, Spartan and then Macedonian — Philip II seized it in 357 BC.

activities.text: Stroll along the Strymon in the afternoon — the river was navigable in antiquity and Amphipolis' strategic position at its mouth explains why so many empires fought over it. The banks are quiet and shaded, with views over the surrounding Macedonian hills. The two Byzantine towers flanking the river, the better-preserved of which dates from 1367, are visible from the bridge.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: A sudden coolness in the water marks the mouth of the Acheron at Ammoudia. The river meets the Ionian Sea here, with noticeable temperature changes near its mouth. The setting is an estuary, not the gorges of Glyki. View the river from its banks and avoid swimming in its channel.

If the Acheron intrigues you, the Necromanteion of Acheron in Mesopotamos extends your visit to Ammoudia. Its stone rooms and crypt have been associated with an oracle of the dead, but this identification is debated: a fortified farmhouse has also been suggested. Stop here before Kassope and check the seasonal opening hours.

activities.text: Board a boat in Ammoudia to follow the Acheron from its mouth, rather than taking an excursion to the gorges. Local boat trips offer views of the riverbanks and the river mouth from the water. The scenery changes without a long drive. Confirm the exact route and return arrangements before heading to Kassope.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: From red thread to painted reception rooms, Schwartz House tells the story of Ampelakia’s wealth. Its owner, Georgios Mavros, headed the textile cooperative; Mavros means “black” in Greek, as schwarz does in German. Look for the painted views of Constantinople in the decorated rooms. Arrive before 3 p.m. and avoid Tuesday, the listed closing day.

Look for an unusual detail in Agios Georgios Church: Saint George appears seated on a throne. This depiction and the carved iconostasis give you a specific reason to step inside during your visit to Ampelakia. Enter only if the church is open and no service is taking place, and ask before photographing the interior.

activities.text: Set aside some time to explore Ampelakia on foot after visiting Schwartz House. The stone mansions, fountains, and café-lined square extend the visit without adding another museum. Take a short loop through the lanes, then continue toward Larissa; the slopes call for sturdy shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: A few galleries are better than a long, aimless wander: the Amphipolis Archaeological Museum helps make sense of the scattered ruins. Funerary objects, sculptures, and coins tell the story of the city and its surroundings. The exhibits also cover the discovery of the Lion of Amphipolis. Check that day’s opening hours and start here before exploring the outdoor site.

The Amphipolis archaeological site takes a little imagination: its remains extend beyond a single monument. Walls, an ancient gymnasium, and buildings from the Christian era reveal several stages of its history. Choose the areas that are actually open instead of trying to cover everything, and bring water for the exposed sections.

Finish at the Lion of Amphipolis, near the Strymon, for a short stop after the museum. This funerary monument from the 4th century BCE is a landmark in the valley landscape; the museum covers its discovery and restoration. Park in a suitable area and keep clear of traffic while taking photos.

days_plan.itin_title: Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

visits.text: It is hard to separate Anavatos from its rocky outcrop: the tightly packed houses seem to extend the slope. This fortified village preserves the memory of the 1822 massacre; a single building housed a press, a school, a water reservoir, and a church. View the site from the open access routes and respect any barriers rather than trying to find a way through the ruins.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: Destroyed and then rebuilt by Philip II, ancient Stagira offers an open-air history lesson. Aristotle’s hometown occupies the Liotopi Peninsula, with ramparts, houses, and an agora among the hills. Bring water and wear sturdy shoes; visit in the morning and avoid Tuesdays, when the site is listed as closed.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

activities.text: If you want to break up the drive before Bassae, stroll through the lanes of Andritsaina. The stone houses and grand residences are reminders that this mountain town has a history of its own, beyond the nearby temple. Keep this stop short and have lunch here before the climb to the sanctuary.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Antiparos Cave is one of Greece's most significant: 85 meters deep, accessible via 411 steps carved into the rock. It harbors an 8-meter-tall stalagmite that's 45 million years old, considered Europe's oldest. The cave was known since antiquity—geometric and classical pottery has been found inside—and it served as a cult site for Artemis. On December 24, 1673, the Marquis de Nointel, Louis XIV's ambassador to Constantinople, celebrated Christmas Mass here before 500 people, using the great stalagmite as an altar. It closes in late afternoon—plan to go in the morning.

The Kastro of Antiparos was built in 1440 by Giovanni Lorendano, the island's Venetian lord, to protect the inhabitants from pirate attacks. The outer walls of the inhabitants' houses form the castle's ramparts. There is a single entrance through a gateway.

Antiparos's Chora is the antithesis of Mykonos: a quiet, authentic village where local life reasserts itself as soon as September arrives. Its bougainvillea-lined lanes, family-run tavernas, and port facing Paros make it a welcome stop to unwind after the more touristy islands.

The islet of Despotiko, reachable by a 10-minute boat ride from Agios Georgios in southern Antiparos, contains an archaic sanctuary of Apollo dating from the 7th century BC, under excavation since 1997. From Chora on Antiparos, plan a day trip by road to Agios Georgios and back, with a boat crossing to reach the islet. The islet's deserted beaches are among the most beautiful in the Aegean - crystal-clear water, a white sandy seabed and no tourist facilities.

activities.text: The Paros-Antiparos crossing from Punta takes 10 minutes by ferry, with connections every 30 minutes from 6 a.m. to midnight in summer. On the Antiparos side, rent a scooter or bike at the port to explore the island at your own pace—roads are flat and distances short.
The beaches of Soros and Glyfa, on the southern coast of Antiparos, are among the island's most beautiful: fine sand, remarkably clear turquoise water and very few people even in peak season.

In the evening in Chora, traditional tavernas serve fresh fish caught that very day, grilled octopus, and homemade mezzes in a relaxed, family atmosphere. Prices are well below those of Paros or Mykonos for equivalent quality.

Paros's assyrtiko, a dry, mineral white wine produced on the island's granite soils, pairs perfectly with seafood and grilled fish. Paros wines have a controlled designation of origin (AOC) and can be found in the island's grocery stores and tavernas.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Island Hopping: Mykonos, Delos, Naxos, Paros & Antiparos
Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Arachova, at 960 m on the slopes of Parnassus, is the village overlooking the Delphi–Athens corridor. Its grey stone houses with red tiled roofs cling to the mountainside on several levels. On the central square, century-old cafés serve local tsipouro and Arachova's PDO formaela cheese – a semi-hard goat's cheese whose production has been regulated since 1996. Shops sell handwoven rugs and woollen textiles, a living craft tradition. In winter, Arachova is a ski resort popular with Athenians – for the Parnassus ski lifts, plan a round trip by road from the village.

On the road to Delphi from Arachova, the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia is the first monument you encounter before entering the main site. The Tholos – a circular temple from the 4th century BC with three Doric columns still standing on a drum 15 m in diameter – is the most photographed image of Delphi. Nobody knows exactly what this building was used for. The Castalian Spring gushes out just opposite: this is where the Pythia and pilgrims purified themselves before consulting the oracle. The spring water still flows into the two ancient basins.

Delphi was “the navel of the world” according to the ancient Greeks – Zeus had released two eagles at the two ends of the earth and they had met here. On the slopes of Parnassus, between the two red cliffs of the Phaedriades towering steeply above, the archaeological site stretches across terraces. Climb the Sacred Way – the path pilgrims from across the Mediterranean followed to consult the oracle. The Temple of Apollo (6th century BC, rebuilt in the 4th) is now only a rectangle of columns, but the view from its foundations – over the valley, olive trees and Gulf of Corinth – is one of Greece's most beautiful. The Pythia delivered her oracles from an underground chamber in a trance, probably induced by ethylene vapours rising from a geological fissure – archaeologists have confirmed the presence of these emissions.

Above the temple, the theatre of Delphi (4th century BC, 5,000 seats) is remarkably well preserved. From its upper seating tiers, you overlook the entire sanctuary with Parnassus in the background – the site's best photo. Higher still, the stadium of the Pythian Games (4th century BC, 7,000 spectators) retains its 177 m track with intact stone starting markers. Allow an extra 30 minutes for the climb.

Delphi's Archaeological Museum is among Greece's finest. Don't miss the Charioteer of Delphi – a bronze statue from 478 BC commemorating a Pythian Games victory, extraordinarily well preserved with enamel eyes and bronze eyelashes. The Sphinx of the Naxians (570 BC) and friezes from the Treasury of the Siphnians (525 BC) illustrate the scale of donations made to the sanctuary by Greek city-states. The omphalos – the marble “navel of the world” – is here too. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: The winding Arachova–Delphi road offers spectacular views over the valley of olive trees descending towards the Gulf of Corinth – according to some sources, Greece's largest olive grove. In the evening, Arachova's central square with its tavernas is one of the most pleasant places on the circuit to dine: valley views, mountain air, and excellent local cuisine centred on roast lamb and Parnassus cheeses.

In the late afternoon, drive down from Arachova to Amphissa (approximately 28 km, 35 minutes by road) or Itea (approximately 25 km, 35 minutes by road) for dinner. Amphissa is a pleasant town with a medieval castle of the Frankish lords (13th century) overlooking the olive plain - a 30-minute climb. The Saturday market in Amphissa is one of the region's most authentic.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South
Central Greece & Gulf Coast
Central Greece & Gulf Coast
Classical Greece Road Trip: Athens To Olympia

visits.text: Aréopoli — 'the city of Ares' — is the gateway to the Deep Mani. Its former name was Tsimova; it was renamed in honour of Petros Mavromichalis, the last bey of the Mani, who set out from here on 17 March 1821 at the head of 300 Maniots to liberate Kalamata — two days before the official start of the War of Independence. His statue stands in the main square. The Church of the Taxiarches (Archangels), built in the second half of the 18th century, has the tallest bell tower in the Mani — a multi-tiered structure decorated with relief carvings and zodiac symbols on its façade, a testament to the Maniots' peculiar bond with Antiquity.

The Diros Caves, 11 km from Aréopoli, are explored by boat on an underground river — one of the most extraordinary experiences in the Peloponnese. A boatman rows you through 1,200 metres of flooded galleries, past stalactites skimming the water's surface, before a final 300-metre stretch on foot. The total mapped network exceeds 14,700 metres, reaching a maximum depth of 80 metres. Speleologists Ioannis and Anna Petrochilos first explored the caves in 1949; they've been open to the public since 1967. Bones of panther, hyena, lion and the largest hippopotamus bone deposit in Europe have been found inside.

Vathia is the ghost village of the Deep Mani: a collective fortress perched on a hill, made of stone towers packed so tightly that they form a continuous rampart against neighbouring clans. Allow a return day trip from Aréopoli. Vathia had up to 200 inhabitants in the 19th century; today a few houses have been restored, but the abandoned part is the most fascinating. Wander the deserted lanes without entering the towers, whose floors are in danger of collapsing. A striking atmosphere, between beauty and melancholy.

Cape Tainaron (or Matapan) is the southernmost point of mainland Greece. It can be reached by car as a day trip from Aréopoli. Leave the car at the car park and walk 45 minutes along a coastal path between two seas: the Ionian Sea to the west and the Aegean Sea to the east merge here into the Mediterranean. The Ancients regarded this cape as one of the gates of the Underworld - a local cave was said to lead straight to the realm of Hades. Near the car park, at the start of the path, lie the ruins of a 4th-century BC temple of Poseidon and a small chapel built on its foundations. The white lighthouse stands 41 metres above the sea.

Kardamyli is the most appealing village of the Outer Mani - Homer mentions it in the Iliad as one of the seven cities offered by Agamemnon to Achilles. Allow a return day trip by car from Aréopoli. The writer and traveller Patrick Leigh Fermor settled here in the late 1960s, and it was here that he wrote “Mani”, the book that revealed this peninsula to the world. Stroll through Kardamyli's old town with its stone houses, and climb up to the church of Saint Spyridon, whose ornate bell tower dominates the village. The path to the Viros gorge, below, is one of the finest hikes in the Mani.

activities.text: The tower houses of the Mani are the emblem of the peninsula: each clan built a stone tower to dominate its neighbours and defend itself during the vendettas that plagued the region for centuries. Around 800 of them still stand. Wander through the alleyways of Aréopoli to spot the Kapetanakos tower and the fortified Koutrakos residence — used in 1826 to resist Ibrahim Pasha's landing at the neighbouring village. Afterwards, drive down to the tiny harbour of Limeni (5 minutes by car): tower houses plunge straight into an emerald cove.

The road through the Deep Mani is the spectacle in itself: landscapes growing ever more barren and lunar, stone towers rising from hilltops, blue sea on both sides. After Vathia, stop for lunch in Gérolimenas — one of the Mani's few harbours, whose name means 'old port'. Waterside tavernas serve fried calamari and shrimp saganaki practically at the water's edge. Continue on to Porto Kagio, the southernmost village on the peninsula, for a swim in a quiet little cove before heading back toward the cape.

The coast between Kardamyli and Stoupa offers a string of quiet little coves - some of fine sand, others of pebbles, all with remarkably clear water. It can be reached by car as a day trip from Aréopoli. Stoupa, the most developed resort on the west coast of the Mani, has sunloungers and seaside tavernas. For something wilder, look for the coves north of Kardamyli, reached by paths from the road.

The hike through the Viros gorge, starting from Kardamyli, is a 3 to 4-hour loop through a canyon covered in plane trees. The trailhead is reached by car from Aréopoli: set aside the whole day. The path is waymarked and accessible. If you don't have time for the full loop, the first hour of walking is enough to feel the beauty of the place.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani
Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani

visits.text: Argostoli has been the capital of Kefalonia since 1757 — before that, the population sheltered inside the Venetian fortress of San Giorgio as protection against pirates. The town thrived as one of the busiest ports in the Greek islands, until the earthquake of 12 August 1953 levelled it entirely. What you see today is therefore a rebuilt city, but it has held on to an authentic Mediterranean character with its palm-lined waterfront and the lively Vallianos Square, which comes alive every evening.

The De Bosset Bridge — also called the Drapano Bridge — is the longest stone bridge over the sea in the world, stretching 700 metres. Originally built in wood in 1813 by Swiss engineer Charles-Philippe de Bosset in British service, it was entirely reconstructed in stone a few decades later. Almost halfway across, you'll come upon an obelisk erected by the British to commemorate their presence — the original plaque reading “To the glory of the British Empire” was destroyed in 1865, one year after the island was united with Greece. The bridge marks the edge of the Koutavos Lagoon, where you can spot Caretta caretta turtles swimming freely.

The archaeological museum of Argostoli, inaugurated in 1960 (architect Pátroklos Karantinós), is closed to the public and its reconstruction is unfinished. Do not plan to visit its collections from Samé, Kranioi, Pronnoi and Paléis. In Argostoli, head instead to Vallianos Square to discover the town rebuilt after the 1953 earthquake, then walk along pedestrian Lithostroto Street, lined with shops and cafés. Finish on the waterfront, where you can walk along the harbour.

The Korgialenios Historical and Folklore Museum, founded in 1963 on the ground floor of the library bearing the same name, traces the history of Kefalonia from the Venetian period through to the 1953 earthquake. You'll find antique furniture, silverware, household tools, traditional costumes and close to 3,000 photographs — a tangible way to understand what the town looked like before it was completely destroyed. The entrance is through the library, which also holds 50,000 rare books and manuscripts.

Saint Theodore Lighthouse, locally known as Fanari (“the lighthouse”), is a neoclassical circular structure with 20 Doric columns, built in 1829 during the British occupation to plans drawn by J.P. Kennedy. Its lantern sits 11 metres above the Bay of Argostoli. Destroyed in the 1953 earthquake, it was rebuilt to the original design in 1960. Come here in the late afternoon: the sun sinking behind the Paliki peninsula on the far side of the bay paints the sea orange — one of the finest sunsets on the island.

The Katavothres are one of the strangest geological phenomena in the Mediterranean: seawater rushes into cracks in the limestone, vanishes underground, crosses the entire island — roughly 15 km — and resurfaces in the Bay of Sami, on the eastern coast, fourteen days later. In 1963, Austrian hydrogeologists Maurin and Zoetl poured 160 kg of fluorescent green dye (uranine) into the sinkholes — and detected it again in the underground lake at Melissani and the springs at Karavomilos. The process remains partly unexplained. As far back as 1835, a British tax collector had the idea of harnessing the current to power corn mills — the ruins of those mills are still visible on site.

activities.text: Lithostroto, the main pedestrian street of Argostoli, is where locals gather every evening for the ritual stroll. Shops, cafés, the Catholic church, the clock tower rebuilt in 1985 — everything is packed into a few hundred metres. Keep walking to Vallianos Square, the large central square, for a Greek coffee facing the palm trees. It's quiet during the day, crowded and lively in the evening.

The Koutavos Lagoon, once a mosquito-infested swamp and a hotbed of malaria, is now a bird sanctuary where migratory species nest. Caretta caretta turtles feed here regularly. You can walk the coastal path or rent an electric boat to get a closer look at the wildlife. Morning is the ideal time — peace and quiet, soft light, and often a few fishermen by the harbour.

Kreatopita is the quintessential Kefalonian pie: puff pastry filled with a mixture of meats (lamb, pork, beef), rice and spices, baked in the oven. It's a festive dish that families still prepare for special occasions. Find it in the bakeries and tavernas around the market — it's the best quick lunch in town.

Robola of Kefalonia is one of Greece's most acclaimed white wines. This ancient grape variety grows on the Omala plateau at an altitude of 700 metres and has AOC status. The wine is dry, mineral and taut, with fine acidity — nothing like the rounded whites from the rest of Greece. Ask for it at any taverna by the harbour: it pairs perfectly with grilled fish and mezze.

days_plan.itin_title: Kefalonia and Zakynthos Tour: Caves and Beaches

visits.text: Armenistis is worth a stop to explore on foot between winding drives. Its small waterfront and pedestrian area offer a change of scale after crossing the island; the long beaches of Livadi and Messakti extend the village eastward. Park away from the narrow passages and locate your accommodations before heading on to Nas.

The Temple of Artemis Tauropolos at Nas takes a little imagination: the sanctuary’s outlines are mostly visible at ground level. The remains line the bay at the mouth of the Chalaris, far from the image of a temple with standing columns. Walk down the steps from the road wearing sturdy shoes, and keep off the ancient masonry.

activities.text: If the sea is calm, Livadi Beach offers a break on the sand near Armenistis. Together with neighboring Messakti, it provides a contrast to the pebbles of Seychelles and lets you stay close to the village. Walk along the water before choosing a spot to settle down; follow the swimming guidance posted on site.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 3 Days: Hot Springs, Beaches, and Villages

visits.text: Look beneath your feet rather than up at the vault. At Agios Stefanos, the Church of St. Stephen in Arnaia, a glass floor reveals the remains buried beneath the place of worship. Built in 1812, the building has suffered several fires; it remains an active church. Visit outside service times and respect the areas reserved for worshippers.

Embroidered roses and colorful rugs catch the eye at the Arnaia Weaving Museum. The collection honors Harikleia Dimitrakoudi and preserves textiles from a craft that once supported the village’s families. Check opening hours before you arrive; if the door is closed, extend your walk among the traditional houses.

activities.text: You can extend your walk through Arnaia’s central square before choosing a few local products. Among Macedonian houses and cafés, shops sell honey, jams, and textiles, among other goods; the village preserves the memory of its women weavers. Ask where the products come from and keep your purchases cool in the car.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

visits.text: Walking over Arta Bridge gives its arches a different sense of scale than viewing them from the road. The bridge spans the Arachthos; a folk ballad tells how it collapsed every night until a sacrifice was made to keep it standing. This story is a legend. Come in the morning to photograph the arches from the riverbank.

You can only see it from outside, but the detour is still worthwhile: Panagia Parigoritissa is an imposing presence in the middle of Arta. This Byzantine church dates to the late 13th century; the Ephorate of Antiquities has announced an extended closure for work. Plan to view the exterior and check the official notice before hoping to go inside.

Head to Arta Castle for a change of scale as you move from the city streets to the ramparts. The fortifications date to the 13th century, although their current appearance owes much to later alterations. Look for the clock tower, then check that day’s access arrangements before counting on a walk inside the walls.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

visits.text: Astypalea's Chora is a cascade of cubic white houses tumbling down a rocky hillside to the old port of Pera Gialos. At the summit looms Querini Castle, built of dark stone by the eponymous Venetian family after 1413—contrasting spectacularly with the village's white walls below. The ramparts once served as exterior walls for three-story houses built against them inside. The 1956 earthquake left ruins within, but the monumental entrance remains intact and the view from the top over the two bays forming the island's isthmus is extraordinary. Free admission.

The eight windmills aligned along the ridge of Chora, between the village and the castle, are Astypalea's symbol. Their position allowed them to capture north and south winds interchangeably according to season. One has been converted into the municipal library, another into a shop. In the evening, this is the locals' meeting point before descending to the tavernas.

Pera Gialos, the old port at Chora's foot, is Astypalea's most authentic spot: painted wooden fishing boats, tavernas with plastic tables facing the sea, fish market in the morning. This is where the island truly lives, far from the tourist animation of Chora. Stroll the quay in late afternoon when fishermen return.

The Church of Panagia Portaïtissa (18th century), just below the castle, is considered one of the Dodecanese's most beautiful: its carved and gilded wooden iconostasis was built over nine years by Agios Anthimos of Cephalonia, who was blind according to tradition. A copy of the Panagia Portaïtissa icon was brought from Mount Athos.

Pera Gialos's archaeological museum sits directly on the old port waterfront. It houses finds ranging from prehistory to the medieval era, including pieces from the Kylindra necropolis—a unique burial site where 2,700 infant skeletons interred in jars were discovered on the castle hill's flank, spanning a thousand-year period. A local cult whose significance archaeologists still debate. The museum is small but dense: allow 30 to 40 minutes.

activities.text: From Pera Gialos, drive or ride a scooter to Livadi, an organized beach below Chora, then continue for about 5 km to Agios Konstantinos. The final kilometre follows a passable dirt road. There, alternate swimming with a walk to the small chapel overlooking the cove and a break beneath the tamarisks or in the serviced area. The beach combines sand and pebbles, facing Chora and Querini Castle. On the way back, stop at Livadi to see Chora's white silhouette again from the other side of the bay.

Reserve half a day to reach Vathy by water taxi from Pera Gialos. This natural fjord on the island's east—accessible only by sea or via a poor-condition track—is one of the Dodecanese's most timeless atmospheres: a silent fishing village at the end of a narrow sea arm surrounded by arid hills. A single taverna serves the morning's catch. Boats generally depart late morning.

Have a drink in front of Chora's windmills at sunset—it's the locals' gathering spot. Illuminated Chora gives the impression the village is either climbing the mountain or suspended in the void, depending on the viewing angle. The atmosphere shifts dramatically once night falls.

Astypalea's 'Kopanisti' is a pungent, fermented soft-paste cheese served as mezze. The local 'Pouggia' are filled with almonds and mastiha (mastic resin), a perfumed variation on the specialty you may have tasted in Patmos. Ask for them in Pera Gialos pastry shops.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos

visits.text: The Parthenon is why you came. Built between 447 and 432 BC by architects Ictinus and Callicrates under the direction of sculptor Phidias, it took 22,000 tonnes of marble quarried from Mount Pentelicus, 17 km away, to raise it. Notice that the marble contains traces of iron that have oxidized over time—at sunrise or sunset, it turns honey-gold. Arrive as early as possible, right when it opens: crowds thicken after 9:30 AM.

The Erechtheion, built between 421 and 406 BC in Ionic style, houses the famous Porch of the Caryatids. These six statues of young women serving as columns are copies—the originals are in the Acropolis Museum. Take time to walk around the building: the north façade, the most ornate, is the best preserved.

The Propylaea form the monumental gateway to the Acropolis, designed by architect Mnesicles starting in 437 BC, in Pentelic marble. This five-opening portico was so imposing that ancient travelers described it as rivaling the Parthenon itself. Look at the ceiling of the central hall—the coffers painted in blue and gold are still partially visible.

The Temple of Athena Nike, perched to the right of the entrance, was built between 427 and 424 BC to celebrate victory over the Persians. It's the oldest Ionic temple on the Acropolis, and also the smallest: only 8 meters long. It was completely dismantled by the Ottomans in 1686 to build a gun battery, then reconstructed stone by stone in the 19th century.

The Theater of Dionysus, carved into the southern slope of the Acropolis in the 6th century BC, is considered the birthplace of Western theater. This is where Aeschylus, Sophocles and Aristophanes first presented their plays, before 17,000 spectators. The marble seats you see date from the Roman renovation, but the original wooden stage goes back to the Great Dionysia festivals.

The Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009 and designed by Swiss architect Bernard Tschumi, houses 4,000 pieces exclusively from the sacred hill. Don't miss the third floor, oriented exactly like the Parthenon: you'll see 160 meters of friezes presented according to their original arrangement. The empty spaces, marked "BM," remind you that two-thirds of the marbles are still in the British Museum. Book your ticket in advance during high season.

If the Acropolis is Athens' symbol, the Ancient Agora is its brain. Here, on these 25 hectares northwest of the sacred rock, democracy took shape: the Bouleuterion housed the Council of 500 members, the Tholos the standing committee. Socrates paced these very porticoes. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours to tour it completely with the museum—don't skip the latter, it preserves history's first voting ballots.

Take time to climb up to the Temple of Hephaestus, perched at the northwest corner of the Agora: it's the best-preserved Doric temple in Greece, built between 460 and 415 BC. Its survival is due to a lucky coincidence—it was converted into a Christian church in the 7th century, preserving its walls and roof. The north and south friezes recount the exploits of Theseus and Heracles. Athenians themselves often mistakenly call it the “Theseion.”

Entering the Stoa of Attalos, you're walking into history's first shopping mall. Built around 150 BC by Attalos II, king of Pergamon, in gratitude to the city that had welcomed him during his studies, this 116-meter portico on two levels now houses the Agora Museum. Reconstructed identically between 1953 and 1956 by the American School of Archaeology, it retains Doric columns on the ground floor and Ionic upstairs. Look for the ostraka—those pottery shards on which Athenians inscribed the name of the citizen to be banished from the city.

Right next to the Roman Agora, don't miss Hadrian's Library: built in 132 AD by the Roman emperor, it was much more than a library—a vast complex of 122 by 82 meters with reading rooms, gardens and a central pool. Today only the façade with Corinthian columns is clearly visible from the street, but the site merits a brief stop. Entry is included in the combined ticket for Athens' seven archaeological sites.

The National Archaeological Museum, founded in 1829, is Greece's largest museum. If you only have time for one room, go directly to the Mycenaean collection: the gold mask called "Agamemnon's," discovered by Schliemann in 1876 at Mycenae, is one of the most striking pieces of Greek antiquity. Reserve at least 2 hours if you want to cover the Cycladic collection and the bronzes.

The Panathenaic Stadium—Kallimarmaro in Greek, "of beautiful marble"—is the world's only stadium built entirely of white marble. Founded in 330 BC by statesman Lycurgus for the Great Panathenaea, it was completely rebuilt in Pentelic marble under Herodes Atticus in the 2nd century AD (capacity: 70,000 spectators). Fallen into ruin then pillaged for its stones in the Middle Ages, it was restored to host the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. You can run on the track: it's included in the ticket. Caution: in summer, the marble heats up—visit in the morning or late afternoon.

Lycabettus Hill rises to 277 meters, Athens' highest point. From the summit, you have 360° views of the Acropolis, Piraeus and, on clear days, as far as the island of Aegina. Climb on foot from Kolonaki (30 minutes) or by funicular from Aristippou Street. In the evening, it's the city's best spot to watch Athens light up.

Athens' National Garden extends over 15 hectares in the city's heart, planted by Queen Amalia in the 19th century. It's the Athenians' green oasis—ducks, turtles, shaded pergolas—a welcome break between visits. At the southern exit stands the Zappeion, a neoclassical palace from 1888 designed by Theophil Hansen, used for official ceremonies and exhibitions.

The Academy of Athens, the University and the National Library form the Neoclassical Trilogy of Panepistimiou Street, all three designed by Theophil Hansen between 1859 and 1902. The Academy is the most impressive: Ionic columns, colored friezes, statues of Apollo and Athena on their pedestals. It's the iconic photo of neoclassical Athens—and often ignored by tourists hurrying off to the Acropolis.

If you're feeling a bit weary of ancient sites, the Benaki Museum is an excellent antidote. Housed in a beautiful neoclassical mansion in Kolonaki, it traces Greek history from prehistory to the present day—Mycenaean, Byzantine, Ottoman, modern—in one fluid journey. It's also one of Athens' museums with the best exhibition design. Go up to the rooftop café terrace: the view over the gardens and city is worth the trip.

After three days of ancient Greece, pause at the Byzantine and Christian Museum—you'll discover another Greece, just as rich. Icons, mosaics, frescoes, liturgical embroideries: the collection covers fourteen centuries, from the 4th to the 15th. Some gold and tempera icons are stunningly refined. Allow about 1.5 hours to enjoy it unhurried.

Don't miss Kerameikos: it's one of Athens' most moving sites, and one of the least crowded. This former potters' quarter was also the city's main necropolis, used from the 12th century BC through the Roman era. You'll find sculpted funerary steles, marble lions, and the Sacred Way that ran from here to Eleusis. The on-site museum houses the finest steles. On weekdays, you'll often have it to yourself.

Kapnikarea Church, nestled right in the middle of Ermou Street since the 11th century, is one of Athens' oldest Byzantine churches. Its central brick dome and golden interior mosaics contrast sharply with the bustle of shops on the street. Step inside—it's often open in the morning.

Syntagma Square is the heart of modern Athens, dominated by the Parliament housed in the former Royal Palace of 1843. In front, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is permanently guarded by the Evzones, presidential guards in traditional costume—white pleated fustanella with 400 pleats, white stockings and shoes with black pompoms. The changing of the guard happens every hour, and on Sundays at 11 AM in full dress with music.

The Museum of Cycladic Art houses one of the world's most important collections of Cycladic art, dating from 3200 to 2000 BC. These white marble figurines with refined forms—barely sketched silhouettes, smooth faces—fascinated Picasso and Modigliani in the 20th century. The effect is striking: they could be contemporary sculptures.

activities.text: Head up to the Acropolis right when it opens (8 AM in summer). The raking morning light gilds the Parthenon's marble and tourists are still scarce—it's the best window of the day to photograph the site without crowds.

After the Acropolis, descend toward Plaka, the historic neighborhood that stretches at the foot of the rock. Its cobbled lanes and stairways, neoclassical houses and bougainvillea make it one of the most pleasant places in Athens to stroll in the shade. Avoid restaurants directly on the tourist thoroughfares—head into the side streets.

Moussaka is the dish to try in Athens: meltingly tender eggplant, spiced ground meat, and béchamel baked until golden on top. The best versions are found in the tavernas of Plaka or Monastiraki, not in terrace restaurants with laminated photos.
In the evening, head back up toward the Acropolis rock at sunset from the Hill of the Muses or from Filopappou—free views, no crowds, of the Parthenon turning orange. It's the day's spectacle.

Monastiraki, right next to the Agora, is the neighborhood of flea markets, shops of every kind and local bustle. On Sundays, the flea market spills into the surrounding lanes - you can find everything from Byzantine icons to old Greek coins.

Head into the Psyrri neighborhood, just north of Monastiraki. It's the haunt of Athenian artists and night owls: walls covered in graffiti, used bookstores, cafés where people play cards until 3 AM. The neighborhood really only comes alive after 8 PM.

Spanakopita—spinach and feta pastry—is the ideal snack to keep you going between visits. You'll find it in all the market bakeries, still warm in the morning. Pastitsio is the day's main dish: baked pasta, ground meat, tomato sauce and béchamel browned on top—a pasta version of moussaka.

In the evening, try ouzo with a few mezze on a Psyrri terrace: cephalopods, olives, taramosalata. Ouzo is drunk diluted with cold water—it turns cloudy and the anise flavor softens. It's been the Athenians' aperitif ritual for generations.

Kolonaki is Athens' upscale neighborhood, at the foot of Lycabettus. Its cafés in Kolonaki Square are perfect for a midday break to watch well-heeled Athenians—it's a local sport. Greek designer boutiques cluster in the streets around the square.

Plan your Lycabettus ascent for late afternoon, so you reach the summit an hour before sunset. When the light shifts over the Acropolis and the city begins to glow beneath your feet, it's one of the most memorable moments of a stay in Athens. The little café at the summit stays open until nightfall.

Dolmades—vine leaves stuffed with rice, fresh herbs and lemon juice—are often served as mezze in the tavernas of Kolonaki or Plaka. Greek salad is always better here than elsewhere: thick slices of tomato, cucumbers, Kalamata olives, a block of feta and dried oregano on top.

If you like Greek wines, look for an Assyrtiko from Santorini when dining out in the evening: a dry white with pronounced minerality and sharp acidity that comes from the island's volcanic soils. It's Greece's most internationally famous white wine, and one of the best to pair with seafood.

For breakfast or a midday break, look for a café in Syntagma Square or the adjacent alleys for bougatsa—warm pastry filled with custard cream or fresh cheese, dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar. It's the traditional Thessaloniki breakfast that's become popular throughout Greece.

Ermou Street, pedestrianized between Syntagma and Monastiraki, is Athens' main shopping artery. This is where you'll encounter locals doing their shopping—not just tourists. Kapnikarea Church cuts it in two, a symbol of two overlapping millennia.

If you have the energy for an evening out, Exarcheia is Athens' most alternative neighborhood—bookstores, politicized bars, walls entirely covered in political graffiti, cafés open until the early hours. It's a very different Athens from Kolonaki or Plaka, and much more authentic.

For dinner, try keftedes—meatballs flavored with mint and cumin, fried and served as mezze. Mavrodaphne from Patras, a sweet red Greek wine, is the ideal companion to finish the meal with honey-based desserts.

visits.text: Starting at the Archaeological Museum of Abdera makes the ruins much easier to understand. In Avdira, everyday objects bring the inhabitants into focus beyond the names of Democritus and Protagoras. Check the museum’s and the site’s opening hours separately: their opening days may differ in winter.

A city that shifted location over the course of its history: the ancient site of Abdera is more than a set of defensive walls. Silting contributed to the relocation of neighborhoods to the south; the Byzantine remains of Polystylon now occupy the ancient acropolis. After visiting the museum in Avdira, drive to the coastal site and save some water for your visit.

visits.text: Do not expect a vast citadel at Avlemonas Castello: its appeal lies in its position near the small harbor. This Venetian fort stands beside a village of light-colored houses and rocky coves. Walk around the accessible grounds to see how the monument relates to the shore; only plan to visit the interior if access is open.

activities.text: Walk along Avlemonas’s small coves to choose a spot for a break by the water. Here, you can swim in rocky inlets, while paved paths connect the areas around the village. Identify an easy way in and out before entering the water; when the sea is rough, stick to walking.

places.name: Bassae

visits.text: An ancient temple beneath a large tent: at Bassae, the protective covering is part of the landscape. The Temple of Apollo Epicurius, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986, combines the Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian orders. Do not expect an open-air colonnade; check the last admission time before leaving Andritsaina and bring a layer to protect against the wind.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

map_keywords: Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae

visits.text: Reeds line the sanctuary of Artemis at Brauron, near the Erasinos River. The portico with its restored columns and the stone bridge recall how this place combined religious ceremonies with a wetland setting. Artemis protected women and children in particular here; arrive around 1:30 PM so you can also visit the museum before 3:30 PM.

You’ll continue your visit at the Archaeological Museum of Brauron, very close to the sanctuary. Statues of children, toys, and figurines make the offerings to Artemis more tangible than the remains alone. Give the everyday objects as much attention as the sculptures; set aside enough time for a proper visit, as the museum also closes at 3:30 PM.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: The Temple of Poseidon raises its 15 surviving Doric columns on a promontory 60 meters high, at the southern tip of Attica. Built between 444 and 440 BC—at the same time as the Parthenon, as part of Pericles' program—it served both as a sanctuary to the god of the seas and as a landmark for sailors returning to Piraeus from the Mediterranean. On clear days, you'll make out the islands of Kea, Kythnos, and in good weather, as far as Serifos in the distance. Time your arrival for sunset: the orange light on the white marble is spectacular.

On one of the temple columns, look for the carved name of Lord Byron, who visited the site in 1810. The English poet was so captivated by Sounion that he recorded his reaction in verses from Don Juan (1819)—an ode to this marble promontory battered by waves that he described as the ideal place to listen to the sea in silence. This kind of graffiti would be a crime today—at the time, Byron was simply an enthusiastic Romantic tourist.

Take time to explore the site beyond the main temple: the cape also encompasses the remains of ancient fortifications and, on the adjacent hill, the foundations of a temple of Athena at Sounion destroyed in the 1st century AD. Less documented, this second sanctuary confirms that Sounion was a major place of worship—not just a navigational landmark for sailors.

As you walk the promontory, keep in mind that you're standing on one of Greece's most mythologically charged places: according to legend, this is where King Aegeus threw himself into the sea, believing his son Theseus dead after the expedition against the Minotaur. Theseus had forgotten to change his black sails to white ones to signal his victory. The sea has borne the king's name ever since. Homer himself mentions Sounion in the Odyssey as 'the sacred promontory of Athens.'

activities.text: The coastal road from Athens follows the Athenian Riviera for 70 km - a succession of beaches, coves and seaside resorts. Plan to leave in the morning to enjoy the water before the summer crowds arrive. The beaches of Vouliagmeni and Varkiza, more than half an hour's drive from Cape Sounion, are the most popular with Athenians.

In Vouliagmeni, more than half an hour's drive from Cape Sounion, stop at the thermal lake of the same name: a turquoise body of water fed by underground hot springs, set within a partially open cave. The water stays around 22 to 29°C all year round. There is an entrance fee but the swim is worth the detour, especially if you have spent several days at the archaeological sites.

Arrive at Cape Sounion about an hour before sunset. The site stays open until sunset—check the exact time depending on the season. Warning: there's no shade at the site, bring a hat and water. The terrain is rocky, avoid light sandals.

After sunset, the tavernas along the Sounion coast serve ultra-fresh locally caught fish: grilled octopus with oregano and lemon, Mediterranean fish soup, calamari and scampi. An ouzo or a Greek Alfa beer while watching the last light fade over the Aegean Sea: hard to beat as an end to the day.
