visits.text: Stop at the historic sliding bridge in the city's heart: you're standing at the narrowest point of the Euripus Strait, where just 38 meters separate island from mainland. Watch the water for a few minutes—the current reverses approximately every six hours, building to speeds of 12 km/h, then achieving eight minutes of eerie stillness before reversing again. This phenomenon, governed by lunar cycles, has mystified scientists since antiquity. Aristotle, whose ancestors hailed from Chalcis, came here to study what seemed to defy the laws of nature. A wooden bridge already spanned this strait in 411 BCE; the current structure dates to 1962.

Karababa Castle towers over the city from the opposite hillside. Constructed by the Ottomans in 1686—just years after they conquered Chalcis from the Venetians—it commands a spectacular vantage over the strait, the bridge, and the terracotta rooftops below. The climb from the center takes about 20 minutes on foot. It's the finest spot for photographing the current phenomenon from above.

Agia Paraskevi Church in the old town is among Greece's rarest surviving examples of Gothic Dominican architecture. Begun around 1250, it housed one of the earliest two Dominican priories approved in the Greek province. The central vault and carved stone sculptures in the southern chapel rank among the finest examples of Italian Gothic in Greece. Don't miss the central arch above the iconostasis.

Chalcis Archaeological Museum holds regional finds: geometric and archaic ceramics, Hellenistic sculpture, and domestic objects from local excavations. The Euboean pottery collection is especially rewarding for understanding Chalcis' pivotal role in Greek colonization. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, Chalcidian colonists founded roughly thirty cities on the Chalcidice peninsula and several in Magna Graecia, including Cumae in Italy.

The historic quarter of Chalcis blends Ottoman lanes, Venetian traces and an old Jewish quarter. The synagogue of Chalcis bears witness to a continuous Jewish presence since Antiquity, one of the oldest in Europe. Stroll through the small streets behind the seafront to find the most distinctive facades.

activities.text: Claim a terrace table facing the old bridge and observe the current shift. Locals do the same—it's free theater and genuinely hypnotic. On "chaotic" days—about 6–7 per lunar month—the current can reverse up to 14 times instead of the usual four. If you hit one of those days, you'll understand why the ancients spoke of Chalcis' "wild waters."

Taste syglino, Euboean smoked pork cured in fat—a highland specialty. Served on local bread with olives, it's the quintessential savory mezze of the region. Pair it with Euboean retsina, that resinous white wine of ancient tradition, here produced locally and superb alongside charcuterie and cheese.

As evening descends, Chalcis' waterfront comes alive. Residents gather at waterfront cafés and tavernas overlooking the strait. Order loukoumades—small fried pastries drizzled with honey and dusted with cinnamon—and watch pleasure boats navigate against the current.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

visits.text: Start with a slow stroll along the Venetian harbour to the lighthouse at the jetty's end – it's the best vantage point over the colourful houses lining the basin. This lighthouse built by the Venetians in the 16th century, then rebuilt by the Egyptians in the 19th century, rises 21 metres and is one of the world's oldest lighthouses still standing. The harbour itself was built around 1320: you're walking on infrastructure that has guided merchant fleets for seven centuries. Plan to return at sunset – the atmosphere is altogether different.

On the harbour itself, don't miss the Hassan Pasha mosque – also called the Janissaries' mosque or Yali Tzami. Built shortly after the Ottomans took Chania in 1645, by an Armenian architect, it's the first mosque ever erected in Crete. Its architecture is distinctive: a cubic building topped with a main dome, flanked by a portico with seven small domes. It's now used as an exhibition space. Just beside it, the Venetian dockyards (Neoria) – 23 vaulted stone halls built in the 16th century to shelter and repair the fleet – are among the few surviving examples of this type in the Mediterranean.

Get lost in the old town lanes beyond the harbour. In the Topanas quarter, look for the Etz Hayyim synagogue, restored in the 1990s after nearly falling into ruin. It recalls a painful chapter: Chania's Jewish community, settled here for centuries, was entirely deported by the Nazis in 1944. Most deportees perished when the ship carrying them was sunk by a British torpedo after being mistaken for a warship.

Just behind the harbour, the Splantzia quarter is Chania's best-preserved – fewer tourists come here, and the atmosphere is more authentic. Look for Saint Nicholas church, a former 14th-century Dominican church converted to a mosque in 1645, which today has the unique distinction of having both an Orthodox bell tower and the old 35-metre Ottoman minaret still standing.

Walk past the Agora, the covered market built in 1913 in the shape of a cross. This dressed-stone building is worth a stop to observe its façade and architecture from outside. It is closed for restoration at the date of this audit: browsing the stalls and shopping inside are not possible. Before travelling, check whether it has reopened; do not plan to buy supplies here for the gorges until the market is operating again.

The Samaria Gorge is among Europe's longest: a 16 km downhill hike from the Omalos plateau (1,230 m above sea level) to the coastal village of Agia Roumeli on the Libyan Sea. The national park, established in 1962 and recognised as a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1981, supports more than 300 plant species, including 70 endemic to Crete. The walls rise up to 600 m, and the narrowest passage - the Sideroportes (Iron Gates) - is just 2.5 m wide. Be sure to organise your return: the last boat to Sougia or Hora Sfakion leaves at 17:30.

The Omalos plateau, at around 1,100 m above sea level, is the last village before the start of the walk. Xyloskalo, the gorge entrance, is 1 km away at 1,230 m. If you're driving, plan to leave Chania around 06:00 – the drive takes about 1 hour 15 minutes and Xyloskalo car parks are free. A few tavernas around the plateau serve breakfast before the descent.

Agia Roumeli, the village at the gorge exit, is accessible only by sea or on foot. A few tavernas and guesthouses welcome hikers who want to avoid the race against time to catch the last boat – a solution we recommend if you're with family or want to enjoy the beach unhurriedly. Otherwise, the evening boat departs around 17:30 for Sougia (45 min) or Hora Sfakion (1 hour 20 minutes), from where buses run to Chania.

If the gorge is too demanding or you prefer an alternative, the village of Loutro on the south coast can be reached by boat from Hora Sfakion (20 min). White houses beside a turquoise cove, no cars, no road - Loutro is one of Crete's most unspoilt corners. A night or an afternoon on its beach is worth all the tourist facilities on the island's north coast.

activities.text: Devote the morning to exploring the harbour and old town on foot. Chania is smaller and easier to explore on foot than Heraklion. Skrydlof Street, parallel to the harbour, is entirely dedicated to leather goods – bags, belts and leather sandals made on the premises. A typical purchase of good quality.

Walk past the covered Agora market to look at its stone building and façade. The market is closed for restoration at the date of this audit: you cannot see its stalls in operation or buy olive oil, aromatic herbs, thyme honey or graviera cheese there. Check whether it has reopened before planning an indoor visit. During the works, this stop remains an opportunity to discover the market's architecture from outside.

For dinner, settle into a taverna on the Venetian harbour by the dockyards – the atmosphere is less touristy than opposite the lighthouse. Taste kouneli stifado (rabbit simmered for a long time with small onions, red wine, cinnamon and cloves), one of the most characteristic slow-cooked dishes of Cretan mountain cuisine. Accompany it with a glass of vidiano, the aromatic local white.

Late evening, wander towards the Splantzia quarter for the more local vibe. The bars and cafés on Splantzia Square are heavily frequented by locals—the atmosphere is distinctly less touristy than at the harbour, and prices a bit more reasonable.

Leave as early as possible – before 07:00 if you can, for two reasons: to avoid the crowds (up to 4,000 people daily in high season in July–August) and to enjoy the coolness of the early hours in the canyon. The first 7 km cross a shaded forest of pines and cypresses and descend gradually; the last 4.5 km, at the canyon bottom, are the narrowest and most striking. Keep an eye out for kri-kri, the endemic wild goats that scale the walls – they're shy but far more visible in the morning. Bring plenty of water (water from the springs along the route is drinkable), good hiking shoes and sunscreen for the last exposed section.

On arrival at Agia Roumeli, the Libyan Sea awaits right ahead. Plunge in—you'll have earned it. The water is clear and the bottom sandy. Take time to lunch in one of the village tavernas before catching the boat.

If you are less athletic or travelling with very young children, there is a reasonable alternative: reach Agia Roumeli by boat, then walk 5 km up the gorge to the Iron Gates – its most spectacular section – and walk back down. Allow 3 hours for the round-trip walk, without the full logistical arrangements.

Rakomelo is the winter version of raki: warmed with honey and cinnamon, it's drunk like a comforting digestif. In the mountain tavernas around Omalos, you'll often be offered it at the start of the meal in the cool morning temperatures—accept without hesitation, it's the local custom.

visits.text: A fortress, but also a neighborhood where life goes on: Chios Castle is more than its ramparts. The fortifications bear the imprint of the Genoese, while the baths recall the Ottoman period. Start by exploring the narrow streets on foot, leaving your car outside the walls.

Light filters through the small openings in the domes of the Ottoman baths at Chios Castle. This 18th-century hammam welcomed men and women at separate times; today, you can admire its restored architecture. Check the opening hours before exploring the rooms: this is a heritage visit, with no bathing.

activities.text: You’ll leave the harbor to walk between the high walls of Kambos, a few kilometers south of Chios. Red stone from Thymiana shelters citrus orchards and former merchant residences. The gardens are hidden behind gateways: stay on public paths unless you are explicitly invited inside.

You will finish with a walk along Aplotaria, Chios’s shopping street, before heading to the port. The town center lies between the waterfront and the castle: this final walk complements the first morning without repeating its visits. Above all, allow enough time to collect your luggage and reach your departure point.

visits.text: At nearly 500 meters above sea level, Christos Raches trades the waterfront for pine trees. The paved square and its church provide a center for this village scattered amid greenery. Its reputation for late-night activity does not mean every shop keeps the same hours: start with the narrow streets, without timing your visit around an assumed opening time.

activities.text: You can extend your break at the cafés around the square in Christos Raches. The village also has a sweets workshop run by the Raches women’s association: another way to experience this stop beyond its reputation for nightlife. Ask what is available that day before choosing a pastry.

places.name: Corfu

visits.text: Corfu's old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007 — a maze of narrow cobblestone lanes known as kantounia, lined with neoclassical facades in pastel hues inherited from centuries of Venetian rule. Venice held the island almost uninterrupted from 1386 to 1797, and it's the Republic that shaped this unique urban fabric, which neither the French nor the British managed to erase. Get up early: the lanes are stunning before 9am, empty and gilded by the morning light.

The Old Fortress (Palaio Frourio) sits on a rocky headland separated from the town by a sea moat — the Contrafossa — which the Venetians dug to turn the citadel into an artificial island. It successfully repelled three major Ottoman sieges: 1537, 1571 and 1716. Inside, don't miss the Church of St George, whose golden facade resembles an ancient temple — the contrast is striking. Climb to the lighthouse at the top for the best panoramic view over the sea and the town.

The New Fortress (Fortezza Nuova), built by the Venetians from 1577 on the hill overlooking the harbour, draws fewer visitors than the Old one — take advantage of that. Its underground galleries, bastions and tunnels carved into the rock form a fascinating labyrinth. The view over the harbour and the Ionian Sea from the battlements alone makes it worth the visit.

The Palace of St Michael and St George, built by the British between 1819 and 1824 in neoclassical style, now houses the Museum of Asian Art — a collection of 11,000 pieces from China, Japan and India, bequeathed by a Greek diplomat. An unexpected combination for a Greek island. The entrance from the People's Garden also offers a fine angle on the Spianada.

The Spianada Esplanade is the largest green public square in Greece. The arcaded Liston that lines its western edge was built during the French occupation, directly inspired by the Rue de Rivoli in Paris. This is where the Corfiots still play cricket, a tradition inherited from the British — one of the few places in Greece where the sport is practised. Late in the afternoon, grab a table on the terrace and watch local life unfold.

The Achilleion is one of the most romantic — and most tragic — palaces in the Mediterranean. Sisi had it built between 1889 and 1891 in a neo-Pompeian style, 10 km south of the capital, on a 200,000 m² plot overlooking the Ionian Sea. She had taught herself Ancient Greek to read Homer in the original and wanted to pay tribute to Achilles, whom she saw as the embodiment of the Greek soul. After her assassination by an anarchist in 1898, Kaiser Wilhelm II bought the palace in 1907 and spent every spring there until World War I. In 1981, the first floor served as the casino set for the James Bond film For Your Eyes Only. Allow at least 1h30 for the gardens and the apartments.

The peninsula of Kanoni, 4 km south of the capital, offers Corfu's most iconic view: in the foreground, Vlacherna Monastery perched on its tiny islet connected to the shore by a causeway, and behind it, the islet of Pontikonisi ('Mouse Island') crowned with dark cypresses. Homeric legend says it's the Phaeacian ship turned to stone by Poseidon after bringing Odysseus home to Ithaca. Arrive in the late afternoon for the best light.

Paleokastritsa, 25 km to the northwest, is one of the most beautiful natural sites in the Ionian Islands: six interlocking bays, crystal-clear turquoise waters and limestone cliffs rising 30 to 50 metres. The Monastery of Panagia Theotokos, founded in 1225 on a rocky headland above the main bay, was according to tradition established after the discovery of an icon of the Virgin. The present buildings date from the 18th century. Modest dress is required to enter — cover-up garments are provided at the door. The view from the monastery gardens over the sea is among the finest on the island.

The hilltop villages of Lakones and Makrades, above Paleokastritsa, offer plunging views over the six coves of the bay - a panorama the locals call the “balcony of Corfu”. These villages of centuries-old olive groves have kept their traditional architecture and their unpretentious tavernas. Plan a day trip from Corfu Town, combined with Paleokastritsa. Stop there for a coffee or a simple lunch on a terrace.

Corfu's Archaeological Museum, in town, houses the pediment of the Artemision, a 6th-century BC temple of Artemis discovered on the island: the central Gorgon stands nearly 3 metres tall and ranks among the best-preserved archaic sculptures in Greece. Allow about 45 minutes.

activities.text: Lose yourself in the Campiello, the oldest neighbourhood in the old town, north of the Old Fortress. It's a tangle of kantounia so narrow that two people can barely pass, with carved Venetian wells popping up in tiny squares. Laundry dries between buildings, bougainvillea spills over ochre walls — the atmosphere is light-years away from mass tourism.

On Orthodox Holy Saturday (in April or early May depending on the year), the people of Corfu celebrate the Resurrection by throwing ceramic jars out of their windows at exactly 11 a.m. - a noisy, festive spectacle unique in Greece. If you are not there for Easter, the religious processions carrying the relics of Saint Spyridon, the island's patron saint, also take place on 11 August and the first Sunday of November, and their atmosphere is worth stopping for.

Pastitsada is Corfu's signature dish: rooster (or veal) braised in a tomato sauce with Venetian spices, served over thick macaroni. The recipe is a direct trace of four centuries of Italian influence. Try it in an old-town taverna — the spots around the Campiello are the most authentic.

Bourdeto is Corfu's other pride: fish (scorpionfish by preference) cooked in a tomato sauce fired up with hot paprika. It's a fisherman's recipe — rustic and bold. Pair it with a glass of Robola, the dry, mineral white from neighbouring Cephalonia, which cuts through the acidity of the sauce.

Book a boat trip from Paleokastritsa to explore the sea caves along the northwest coast. Small boats slip into limestone cavities where sunlight creates blue and green reflections on the water — local guides call one of them the “Blue Light Cave”. The experience is at its best in the morning, when the sea is calm.

Take a dip in Agios Spyridon bay at Paleokastritsa — it's the most accessible beach in the resort, a mix of sand and pebbles with shallow waters. Several outfitters rent sea kayaks to explore the coves that can't be reached on foot. Expect to pay around €25–35 for a half-day kayak rental.

Sofrito is Corfu's quintessential Venetian dish: thin slices of veal pan-fried in a sauce of garlic, parsley, white wine and vinegar. The recipe dates back to 16th-century Venetian cooks. Pair it with a glass of Verdea, the dry white from Zakynthos — slightly oxidised and full-bodied, it holds its own against the bold flavours of the sauce.

Mantolato, a hard nougat made with roasted almonds and thyme honey, is Corfu's traditional confection — old-town delicatessens have stocked it since the 19th century. It's the ideal edible souvenir to bring home: it travels well and keeps for several weeks.

visits.text: The Temple of Apollo immediately gives you a sense of the scale of Ancient Corinth: its columns still tower over the surrounding remains. Dating from the 6th century BCE, it stands alongside the Roman forum, a reminder of another era. Start early on this exposed site, then continue to the museum using the same ticket.

Up close, the objects in the Archaeological Museum of Corinth make the ruins feel less abstract. Built in 1932, the museum houses finds from excavations of the city and stands within the archaeological site. Keep your ticket and enjoy this indoor visit before getting back on the road.

Save some energy for Acrocorinth: the climb is part of the visit. This fortress occupies the rocky height that protected the ancient city; from the ramparts, the ruins and the modern city share the same panorama. Wear shoes with good traction and check the closing time before heading up.

visits.text: It helps to understand the landscape before looking for raptors: start at the Dadia information center. The exhibition explains the park’s habitats and provides context for a forest scarred by the 2023 fire. Stop here before the minibus departs, then ask which routes are actually accessible that day.

activities.text: If you want to watch vultures without approaching them, book the minibus to the Dadia raptor observatory. The supervised trip takes you to a viewing station equipped for watching birds from a distance; sightings remain unpredictable. Choose an early morning departure and confirm it the day before: extreme heat and fire risk can suspend the service.

visits.text: Gold catches the light in the mosaics of Daphni Monastery. Beneath the dome, Christ Pantocrator presides over decoration dating from the late 11th century, while the wall paintings are later additions. Let your eyes adjust to the interior before studying the faces; the monument is closed on Tuesdays.

visits.text: The Sanctuary of Apollo clings to the slopes of Mount Parnassus at 600 meters—a site that functioned as an oracle for over a thousand years, from the late 7th century BC through the 4th century AD. According to tradition, this is where the omphalos stood, the stone Zeus designated as the center of the world. Don't expect a peaceful museum experience: tour buses arrive early in summer. Plan your ascent for opening time (8 AM) to catch the site while it's still quiet.

The Temple of Apollo you see today dates from the 4th century BC—actually the sixth temple built here, after an earthquake in 373 BC destroyed its predecessor. A Doric structure measuring 60 meters long by 24 meters wide, with six columns on the facade and fifteen along the sides, it housed the Pythia seated on her tripod inside the cella. This is where the maxim Socrates would make famous was carved: "Know thyself." Three columns still stand—they give you a sense of the original building's scale.

The theater, built in the 4th century BC and restored by the Romans in the 2nd century, seated 5,000 spectators during the Pythian Games, held every four years in honor of Apollo. Climb to the upper tiers: the view over the Pleistos valley, the olive groves, and the Gulf of Corinth in the distance is one of the finest at the entire site. Take time to examine the proscenium's bas-reliefs depicting the labors of Heracles before moving on.

Don't rush past this small building in Parian marble: the Athenian Treasury, built between 510 and 480 BC to celebrate the victory at Marathon, is one of the few Delphi monuments completely reconstructed—French archaeologists reassembled it stone by stone between 1903 and 1906. Its friezes depict Theseus, Heracles, and an amazonomachy. And on the exterior walls, carved into the marble, you can still see two hymns to Apollo with their musical notation—among the only sonic documents to survive from antiquity.

After the theater, take time to look at the seating and the Pleistos valley below. The stadium lies higher up the site, but access is currently closed for work to protect against falling rocks. The theater remains a place to imagine the Pythian Games and view the sanctuary of Apollo from above.

The Castalian Spring lies in the ravine between the two Phaedriades rocks, just before entering the sanctuary. Every pilgrim had to purify themselves here before consulting the oracle—washing their hands, or their entire head for first-time visitors. Today it's a basin carved from rock, with water still flowing. The setting, between cliffs rising over 200 meters, has a stark beauty.

Below the main sanctuary, the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia is often less visited—wrongly so. Its most famous monument is the tholos, a 4th-century BC circular building whose exact function remains unknown. Three Doric columns and three interior Corinthian columns have been re-erected—they give the site an almost photogenic appearance. Allow 20 to 30 minutes to descend from the main site entrance.

The gymnasium at Delphi, midway between the tholos and the main sanctuary, was the training ground for athletes competing in the Pythian Games. You can still make out the running track (xystos) and the cold bath basins. A quiet spot, often deserted, that you may have entirely to yourself.

Arachova (960 meters elevation) deserves at least an hour's stop. Its steep alleyways open onto craft shops—hand-woven rugs, cheeses, local liqueurs—and viewpoints over the valley. In winter it's a lively little ski resort; in summer the village is considerably calmer. Look for the overlook above the main church for the best view of the surroundings.

Make the detour to Hosios Loukas, 37 km from Delphi—it's an hour's drive well worth the trip. This monastery founded in 945 by the hermit Saint Luke of Steiris has been UNESCO-listed since 1990 and preserves 11th-century gold-ground mosaics among the best preserved in the entire Byzantine world. The great katholikon, built in 1011, introduced an architectural plan—octagonal inscribed cross—that would become standard throughout Byzantine Greece. Inside, look up at the dome: Christ Pantocrator gazes down at you. The site is open mornings; check hours before departing as midday closures often surprise visitors.

activities.text: Take your time walking slowly along the Sacred Way from the sanctuary entrance to the temple. On either side once stood dozens of statues and treasuries offered by Greek city-states competing for prestige. The empty pedestals you see today once bore bronzes long since melted down. This gradual ascent with the oracle at the end creates an atmosphere that even the crowds can't quite dispel.

The Delphi Archaeological Museum deserves half a day on its own. Its centerpiece is the Charioteer (Hêniokhos): a 1.82-meter bronze discovered in 1896 beneath the Sacred Way, buried during the earthquake of 373 BC. Cast around 470-466 BC to commemorate the tyrant of Gela's victory at the Pythian Games, it's one of only five major classical bronzes preserved worldwide. Look closely at the eyes: irises in brown chalcedony, pupils in obsidian, tear ducts in pink coral—a staggering level of detail for a work 2,500 years old.

In late afternoon, from the heights of the site, the panorama over Parnassus (2,457 meters according to official sources) and the valley of olive trees descending toward the Gulf of Corinth is at its finest. The oblique light brings out the nuances of the temple's honey-colored stone. If you're staying in Delphi or Arachova, you can walk down via the trail along the ravine—allow 30 minutes and wear sturdy shoes.

Formaela from Arachova, a PDO sheep's milk cheese, can be purchased in shops in the neighboring village. Grill it and drizzle with local honey—a combination you won't find everywhere in Greece. Arachova is 10 km from Delphi via a road offering some beautiful valley viewpoints.

Kleftiko lamb—slow-cooked in a paper parcel with herbs and garlic—is the mountain specialty of the region. You'll find it in most tavernas around Delphi and Arachova. The name comes from the "klephtes," brigands who cooked meat underground so the smoke wouldn't give them away.
Agiorgitiko, a red wine from Nemea (Peloponnese), pairs beautifully with the region's mountain cuisine. Full-bodied with soft tannins, it drinks young. You'll find it by the carafe in local tavernas.

The walk through the Pleistos Gorge, the river flowing below Delphi, is accessible from the village and takes 1.5 to 2 hours round trip. The trail winds through thousand-year-old olive groves—some trees are said to be over a millennium old. The quiet contrasts with the bustle of the archaeological site. Hiking shoes recommended; the path can be slippery.

In the village of Arachova, step into the craft shops lining the main street. Hand-woven rugs and kilims are the village specialty going back several generations—red and black geometric patterns you'll only see here. Local cheeses (formaela, fresh goat cheese) are sold directly from producers.

On the route to Hosios Loukas from Delphi, stop in the village of Distomo—known for the 1944 tragedy when the SS massacred 218 residents in reprisal. A sober memorial marks the village center. This context adds another dimension to the monastery visit that follows, a place of cultural continuity and resistance for a thousand years.
Hilopites—square dried pasta typical of the region—are eaten in soup or baked with cheese. A simple, hearty dish you'll find in mountain tavernas around Arachova.

Feta saganaki, pan-fried in olive oil and served with honey and sesame seeds, is a classic appetizer in the region's tavernas. The sweet-salty balance works particularly well with a glass of dry white wine.

Tsipouro from Thessaly, a grape marc eau-de-vie sometimes lightly anise-flavored, is served ice-cold with mezze—olives, cheese, mountain charcuterie. It's the aperitif drink throughout central Greece. Don't confuse it with ouzo: tsipouro is more concentrated and without added sugar.

activities.text: If the ferry schedule leaves you some time, take one last break on Diakofti Beach. The pale sand and shallow water contrast with the village’s role as a port. Settle in the area reserved for swimmers, then head to the dock at the time requested by the ferry company, without waiting for the last call.

visits.text: A good introduction: Diakopto station tells the story of the Odontotos before you even head into the mountains. Inaugurated in 1896, the line uses a rack-and-pinion system to climb steep slopes. However, Hellenic Train has announced that service is suspended: stick to accessible areas around the station and only plan a ride once the resumption of service has been officially confirmed.

activities.text: If you still feel like walking, return to the waterfront in Diakopto after the slopes of Helmos. The Vouraikos flows into the Gulf of Corinth here: the river you saw in the mountains ends its journey near town. Keep this late afternoon flexible and stay overnight to avoid a long drive after sightseeing.

visits.text: The climb offers more than the silhouette glimpsed from the road: Didymoteicho Castle overlooks the Erythropotamos and the lower town. Within the walls, cavities carved into the rock once served as dwellings. Leave Soufli early and wear sturdy shoes to explore the permitted routes to the ramparts.

A roof lost to flames transformed the silhouette of the Bayezid Mosque in Didymoteicho. Completed in 1420, the monument suffered a fire in 2017 and is undergoing restoration documented in 2026. Plan to view the exterior from the square and ask on site whether the interior is open to visitors.

visits.text: On the way to Dikella, make a detour through Kavala — a port city built into a hillside descending to the Aegean, facing the island of Thasos. Its old Ottoman quarter of Panagia is best explored on foot from the 270-metre Kamares aqueduct, built in the 16th century under Suleiman the Magnificent. Climb to the citadel for the sea view. In the quarter's streets, look for the birthplace of Mehmet Ali, an Ottoman officer born here in the 18th century and considered the founder of modern Egypt.

Twenty-five minutes north of Kavala, the site of Philippi is an essential stop. Founded in 360 BC by settlers from Thasos, fortified by Philip II of Macedon in 356, it witnessed the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC where Octavian (the future Augustus) and Mark Antony crushed Brutus and Cassius. In AD 50, the Apostle Paul founded the first Christian church in Europe here. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the grounds include an ancient theatre still used in summer, early Christian basilicas, a Roman forum and a museum. Allow at least 2 hours.

Dikella beach, on the northern coast of the Aegean Sea, is a long, well-equipped stretch of golden sand and smooth pebbles — with sun loungers, showers and a gently sloping entry into the water — popular with families from the Alexandroupolis area. It's quiet, not heavily visited by foreign tourists, and offers a peaceful end to the trip before heading back via Kavala.

activities.text: Spend the afternoon at Dikella beach — the water is clean and shallow, the Aegean sunset is serene and crowd-free. Mesi beach, a few kilometres along, is even wilder if you're looking for total solitude.

Finish with a seafood dinner at one of the waterfront restaurants in the nearby village of Agia Paraskevi — octopus, Thracian mussels and grilled fish have been served here for decades by local fishing families. The cuisine of Eastern Macedonia blends Greek, Turkish and Balkan influences in a way quite different from the islands.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: Dimitsana’s stone houses stretch above the Lousios Valley, with bell towers rising above the rooftops. The lanes reveal the terrain: a few steps completely change the view. Save this stroll for the end of the first day and leave the water power museum for the following morning.

Water used to make gunpowder: in Dimitsana, this contrast sums up an industrial history. The Open-Air Water Power Museum brings together a mill, a tannery, and a gunpowder mill linked to the uprising of 1821. Since access is reported to be partial during construction, check which areas are open before your visit; the museum is closed on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Water between the columns: in places, Dion Archaeological Park resembles a garden dotted with ancient remains. Sanctuaries, thermal baths, and ancient streets share the grounds at the foot of Mount Olympus, with an area dedicated to Isis. Start with the park when it opens, then head to the museum before the hottest part of the day.

An organ in an archaeological museum: in Dion, the hydraulis briefly draws attention away from the statues. The Archaeological Museum of Dion displays this ancient instrument among finds from the sanctuaries and thermal baths. Ask where it is displayed and check access arrangements for the nearby archaeotheke if you want to see the Dionysus mosaic.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: The monastery of Osios Loukas is one of the most beautiful in the entire Mediterranean – and one of the least familiar to French-speaking travellers. Perched on the slopes of Mount Helicon in a bowl of olive and almond trees, it was founded by the hermit Luke of Steiris, born in Delphi in 896, who died in 953 after predicting the reconquest of Crete from the Arabs (a prediction fulfilled eight years after his death). UNESCO-listed since 1990, its katholikon (completed around 1011) houses Greece's most complete 11th-century gold-ground mosaics: Crucifixion, Descent into Limbo – an iconographic programme of rare coherence and beauty. The polychrome marble, jasper and porphyry pavements are also exceptional. The saint's relics remain in the crypt. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

On the road between Thebes and Osios Loukas, a stop in Levadia (Livadia) is worth the detour. From Distomo, allow approximately 22 km and 20 minutes by car. The city centres on the spring of Trophonius, an ancient oracle contemporary with Delphi that made those seeking its advice enter a terrifying cave – Pausanias, the Greek traveller of the 2nd century AD, left a striking description. The springs still gush from the foot of a rocky cliff, where a promenade with watermills and cafés has now been laid out. The medieval castle of Levadia (14th century) overlooks the city from the hill – a 30-minute climb.

activities.text: In the monastery shop, monks sell their honey, olive oil and preserves. These are products of exceptional quality at very reasonable prices. Before leaving the site, have a coffee on the small terrace facing the valley – the view of olive trees descending towards the sea, the silence and the mountain air form a combination you won't find anywhere else on this circuit.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

visits.text: The best introduction to the caves is still the Archaeological Museum of Drama. Its collections connect the finds from Maaras with the region’s first farming communities, while a reconstructed Neolithic dwelling brings this past to life. Start with the prehistoric galleries to make the connection with your visit to Maaras.

From Byzantine sanctuary to mosque, Agia Sophia has changed uses while remaining in the center of Drama. The church dates to the 10th century, and its architecture preserves this history of transformations. Take in the building’s overall shape from the outside, then visit the interior outside service times.

activities.text: The sound of water takes over at Agia Varvara Park in Drama. Springs feed pools and channels among plane trees, small bridges, and old mills: here, water flows through the urban landscape. After the two caves, save this walk for late afternoon and choose shoes suitable for the damp areas around the water.

From the tobacco trade to today’s streets, Drama’s old town preserves traces of several eras. The remains of the city walls and the old facades offer a change of perspective after your day in the forest. Explore the central streets on foot, focusing on facades and remains visible from public spaces.

visits.text: Echinos changes the scale of the journey: valleys take over from the streets of Xanthi. The Eski and Teke mosques are among the landmarks of this Pomak village in the Rhodope Mountains. View their exteriors first, ask permission before entering, and avoid prayer times when sightseeing.

You can stop in Myki and Kentavros on the climb toward Echinos. These neighboring villages belong to the same group of Pomak settlements, but each deserves a short walk rather than a passing glance through the windshield. Park without blocking the narrow streets and ask residents for permission before photographing them.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: You hear the roar before you see the waterfalls of Edessa: Karanos and the double waterfall come into view at the edge of the city’s plateau. The Edessaios River splits into branches in the city before falling into the plain, explaining the abundance of water amid the streets. Follow the open paths and wear shoes with good traction near the spray.

Varosi overlooks the plain of Edessa from the site of the ancient acropolis. This neighborhood retains houses built in the Macedonian architectural tradition and cobblestone streets; its remains are a reminder that the ancient city also had fortifications on the plateau. Explore it on foot after visiting the waterfalls, allowing time for the viewpoints and historical information panels.

Before attracting walkers, water powered the workshops of Edessa: the Open-Air Water Museum tells this industrial history. The mills form a group of buildings near the waterfalls, rather than an exhibition confined to a single room. Check which buildings are actually open on the day you visit before planning to go inside.

activities.text: Head to Kioupri Bridge in Edessa to finish with a walk along the Edessaios River. This arched stone bridge is part of the urban heritage of a city where waterways still run alongside streets and cafés. Plan a short route if you are leaving afterward, and allow extra time to reach your transportation.

visits.text: Elafonisi isn't really an island: in calm weather, you can walk across the shallow lagoon separating it from shore—the water comes up to your knees. The pink sand is real but nuanced: it's not uniformly pink, but sprinkled with pink grains where the waves deposit crushed shells of micro-organisms called Foraminifera. Local legend says the sand was stained by the blood of an Ottoman massacre on April 18, 1824: several hundred Cretans, including many women and children, were killed here while waiting for a rescue boat. The area is protected by the Natura 2000 network—it's strictly forbidden to take sand, shells, or plants; inspections are real. Arrive before 9:30 a.m.: afterward, tourist buses pour in hundreds of people.

The Monastery of Chrissoskalitissa stands on a coastal rock 10 minutes by car from Elafonisi. Its name means “Golden Step”—legend says a 90-step staircase carved into the rock has one golden step, visible only to those who haven't sinned. The view over the west coast from the terraces is magnificent, and the visit takes only 20 minutes.

activities.text: Walk across the lagoon from the main beach (barely 100 meters, warm and shallow water) and follow the island's northern shore: the beach on the north side is less crowded, the waters slightly deeper and turquoise. Plan to stay until the tourist buses leave around 4–5 p.m.—the site then regains a remarkable calm, ideal for sunset.

If you want to extend this stop, plan a return drive from Elafonisi to Falasarna. This long, wind-exposed white-sand beach offers spectacular sunsets. Two distinct beaches frame a rocky headland with ancient remains.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: Agios Spyridon has its own small islet at the entrance to Elafonisos harbor, connected to the village by a bridge. The white church shares this rocky outcrop with trees, like a miniature version of the island you have just reached. Walk across, look at the harbor from the grounds, and save the interior for a time when no service is taking place.

activities.text: Follow Kontogoni Beach from Elafonisos village to end the day without getting back in the car. This beach lies west of Agios Spyridon, alongside the houses and harbor amenities. Walk along the water or enjoy a short swim if the light and sea conditions allow.

Underfoot, the sand of Simos replaces the rocks of Kythira’s coves. About 4.5 km from Elafonisos village, this beach lies between two headlands, with dunes in the background. Settle in near an existing access point without crossing the vegetation, and choose where to swim based on the day’s wind.

Continue walking toward Sarakiniko, also called Megali Paralia, to see the other part of this sandy coastline. Next to Simos, it is lined with dunes and trees referred to as kedros in local tourism. Stay on sand that is already used by visitors, without climbing the dunes, then return to the village for a second night on Elafonisos.

visits.text: Elatia, also called Kara Dere, sets the scene: this forestry village serves as the gateway to a vast forested mountain area near the Bulgarian border. Its history remains tied to forestry, far removed from the image of a Greek seaside village. Before walking, locate the forestry village on your map so you can easily find your starting point again.

activities.text: You’ll leave your car at the forestry village of Elatia to walk beneath the conifers. Spruce and pine trees give this part of the Rhodope Mountains a very different feel from the dry coastal hills. Choose an out-and-back route suited to the day’s conditions and set your turnaround time before leaving.

visits.text: You can explore everything at Eleusis except the secret that made it famous. At the sanctuary of Demeter, initiates were forbidden to reveal the rites of the Mysteries. Go through the propylaea to the foundations of the Telesterion, the ceremonial hall. Arrive at opening time and consult the map before exploring these remains that stand little above ground.

A useful follow-up to the ruins, the Archaeological Museum of Eleusis provides context for the sanctuary’s finds. Its displays shed light on the cult of Demeter and Persephone, which is difficult to understand from the foundations alone. Keep your ticket: it covers both the site and the museum, which you should visit immediately afterward.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: Spinalonga is the most history-laden place in all of eastern Crete. The Venetians began fortifying this 34-hectare rocky islet in 1579 to protect Mirabello Gulf—the fortress was so solid that even after the Ottomans took Crete in 1669, it held out another 46 years before falling in 1715. Entry is through a long dark tunnel that the lepers deported here between 1903 and 1957 nicknamed 'Dante's Gate.' For over 50 years, between 300 and 400 patients lived here as a community—with a baker, a barber, a priest. The last inhabitant, a priest, didn't leave the island until 1962. Allow 90 minutes to explore it fully. From Plaka (5-minute crossing) or from Elounda (20 minutes), boats depart regularly in high season.

Between Elounda and the peninsula, a causeway runs along the ancient city of Olous, submerged since antiquity. At low tide, you can see the mosaics of a 4th-century early Christian basilica with the naked eye—just beneath the surface, among the rocks. Olous was one of the great cities of Minoan and Classical Crete, mentioned as early as 3000 BC. With a mask and snorkel, the walls of the ancient acropolis are visible in shallow water. Swimming in this small lagoon sheltered from the wind is among the most pleasant in the region.

Elounda is the most comfortable base for this day. The resort is upscale—international resorts have set up here since the 1970s—but the waterfront of the original fishing village, the old salt pans between the town and the Olous peninsula, and the fish tavernas at the harbor are worth a detour beyond the hotels. The view of Spinalonga from the lagoon beaches is one of the finest in the region, especially late afternoon when golden light falls on the fortress walls.

Plaka is a fishing village 5 kilometers north of Elounda, facing Spinalonga. It's the closest departure point for the island (5-minute crossing) and also a remarkably preserved village with tavernas on the harbor, colorful boats, and nets drying in the sun. The grilled catch of the day here is impeccably fresh—Spinalonga's residents used to get their supplies here. Reserve a table for sunset over the island.

activities.text: The boat trip to Spinalonga is unmissable—but organize it early in the morning. By 10 AM in summer, groups land in waves and the vaulted passages become packed. Leaving Plaka at 8:30 or 9 AM, you stand a good chance of exploring the fortress in relative calm. Bring water and a hat: there's virtually no shade on the island.

After Spinalonga, swim in the lagoon between the Olous peninsula and Elounda: calm, shallow, and remarkably clear waters. With a mask and snorkel, you can search for the underwater ruins of the ancient city in shallow depths. The sandy beach on the way to the peninsula is one of the least crowded in the area.

For breakfast or brunch, order sfougato at a harbor taverna in Elounda: a thick omelet of zucchini with sheep's cheese and Cretan herbs. Several places serve it in the morning. In season, also look for clusters of octopus drying in the sun outside the Plaka tavernas—order it grilled, it's one of the best things you'll eat on this coast. A white Cretan Assyrtiko, mineral and dry, pairs perfectly with both.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Crete: Minoan Palaces, Gorges and Eastern Coast
Crete Road Trip: Agios Nikolaos, Elounda & Spinalonga

activities.text: If the sea is calm, treat yourself to a swim at Mavra Volia, near the harbor of Emporios. The black pebbles give the water its dark hue, and it gets deep quickly. Bring water shoes, keep an eye on children, and skip swimming if waves make entering the water difficult; leave the pebbles where they are.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: Potamos beach at Epanomi, 35 km south of Thessaloniki, is a pointed sandy spit jutting into the Thermaic Gulf — its shape recalls Croatia's Zlatni Rat, but with far fewer people. On a clear day, Mount Olympus is visible across the gulf. What makes the site truly unusual is the wreck of a cargo ship that ran aground more than 50 years ago just off the shore: locals say Saint Antonios himself sank the vessel to protect the adjacent 550-hectare wetland, a refuge for migratory birds. Arrive in the morning for the calm before the Thessaloniki families descend.

The Epanomi wetland stretches across 550 hectares between dunes and marshes — a sanctuary for migratory birds, with herons, passing flamingos and numerous aquatic species. A trail runs along the lagoon from the east car park of the beach. The site is especially active in spring and autumn during the migrations.

activities.text: The wreck offshore is reachable by swimming or snorkelling from the beach — the water is clear and shallow here, making it an excellent snorkelling spot suitable for all levels. The west side of the bay, exposed to the wind, is popular with kitesurfers.

The Epanomi area is known for its vineyards: the soil and microclimate produce characterful dry whites. A short drive through the surroundings will take you past several wineries open for visits in summer. End the day at sunset facing the gulf — Olympus turns orange.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: The Theatre of Epidaurus is probably the most impressive surviving ancient theatre in the world. Built in the 4th or early 3rd century BC on the slopes of Mount Kynortion, it originally had 34 rows of seats for 6,200 spectators — the Romans added 21 more rows, bringing capacity to nearly 14,000. Walk to the centre of the orchestra (the circular slab on the ground) and drop a coin: you'll hear it from the back rows, 60 metres away. Researchers at the Georgia Institute of Technology discovered that the limestone seating filters out low-frequency background noise, allowing voices to travel without amplification. Arrive in the morning to avoid the groups that flood in after 10 am.

Five hundred metres from the theatre, the Sanctuary of Asklepios served for six centuries as the foremost healing centre in the Greek world. Pilgrims came from across the Mediterranean to practise incubation: sleeping in the abaton (a sacred dormitory) in the hope that the god of medicine would appear in their dreams and cure them. Votive stelae found on the site describe cures for hernias, blindness and paralysis that would make a modern doctor smile, yet testify to a thousand-year-old belief. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

The Tholos of Epidaurus, dated to around 360 BC, is the most mysterious building in the sanctuary. This circular building with a triple ring of columns (6 Doric columns on the outside, 14 Corinthian columns on the inside) had a function that no historian has yet clearly established — healing ceremonies, housing the sacred snakes of Asklepios, or an initiation ritual? Don't look for the answer in the museum: it isn't there. Take the opportunity to examine the perfectly preserved Corinthian capitals.

The Epidaurus Museum, at the foot of the site, displays sculptures and architectural elements discovered during the excavations. Don't miss the reconstruction models of the sanctuary — they give an idea of what this complex was like at its Hellenistic peak, far larger than what you've just walked through. Allow 45 minutes.

activities.text: Test the theatre's acoustics for yourself: from the central slab of the orchestra, whisper a sentence. Ask a companion to climb to the top rows - they will hear you clearly. If you are alone, drop a coin onto the slab. It is the experiment every guide has performed for centuries, and it never disappoints. The Epidaurus Festival stages ancient tragedies every Friday and Saturday evening from late June to late August: if you are there at that time, book in advance.

Swimming in the coves between Paleá Epídavros and Nea Epidavros, a few kilometres from the site: small pebble beaches framed by pine trees, with very clear water. The village of Paleá Epídavros has a fishing harbour with seafood tavernas whose terraces overlook the water — ideal for dinner.

Try gemista: tomatoes and peppers stuffed with rice, aromatic herbs and sometimes minced meat, slow-baked in the oven. It's a summer dish found everywhere in Peloponnese tavernas, much better than the name suggests. Pair it with a white assyrtiko — dry and mineral, with a sharp acidity that makes it perfect with stuffed vegetables.

days_plan.itin_title: Peloponnese Road Trip: Mycenae, Epidaurus & Olympia

visits.text: Take time to walk through Eresos before heading down to the beach. The inland village and Skala Eresou offer two sides of the same stop, separated by about four kilometers; ancient Eresos is associated with Sappho and Theophrastus. Park on the outskirts of the old center and take the main road toward the coast.

activities.text: The gray sand and open horizon bring a change of pace at Skala Eresou Beach. Below Eresos, the coastal village’s terraces extend to the waterfront; this break lets you take off your sightseeing shoes after Sigri. Swim only if sea conditions allow, then return to Eresos for the night.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Eretria's archaeological site spreads beneath the modern town—you'll circulate among open-air ruins with a map available at the museum (€5). At the site's heart stands the Temple of Apollo Daphnephoros: its earliest phases date to the late 8th century BCE, with the Doric version of 520–490 BCE destroyed by the Persians during the 490 BCE sack. Foundation stones and sculptured pediment fragments remain. Bring water and a hat in summer—the site offers no shade.

The House of the Mosaics, dated to the 4th century BCE, stands among Greece's finest preserved Hellenistic dwellings. Its floors showcase pebble mosaics depicting mythological scenes—Nereids astride sea creatures, griffins, panthers. Check before visiting: travelers report it's occasionally closed early despite posted hours.

Eretria Archaeological Museum, founded in 1960 and expanded by the Swiss School of Archaeology in Greece (excavating since 1964), displays remarkable finds. Don't miss the sculptured group of Theseus and Antiope, attributed to the Athenian sculptor Antenor (circa 510 BCE), and a black-figure funerary amphora dated 560 BCE depicting Heracles battling Centaurs. Labels appear in Greek and French.

Eretria's ancient theater, with earliest phases from the 5th and 4th centuries BCE, is remarkable for an underground tunnel still visible—actors vanished through it for stage effects, a rarity of ancient theatrical machinery. Climb to the acropolis in the north for a commanding overview of the site and the coastline.

The Persians destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE—Darius sought vengeance for the city's aid to the Ionian Revolt. The male population was slaughtered; women and children were enslaved and deported to Persia. The city rebuilt swiftly, sent 600 hoplites to the Battle of Plataea in 479 BCE, flourished in the 4th century, then fell to the Romans in 198 BCE and was finally abandoned after 87 BCE. Marshland reclaimed it until 1824, when refugees from Psara resettled the site.

activities.text: Swimming along Eretria and Amarynthos beaches—a neighboring village to the east celebrated for seafood tavernas and grilled shellfish spreads. Waters here are calm and shallow, ideal for children. If you're motoring about, Amarynthos merits a detour for dinner: locals prefer its fish freshness to Eretria.

Sample fava: a creamy yellow-pea purée dressed with excellent olive oil, capers, and lemon juice. It's among Greece's finest yet most underappreciated mezzes. Pair it with local Savatiano white—a dry, fruity Euboean varietal that harmonizes beautifully with legumes.

Pasteli—sesame bars bound with thick honey—sells in waterfront shops and groceries. It's one of Greece's oldest candies, energy-dense and nourishing, perfect to carry for tomorrow's hike to Kymi or Karystos.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

visits.text: Closely packed façades rise in tiers above the harbor of Evdilos. This town was the capital of Ikaria from 1834 to 1912, before Agios Kirykos; its old residences recall a role that went beyond that of a maritime stopover. Take time to view the whole scene from the quay, keeping clear of areas where vehicles are maneuvering.

activities.text: Follow the paved narrow streets of Evdilos on foot to leave the quays behind for a while. They connect the neighborhoods arranged in tiers, then lead back toward the waterfront cafés: the walk alternates stretches of walking with breaks rather than following a long marked route. Leave some extra time before driving back to Agios Kirykos, and keep your luggage out of sight.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 3 Days: Hot Springs, Beaches, and Villages

activities.text: Sand replaces cobblestones on Fanari Beach, on the shores of the Thracian Sea. The village also retains a fishing harbor: this stop takes you from the lagoon shores to the coast. Walk along the beach or swim if conditions allow; check the wind before settling in.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

places.name: Fira

visits.text: Fira, Santorini's capital, clings 250 meters above the caldera. The caldera itself resulted from one of the largest eruptions in human history: around 1600 BC, the island's central volcano exploded and collapsed, creating a 12 km diameter crater now filled with sea. The multicolored cliffs - black basalt, red, white pumice - tell the stratigraphy of this catastrophe. If you're afraid of heights, walk carefully along the edges.

The Museum of Prehistoric Thera in Fira displays objects discovered during Akrotiri excavations - a Minoan city buried under volcanic ash around 1600 BC, comparable to Pompeii. The original frescoes from the city are among the finest in the Aegean Antiquity: fishing scenes, navigation, young men in action. Allow an hour for the visit.

Oia is Greece's most photographed village - its cave houses carved into the cliff, cobalt domes and flowered alleyways make it a worldwide postcard. Arrive early morning, before 9am, to see it almost deserted. Oia's Byzantine castle is the best viewpoint for sunset - plan to arrive 90 minutes early to find a spot.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is often compared to Pompeii: a Middle Bronze Age Minoan city, buried under meters of volcanic pumice around 1600 BC and preserved intact. Unlike Pompeii, no bodies were found here - the inhabitants had time to flee. The two-story alleyways, oil jars still in place, and house structures are protected by a massive covered structure. Allow 90 minutes.

Kamari beach, on the east coast, is Santorini's main black sand beach. This volcanic sand heats up very quickly in summer - wear shoes to walk to the water. The water is clear and quite deep quickly. The beach is long, well-equipped, with seaside tavernas.

Red Beach, west of Akrotiri, is a cove enclosed by bright red lava cliffs that plunge into a deep blue sea. Because of rockfalls and access restrictions, view it only from a distance and comply with any prohibition posted on site.

Pyrgos is the best-preserved medieval village on Santorini, perched at an elevation of 350 meters. Built around a 13th-century Venetian kastro, it has preserved its maze-like lanes and crenellated houses. The chapel at the top offers a 360° view over the entire island. It is far less crowded than Oia.

Megalochori is one of Santorini's most authentic villages, built in the 17th century by merchants and shipowners. Its main square with vaulted arches and small church is one of the island's most beautiful. Much less crowded than Fira or Oia, this is where you'll see the island as it was before mass tourism.

Imerovigli, between Fira and Oia, is nicknamed 'the balcony of the Aegean Sea'. Skaros Rock, a former 13th-century Venetian fortress partially collapsed into the sea during the 1956 earthquake, offers a 270° view over the Kameni islets and caldera - less crowded than Oia castle for sunset.

activities.text: In the evening, settle in Oia for sunset. It's the most famous in the Cyclades: in July-August, hundreds of people crowd the cliff edge. Go anyway, but arrive early and position yourself slightly back from the castle for an unobstructed view without fighting for space.

Santorini fava, yellow split pea puree grown on the island since antiquity and protected by PGI, has incomparable sweetness. Tomatokeftedes, fritters made from cherry tomatoes concentrated by volcanic sun, are worth trying as meze. You'll find both in all Fira and Oia tavernas.

Santorini's assyrtiko, a white grape variety grown in baskets close to the ground to protect it from the wind, produces a mineral, dry and slightly saline wine. Vines have thrived on the island's volcanic soils for centuries. Several estates offer tastings overlooking the caldera.

The Fira-Oia hike along the caldera is one of the most beautiful in the Mediterranean: 10.5 km on the cliff edge, between 250 and 350 meters height, with constant views over the 12 km diameter crater and volcanic islets at the center. Allow 3.5 to 4 hours with breaks. Start early morning in summer - midday heat on the volcanic stones is crushing. The trail passes through Firostefani and Imerovigli before reaching Oia.

Amoudi Bay, at the foot of Oia's cliffs accessible by 300 steps, is the island's most authentic spot for fish. A few fishing tavernas serve dried octopus, sea urchins and grilled fish at the water's edge. You can also dive from the rocks directly into the sea. Avoid going between noon and 3pm - the return climb in the heat is exhausting.

Boat excursion to Nea Kameni volcano in the caldera's center: shuttles depart from Fira's old port (accessible by 580 steps or funicular). On the islet, a trail climbs to the volcanic cone's summit at 150 meters - sulfurous fumaroles remind you the volcano remains active, its last eruption dating from 1950. You can then swim in neighboring Palaia Kameni's natural hot springs, slightly ferruginous and sulfurous water.

Wine tasting in Santorini is a unique experience: vines are cultivated in ground-level basket coils to protect from wind, a millennial technique unique here. The mineral, dry assyrtiko white is most renowned - but vinsanto, sweet wine from sun-dried grapes, is also worth experiencing. Several estates offer tastings with caldera views.

visits.text: If the ruins of Prespa have left you with questions, the Archaeological Museum of Florina offers artifacts to help answer them. The collections bring together finds from the region, from the Neolithic period to Byzantine times. Make it your main indoor visit for this half-day; the museum is closed on Tuesdays.

activities.text: You will follow the Sakoulevas River in Florina, moving from building facades to small scenes of street life. Old houses line both banks, particularly in the Varosi neighborhood; the city also inspired the films of Theo Angelopoulos. Walk along the waterfront without trying to cover everything, then allow some extra time to reach Lake Vegoritida.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: Frangokastello Fortress was built by the Venetians between 1371 and 1374 to keep order in the rebellious Sfakia region. The locals never accepted it and renamed it “Frangokastello”—the Castle of the Franks—as a sign of contempt. The rectangular plan with four corner towers still bears the coat of arms of the Lion of St. Mark above the entrance. In 1828, during the Greek War of Independence, 385 Greek fighters led by Hatzimichalis Dalianis were massacred here by the Ottomans. A persistent legend says that every year in May, on the battle's anniversary, the shadows of the dead soldiers—the Drosoulites, literally “dew men”—appear in the morning mist and parade before the castle. The phenomenon has been documented but never fully explained.

activities.text: Imbros Gorge is the southern coast's most accessible hiking route: the descent from the Askifou Plateau to the village of Komitades takes 2 to 3 hours. The walls reach up to fifty meters high in places and the vegetation is dense—a striking contrast to the coastal aridity. The hike is relatively easy, doable year-round.

Frangokastello beach stretches for about 500 m along the castle walls, with fine sand and a gentle slope into calm, shallow water that suits families. To the east, Orthi Ammos beach is wilder, with a rocky seabed suited to snorkeling. You can visit both in one afternoon.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

places.name: Galaxidi

visits.text: Galaxidi appears around a bend in the coastal road between olive trees and the Gulf of Corinth like a 19th-century print. This port of 1,700 inhabitants has two natural harbours and a collection of neoclassical houses built by ship captains who made their fortunes in the Mediterranean. In the 18th–19th centuries, Galaxidi had a fleet of 350 vessels trading as far as Marseille and the Black Sea – maritime power disproportionate to such a small town. The War of Independence of 1821 largely put an end to this. Today its cobbled alleys and softly coloured façades make it one of mainland Greece's most photogenic villages.

Galaxidi's Maritime Museum occupies a renovated former shipyard – excellent for understanding the port's history in a few well-designed galleries. The collection includes 19th-century sailing-ship paintings (Greece's largest selection), navigation instruments, travel journals and nautical charts. Outside the museum, the PeraPanta coastal promenade leads to the statue of a sailor's wife waving her handkerchief towards the sea – a melancholic image that encapsulates the village's history.

activities.text: The Gulf of Corinth coves below Galaxidi are calm and the water is clean. The coastal walk between the village's two ports (Hiriolakas and the main harbour) skirts small pebble beaches with views of the Byzantine islets opposite. If you're here on a Saturday, Amphissa's market 30 km away merits a morning detour before heading down to Galaxidi.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

map_keywords: Port of Galaxidi Gulf of Corinth

visits.text: Vathia is the ghost village of the deep Mani: a collective fortress perched on a hilltop, made up of stone tower houses packed so tightly together they form a continuous rampart against rival clans. Vathia had as many as 200 inhabitants in the 19th century; today a few houses have been restored, but it's the abandoned section that is most haunting. The atmosphere is unique — beauty and melancholy intertwined, and not a tourist in sight outside July and August.

Cape Tenaro is the southernmost point of mainland Greece. From the car park, walk 45 minutes along a coastal trail running between two seas: the Ionian Sea to the west and the Aegean to the east merge here. The ancients regarded this cape as one of the gates to the Underworld. You'll find the ruins of a 4th-century BC Temple of Poseidon and a small chapel built on its foundations. The white lighthouse stands 41 metres above the sea.

activities.text: The Diros Caves, 11 km from Aréopoli on the road to Gérolimenas, can currently be visited on a short boat section and in the land section. The boatman rows you past stalactites that almost touch the water. The total mapped network exceeds 14,700 metres. In summer, check visiting arrangements before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South

visits.text: A park of wooden mushrooms: Grevena celebrates its specialty even in its public spaces. Mushroom Park, on the way out of town toward Kozani, features sculptures inspired by the forest and its mushrooms. It is an easy stop before the return drive; take a short walk and watch children near road entrances.

activities.text: Continue discovering Grevena through its food by asking which mushrooms accompany the day’s dishes. The region’s forests supply a cuisine that makes these ingredients part of the local identity, beyond simple garnishes. Choose a dish prepared by a restaurateur and save wild mushroom foraging for a guided outing.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

visits.text: Gytheio is the capital of the eastern Mani and the former naval port of Sparta — the Spartans, who scorned the sea, needed a maritime outlet and established their arsenal here. The pastel façades with wrought-iron balconies descending towards the quay, the bustle around the fishing harbour and the tavernas that open at dawn for the fishermen make it one of the most authentic small towns in the Peloponnese. Stroll along the waterfront in the late afternoon when the light is golden.

The islet of Marathonisi (formerly known as Cranae) is linked to the port by a narrow causeway. It was here, according to Greek mythology, that Paris and Helen spent their first night of love before fleeing to Troy. On the island stands the Tzanetakis Tower, built in 1829, which now houses the Historical and Ethnological Museum of the Mani. The octagonal lighthouse at the tip of the island offers a fine view over the gulf.

The museum inside the town hall (1890), on the waterfront, displays archaeological finds from Gytheio and the Mani: ossuaries decorated with reliefs, engraved inscriptions, pottery and sculptures from the Roman period. It's a useful addition to the visit, helping you understand the commercial history of this town, which was one of the main trading centres of the Free Laconians under the Roman Empire.

Take a detour along the Mani coast road to the village of Vathia - one of the best preserved on the peninsula. Its medieval stone towers, built tightly against one another and now almost deserted, tell of the centuries of clan vendettas among the Maniot families, who protected themselves from their neighbours in this way. The road leading there is arid, rocky and spectacularly bare. Allow for a round trip within the day from Gytheio.

activities.text: Mavrovouni beach stretches for several kilometres near Gytheio - a long strip of fine sand with a view of the Laconian Gulf and the peaks of Taygetus in the background. The water is calm in the morning, ideal for a family swim. In the afternoon the sea breeze picks up and makes it a good kitesurfing spot. This is the beach used by Gytheio's residents: simple, authentic.

Synglino is the Mani's iconic cured meat — pork smoked over myrtle or orange wood and preserved in lard. Before the age of refrigeration, every Maniot household kept a supply. The harbour tavernas serve it as a starter, often alongside the orange-spiced sausage. Kakavia, a Mediterranean fish soup with saffron and lemon, is the other must-try for an evening on the quayside.

days_plan.itin_title: Laconia Road Trip: Sparta, Mystras & Monemvasia

visits.text: Ten rows of seats: at the theater of Hephaistia, they belong to the first stone structure, built at the end of the Classical period. Hellenistic and then Roman expansions altered the complex, which was built over older sanctuaries. Identify the orchestra and tiered seating from the designated paths; drive slowly along the unpaved access road and check the theater’s opening hours before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 3 Days: Villages, Ancient Sites, and Dunes

visits.text: At the Heraion of Perachora, ancient remains stand so close to the sea that they change your perspective on a sanctuary. Around the Temple of Hera, surviving structures include an L-shaped colonnade and a large cistern above a small cove. Come in the morning and wear closed-toe shoes for the descent over uneven ground.

Head up to Melagavi Lighthouse for a different perspective on the Heraion of Perachora. Set above the cliffs, the lighthouse overlooks the natural harbor around which the sanctuary was laid out. Stay on the permitted access route and enjoy the views from outside; this walk does not depend on the building being open.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: Plan to arrive at Knossos as soon as it opens at 08:00 – groups arrive from 10:00 onwards and the site quickly becomes stifling in summer. This Minoan palace built around 1900 BC and remodelled after an earthquake around 1700 BC covered more than 20,000 m² with some 1,300 rooms: administrative offices, sanctuaries, workshops and royal quarters, all linked by labyrinthine corridors that probably inspired the Minotaur myth. Pay close attention: the frescoes visible on site are copies; the originals are in the archaeological museum. British archaeologist Arthur Evans, who excavated the site from 1900 to 1935, reconstructed the palace in reinforced concrete – a highly controversial decision that explains the bright, somewhat artificial colours of certain areas.

Visit the Heraklion archaeological museum before or after Knossos – a combined ticket lets you enter both at a better rate. This museum, founded in 1883 and housed in a building whose renovation continued until 2014, is Greece's second most visited museum and holds the world's largest collection of Minoan objects. Don't miss the four highlights: the Snake Goddess in faience (around 1600 BC) discovered at Knossos, the black steatite rhyton shaped like a bull's head with rock-crystal eyes, the Bull-Leaping Fresco, and above all the Phaistos Disc – a fired clay disc discovered in 1908, covered with 242 signs arranged in a spiral, belonging to a script still undeciphered to this day.

The Koules fortress dominates the old harbour entrance, at the end of the jetty. Built by the Venetians between 1523 and 1540 on a site fortified since the 9th century, this massive Rocca al Mare was constructed to counter the Ottoman threat in the time of Suleiman the Magnificent. Its outer walls reach 9 metres thick. It reopened in 2016 with a permanent exhibition—including pieces brought up from the seabed by Cousteau's team in 1976. Climb to the terrace: the view over the harbour and city is Heraklion's best.

Push open the door of Saint Titus Cathedral in the city centre. This church dedicated to Crete's patron saint—Titus, disciple of Saint Paul—has a turbulent history: built in the Byzantine era, converted to a mosque under the Ottomans, it was returned to Christian worship in 1925. It houses a relic of Saint Titus, brought to Venice when the Ottomans took Crete in 1669 and returned to Heraklion in 1966.

Just beside the cathedral stands the Loggia, a Venetian edifice rebuilt in 1628 that served as a meeting place for Candia's nobility (Heraklion's former name). Now the town hall, this building with its Renaissance porticos perfectly illustrates Venice's imprint on the city. Spend a few minutes walking around it—the façade is one of the old town's most elegant.

If Knossos gave you Minoan Crete, the historical museum gives you everything else: Byzantium, Venice, the Ottomans and 20th-century Crete up to the Second World War. Don't miss the room devoted to El Greco – Dominikos Theotokopoulos was Cretan, born around 1541 in Fodélé, and the only work by him kept in Crete is here. Also look for the reconstruction of the library of Nikos Kazantzakis, the author of Zorba the Greek, born in Heraklion in 1883 – an intimate and moving room.

Make the detour to the Martinengo bastion, in the Venetian walls encircling the city – these ramparts rank among the best-preserved in the entire Mediterranean. You'll find the tomb of Nikos Kazantzakis, who chose his own epitaph: “I hope for nothing, I fear nothing, I am free”. You can climb certain sections of the ramparts; the view over the city from the wall walk is worth the effort.

Take a tour down 1866 Street, the liveliest covered market in the city, where locals actually do their shopping. You'll find aged graviera, fresh mizithra, mountain thyme honey, aromatic herbs and marinated olives—all at better prices than at the harbour. Plan to pass through in the morning: some stalls close around 14:00, especially at weekends.

If you have a car, an excursion to the palace of Phaistos (allow for a day trip from Heraklion) is well worth the journey. The second Minoan palace of Crete after Knossos, Phaistos is much less crowded and far more authentic: no concrete reconstruction here, just open-air ruins on a plateau overlooking the Messara plain, with Mount Psiloritis (2,456 m, Crete's highest peak) in the background. This is where the famous Phaistos Disc was found, now in Heraklion museum.

activities.text: Leave for Knossos first thing in the morning – allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours on site. Be sure to use an audio guide or hire a local guide: without explanations, it's very difficult to distinguish original ruins from Evans's concrete reconstructions, and the site loses much of its meaning. A guide will also stop you from missing the Royal Road, considered Europe's oldest paved road.

Follow up with the archaeological museum – ideally after Knossos, to see the originals of the copies you saw there. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes. A practical tip: buy the combined museum + Knossos ticket, valid for 3 days – you save on both admissions and avoid the queue at the museum ticket office.

In the evening, head back towards the old Venetian harbour for golden hour. The tavernas lining the harbour serve seafood and grilled fish facing the illuminated fortress. If you arrive before sunset, walk to the jetty's end: the view over the city and the hinterland mountains is striking.

Take advantage of your Cretan evening to taste dakos, the cornerstone of local cuisine: a barley rusk soaked in olive oil, topped with fresh tomato and feta, scattered with oregano. Accompany it with a glass of raki (or tsikoudia), the local eau-de-vie distilled from grape pomace—served chilled and often offered at meal's end.

The morning in Heraklion is ideal for leisurely exploring the old town streets around Venizelou Square, with its Morosini fountain from 1628—locals simply call this spot 'Lions Square' because of the carvings on the old basin. The surrounding cafés are perfect for a Greek coffee while watching the morning buzz before hitting the road.

If you make the excursion to Phaistos, plan to stop en route at Agia Triada, just 3 km from the palace. This small Minoan site has yielded some of the finest works in Heraklion museum, including the Agia Triada Sarcophagus and the Harvester Vase. Allow 30 to 45 minutes on site.

Cretan vineyards merit a stop: indigenous grape varieties like vidiano (aromatic white with notes of citrus and white flowers) or kotsifali (fruity, sweet red) are found practically only on the island. If you pass through the Messara plain on the way to Phaistos, several wineries offer tastings – ask at your hotel for current recommendations.

In Heraklion, taste kalitsounia, little turnovers made with thin pastry and filled with mizithra and aromatic herbs. They come in both sweet versions – with honey and cinnamon – and savoury ones. Town-centre bakeries generally have them at all hours.
