visits.text: The Historical Archives Museum of Hydra deserves more than a hurried visit between boats. Documents and objects place the harbor mansions in the context of the island’s maritime history; the current building also houses archives and a library. Visit as soon as you arrive if opening hours allow, then save your walk for the end of the day.

activities.text: Car-free does not mean quiet: Hydra’s harbor is a hub of arriving passengers, outdoor cafés, and small boats. For a change of pace, you can leave the dock and walk through lanes lined with stone houses that reflect the wealth of the shipowners. Travel light and choose luggage that is easy to carry through the sloping lanes.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses

visits.text: Ierapetra holds a title few cities can claim: Europe's southernmost, nicknamed 'the bride of the Libyan Sea.' Its position at the southern tip of Crete's isthmus has made it a strategic crossroads since antiquity—the ancient city of Hierapytna was already famous in the 3rd century BC for its piratical tendencies, before being destroyed by the Romans in 67 BC. Climb up to Kales Fortress, rebuilt in 1626, for a view over the fishing harbor—allow 30 minutes. And if you want a local oddity: Ierapetra is also one of Crete's wealthiest towns, thanks to the 13 square kilometers of greenhouses supplying all of Greece with off-season vegetables.

Twelve kilometers offshore from Ierapetra, the island of Chrissi—'the golden island'—is a protected, uninhabited nature reserve, except for a few seasonal caretakers. It's famous for its forest of two-hundred-year-old Lebanon cedars, the only one in Europe, and for its beaches of white sand and intensely turquoise waters. Facing an influx of 200,000 visitors per year, the Greek government imposed access restrictions in summer starting in 2022—prefer May-June or September-October to find it nearly empty.

Wander down into the alleyways of Kato Mera, Ierapetra's old town: a medieval quarter of narrow lanes and dead-ends leading to the fishing harbor. You'll find the Ottoman mosque, a former Christian church converted under Turkish rule, and 'Napoleon's House'—an 18th-century dwelling where, according to local legend passed down since 1798, Bonaparte spent one night during his Egyptian expedition. Undocumented, but locals will tell you the story with infectious pride.

The Archaeological Museum of Ierapetra is small, calm, and often empty—the anti-Heraklion. You'll find collections spanning the Minoan era through the Greco-Roman period: amphorae, decorated sarcophagi, statuettes, and ceramics testifying to Hierapytna's importance in antiquity. Ideal for an hour mid-day, before the Chrissi excursion or after.

If you have time at the end of the day, the coastal road between Ierapetra and Makrygialos offers several wild, quiet beaches, particularly around Agia Fotia. You can also take this direction if you are heading to Sitia Airport (56 km, about 1 hour 5 minutes) or to Heraklion for an international flight (allow at least 1 hour 45 minutes; set off in the middle of the morning so you are not pressed for time).

activities.text: The boat trip to Chrissi Island is the day's highlight in Ierapetra. Book the morning crossing (departure around 10 AM) to maximize your time on the island. Once ashore, follow the marked trails to the cedar forest—the scent of resin beneath the centuries-old trees, with the turquoise sea glittering between the trunks, is striking. Belegrina Beach, covered in a carpet of bleached fossil shells, is a unique natural curiosity. Bring your lunch: the island's only taverna is rudimentary.

Walking exploration of the old town: start from Kales Fortress, then into the alleyways of Kato Mera, the Ottoman mosque, Napoleon's House, the 17th-century Venetian fountain, and the lanes leading to the waterfront. The waterfront promenade runs along a long beach of gray-gold sand to the modern neighborhoods—the perfect spot for a final Cretan swim late in the day.

For dinner, settle into a waterfront taverna and order chtapodi krasato: octopus simmered slowly in red wine with onions and herbs until it's tender—the house specialty at most local establishments. Finish with loukoumades, fried doughnuts served hot and drizzled with honey, dusted with cinnamon. Tsikoudia (Cretan raki) usually arrives unbidden as an end-of-evening digestif.

Return to the airport: if you are flying from Sitia (a small airport with seasonal flights to Athens and a few European destinations), allow about 56 km and 1 hour 5 minutes' drive from Ierapetra. For an international flight from Heraklion, allow at least 1 hour 45 minutes; leave in the middle of the morning to avoid rushing. The faster northern coastal road passes through Agios Nikolaos.

visits.text: A canal without water: near Nea Roda, the Xerxes Canal is discernible mainly in the terrain. Its course connected the Gulf of Ierissos to the Singitic Gulf to avoid sailing around Athos; it is now filled in. Make it a brief historical stop as you continue toward Ouranoupoli, without expecting a navigable waterway.

activities.text: You can walk along the Ierissos waterfront before heading to Nea Roda. The promenade runs alongside a sandy beach, while the town maintains a tradition of wooden boatbuilding. Keep this stop flexible for lunch, then continue to the canal on the road to Ouranoupoli.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

visits.text: It is better to start at the Archaeological Museum of Igoumenitsa than to visit one ruin after another without context. Its collections introduce Thesprotia, including a silver helmet and other pieces of ancient military equipment. Artifacts and models make this history easier to understand before the next stops. On Tuesdays, stick to the waterfront walk: the museum is closed.

activities.text: Walk along the Igoumenitsa promenade for a change of scale after the museum. The city stretches around a gulf, its daily rhythm shaped by ferry connections to Italy and Corfu. This waterfront offers a break without a detour north. Stay on the public promenade, then get back on the road toward Sivota.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: Take the boat from the dock facing the fortress—the crossing takes five minutes and departures are regular. Nisi Island, in the middle of Lake Pamvotis, is smaller than it appears but brings together several Byzantine monasteries and a gripping history: it was in Agios Panteleimon monastery that Ali Pasha took refuge in 1822, pursued by Ottoman troops who had withdrawn the sultan's trust in him. He was executed there at 82, and his decapitated body was buried within the walls. His head was sent on a silver platter to Constantinople. Walking around the island takes 20 minutes.

Ioannina fortress occupies a rocky promontory jutting into Lake Pamvotis—three of its four sides are surrounded by water, making it a naturally defensible position. Justinian laid its first stones in the 6th century; Ali Pasha almost entirely rebuilt it in the early 19th century, completing work in 1815. He made it what you see today. Stroll through the old town's alleys within the walls: at the entrance, by the plane tree where Turks tortured rebels, cafés and silversmiths' shops coexist with the remains of Ali Pasha's palace. One of the few Ottoman town centers in Greece that are still inhabited.

In the fortress's northeast citadel, don't miss the Aslan Pasha mosque—built in 1618 on a Byzantine church's site after the Christian population's expulsion. It now houses the municipal ethnographic museum, documenting the coexistence of Ioannina's three communities: Christian, Muslim and Jewish. What few know is that the city was long one of the great Sephardic Jewish communities of the Balkans. The costumes, silver jewelry and weapons on display give a concrete image of what the city was before the 20th century.

Five km from the center, Perama Cave merits the detour. Discovered by chance in 1940 by villagers seeking shelter during the war, it extends over a kilometer of galleries covering 14,800 m². Archaeologists found the skeleton of a cave bear there—the species is extinct, no worries. Visits are guided group tours (Greek and English), lasting about 45 minutes. Bring a sweater: even in midsummer, the 15°C temperature inside can come as a surprise. Last entry around 5:30 PM.

Head down to the old bazaar's alleys, around the fortress, and step into a silversmith's workshop if you find one open. Ioannina was nicknamed “the city of silversmiths”—an Epirote tradition dating at least to the Ottoman era, with a few artisans still practicing its traditional techniques. The Silversmithing Museum, inside the citadel, displays worked silver pieces from the Ottoman period giving an idea of the region's craftsmanship. The bazaar street is also the best place to buy homemade pita to go.

activities.text: Late in the day, settle on a lakeside terrace by Lake Pamvotis and order local fish: smoked eel, carp, trout—fishermen directly supply the lakefront tavernas. Ioannina is also known for its frogs, exported as far as France. Stay until sunset: the lake reflects the mountains turning violet, and the fortress silhouette stands out against the water.

The walk on the fortress ramparts lets you follow the walls on the lakeside with spectacular views over Pamvotis and the mountains beyond. In the evening, the reflection of the city lights on the water is striking. The café in the elevated Its Kale acropolis is a good place to stop.

Bakaliaros skordalia, fried cod served with a garlic and potato purée, is the signature fried dish of everyday Greek cooking. You'll find it in traditional tavernas around the fortress, often on Fridays—a legacy of the Orthodox calendar.

Ioannina pita differs from mass-produced flaky pitas: a thick pie of homemade phyllo dough, filled with spinach and local cheeses, baked in a wood-fired oven. Each taverna has its recipe. It's THE specialty, wrapped in paper and eaten standing or sitting by the lake.

Epirus tsipouro differs from Thessaly's by the total absence of anise: it's dry, almost neutral, and lets the mezze take center stage. In kafeneia (traditional cafés) around the fortress, you'll be served a small carafe accompanied by a few slices of cheese and mountain charcuterie—a local institution.

visits.text: Less monumental than Corinth, the Sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia calls for a little more attention. Its remains are a reminder that the isthmus also hosted ancient athletic contests, as well as travelers passing through. Start with the site’s information panels to make sense of the foundations, then head to the nearby museum before it closes.

Pictures made of glass rather than paintings on canvas: that is the surprise awaiting you at the Archaeological Museum of Isthmia. Its panels come from the ancient port of Cenchreae, while other objects shed light on the Sanctuary of Poseidon. Save the canal for after the museum: the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

At 6,343 meters long, the Corinth Canal cuts a channel through the land that is easier to grasp from a bridge than on a map. Completed in 1893, it connects the Saronic Gulf and the Gulf of Corinth. Park in a permitted area, head to the pedestrian walkway, and do not count on seeing a boat pass through.

places.name: Ithaca

visits.text: Vathy, the capital of Ithaca, is a small town of 1,700 people tucked at the end of a horseshoe-shaped gulf — one of the best-sheltered natural anchorages in the Ionian Sea. Most of the Venetian-style buildings were rebuilt to their original designs after the 1953 earthquake; one of the painter El Greco's earliest works is said to be in the local cathedral. Stroll along the harbour, stop at one of the quayside tavernas — the atmosphere is gentle, far from mass tourism.

The Archaeological Museum of Vathy holds over 1,000 objects unearthed on the island, covering the Mycenaean through Roman periods. The star exhibit is a pottery fragment inscribed with the name “Odysseus”, found during excavations at the Alalkomenes site. There is also a small bronze sculpture that some identify as depicting Odysseus himself, along with Mycenaean votive tripods. Admission is free. The museum is closed on Tuesdays.

Aetos Hill, 4 km from Vathy, rises to 380 metres. From the church of Aï Giorgios, a steep trail climbs in 20 minutes to the ruins of the ancient city of Alalkomenes — this is where Heinrich Schliemann dug in 1868 and 1878, convinced he had found the palace of Odysseus. Modern archaeologists are more cautious: the fortifications date from the 7th century BC, after the events of the Odyssey. But the view from the top, over both coasts of the island and Kefalonia across the water, is worth the trip on its own.

Kathara Monastery stands at around 600 metres above sea level, on the mountain Homer called Nirito. Founded in the late 17th century, it offers a 360° panorama of Vathy, the southern part of the island and Kefalonia. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Even if the monastery itself does not interest you, make the trip for the view - it is among the most beautiful in all the Ionian Islands.

The Cave of the Nymphs, known locally as Marmarospilia, lies a few kilometres north of Vathy. According to the Odyssey, this is where Odysseus hid the gifts of the Phaeacians on his return. Its interior is closed to the public: do not plan to enter to see the stalactites or the ancient altar. To explore Vathy's links with the Odyssey without relying on this access, walk along the harbour and visit the archaeological museum of Vathy, which displays finds from the island.

activities.text: Ithaca is tailor-made for gentle hiking. Signposted trails connect the villages through olive groves and scrubland of kermes oak. The island is home to just 3,000 people, and the paths are often deserted — one of the most authentic experiences in the Ionians. Ask in Vathy for details on the marked routes.

Revithokeftedes are chickpea fritters laced with fresh herbs, typical of the Ionian Islands. In Ithaca, they're usually served with yoghurt or skordalia (garlic mash). A simple, delicious vegetarian starter — one of the best things to order in a harbourside taverna in Vathy.

The village of Stavros, in northern Ithaca, is worth a stop: its central square has a bust of Odysseus and a model of his “idealised” castle, while a small archaeological museum displays finds from excavations conducted by the British School of Archaeology in the 1930s. Allow for a return drive from Vathy for this visit. Do not confuse it with the museum in Vathy - this one focuses on the north of the island and its connections with the Odyssey.

visits.text: An open panorama, but rituals hidden from view: Kabirion played on this contrast. At Cape Chloi, the sanctuary occupied two artificial terraces, with initiation halls concealed from the uninitiated. Focus on the accessible remains and bring protection from the wind; the visit does not include the descent to the Cave of Philoctetes.

visits.text: The view is worth the climb when the sky is clear: Kaimaktsalan, also known as Voras, rises above 2,500 meters on the border with North Macedonia. The road leads to the ski resort, while the summit is reached on foot. Check the weather and road access; do not try to reach the summit by car.

activities.text: If the trail is dry and the weather is stable, hike to the Profitis Ilias Chapel on Kaimaktsalan. This border monument commemorates the fighting of World War I. Plan a round-trip hike from the ski resort, and bring hiking footwear and a warm layer; give up on the summit if there is snow, fog, or a thunderstorm.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: A monastic bathhouse survives at Kaisariani, within the monastery walls. Along with the church, it dates to the earliest phases of the complex, founded in the late 11th or early 12th century. Also look at the refectory and the cells around the courtyard; enter before 2:30 PM, as closing time is 3:30 PM.

activities.text: You’ll walk to Taxiarches Hill from Kaisariani Monastery. In the woods of Mount Hymettus, this short route brings together Early Christian, Byzantine, and Frankish remains, including the Church of Saint Mark. Take the walk after visiting the monastery; wear closed-toe shoes and check forest access restrictions during periods of wildfire risk.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: Perched on the hill above Kalamata, the Castle of Villehardouin is well worth the climb. Built after 1205 by Geoffrey I of Villehardouin on the site of an ancient acropolis, it was the family's fief for two centuries before passing to the Venetians and then the Turks. The ruins are not spectacular, but the panoramic view over the Gulf of Messenia and the peaks of Taygetus rising behind the city is worth the detour on its own. Allow an hour for a leisurely stroll.

The Archaeological Museum of Messenia, housed in the former municipal market hall, has an attractive modern exhibition design. You can follow the region's history from prehistory to the Byzantine era through finds from Kalamata and across Messenia — pottery, mosaics, gold jewellery including a Mycenaean ring dating to the 16th century BC. The English information panels are well done. Allow 45 minutes.

The church of Agioi Apostoloi (Holy Apostles) holds a story of a founding moment: it was here, in this 13th-century Byzantine church, that the oath of the Greek Revolution was sworn on 23 March 1821 — two days before the date recorded in official history books. The façade is unassuming, but the interior retains an intact Byzantine chancel and an atmosphere of contemplation rarely found in such a lively city.

Kalamata's seafront stretches for 2.5 km along the Messenian Gulf. Stroll here at the end of the day, when the low light gilds the neoclassical façades - you can make out German, Italian and Venetian influences in the buildings of the old town. Every Wednesday and Saturday morning, Kalamata hosts one of the finest markets in the region: vegetables, cheeses, dried figs and local olives abound.

activities.text: Kalamata olives have held PDO status since the 1990s — their oblong shape, fleshy texture and deep purple colour set them apart from all other varieties. The region also produces extra-virgin olive oil from the Koroneiki variety, prized for its high antioxidant content. Ask at the delicatessens in the market or at nearby farms for a tasting — you'll surely leave with a few bottles in your luggage.

Kalamata market (Wednesday and Saturday mornings) is one of the richest food markets in the Peloponnese. Messenia is one of the most fertile areas of the country: you will find dried figs, Taygetus honey, pasto (local smoked pork) and, of course, the famous black olives. Arrive early for the atmosphere and for the best pick.

Try Kalamata's pasteli — a dense, crunchy bar of toasted sesame seeds and honey that Greeks have been making since antiquity. Local pastry shops also offer imam baildi, aubergines stuffed with tomato and onion and baked in olive oil until meltingly soft, and the famous marinated olives served with feta. Dinner on the terrace of a waterfront taverna makes for a perfect evening.

places.name: Kalambaka

visits.text: When you arrive in Kalambaka and see these sandstone pillars surging from the plain for the first time, you understand why monks chose this place in the 11th century. These rocks formed 60 million years ago from river sediments, uplifted then sculpted by erosion into pinnacles over 400 meters high. At their peak in the 15th century, 24 monasteries occupied the summits—built without roads, with materials hoisted in nets by pulley. Six remain active. A 17-km circuit from town lets you tour them by car with stops; allow a full day.

Start with the Great Meteoron—the largest, the oldest, the most visited, and for good reason. Founded in the 14th century by Saint Athanasius of Meteora, its main church was rebuilt between 1545 and 1582 on the Mount Athos model, with frescoes of the Cretan school covering the walls floor to ceiling. Bring good shoes: you must climb 300 steps carved in rock from the parking lot. Arrive at opening (9 AM in season) or late afternoon—between 11 AM and 2 PM buses disgorge hundreds of people at once. Don't leave without taking a look at the museum of manuscripts and icons from the 14th to 20th centuries.

Varlaam Monastery, perched at 373 meters on its pinnacle, is Meteora's second largest. Founded in the 16th century by brothers Theophanes and Nectarios Apsaradas, its katholikon preserves frescoes painted in 1548 by Frangos Katelanos, one of the great masters of post-Byzantine painting. Don't miss the old winch system and net—still on display—used to hoist people and provisions before the stairs were built. And look at the immense 16th-century wooden barrel: 12,000-liter capacity.

Roussanou is a nunnery founded in the 16th century, built on a narrow rock and accessed by bridge. Its Cretan-school frescoes, still vivid in color, are among Meteora's finest. The garden extending to the cliff edge is tended and peaceful. It's often the least crowded monastery on the loop—go last, when the buses have left.

Agios Nikolaos Anapafsas is the first monastery on the road from Kastraki, the smallest and often least visited. Founded in the late 14th century, it's famous for its frescoes executed in 1527 by Theophanes the Cretan, considered the founder of the Cretan school of post-Byzantine painting. The interior space is tiny but the paintings are of exceptional quality. The terrace offers one of the best viewpoints over the rock pillars.

Agios Stefanos is Meteora's most accessible monastery—no steps, just a bridge spanning the gap between the parking lot and entrance. Founded in the 14th century, it was transformed into a women's convent in 1961 after heavy damage during World War II. The nuns have carefully restored the spaces. The view from the terrace over the Thessaly plain is open and impressive.

Agia Triada (Holy Trinity) is the most difficult monastery to access: 147 steps carved in rock to reach a narrow pinnacle where gardens extend to the edge of the drop. This is where the 1981 James Bond film “For Your Eyes Only” was shot—filming equipment had to be winched up by helicopter. The view from the gardens is dizzying. If you only visit one monastery that's difficult to reach, make it this one.

The Cathedral of the Dormition of the Virgin in Kalambaka is often ignored by visitors heading straight for the monasteries. Built on an ancient temple's foundations, it preserves 12th-century Byzantine frescoes and a marble pulpit placed at the nave's center—a unique arrangement in Greece. Allow 30 minutes and it's a fine introduction to the region's religious art.

The natural history museum in Kalambaka displays taxidermied animals and mushrooms in settings that recreate their habitats. Observe the birds and mammals, then discover the diversity of mushrooms in the section of the museum devoted to them. A clear, well-illustrated exhibition, especially useful if you have children. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.

The Pineios gorges, east of Kalambaka, are accessible by car and offer unspoiled nature very different from Meteora's rocky landscape. The river flows between wooded gorge walls, with several old Ottoman stone bridges along the route. Traditional villages are hidden in valleys running perpendicular to the river. A half-day excursion to get off the usual tourist routes.

activities.text: The Meteora scenic road runs 17 km and links all the monasteries with spectacular viewpoints between each stop. Some overlooks let you see several monasteries standing out against the sky at once. In late afternoon, the golden light on the sandstone rocks is remarkable for photography. Kastraki village, at the foot of the rocks, is a calmer and more photogenic place to stay than Kalambaka.

Hiking trails link some monasteries via ancient paths—those monks traveled before roads were built. One of the most interesting descends from the Great Meteoron to Kastraki (about 1 hour). Caution: some passages run along cliffs without guardrails. Maps available at Kalambaka tourist office.

In Kalambaka and Kastraki, artisans have studios where icons are painted using the traditional Byzantine technique—gold ground, natural pigments, egg binder (tempera). These studios often work on commission but sometimes welcome visitors. Ask at your hotel or the tourist office.

Kontosouvli, a pork skewer spit-roasted over charcoal, is Thessaly's meat specialty. You'll find it in Kalambaka tavernas, often served with country bread and Greek salad. A simple dish, but particularly well prepared in establishments that build their own fire.

Boureki is a savory pie with zucchini, potatoes and feta, enclosed in crispy phyllo pastry. It varies from house to house according to cheese proportions and herbs used. In Thessaly, it's often made thicker than in Crete, where it's also popular.

Xinomavro from Naoussa, a red wine from northern Greece, is tannic and full-bodied with aromas of black cherry and spices. It pairs well with roasted meats and aged cheeses. Producers from the Naoussa region often age their cuvées several years in oak barrels.

Sunrise at Meteora is an experience all its own. Several viewpoints below the monasteries (notably near Kastraki) let you watch the rocks emerge from valley mist in golden, low-angle light. Plan to be on site before 7 AM—in summer the sun rises early. It's the ideal moment for photography and total silence.

The Kalambaka market (on Friday mornings) offers products from the monasteries and neighboring farms: mountain honey, dried herbs from the Pindus, olive oil and green walnut jam. The shops around the main square also sell icons and handmade goods.

If you have a car, leave early morning to explore the 50-km loop from Kastraki toward the mountain villages of Agios Dimitrios, Gavros and Vlachava at 1,000 meters altitude. The ridge road offers a panorama over Meteora from above—a completely different perspective from below. En route: beekeepers, goat herds, troglodyte chapels and Liakou estate vineyards.

Galaktoboureko is central Greece's emblematic pastry: vanilla-scented semolina custard, enclosed in phyllo pastry and drizzled with lemon syrup. You'll find it in all Kalambaka pastry shops, often still warm late morning.

Stifado, beef stew with pearl onions, red wine, cinnamon and cloves, simmers for hours and is served in an earthenware pot. It's a seasonal dish that Kalambaka tavernas often cook in the evening. Order ahead if you want to be sure to find it.

Retsina Malamatina is a resinated white wine produced in Attica according to a tradition dating to antiquity—originally pine resin was added to amphorae to preserve them. Very distinctive, it rarely appeals at first tasting, but you acquire a taste for it alongside rich Greek food. Regional tavernas always serve it by the carafe.

visits.text: Sithonia, Halkidiki's middle peninsula, is a different world from Kassandra. Here, pine forests plunge straight into emerald coves, winding roads reveal a new bay at every turn and the fishing villages haven't been swallowed by hotels. Drive the loop starting from the east coast — the views across to Mount Athos are breathtaking.

Karydi Beach, near Vourvourou, regularly ranks among the finest beaches in northern Greece: powdery white sand, turquoise water barely knee-deep, set against pines and sculpted rocks. It's a wild beach — no sunbeds, no umbrellas — so bring everything you need. Arrive before 10am in summer; it fills quickly.

Kavourotripes, also known as Orange Beach or Crab Holes Beach, is a chain of small coves separated by white cliffs tinged with orange. The water shifts from azure blue to emerald green. It's the most famous organised beach on Sithonia — sunbeds are available at the main cove, the others remain wild. If you're worried about the parking situation (it's chaos in August), arrive early.

Neos Marmaras is Sithonia's liveliest port — dozens of waterfront tavernas, excursion boats and a marina. It's a practical base for exploring the peninsula, but also the place to enjoy fresh seafood in the evening under the harbour lights.

activities.text: Rent a boat (no licence required) from Neos Marmaras or Vourvourou to explore the coves that can't be reached by road — particularly the beaches of Platanitsi and Armenistis, which look even wilder from the sea. Organised excursions from these ports also offer views of the Mount Athos coastline opposite.

Porto Koufo, at Sithonia's southern tip, is an almost enclosed natural harbour: two sheer cliffs leave a 300-metre opening onto the sea. The effect is dramatic and the waters inside are perfectly still. Stop here for a lunch of grilled fish at a waterside taverna.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: If the door is open, Kipina Monastery looks as though it is embedded in the cliff. A path cut into the rock followed by a wooden footbridge leads to its buildings, near Kalarrytes. Ask for the monastery keys at the café in the village of Kipina; from the narthex, a 240 m cave follows an old underground riverbed.

Kalarrytes reveals itself through its stone houses more than through a list of monuments. Alongside Syrrako, it is one of the mountain range’s protected traditional villages, which explains the consistency of its built landscape. Explore the lanes on foot and check where parking is permitted before entering the narrow passages.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

visits.text: In Kalavryta, walk up to the memorial to the 1943 massacre, on the spot where the men of the village were executed. The victims' names give this history a tangible dimension, beyond the mountain landscape surrounding the town. Take time to explore the memorial, then head back down to the Orthodox church: its stopped clock also recalls the massacre. The visit puts the streets and houses you see today into perspective. The museum dedicated to the massacre allows you to continue this exploration through the testimonies and documents on display. This stop takes place in Kalavryta, without planning an excursion to the Corinth Canal from the town where you are stopping.

Kalavryta, at an altitude of 735 meters in the mountains of Achaea, is one of the Peloponnese's most moving villages. On December 13, 1943, soldiers of the Wehrmacht's 117th Jäger Division encircled the village and shot the entire male population over the age of 12—an estimated 1,436 people—in reprisal for the deaths of 81 German soldiers. The women and children, locked in the school, managed to escape during the massacre. Only 13 men survived. Since then, the clock on the Orthodox church has been stopped at 2:34 PM, the exact time of the executions. A memorial at the massacre site bears the names of all the victims—it's understated, without theatrics, and that's all it needs.

Six kilometers from Kalavryta, the Monastery of Agia Lavra (the Holy Lavra), founded in 961, has two significant chapters in its history. It was here that on March 25, 1821, Archbishop Germanos of Patras raised the banner of revolt against the Ottomans—a gesture that sparked the Greek War of Independence and made March 25 the national holiday. The monastery was burned by the Germans the day after the 1943 massacre and has since been rebuilt. It houses a small collection of relics and historical objects related to the revolution.

activities.text: Kalavryta is also a pleasant mountain resort, perched at an altitude of 735 m in Chelmós-Vouraïkos National Park, designated a UNESCO Global Geopark. For lovers of local produce, the pedestrian street of 25is Martiou has grocery stores where you can find Kalavryta PDO feta, award-winning mountain honey and chestnut specialties.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Greece: Epirus, Peloponnese and Athens
Achaea in 3 days: gorges, Cave of the Lakes, and Helmos

activities.text: If you have binoculars, take them out at the Kalloni saltworks before trying to get closer to the birds. The production ponds sit alongside marshes and other wetlands; nature and industry share the landscape. Favor the Tholonia observation point in the morning and watch from a distance, without entering the saltworks facilities.

Settle in for a break in Kalloni to sample seafood from the gulf. Sardines caught in this bay are among the specialties of Lesbos, but their availability on the menu depends on supplies. Ask where they come from and how they are prepared before ordering; then leave time for the drive to Agiasos.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Pothia, Kalymnos's capital, welcomes you with its amphitheater of colorful houses as soon as you leave the ferry. Along the waterfront, stalls displaying natural sponges of all shapes and sizes immediately remind you which island you're on. Homer already mentioned this tradition in the Iliad—Kalymnos was long the world's leading exporter of natural sponges. Wander through Pothia's lanes to see the neoclassical buildings inherited from this prosperity, and spot the coats of arms of the Knights Templar engraved on certain facades.

The Maritime Museum of Pothia (Vouvalio district) is the best introduction to the island's history. You'll see the archaic diving suits used by divers until the 1960s to descend to depths of several dozen meters, archival photos of seasonal expeditions to North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, and sponge-processing equipment. Decompression accidents were so frequent that the island had an abnormally high number of disabled men—the museum doesn't hide this reality.

Chrysocheria Castle dominates Pothia from a promontory above town. Byzantine in origin, it was reinforced by the Knights of St. John. The climb on foot from the center takes 20 to 30 minutes—the view over the harbor and sea is well worth the effort. Two small churches with post-Byzantine murals stand within the walls.

Vathy, on the island's east side, is one of Kalymnos's most unusual sites: a narrow fjord of turquoise water cuts inland between limestone cliffs, opening onto a peaceful village surrounded by orange and mandarin groves. The road leading there is winding but passable. Avoid lunchtime when excursion boats from Kos and Bodrum discharge their groups—the village regains its calm by mid-afternoon.

activities.text: Since the early 2000s, Kalymnos has become one of the world's premier sport climbing destinations, with over 3,500 equipped routes across roughly eighty sectors. The Grande Grotta sector, near Myrties, is the most photographed: its stalactites overhang the Aegean directly. Even without experience, you can try it out—several local centers offer guided sessions on beginner sectors like “Afternoon,” with sea views. French-speaking instructors are active on the island. A Climbing Festival is organized every autumn, attracting climbers from around the world. Book the day before in high season.

Take a taxi-boat from Myrties to reach the island of Telendos, directly opposite—10 minutes crossing. Since an earthquake in AD 554, Telendos has been separated from Kalymnos, and local legend has it that the vestiges of an ancient city still rest on the seabed between the two islands. On site: a few tavernas, a quiet beach, and rare peace. Ideal for sunset.

In Pothia, waterfront tavernas serve grilled octopus with vinegar, fresh squid, and fava (split pea purée) drizzled with olive oil and raw onion—fishermen's cuisine at its most authentic. As a souvenir, leave with a natural sponge bought from one of the harbor shops or a processing workshop.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos

visits.text: Kamari is the main beach resort on Santorini's east coast. Its black volcanic sand beach stretches nearly 2 km at the foot of the imposing Mesa Vouno mountain (369 metres). The sand, of volcanic origin, heats very quickly: bring sandals or water shoes if you're visiting in the height of summer. The pedestrian promenade running the beach's length is lined with tavernas and bars. The atmosphere is more family-friendly and affordable than Oia or Fira. Santorini airport sits 3 km to the north - for your final day, it's a practical base.

Ancient Thera, perched atop Mesa Vouno at 369 metres altitude, is an archaeological site founded in the 9th century BC by Dorian colonists led by King Theras. It was continuously inhabited until the Byzantine era. You'll find remains of an Apollo temple, a theatre, a gymnasium and numerous inscriptions. The climb from Kamari takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes on foot. There's also a winding road open to vehicles from 7:30am to 5:30pm, or a shuttle from the village. The combined ticket purchased in Fira is valid here.

On the path climbing to Ancient Thera from the Perissa side, don't miss the rock-cut chapel of Panagia Katefiani, carved directly into the cliff. The stop takes ten minutes and the view over the east coast and Kamari below is well worth the detour. Few visitors stop here - it's a calm and unexpected spot on an otherwise well-trodden path.

Perissa, on the far side of Mesa Vouno, is Kamari's sister beach - same black volcanic sand, slightly younger and more festive atmosphere. The two villages are separated by the mountain and linked only by the inland road (roughly 25 minutes' drive) or a paid boat shuttle. If you have time, make the round trip to compare the vibe.

activities.text: The hike to Ancient Thera from Kamari is the finest walk on the east coast. The path switchbacks through dry, aromatic vegetation, with progressive views over the bay. Leave early in the morning, bring water and take your time on site - the ruins are scattered across a windy ridge with panoramas of both the island's coasts.

If you haven't yet done the caldeira volcano excursion, now is the time: boats depart from Athinios port (12 km from Kamari) or Fira Skala port. You'll walk on the crater of Nea Kameni - still active, with visible fumaroles - then swim in the sulphurous hot springs of Palea Kameni, whose water takes on an ochre tint around the hydrothermal vents. Allow roughly 4 hours. Book in advance in July-August: spots go quickly.

Kamari's open-air cinema, operating since 1987, screens from May to September under the stars with blockbusters in original language subtitled in Greek. The place is convivial, with loungers and a snack bar. Arrive early for the best seats - it's a far more local way to end an evening than Fira's crowded bars.

Mavrotragano is Santorini's grand red, produced from an almost-extinct indigenous grape saved by a handful of passionate winemakers. It yields wines of deep colour, firm tannins and remarkable structure - very different from the light reds typical of the Cyclades. If you find it by the glass in a Kamari taverna, seize the chance.

Swimming at Kamari is a good option early or late in the day. The water is clear, supervised, and facilities (loungers, fresh-water showers) are well-organised. Heads up: black sand absorbs heat enormously - avoid walking barefoot between 11am and 4pm.

days_plan.itin_title: Santorini Road Trip: Caldeira, White Villages and Minoan Sites

visits.text: The Karlovasi Tannery Museum tells the story of an island that worked leather as much as it made its living from the sea. Housed in a former tannery, it brings together tools, machinery, and photographs of the workshops. Visit before heading to the waterfalls: the national tourism office lists opening hours as Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Beneath the trees, the Church of the Transfiguration in Potami offers a pause before the gorge. Also known as Panagia tou Potamiou, it combines Byzantine, Genoese, and more recent elements: a small building with several layers of history. Walk there from the beach area and wear clothing that provides adequate coverage to visit the interior.

activities.text: Follow the stream toward the Potami waterfalls, near Karlovasi. The first stretch follows the water beneath the trees, but reaching the first waterfall then requires wading and swimming. Bring suitable shoes and a waterproof bag; after heavy rain, or if you are not comfortable in the water, stick to the approach trail.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls

visits.text: Olympos is arguably the Dodecanese's most spellbinding village. Founded between the 7th and 9th centuries on the heights of Mount Profitis Ilias to escape Saracen raiders, it remained cut off from the rest of the island for centuries—the paved road only opened in 2011. The result: women still wear traditional embroidered costumes daily (not for tourists), the local dialect preserves Doric Greek phrasings, and single-room houses are built in intact medieval architecture. The 75 windmills along the ridge, many still operational, are the island's symbol. Plan a full day.

Pigadia, Karpathos's capital and main port, is the island's logistical hub. Its natural semicircular harbor is one of the Dodecanese's most sheltered. Take time to visit the archaeological museum housed in the Prefecture Palace: Mycenaean ceramics, ancient coins, Roman statues—the collection documents 3,000 years of human presence on the island.

Aperi, Karpathos's former capital until the 19th century, clings to the hillside with stone houses and flower-filled courtyards. The village is famous for its grand 19th-century mansions built by wealthy shipowners—some feature neoclassical facades that seem transported from another Mediterranean entirely. It's also one of the island's best-maintained villages.

Menetes, at 350 meters elevation in the southern hinterland, is the birthplace of the Karpathos lyre—the traditional stringed instrument that has accompanied dances for centuries. The Church of the Dormition of the Mother of God is considered the island's most beautiful. The view across the sea from the village edge at sunset alone justifies the detour.

At Apella, the beach combines pale sand and pebbles beneath red cliffs, in a bay of turquoise water. The paved but winding road descends to the beach; parking quickly becomes difficult in summer. Part of the shore then offers sunbeds and umbrellas for rent, while a taverna a few metres above serves food and drinks. Enter the water carefully, as it deepens quickly, then follow the rocks with a mask if the sea is calm.

activities.text: If you're in Olympos on August 15th, don't leave under any circumstances: the Feast of the Dormition of the Virgin is celebrated here with epic songs transmitted orally for generations, costumed dances, and music played on lyre and tsambouna (local bagpipe) until dawn. Diaspora residents return from abroad just for this.

The hike between Olympos and the port of Diafani descends about 8 km via a mountain trail that overlooks the sea. The view is vertiginous and the vegetation changes at every elevation. Count on 2.5 to 3 hours of walking. Boats connect Diafani to Pigadia for the return journey.

'Makarounes' are Olympos's signature handmade pasta: shaped by hand through rolling between the palms, they're served with melted butter, fried onions and grated mizithra. You'll find them in Olympos tavernas—one of the rare places where they're still made fresh on site every morning. 'Kserotigana,' ribbons of fried dough drizzled with honey, are served at festivals.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos

visits.text: Bourtzi Castle stands harborside in Karystos, steps from waterfront cafés—a two-story, horseshoe-shaped hexagonal Venetian fortress from 1350 built partly with marble salvaged from a nearby Roman mausoleum. It's among southern Euboea's finest-preserved fortifications. In summer, the courtyard hosts concerts and exhibitions. Entry is free.

From town, gaze toward the heights 4 km away: Castello Rosso (Kokkino Kastro) crowns a rocky spur. Early Byzantine fortifications date to 1030. The Lombard baron Ravano dalle Carceri rebuilt the castle between 1209 and 1216. It later passed to Franks, Venetians, and Ottomans before 1470. A ten-minute car journey from the center rewards you with vistas spanning the bay and surrounding mountains.

Karystos Archaeological Museum, housed in the Yokaleio Cultural Foundation, presents local excavation finds including ceramic sherds recovered in 1959 during Professor Moutsopoulos' excavation of the Drakospito on Mount Ochi. Pieces related to ancient quarries and maritime history appear as well. Small but well-documented.

About 4 km north of Karystos, above the village of Myloi, you'll find the ancient quarries known as "Kolones": monolithic columns of green cipollino marble (marmor Carystium), some reaching 12 meters in length, abandoned in situ two millennia ago before they could be shipped out. This veined green marble, quarried since the 1st century BCE, was exported as far as Rome for the imperial forums, temples, and baths. Columns from Karystos still adorn Hadrian's Library in Athens. The site is accessible on foot from Myloi.

The Drakospita—Dragon Houses—rank among Euboea's most enigmatic monuments. Twenty-three exist across southern Euboea; the largest and best-preserved crowns Mount Ochi's 1,389-meter summit. These megalithic structures, raised without mortar from slabs weighing up to 10 tons, likely date to the Classical or Proto-Classical period (5th–4th centuries BCE). Their purpose remains baffling: temple to Zeus and Hera? Watchtower? Quarryman's lodge? Astronomical observatory? One doorway slab measures 4 meters long, 2 meters wide, yet weighs 10 tons. Their first scholarly mention came October 21, 1797, when British geologist John Hawkins ascended Mount Ochi and documented what he found.

activities.text: Hike up Mount Ochi to reach the Drakospito at the summit: this is the big excursion of the day. Start from the parking area above the village of Myloi (via the forest road that climbs up from the national road), pass the refuge at 1,050 meters and reach the Profitis Ilias chapel. The Dragon House is just a few meters from the summit. Allow about 7 hours there and back, start early, and bring water and a jacket—the wind can be strong at the summit even in summer. The trail crosses the Kastanologos chestnut grove, a haven of rare vegetation.

Visit the Myloi quarries (alternative to the Ochi hike or complementary short excursion): chisel marks in living rock, abandoned columns, and ancient transport systems remain perfectly legible. The open-air, unfenced site commands spectacular vistas over Karystos Bay and the Aegean.

Taste matsata—homemade Karystos pasta served in sauce with braised cock and tomato: this is the town's festive specialty, rustic and generous. Seek it in central tavernas, preferably at dinner. Wash it down with Karistia Gi white, a local blend of Savatiano, Malagouzia, and Assyrtiko.

Before departing toward Rafina or Athens via ferry from Marmari (10 km from Karystos, regular service to Rafina in 1h15), take one last café on the waterfront facing Bourtzi. This ranks among the island's most tranquil waterfronts—fishermen, a handful of pleasure boats, waves lapping stone beaches. The whistled language of nearby Antia village (10 km away) is one of the world's last remaining systems of long-distance vocal communication: a detour there is delightfully offbeat if time permits.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

visits.text: Climb toward Karytaina Castle to understand why this hill controlled the routes through the valley. The Frankish fortress towers over the village like a lookout above the Alfeios River. The climb matters as much as the visit: wear shoes with good traction and save water for the exposed stretches.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Discover the Kassandra Peninsula, the westernmost finger of Halkidiki renowned for its stunning white sand beaches and turquoise Aegean waters. This popular resort area offers some of the finest beaches for swimming and sunbathing in northern Greece, ranging from lively resort strips to secluded coves. The warm, crystal-clear waters and gentle coastline make Kassandra ideal for water sports and family beach vacations.

Explore the picturesque village of Afitos, a traditional settlement perched on cliffs overlooking the sea with panoramic views across the Toroneos Gulf. Charming stone houses, artisan workshops, and tavernas line cobbled streets that have preserved their authentic Macedonian character. The village's elevated position provides spectacular sunset vistas over the Aegean that draw visitors from across Halkidiki.

activities.text: Swim in the pristine waters of Halkidiki's beaches, consistently ranked among the cleanest and most beautiful in the Mediterranean. The three peninsulas jutting into the Aegean like Poseidon's trident offer hundreds of kilometers of coastline, from developed beaches with water sports to hidden coves accessible only by boat. The region's clear, warm waters and pine-fringed shores create a quintessential Greek summer experience.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Greece Tour: Thessaloniki, Macedonia and Meteora

visits.text: Streets meet at right angles against a backdrop of the sea: Kassope reveals an ancient city rather than a single monument. Its street grid, houses, and theater make up this site above the coast. Visit Kassope before heading up to Zalongo: the site closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays and in winter.

Save your energy for the 410 steps to the Zalongo Monument. Its six female figures commemorate the Souliotes’ tragedy of 1803; Georges Zongolopoulos created this sculpture, inaugurated in 1961. The approach starts at Agios Dimitrios Monastery. Make the climb outside the hottest hours, bringing water and wearing closed-toe shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: Stone warms in the sun in Doltso, while the lake comes into view at the end of the narrow streets. The grand houses in this neighborhood of Kastoria recall the prosperity of the fur trade; their projecting upper stories contrast with the narrow passageways. Explore the neighborhood on foot rather than by car, then head to the waterfront: you will better understand how these houses face the water.

Small in stature, full of character: Panagia Koubelidiki invites you to see Kastoria’s churches in a new light. Also known as Panagia Kastriotissa, this Byzantine church stands on the ancient acropolis and is distinguished by its compact form topped with a dome. Walk around it before looking for the entrance: its architecture is already clear from the outside. Ask locally about opening hours to see the paintings inside.

Faces from the 12th through the 18th centuries seem to converse at the Byzantine Museum of Kastoria. Its collection brings together portable icons from churches in the city and surrounding area: images designed to accompany religious practice, rather than simply serve as decorative paintings. Take time to compare their gazes and colors. Schedule this visit for a day other than Tuesday, when the museum is closed according to the Ministry of Culture.

Dispilio tells the story of another way of living beside Lake Orestiada, long before the churches. This Neolithic lakeside village evokes communities of farmers and herders; the archaeological collection explores their dwellings, techniques, and economy. Water has therefore not erased every trace of the past. Contact the Ephorate of Antiquities of Kastoria before traveling there: the collection can be visited on request.

Cool air suddenly replaces the air by the lake inside Dragon’s Cave, Spileo Drakou, in Kastoria. Stalactites and underground lakes feature on this visit; the site reports a year-round temperature of 16 to 18 °C. Bring a light layer and wear shoes with good traction, then confirm tour departure times: the usual advertised closing day is Monday.

Panagia Mavriotissa offers a stop beneath the plane trees on the shore of Kastoria’s lake. The monastery preserves fragments of early 13th-century wall paintings, which can also be seen on the church’s exterior. Look for them on the facades before heading inside, then plan your visit around opening hours and the customs of this religious site.

activities.text: You will walk along Lake Orestiada to see Kastoria’s silhouette change with every curve of the shoreline. The city occupies a peninsula, so its houses and churches present different profiles from different stretches of the waterfront. Choose a short walk near the center instead of a full circuit if you are adding Dispilio to the day. Save this walk for late afternoon, and bring an extra layer for when the wind picks up.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes
Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: Katapola, one of Amorgos's two ports, opens onto spectacular mountain scenery. Amorgos Chora, at an elevation of 320 meters, is linked to the port by a winding road—take the municipal bus or walk for 45 minutes along the switchback trail. At the top, white windmills keep watch over the village from a ridge exposed to the wind, and Venetian coats of arms still adorn the doors of old houses.

The Panagia Hozoviotissa monastery is one of the Aegean's marvels. Founded in the 11th century by Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos to shelter a miraculous icon from Palestine, it's built literally into a cliff face 300 meters above the sea. The building stands 40 meters tall yet only 5 meters wide in places—8 floors carved into rock, a labyrinth of small rooms and narrow staircases. You'll need to climb about 300 steps to reach it from the road. The monks (3 or 4 remain) welcome visitors with Amorgian raki, loukoumi, and Greek coffee. Modest dress required—garments are loaned at the entrance. Luc Besson filmed scenes from The Big Blue here in 1987.

Agia Anna beach lies below the monastery at the foot of the cliffs. Turquoise water, pebbly bottom, access via stairs from the road. This is where the monastery's icon supposedly washed ashore mysteriously on a boat from Palestine. Open sea, sometimes with swell.

activities.text: Waterfront stroll at Katapola and provisioning: Amorgos is known for its honey, local wine, and sun-dried octopus. The harbor market is modest but authentic.
Easy hike between Chora and the windmills for panoramas over the archipelago—on clear days, the view reaches Naxos and Paros.
Swimming at Agia Anna (open sea, possible swell)—diving from the rocks is an island classic.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Seli, also called Kato Vermio, offers a mountain break after the museums on the plain. This village with Aromanian heritage sits at about 1,450 meters in Vermio; its identity extends well beyond that of the nearby ski resort. Keep a warm layer handy, even if the weather in Veria was mild.

activities.text: Head to the area around the Seli National Ski Center for a walk when the slopes are free of snow. The facilities are located in Vermio, very close to the village, in a mountain landscape that can also be explored outside the ski season. Choose a short out-and-back walk on a permitted trail and check local conditions before setting out.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: Set against a cliff rather than atop a hill, Mega Spileo Monastery surprises visitors with its vertical silhouette. Its name refers to the large cavern around which the sanctuary is built. Wear clothing that provides adequate coverage and check access to the monastery before heading up from Zachlorou.

activities.text: Reach Mega Spileo Monastery via the trail from Zachlorou, provided its condition allows the climb. The path connects the village to the sanctuary through the trees, without requiring you to follow the railroad through the gorge. Allow this time for the round-trip walk, in addition to the visit; after rain, use the road access instead.

The sound of the Vouraikos accompanies your walk in Kato Zachlorou, between the village and the area around its small station. The river and the Odontotos line share the narrow valley here. Stay on the village’s public paths: the suspension of train service does not make the tracks or tunnels authorized walking routes.

days_plan.itin_title: Achaea in 3 days: gorges, Cave of the Lakes, and Helmos

visits.text: The fortress of Kavala commands the entire peninsula from the summit of Panagia hill. Its current form dates from the first quarter of the 15th century, though it rests on Byzantine foundations subsequently reworked by the Venetians and the Ottomans. Climb up to the outer walls for the view: at your feet, the red-tiled roofs of the old town, the turquoise harbour, and in the distance the silhouette of Thasos on the horizon. The open-air theatre nestled within the walls hosts performances in summer — check the programme if you're here in July or August.

The Kamares Aqueduct is the most photographed monument in the city, and it deserves every shot. This double-tiered structure — 11 large arches below, narrower arches above — stretches 270 metres long and stands 25 metres high. It was built between 1520 and 1536 on the orders of Ibrahim Pasha, Grand Vizier to Suleiman the Magnificent, after the city was destroyed in 1391. Made of local granite with Ottoman brick detailing, it supplied Kavala with water from Mount Pangaion until 1911. The best angle for a photo: from Lahana Street in the late afternoon, when the golden light brings out the stone.

In the old quarter of Panagia, look for the house of Mehmet Ali (1769–1849) — the founder of the last dynasty to rule Egypt, born right here in this modest cantilevered stone building. The house is preserved as a museum and gives a good sense of Ottoman domestic architecture of the era. Across from it, the square bearing his name features an equestrian statue of the pasha — one of the rare depictions of a human figure tolerated within Islamic tradition.

The Panagia quarter, perched on the peninsula between the fortress and the sea, is the historic heart of Kavala. Its cobbled alleyways, colourful houses with cantilevered balconies (sachnisia), and hidden courtyards make it one of the best-preserved Ottoman neighbourhoods in northern Greece. Don't miss the Halil Bey Mosque, built on the foundations of an early Christian basilica — during the population exchange of 1922–1923, it served as temporary shelter for Greek refugee families.

The Imaret, on the western flank of the Panagia peninsula, is one of the largest Islamic complexes from the Ottoman era still standing in Europe. Built in the early 19th century by Mehmet Ali to serve as a soup kitchen, madrasa and mosque, it combines Ottoman arches and slender columns in a remarkable inner courtyard. The interior is now privately managed, but the exterior can be viewed from the lane.

The site of Philippi has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2016 — the 18th Greek site to join the list. Founded in 360 BC by colonists from Thasos under the name Krenides, the city was conquered in 356 BC by Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, who gave it his name. Allow at least two hours to cross the entire site — it covers 67 hectares, slightly larger than Pompeii.

The theatre of Philippi was built by Philip II in the mid-4th century BC and remodelled under the Romans in the 2nd century AD into a theatre with a monumental three-storey stage façade. In the 3rd century it was converted into an arena for gladiatorial combat: the wild animal pit beneath the orchestra is still visible. Since 1957 it has hosted the Philippi Festival every summer — one of the oldest ancient-theatre festivals in Greece.

The Roman forum of Philippi is one of the best-documented in the eastern provinces of the Empire: a vast square surrounded by temples, shops, the orators' tribune, and a meeting hall for the decurions. A monumental inscription at least 20 metres long, with metal letters 62 cm high set into the paving, honoured the flamen of the divine Augustus. Look for the ruts left by chariots on the Via Egnatia — they're still visible in the stone.

The early Christian basilicas of Philippi are among the most impressive in Greece. Basilica A (late 5th century) measured 130 by 50 metres, with a transept, galleries and atrium. The Octagon, an episcopal complex built on the presumed site of Saint Paul's house of prayer, went through three construction phases from the 4th to the 6th century. It was here, in AD 49–50, that the Apostle Paul founded Europe's first Christian community — and was briefly imprisoned in a Roman cistern traditionally identified as the 'Prison of Paul'.

The Archaeological Museum of Philippi, spread over two floors, presents the site's collections chronologically: sculptures, vases, coins and gold jewellery from prehistoric through Roman times on the ground floor, Christian heritage and the city's decline upstairs. Allow 45 minutes to an hour — the Macedonian jewellery and coins from the era of Philip II are particularly worth your time.

activities.text: Stroll along the Kavala waterfront down to the fishing harbour: the blue-and-white boats, nets drying on the quay, and fish tavernas lined up along the water give the city the feel of an authentic Greek port, well away from the mass-tourism circuit. This is where Saint Paul landed on his first journey to Europe — a commemorative plaque near the harbour marks the event.

Sample sardeles pastes: salted, dried and pressed sardines are Kavala's signature culinary speciality, going back centuries. They're eaten on toasted bread, simply drizzled with lemon juice, alongside a glass of Macedonian tsipouro without anise — the local spirit served chilled with olives and feta. The tavernas along the harbour serve both without ceremony.

In the evening, order a saganaki: a slice of graviera cheese, breaded and fried in olive oil, served still crisp with a wedge of lemon. Simple, no-nonsense, and far better than it looks — it's the essential meze to start a meal across the entire region.

Side trip to the Baptistery of Saint Lydia, a few hundred metres from the archaeological site, on the bank of the Zygaktis River. Lydia, a wealthy purple-cloth merchant from Thyatira, was the first European baptised by Paul in AD 49–50 in this river. The modern octagonal baptistery dates from 1974, but an open-air baptism ceremony takes place every 20 May — if you happen to be here on that date, you can attend.

Try kavourmas: pork or veal slow-cooked in its own fat with spices — a traditional Macedonian winter preservation method you'll find in tavernas around the Kavala area, served as a hot or cold meze. Pair it with an assyrtiko from Drama: this mineral white wine, produced in the highland vineyards to the west, is dry, bright and sharply acidic.

The evening drive back to Kavala follows the Philippi plain, dominated by Mount Pangaion to the south-west — it was from its gold and silver mines that Philip II bankrolled his conquests. If you have time, stop at Krinides, the small modern village on the site of ancient Krenides, to see the remains of the Hellenistic city walls on the outskirts of the UNESCO site.

days_plan.itin_title: Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi
Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi

visits.text: To understand what lies beyond the reeds, start at the Nestos Delta Information Center in Keramoti. It explains how the wetlands function and their ecological importance. Ask which observation areas are accessible at this time of year.

activities.text: You’ll bring your binoculars to observe the Nestos delta from authorized access points around Keramoti. Lagoons, channels, and riverside vegetation provide different habitats for migrating birds and resident species. Favor the late afternoon and keep your distance: sightings of any particular species are never guaranteed.

Keramoti Beach offers a place to linger as the day continues, on a strip of sand facing the Aegean Sea. The nearby port provides a connection to Thassos, but you can also enjoy this stop without boarding a boat. Walk along the beach toward the end of the day, keeping clear of port operations.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: Artificial, yet very much alive: Lake Kerkini owes its existence to a dam built on the Strymon in 1932. Dalmatian pelicans, cormorants, and herons frequent this landscape of reeds and mountains, whose appearance changes with the water level. From the shores near the village of Kerkini, you can observe the habitat without boarding a boat. Bring binoculars and keep your distance from the birds.

activities.text: Book your boat trip on Lake Kerkini before arriving at the dock. These outings let you observe the landscape and birds from the water with a boat operator who knows the area. The species present and the appearance of the shores change with the season. Confirm the departure point and weather conditions, and bring a jacket for the wind on the water.

The sound of hoofbeats accompanies your ride along Lake Kerkini. Horseback rides offered in the area follow a lakeside path, providing a different perspective on the shores. The local boat operator also offers this activity through a partner. Book before you arrive, describe your riding experience, and ask for a route suited to your ability, along with the necessary instructions and equipment.

If a farm welcomes visitors, Kerkini’s water buffalo are worth a guided detour. These animals are part of the landscape of wet meadows around the lake, and their milk is used in several local specialties. Visits depend on the provider’s availability. Book ahead: some visits are offered only to groups by appointment, and you need the farmer’s permission to approach the animals.

Try water buffalo milk in Kerkini as yogurt or kazan dipi. This caramelized cream dessert is among the area’s dairy offerings and provides a tangible extension of a visit to the buffalo farms. Choose a small portion if you want to compare several preparations. Ask the seller about the ingredients, since not all the desserts offered are made with water buffalo milk.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Greece Tour: Thessaloniki, Macedonia and Meteora
Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

visits.text: Falassarna beach is actually five consecutive beaches stretching over 3 km — the main one, Pachia Ammos, runs for over a kilometre. The sand is thick and white, the water an intense turquoise, and the full-west orientation produces the most beautiful sunsets in all of Crete: the sun drops straight into the sea with nothing in its way. Settle in late afternoon for the show. Be aware that the beach can be windy — on meltemi days, the waves attract windsurfers but make swimming less enjoyable.

Take 30 minutes to explore the ruins of the ancient city of Falasarna at the northern end of the beach — it's a story few people know. The city thrived from the 4th to the 1st century BC as a naval power, boasting the only natural harbour in western Crete. In 69 BC, the Romans destroyed everything and sealed the harbour to put an end to what they called a pirate stronghold. Excavations begun in 1986 have uncovered the docks, the acropolis, and tombs from the 6th century BC — you're literally walking on 2,500 years of history between beach towels.

Kissamos — also known as Kastelli — doesn't look like the other tourist towns in Crete, and that's exactly why it's worth a stop. No restored Venetian harbour for the tourists, no souvenir-shop alleyways: just a genuine waterfront with fishermen's tavernas serving whatever they pulled from the sea that morning. Enjoy a simple dinner by the water before sorting out your Balos excursion for the next day — Kissamos port is where the ferries depart.

activities.text: Ferry excursion from Kissamos port to the Balos lagoon and Gramvousa island. The Balos lagoon can be reached either by this boat trip (departing around 10 am, returning late afternoon) or via an unpaved 8 km track by car (note: rental contracts typically don't cover damage on dirt roads) followed by a 20- to 30-minute walk. From the heights overlooking the lagoon, the view is genuinely breathtaking: a tongue of white-pink sand between two arms of intensely blue sea. The sand owes its pink tint to the same micro-organisms (foraminifera) and crushed shells as Elafonisi. Get there early — the first ferries let you arrive before the midday rush. Book ahead in high season.

days_plan.itin_title: Southwest Crete Road Trip: Gorges and Beaches

visits.text: Touristy, certainly, but Kokkari’s small harbor retains its village scale. Houses cluster on a tongue of land between the boat basin and the pebble beaches. Explore the lanes behind the outdoor dining areas before choosing where to have lunch; park on the outskirts to avoid the narrow passages.

activities.text: If the sea is calm, Kokkari Beach offers a swimming break after the museums. Pebbles replace sand, and the water gets deep quickly; the wind can also whip up waves along this northern coast. Bring water shoes and skip swimming if conditions are poor.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls

visits.text: The gold bust alone is worth a stop at the Archaeological Museum of Komotini. This effigy of Septimius Severus was carried on a pole in the Roman army; it changes how you view an imperial portrait. Visit the museum before your city walk and check its hours, which are shorter in winter; it is closed on Tuesdays.

Komotini’s old town reveals itself around the clock tower as much as along its shopping lanes. The tower, built in 1884 and later remodeled, stands beside the Yeni Mosque; Ermou and Hephaestus Square extend this compact area. Explore on foot and visit the interiors of places of worship during permitted hours.

An Ottoman building housing Christian collections: Komotini’s Imaret offers this unexpected pairing. This former charitable institution houses the ecclesiastical museum, with icons, liturgical vestments, and manuscripts. Check the opening hours before setting aside the end of your day for a visit; if the interior is closed, the brick-and-stone building is still worth a look from the street.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: Konitsa is built amphitheater-style on a Pindus slope, overlooking the confluence of the Aoos and Voidomatis rivers. Its stone bridge is one of the largest single-arch bridges in the Balkans: 20 meters high, with a span of nearly 40 meters, built between 1823 and 1871 by master mason Zioga Frontzo from the village of Pyrsoyianni. Cross it on foot—the wind blows hard at the arch's summit, and the masons hung a small bell underneath to keep rhythm during construction.

Panagia Stomiou Monastery lies upstream of Konitsa Bridge, clinging to the rock face at an altitude of 650 meters and accessible on foot along the Aoos Gorge trail. Built in 1774, it was inhabited for several decades by the monk Paisios, who lived there as a hermit before moving to Mount Athos. The trail leading to it follows the turquoise river through a magnificent setting—swimmers bathe there in summer; the water is icy and the current strong.

activities.text: The Aoos River below Konitsa is one of Europe's last wild rivers: clear water, a pebble bed and steep-sided gorges. From Konitsa's stone bridge, set out on foot along the trail entering the gorge toward Panagia Stomiou Monastery. The path lets you observe the cliffs, pebbles and riverside vegetation as you follow the river. Return along the same route to the bridge, choosing your turnaround point according to your fitness.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld

places.name: Kontias

visits.text: The windmills of Kontias are a reminder that the wind also helped feed the island. These restored stone buildings bear witness to grain milling; some now serve as accommodations. View them from public areas, then head toward the village’s stone houses: do not count on visiting the windmill interiors.

If you enjoy a change of perspective, the Balkan Contemporary Art Gallery in Kontias offers a break between ancient sites. Its collections bring together works by artists from several Balkan countries, often inspired by Lemnos. Confirm its opening hours before setting out, and plan this stop early enough to reach Poliochni before it closes.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 3 Days: Villages, Ancient Sites, and Dunes

map_keywords: Gallery of Contemporary Balkan Art Kontias

places.name: Kos

visits.text: The Asclepeion of Kos sits 4 km southwest of town, and it's the island's most important archaeological site. Founded in the 4th century BC, it was simultaneously a religious sanctuary, healing center, and medical school—one of history's first hospitals, capable of receiving up to 4,000 patients according to some ancient sources. Hippocrates, a native of Kos, supposedly taught here. The sanctuary spreads across three terraces connected by marble staircases: Roman baths and consultation rooms on the first level, temples of Apollo and Asclepius on the second, grand Doric temple and porticoes on the third. From the top, the view sweeps across Kos town, the sea, and the Turkish coast opposite. Bring a hat and water—there's little shade on site.

Opposite the Castle of the Knights, on Platanos Square, stands the plane tree of Hippocrates. The tree measures 4.7 meters in diameter and spreads over a radius of more than 12 meters; botanists estimate it to be about 500 years old rather than the 2,400 years of legend. Either way, the spot is pleasant and shady, and tradition has it that Hippocrates taught medicine beneath its branches.

The Castle of the Knights of Kos (Neratziá), built from 1315 directly atop the ruins of an ancient fort, controls the harbor entrance from its promontory. The Knights of St. John reused ancient marble blocks for its walls—you can still clearly spot them in the lower courses. The interior houses a collection of ancient and medieval sculptures. Until the early 20th century, the castle was separated from town by a moat filled with seawater.

The ancient agora of Kos, south of the castle, is one of the region's best-preserved ancient urban centers. Founded in the 4th century BC on a geometric plan, it features a massive colonnaded stoa, ruins of a sanctuary to Aphrodite, a 2nd-century BC Temple of Hercules, and a 5th-century Christian basilica. The site is generally open and lightly monitored—ideal for peaceful exploration.

The Archaeological Museum of Kos, on Eleftherias square, houses the collection of discoveries made on the island since antiquity. The centerpiece: a marble statue of Hippocrates, and several remarkable mosaics from the Hellenistic and Roman periods. Combined ticket with the Asclepeion available.

activities.text: Kos is one of the Dodecanese's most bikeable Greek islands—flat, well-served by bike paths, and crossed end-to-end by a coastal road. Rent a bike in the morning to reach the Asclepeion (4 km), then head toward the beaches of Tigaki or Marmari on the north coast, with their fine sand and shallow waters. The total journey from Kos town represents about twenty kilometers round-trip—very accessible for any level.

In the evening, explore the lively center of Kos town with its blend of Ottoman architecture (mosques, fountains) and Greek and Roman remains around street corners. Apellou street and the areas around Eleftherias square concentrate tavernas, bars, and restaurants for ending the day on a terrace.

Try patatato, Kos's traditional dish: veal slowly braised with potatoes, white wine, and cumin. Simple, generous, rooted in the island's rural tradition. For dessert, sample the local baklava, more generous with walnuts and cinnamon than the neighboring Turkish version.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos

map_keywords: Neratzia Castle of the Knights Kos

places.name: Kozani

visits.text: From costumes to taxidermied animals, the atmosphere at Kozani’s Museum of History, Folklore, and Natural History changes from room to room. Its collections bring together domestic life, regional wildlife, and local history; reconstructed homes give the objects a human scale. Check opening hours and focus on selected sections to leave time for Aiani.

On a road trip, Kozani’s municipal map library makes a worthwhile detour. Housed in the home of Georgios Lassanis, its permanent exhibition places the city within the history of maps: seeing how roads were depicted gives you a different perspective on your route. Check opening hours before making the trip.

“Mamatsios” is the name given to the clock that towers over Agios Nikolaos in Kozani. Beside this urban landmark, the church preserves frescoes and a carved iconostasis, while the bell tower was built separately. Enter only outside service times, then view the complex from Nikis Square to see how the buildings relate to one another.

activities.text: For a food-focused break in Kozani, look for Krokos Kozanis in grocery stores. This saffron is grown around the nearby village of Krokos, rather than in the heart of the city. Check its origin on the label and choose a small, sealed package for transport, or try a saffron dish if one is on the menu.

Finish the circuit with a café break on Nikis Square in Kozani. The clock, city hall, and Agios Nikolaos Church form a compact group that you can explore on foot after traveling the country roads. Choose a table away from traffic and allow plenty of time before your departure.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece
Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

map_keywords: Historical Folklore and Natural History Museum Kozani

visits.text: Kymi perches 200 meters above the Aegean Sea, hidden behind forested hills—locals call it "the Balcony of the Aegean." Shipowner mansions from the 19th century, when Kymi commanded 400 sailing vessels and ranked second only to Chalcis in island prominence, lend the center a rare architectural character. Climb to the main square for vistas across the open sea. A statue in the square commemorates the town's most celebrated son.

Kymi's folk museum gathers embroidered costumes, maritime documents, traditional tools, and daily-life artifacts chronicling this sailors' town. It also houses archives connected to Dr. George Papanicolaou, born here May 13, 1883. This Greek physician, who emigrated to the United States in 1913, developed the cytological test known as the "Pap smear"—a screening method for early cervical cancer detection that has saved millions of lives worldwide. His birthhouse is visible nearby.

Descend the serpentine 5-km road to Paralia Kymis at the clifftop's base. This is where ferries depart for Skyros, Skopelos, and Alonissos. The atmosphere is that of an animated fishing harbor: seaside tavernas line the quay, blue-and-white boats bob at anchor, nets dry in the sun. If timing allows, dine here rather than in the upper town.
