The Monastery of the Transfiguration (Metamorphosis), founded in the 16th century by monks from Mount Athos, nestles in greenery along the route between Kymi and the sea. It's a peaceful sanctuary with characteristic monastic architecture and small-batch honey production sold on-site. The nuns who inhabit it today welcome visitors outside service hours—dress appropriately.

activities.text: Kymi's dried figs are among Euboean products most prized: fumigated with sulfur by the local cooperative, they acquire a pale hue and slightly tart edge distinguishing them from standard dried figs. Search for them in central-town groceries—they're the edible souvenir worth bringing home.
Hike to Maniakiatis Falls: the Maniakiatis River originates on Mount Kserovouni. A 50-minute trail leads to a 15-meter waterfall amid lush vegetation. Start early to enjoy the cool morning air.
Savor Kymi's baklava: the local pastry craft is celebrated for its quality, crafted with Euboean walnuts and honey. Pair it with amygdalota—tender almond cakes found in every pastry shop in town.

days_plan.itin_title: Euboea: Ancient Spas and Villages

visits.text: To get a sense of Chora, start by heading up to Kythira Castle. The ramparts overlook Kapsali, while the capital’s houses rise in tiers below the castle entrance. This Venetian past is also reflected in the town’s architecture. Head up before the intense heat, with water and shoes with good traction.

A register of nobility burned in a square: Chora also has a revolutionary history. In Estavromenos Square, the French proclaimed the abolition of privileges and destroyed the Libro d’Oro. The square takes its name from the cathedral. Walk there through the narrow streets and respect services when visiting the church.

activities.text: Head down to Kapsali to view the castle from the sea after seeing it from above. The two bays of Chora’s port offer a very different landscape from the narrow streets perched above. Walk along the waterfront, then choose a swimming area away from boats; leave time to head back up to Chora for the night.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 4 Days: Coves and Villages

visits.text: The Sfagnonas of Lailias looks more like a small wetland than a picture-postcard forest. This protected habitat, at an elevation of around 1,470 meters, is of paleobotanical interest. Observe it from designated paths and stay on firm ground: the peat bog should not serve as a shortcut during your walk.

activities.text: The shade of the beech trees changes the mood in Lailias after the heat of the plain. Paths pass through a forest of beech and pine in the Vrontous mountain range, which is crossed by hiking routes. Choose a short walk suited to the conditions, bring a warm layer, and turn back if the trail markings become unclear.

days_plan.itin_title: Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

visits.text: Artificial, though you would hardly guess it at first glance: Lake Aoos carves the plateau into coves and islets. This hydroelectric reservoir lies at an elevation of around 1,350 meters, between the Valia Kalda and Vikos-Aoos areas. Stop in a designated spot and keep a warm layer within reach, even in summer.

activities.text: Follow an accessible stretch of Lake Aoos to leave the pace of the road behind for a while. Meadows and pine or beech woods alternate along its indented shores; the lake lends itself to a short walk as well as cycling. Decide where you will turn back before setting out, rather than improvising a full circuit.

days_plan.itin_title: Metsovo and the Northern Pindus: 3 Days Among Villages and Forests

visits.text: Despite its natural appearance, Lake Doxa is a reservoir created for irrigation in the 1990s. The chapel of Agios Fanourios extends into the water at the end of a narrow strip of land, surrounded by wooded slopes. Walk to it from an authorized parking area and keep the path clear for other visitors.

Beyond its fortress-like exterior, Agios Georgios Feneou Monastery offers a view down over the Lake Doxa area. The old monastery was relocated to higher ground because of flooding. Make this an optional visit, depending on opening hours; wear clothing that provides adequate coverage and skip it if it would delay your return.

activities.text: Walk along Lake Doxa to enjoy the reflections of the wooded slopes without adding a mountain hike to the itinerary. The small lakeside road offers a walk you can adapt to the time available. Choose a short out-and-back route, watch for vehicles, and bring an extra layer for this high-elevation area.

Better than a bulky souvenir, legumes from Feneos let you continue your discoveries at the table. The region produces yellow split peas, among other crops, and producers sell their products near Lake Doxa. If there are stalls, ask where the products come from and how to cook them; otherwise, look for these specialties at lunchtime.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: The birds of Heracles belong to myth; at the Environment Museum of Stymphalia, the focus returns to the natural habitats and people of the basin. The exhibition connects water, traditional trades, and changes in the landscape. Arrive at or after 10 a.m. and avoid Tuesdays, when the museum is closed, before heading out onto the outdoor trail.

activities.text: Follow the Lake Stymphalia interpretive trail to connect the museum’s explanations with the landscape. Its 1.8 km linear route takes in wetlands, a bird observatory, and the remains of ancient Stymphalos. Plan to return along the same path, bring binoculars, and stay on the sections accessible under current ground conditions.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: The First Ancient Theater of Larissa comes into view among the streets of the modern city. Its tiered seating recalls that the site hosted political assemblies of the Thessalian League as well as performances. Walk around it from public areas if the grounds are closed, then head to your accommodations for the final night.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: Approaching from Heraklion—about 90 minutes by car—or from Agios Nikolaos (75 minutes), you emerge onto a sight nothing on the coastal drive could have prepared you for: the Lasithi Plateau, a green basin 850 meters above sea level, 11 kilometers long, ringed by the Dikti Mountains that soar above 2,100 meters. What strikes you first are the cultivated fields and, dotted here and there, restored windmills. The Venetians once built up to 5,000 of them to irrigate the land through a network of canals called linies. Stop at Seli Ambelou at the plateau's entrance to see them lined up against the sky—it's the most photographed viewpoint in Lasithi.

The Dikteon Cave, known as the Cave of Zeus, clings to the mountainside at 1,025 meters above the village of Psychro. According to Greek mythology, this is where Rhea hid her infant son Zeus from his father Cronos, who had a nasty habit of devouring his own children. Descending the 314 steps into the mountain's belly is a bit of a workout, but the payoff is real: a forest of stalactites and an underground lake in an atmosphere that feels genuinely mystical. Bring a sweater—it's cool inside year-round, no matter how scorching it is outside. The cave draws over 200,000 visitors annually; arrive early in the morning to explore without the crowds.

On the road climbing toward Lasithi, stop at the Kera Kardiotissa Monastery, perched at 650 meters on the northern slopes of Mount Dikti. Its first written mention dates to 1333. What sets this place apart is the story of its miraculous icon: stolen three times by the Turks, it returned three times on its own. The third time, they chained it to a marble column to prevent another escape—it came back anyway, bringing the column with it. You'll see the column in the courtyard and the chain beside the icon. The original has been in Rome since 1498; the copy that replaced it in 1735 is also considered miraculous.

Make a stop in Tzermiado, the plateau's 'capital.' Its folklore museum reconstructs two Cretan interiors: one traditional mountain dwelling, the other a neoclassical home from the post-Ottoman period. If you have time, head to the Kronion Cave at the village entrance—a Minoan cult site frequented since the Neolithic, far less known than the Dikteon Cave and often completely deserted. The plateau is one of the rare places in Crete where people live year-round, even under winter snow: take the time to chat with locals in the village cafés.

Agios Georgios houses a museum dedicated to daily life on the plateau—better curated than its modest size might suggest. You'll find a carefully reconstructed Cretan mountain house and a room devoted to Eleftherios Venizelos, the great Greek statesman whose family hailed from the region. Between May and October, the museum is open Monday to Saturday from 10:30 AM to 5 PM. Nominal entrance fee.

activities.text: The drive up to the plateau from Heraklion or Agios Nikolaos is a pleasure in itself: the road winds through panoramic mountain passes and perched villages. From Agios Nikolaos (about 75 minutes), the approach from the south side of the Dikti massif is particularly beautiful. If you're coming from the north coast, stop at the Seli Ambelou viewpoint to see the windmills lined up with the valley below—and in the distance on clear days, the Aposelemis reservoir and the submerged village of Sfendyli.

The Seli windmill loop is an easy 3-kilometer walk among the 19th-century stone windmills and orchards. The E4 trail also crosses the plateau for those who want to push on to the Minoan ruins at Mount Karfi, with spectacular views over the coast. Bring sturdy shoes and water.

In the tavernas of Psychro or Tzermiado, ask for stakovoutyro: a fermented mountain butter from the Lasithi highlands, made by churning sheep's milk, that you eat spread on grilled bread. Rare—you'll find it almost nowhere else in Crete. If you're there in season, the taverna tables overflow with local products: fresh cheeses, wild thyme honey, mountain potatoes.

For dinner, order ofto at a plateau taverna: a whole lamb slow-roasted in an earthen oven with potatoes, garlic, and wild herbs—meat so tender it falls apart, juices concentrated and rich. Lasithi tavernas serve it mostly on Sundays as a traditional dish. Pair it with a glass of Romeiko, the rustic and ancient red grape of eastern Crete, vinified naturally by local producers.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Tour of Crete: Minoan Palaces, Gorges and Eastern Coast
Crete Road Trip: Agios Nikolaos, Elounda & Spinalonga

visits.text: To understand silver in antiquity, nothing beats the Archaeological Museum of Lavrio. Finds from the metalworking workshops explain how the ore was processed, while reliefs from the Temple of Poseidon already establish the town’s connection to Sounion. Start here on the third morning, then head to Thorikos; make sure to visit the mining sites before they close in the afternoon.

An ancient quarry forms the foundation of the theater at Thorikos. Its elongated seating departs from the expected semicircle, amid a landscape where performance spaces and mining facilities stood side by side. Study the layout from the designated paths; bring water and keep away from mine openings, which are not part of the visitor route.

You’ll follow the designated paths through the ancient ore-washing installations at Souriza, inland from Lavrio. The basins bear witness to an ore-processing method that recycled water to recover silver and lead. Stay above ground, away from the shafts; from April to October, aim to arrive before 2:30 PM, and book by phone in winter.

activities.text: If you’ve left time for a break, walk along Lavrio’s harbor after visiting the mining sites. Departures for Kea and Kythnos reveal another side of this town shaped by silver mining. Settle in for lunch on the waterfront, then head toward Sounion; this itinerary does not include a ferry crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: The castle of Agia Mavra (Santa Maura), standing at the edge of the channel that separates the island from the mainland, is the first thing you'll see as you cross the bridge. Built in the 14th century by the Orsini counts, it gave its medieval name to the entire island — Lefkada was known as Santa Maura until the 19th century. The Turks held it from 1479 to 1684, before the Venetians took it back. The grounds are freely accessible and the view over the lagoon and salt flats is beautiful in the late afternoon.

Cape Lefkatas, at the south-western tip of the island, is one of the sites most steeped in mythology in all of Greece. Plan a day trip from Lefkada Town. The white cliff drops 72 metres into the Ionian Sea. In Antiquity, according to tradition, those suffering from an impossible love came to throw themselves into the sea from this headland - surviving the leap meant being cured of one's passion. The poet Sappho (c. 630-580 BC) is said to have died here for Phaon, according to legend. A lighthouse built in 1913 now stands on the site of the ancient temple of Apollo. On a clear day the view reaches as far as the coasts of Epirus.

Nydri, on the east coast, is the launching pad for boat trips to the small islands of the archipelago: Meganisi, Madouri, Sparti and, most famously, Skorpios — formerly owned by Aristotle Onassis, where he married Jackie Kennedy in 1968. Water taxis and organised excursions leave from the harbour throughout the day in summer. The marina is lively, with plenty of waterfront tavernas.

The Faneromeni monastery, perched on a wooded hill 3 km from the capital, offers the finest view down over Lefkada Town and the channel separating it from the mainland. The current buildings date from the 17th-18th centuries. Allow 20 minutes' walk from the car park.

The town of Lefkada itself is worth an hour's wander through its lanes: the facades are built of painted corrugated iron on wooden frames — an earthquake-resistant technique honed over centuries of seismic experience, which gives the houses a Caribbean feel unique in the Ionians. The archaeological museum, in town, displays finds from the excavations of Dörpfeld, the German archaeologist who came here searching for the homeland of Odysseus.

activities.text: Rent a boat from Nydri and explore the islets off the east coast at your own pace. Skorpios remains private property, but you can anchor nearby; Meganisi has several superb coves accessible only by sea. The east coast of Lefkada is sheltered from the prevailing winds — ideal for a relaxed day on the water, even without sailing experience.

Eglouvi lentils are Lefkada's most prized agricultural product — this small mountain village at 700 metres altitude grows tiny, flavourful lentils that carry a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO). In soup with local olive oil or as a cold salad, they're simple and outstanding. Look for them in the grocery shops of the capital.

Ladopita is a rustic Lefkadian cake made with olive oil, flour and raisins — no butter, no milk. It's a Lenten recipe handed down from the Venetian centuries. Dense and mildly sweet, it pairs perfectly with a Greek coffee on a terrace. You'll find it in the traditional bakeries of the old town.

Agios Nikitas, 12 km northwest of the capital, is the most charming seaside village on the coast: its pedestrian lanes lead straight down to a small sandy beach, the tavernas sit at the water's edge and the crowds are more manageable than in Nydri. It's a good option for dinner or a late-afternoon swim.

days_plan.itin_title: Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada

visits.text: The Kastro of Panagia, perched on Apityki hill 200 meters above the sea, is visible from the ferry long before you dock at Leros. Built by the Byzantines in the 11th century and reinforced by the Knights of Rhodes in the 15th, it shelters the miraculous icon of the Virgin who, according to legend, emerged from the sea of her own accord before being installed in the powder magazine chapel. Climb the 300 steps from Platanos—the view of Agia Marina and Panteli bays spreading on either side of the hill is one of the Dodecanese's finest. The 1745 iconostasis and the bronze-and-silver bell cast by Russian artisans are worth the ascent.

Platanos, Leros's former capital, is a quiet village squeezed between two hills, with sand-colored neoclassical houses and small squares shaded by plane trees. This is where the island's administrative heart beats, far from the port bustle. Take time to wander its lanes—several buildings date from the 19th century, when local shipowners were at the height of their prosperity.

Lakki is one of Greece's most bizarre architectural curiosities. Founded in the 1930s by the Italians under the name Porto Lago, this port was designed from scratch according to fascist rationalist principles: wide boulevards, buildings with rounded facades, a cinema and town hall resembling beached ocean liners. Lakki Bay is one of the Mediterranean's largest natural harbors. It's hard not to feel disoriented strolling these nearly deserted streets off-season—like wandering a forgotten 1930s film set.

The War Museum, installed in an authentic underground tunnel at Merikia, is unique in Greece. The Italians excavated it as a munitions depot; in 1943, the Battle of Leros left scars here when the Germans bombarded for 42 days before seizing the island from the British, Greeks and Italians. The museum, opened in 2005, preserves weapons, uniforms, munitions and maps from the 1912-1943 period. Allow 45 minutes.

Alinda's Belleni Tower, built between 1925 and 1927 by expatriate Parisi Belleni, is a neo-Gothic turreted stone building that now houses the island's folklore museum. Exhibits include the watch from the destroyer 'Queen Olga,' sunk in the harbor during the 1943 battle, and artwork painted by political prisoners interned on Leros under Greece's dictatorship (1967-1974).

activities.text: Leros's beaches are perfect for families: Alinda, the longest, is lined with tamarisks and its shallow waters suit children. Vromolithos offers a beach bar and crystalline water. Panteli, at the castle's foot, is the ideal spot in late afternoon when light settles on the ruined windmills along the ridge. For diving, Xirokampos in the south is renowned for its World War II wrecks—a good dozen ships and planes rest at 10 to 30 meters depth.

'Koukouvadès,' fish marinated with rosemary, are Leros's signature seafood specialty. 'Pitakia,' pies stuffed with fava beans, and 'Kakavia,' bouillabaisse prepared with fish pulled from caïques that very morning, are essential at tavernas in Panteli or Agia Marina. For dessert, 'Melopita'—honey-and-mizithra-cheese cake—is the local sweet touch.

Ride a scooter (ideal for this reasonably sized island) up to the castle at sunset, when the last visitors have left and bats begin circling the battlements. The panorama of both bays in orange light is one of the Dodecanese's most memorable views. Scooter rentals are available at Agia Marina and Lakki ports.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos

activities.text: If you want a break between the ruins and the mountains, stop in Levidi. The town sits on the northeastern slope of Mainalo, where the roads from the plateau and Vytina meet. Take a short walk through the center and have a coffee before continuing toward the fir forests.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Stand in the shadow of Mount Olympus, the legendary home of the ancient Greek gods rising 2,918 meters as Greece's highest peak. This mythical mountain where Zeus and the Olympian deities held court dominates the landscape of Pieria with its snow-capped summit visible from Thessaloniki on clear days. Olympus National Park, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, protects pristine forests and rare alpine flora surrounding the sacred mountain.

Explore the Archaeological Site of Dion, the sacred sanctuary of the ancient Macedonians dedicated to Zeus at the foot of Mount Olympus. Philip II and Alexander the Great celebrated their military victories at this sacred site where the Greeks believed the gods descended to earth. Remarkably preserved temples, theaters, and Roman baths reveal the religious importance of this pilgrimage destination.

Stroll through the enchanting village of Palaios Panteleimonas, a hidden gem perched at 700 meters on the slopes of Mount Olympus. This eighteenth-century settlement, with traditional stone houses adorned with flowers, offers spectacular views stretching from the Aegean Sea to the snow-capped peaks. Time seems to stand still in the cobbled lanes, where local tavernas serve traditional cuisine on terraces overlooking the sea. Allow for a same-day round trip from Litochoro.

activities.text: Cool off in the crystal-clear pools of the Orlias waterfalls, a paradise of 25 waterfalls nestled in a wooded canyon near Dion. Natural pools formed beneath each waterfall offer refreshing relief during the warmer months, surrounded by lush vegetation. From Litochoro, drive to the trailhead near Dion, then continue to the pools on foot.

Explore the Byzantine Castle of Platamonas, a crusader fortress dramatically positioned on a hill overlooking the Aegean Sea. Built between 1204 and 1222 to guard the entrance to the Temple Valley, this impressive stronghold features distinctive medieval European architecture rare in Greece. The imposing keep and well-preserved walls command sweeping views over the coastline and toward Mount Olympus.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Greece Tour: Thessaloniki, Macedonia and Meteora
Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa
Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: Welcome to the Lesser Cyclades. Iraklia has just 150 permanent residents across 18 km² and electricity only arrived in 1982. The port of Agios Georgios is endearing: the entire village comes down to greet the ferry, collect deliveries, and chat under the tamarisks. Livadi beach, 1.5 km from the port, is the island's finest—a long crescent of golden sand with turquoise water where you'll find space even in the middle of August. No umbrellas are available to rent on site; bring your own.

activities.text: Snorkeling and swimming in Livadi bay: the crystalline waters let you spot fish, sea urchins, and if you're lucky, sea turtles that regularly visit the bay.

Hike to the village of Panagia (Chora), 4 km from the port via a marked trail. This inland hamlet is the island's traditional capital, with its Cycladic stone houses and whitewashed church. Those with energy left can continue to the Agios Ioannis cave, considered the largest in the Cyclades with 2 km of stalactite-adorned galleries—bring a flashlight and closed-toe shoes.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The waterfalls at Loutra Pozar add a natural dimension to this thermal spa stop in Pella. The complex extends through a gorge at the foot of Voras, with flowing water and areas developed for visitors. Approach accessible viewpoints without leaving the permitted paths, and protect your phone from splashes.

activities.text: Warm water even when the air turns cool: that is the pleasure of a soak at Loutra Pozar. The thermal water emerges at 37°C and feeds indoor and outdoor pools set amid the mountain landscape. Bring a swimsuit, towel, and sandals, then check the price and availability of your chosen pool before paying.

Follow an established trail at Loutra Pozar to extend your break beyond the pools. Paths and bridges follow the contours of the gorge; some branches lead toward caves in the area. Ask at reception which route is open, stay on a suitable route, and allow extra time to return before getting back on the road.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: The sound of water accompanies your break at the Loutraki waterfalls, near the old thermal springs. Their landscaped appearance can be misleading: they are an artificial feature that has become a landmark along the promenade. Make this a brief stop in the late afternoon; the wet ground is a reminder to watch your footing, too.

activities.text: Walk along the Loutraki promenade once the day’s visits to stone monuments have filled enough of your time. The pebble beach and outdoor terraces share the waterfront, facing the gulf. Walk as far as your energy allows, then stop for dinner; water shoes are useful if you choose the beach.

If you prefer warm water to the beach, Loutraki Thermal Spa offers another option for a break. The facility uses the local thermal springs, whose presence explains the town’s role as a spa resort. This session remains optional: book directly and confirm opening hours before adding it to this first day.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: Hora Sfakion is the embarkation point for Loutro—leave your car in the harbor parking lot and buy your ticket at the ferry company counter before boarding. The crossing takes about 20 minutes and runs along sheer cliffs that plunge directly into the Libyan Sea. It's already a spectacle in itself.

Loutro is one of Greece's most unusual villages: no road reaches it. White houses with blue shutters cascade down to a small bay of emerald water, completely sheltered from the wind. The village was once the port of Anopolis, a prosperous city in Roman and Byzantine times—the Bible even mentions this anchorage as the place where the Apostle Paul took shelter during his journey to Rome. Today, no cars, no engines—just the sound of waves and taverna terraces.

activities.text: Before taking the ferry, drive up to the village of Aradena (20 minutes by car from Hora Sfakion). The Vardinogiannis Bridge spans an impressive precipice several dozen meters deep—kids generally love it, drivers a bit less so. In the abandoned village, a 14th-century Byzantine chapel dedicated to the Archangel Michael stands at the gorge's edge.

From Loutro, take a water taxi to Glyka Nera beach—the sweet water beach. Natural springs gush between the pebbles directly into the sea, creating slightly cooler water with a curiously sweet taste. The 500-meter cliffs looming above cut it off completely from the world. Marmara Beach, the starting point for Aradena Gorge, is accessible the same way.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: A giant’s name for a modest cave: the Cyclops Cave in Makri has two small chambers. Local tradition places Polyphemus here, while archaeological finds attest to prehistoric human occupation of the area. Wear shoes with good traction; if access to the interior is closed, stay in the permitted areas outside, facing the sea.

activities.text: Gnarled trunks and silvery foliage line your walk through the Makri olive grove. Here, the trees are more than scenery: they are part of an agricultural landscape still devoted to oil production. Follow public paths and take photos from them without entering cultivated plots.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Portaria, 13 km from Volos, is the first village on western Pelion — its nickname "lady of welcome" is well earned: centuries-old plane trees, fountains, stone houses with carved wooden balconies. During Ottoman rule (15th–19th c.), Pelion was a refuge for Greek intellectuals fleeing Constantinople and for merchants who traded freely with Europe. That era left behind exceptional architecture, libraries, and secret schools in every village.

Makrinitsa - “the balcony of Pelion” - lives up to its reputation. At 650 m above sea level, its cobbled lanes open onto a main square with a view over Volos, the Pagasetic Gulf and, on clear days, the Sporades islands. The 18th-century houses of local stone, with projecting upper floors in carved wood, are among the best preserved in Greece. On the square stands the church of Agios Ioannis Prodromos (St John the Baptist). The fountain with four lion heads from 1809, known as the “Spring of Immortal Water”, still flows. Allow at least 2 hours to wander.

The Topali house museum, built in 1844 and now the Folklore Museum, is a dive into the bourgeois life of Pelion: furniture, jewellery, costumes, weapons and mountain utensils. Take the opportunity to also visit the church of Agia Magdalini (1737) with its icons and wall paintings - the interior is unexpectedly rich for such a small village.

activities.text: The shops of Makrinitsa sell local produce from Pelion - mountain herbs, honey, preserves of local fruit (apples, chestnuts), liqueurs, handmade pasta. Try the spicy Pelion sausage and mountain tea (tsai tou vounou) in a taverna with a view over the bay. It is a distinctly Thessalian food experience - far removed from the tourist spots of the islands.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: The drive uphill is as worthwhile as the stop in Manolates: you leave the shore for a village surrounded by vineyards. Artists and potters work here, behind the facades lining the narrow lanes. Leave your car at the entrance, browse the open workshops, and keep this stop short so you can reach Karlovasi before noon.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls

visits.text: An icon in relief, rather than a painted image: at the Monastery of the Taxiarchs in Mantamados, this detail catches the eye. The current basilica dates to 1879 and forms part of a fortress-like complex. Enter outside service times, with your shoulders and knees covered, and ask before photographing the interior.

activities.text: Set aside a few minutes for the potters of Mantamados before getting back on the road. The village maintains pottery workshops alongside its cheesemaking traditions, so there is more to this stop than the monastery. Ask which pieces are made on site and have your purchases packed securely for the rest of the trip.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: In Mantinea, the theater helps you understand the ancient city without a monumental reconstruction. The remains of the agora and city walls place the tiers of seating within a city set in the middle of the plain. Stay within permitted areas and bring a hat: much of this archaeological visit is in the open.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: The lagoon of Etolikou (Etoliko), on the coastal route between Preveza and Marathias, is an unexpected stop that contrasts sharply with the beaches you have already seen. Here there is no sand, but a large coastal marsh—one of Greece's most important—home to flamingos, herons and many species of shorebirds. If you enjoy birdwatching, bring binoculars and stop beside the road to observe them. The landscape, with the village houses suspended between sky and water, is truly distinctive. From Marathias, allow for a round trip by car during the day for this stop.

Marathias is a small fishing village on the Ionian Sea, little-known to foreigners and visited mainly by Greeks. It's far from the tourist bustle: a fishing harbor, a handful of hotels, and tavernas serving the catch of the day. What really makes it worthwhile is the view from the seafront: across the water, the Peloponnese mountains rise in bluish silhouette. In the evening, locals gather along the waterfront for dinner and sometimes informal performances—ask when you arrive if there's anything happening tonight.

activities.text: Settle in along Marathias' seafront at sunset. With the Peloponnese ridges enclosing the horizon, the late-day light is often spectacular. It's also an opportunity to try a pita gyros with a sea view—local tavernas serve them at very modest prices, with fresh ingredients. To round out the evening, a short stroll along the harbor is enough to discover the unhurried rhythm of this village where life moves slowly.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Greece: Epirus, Peloponnese and Athens

visits.text: Egyptian-style statues await you at the Archaeological Museum of Marathon. They come from the sanctuary of the Egyptian gods founded by Herodes Atticus in the area, long after the battle. Look for the fragments of the victory trophy as well; start with the museum in Vrana, then head to the burial mound at a separate site.

The burial mound of the Athenians at Marathon looks like a simple grassy hill. Yet it covers the Athenian soldiers who died in the battle of 490 BCE: the memorial lies in this mound, rather than in a temple. Walk around it without leaving the path, and allow time to reach Brauron before it closes.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: From performances to combat: the ancient theater of Maroneia changed function during the Roman era. Its conversion into an arena followed an earlier period of theatrical use in a city oriented toward the Thracian Sea. Start here in the morning: the site lists a closing time of 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

After the theater, you can continue to the signposted ruins of Maroneia without looking for a single enclosed museum site. The ancient city extends among olive groves and the hills of Ismaros; a propylon, a sanctuary of Dionysus, and an early Christian basilica are among the identified monuments. Follow the signs, check which areas are open, and drive between groups of ruins that are farther apart.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: The caves of Matala are carved straight into the golden limestone cliff that closes off the bay to the south — some date back to the Neolithic era, while others served as Roman tombs in the 1st and 2nd centuries AD. But it's their later chapter that made Matala famous: in the 1960s and 70s, hundreds of hippies from around the world moved in, living rent-free in the seaside caverns. Joni Mitchell stayed here and immortalized the place in her song "Carey" (from the album Blue, 1971). Allow 30 to 45 minutes to explore the accessible caves from the beach — admission to the main complex is €2. On the harbour wall, look out for the painted slogan that captures the spirit of the place: "Today is life. Tomorrow never comes."

Matala beach stretches 250 m long and 45 m wide — not the biggest in Crete, but the setting is one of a kind: tamarisk trees on one side, cave-riddled cliffs on the other, and in the background, the snow-capped peaks of Crete in winter. The water is perfectly clear, and the westward orientation delivers genuinely stunning sunsets. Come in late afternoon to watch the sun drop right between the two rocky arms of the bay — one of the finest moments on the south coast. The beach holds a Blue Flag label.

To escape the crowds on the main beach and take in some scenery, walk to Red Beach, reachable in 15 to 20 minutes along a coastal trail from the far end of Matala beach. Its reddish sand — formed from iron-rich sandstone eroding off the surrounding cliffs — creates a striking contrast with the blue of the Libyan Sea. The cove is quieter because it weeds out the less motivated: bring proper shoes, the path is rocky. It's also one of the most popular nudist beaches on this coast.

If you still have energy, drive to the Palace of Phaistos, 11 km east — the second-largest Minoan palace in Crete after Knossos, built around 2000 BC. What made the site world-famous: the Phaistos Disc, a clay tablet covered in spiral symbols discovered in 1908 that no one has managed to decipher to this day. Go in the late afternoon: the low-angle light over the Messara plain is gorgeous, and the crowds thin out noticeably compared to midday.

Take some time to wander the village lanes: psychedelic murals on the facades, driftwood sculptures, cafés where Bob Marley plays late into the night. The hippie soul lives on in tourist form, but the vibe remains laid-back — you won't find the designer shops of Mykonos here. Every June, a three-day festival of seventies rock and reggae takes over the beach to keep the myth alive. If you're around at that time, don't miss it.

activities.text: Snorkeling around the rocks at the edge of Matala bay offers clear water and diverse marine life — grouper, octopus, sea urchins. The best spots are at the southern end of the beach, where the cliff plunges straight into the sea. Bring your own gear if you can — rental shops on site aren't always open outside peak season.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Traverse of Crete
Southwest Crete Road Trip: Gorges and Beaches
Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: Megalo Livadi is a timeless village in southwest Serifos, a 30-minute drive along winding roads from the port. This is where the island's major industrial history unfolded—until 1963, Serifos's iron mines (worked since antiquity, reopened on a large scale in 1880 by a Franco-German company) loaded their ore from this quay onto cargo ships bound for Europe. The rusted metal loading bridge is still there, bulky and poetic. In 1916, a miners' strike led to a bloody confrontation with the gendarmerie—4 miners were killed. It's considered the first bloody labor strike in modern Greek history. A memorial on the quay commemorates this episode.

activities.text: Sunset from anchorage or the surrounding hills—Megalo Livadi bay is well sheltered and faces west. A small waterfront taverna serves good fresh fish.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: At Mesimvria-Zone, inverted amphorae were also used to build houses. Placed beneath the floors, they may have helped regulate moisture: look for this feature among the streets, sanctuaries, and homes of this former colony of Samothrace. Arrive before lunch; the Greek tourism board lists a closing time of 3:30 p.m. and closure on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Messenikolas, nicknamed "the balcony of Thessaly", is built in an amphitheatre on a promontory with views in two directions: on one side Lake Plastiras, on the other the Thessalian plain. With fewer than 500 inhabitants, the village has kept its traditional stone houses and an end-of-the-world atmosphere. It's also the starting point for the Megalo Rema gorge, a moderate-level hike through a narrow ravine.

Fylakti, a viewpoint village on the southern shore, offers one of the finest panoramas on the circuit. From its square, the winding dam road is visible below — a 1950s structure that's still impressive, passable by car in a single lane. The Tavropos Dam is the engineering feat that created this entire landscape: 82 m high, 275 m long.

activities.text: Drive the full loop around the lake (70 km) at your own pace, stopping at the viewpoints and villages that appeal to you. Morning is the best time - the low light on the lake is perfect and the roads are empty. Finish in Karditsa for lunch: the town is a lively farming market, and its tavernas serve game from the Agrafa mountains - wild boar, roe deer - depending on the season. From Karditsa, the road to Volos (1.5 hours) makes for an easy return to the airport.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Messolonghi is the city of heroes. In 1826, after two successive sieges, the exhausted Greek garrison attempted a desperate breakout against Ottoman besiegers—the Exodus of Messolonghi. More than 5,000 people, soldiers and civilians, perished. The Garden of Heroes, created in 1830 by Governor Kapodistrias, holds their graves and that of poet Lord Byron, who died here in April 1824 of fever, age 36, after financing and supporting the Greek cause. His heart is buried here; his body was returned to England. It has become a pilgrimage site for Greeks.

Just outside town, Kleisova Lagoon is a remarkable ecosystem: 320 km² of lagoons and salt pans hosting nearly 270 bird species and constituting Greece's largest salt reserve. The “pelades” – small fishermen's houses on stilts in the lagoon – form a landscape unique in the Mediterranean. The Salt Museum, housed in a restored former saltworks, tells the story of the salt economy that has shaped the region since antiquity.

Messolonghi's Museum of Art and History, in a well-restored 1932 neoclassical building, displays archaeological objects from the region (from prehistory to the Roman era) and a comprehensive section on the War of Independence of 1821–1826, with documents, weapons and portraits of combatants. The four Greek prime ministers born in this town give an idea of Messolonghi's political importance in modern Greece.

activities.text: A boat ride in Kleisova Lagoon, offered by local fishermen, is one of the circuit's most unusual experiences – fishing structures on stilts, pink flamingos in season and the silence of this expanse of water at sunset contrast completely with the previous days' archaeological sites.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

visits.text: Mesta makes you work out which way to go, which is a good way to understand its defenses. The adjoining houses themselves formed the outer wall; covered lanes connect the village’s interior. Follow a few passageways from the square, then retrace your steps if necessary, without trying to cross private courtyards.

You’ll pause in Mesta’s square in front of Megalos Taxiarchis. This large church stands on the site of the former central tower: the village’s defensive heart has changed its function. Go inside if it is open, wearing appropriate clothing, then have lunch before taking the winding road northwest.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: The citadel of Methoni is one of the finest fortresses in Greece — 9.3 hectares on a peninsula surrounded by the sea on three sides, cut off from the mainland by an artificial moat. The Venetians built it from 1209 after seizing it from Geoffrey de Villehardouin, turned it into a vital staging post on the route to the East, and held it until 1500 when the Ottomans took it after a bloody siege. At the end of a 70-metre causeway, the octagonal Ottoman Bourtzi tower — topped with a dome — offers stunning views of the sea at sunset. Chateaubriand landed here on 10 August 1806 for his only journey to Greece. Allow at least 2 hours.

The castle of Koroni, 35 km to the east, spreads across 62,000 m² on a low peninsula overlooking the Gulf of Messenia. It's one of the rare medieval castles in Greece that is still inhabited: a few families live inside, olive trees grow within its walls, and the Timios Prodromos convent occupies the original Byzantine acropolis. The church of Agia Sophia, built on the ruins of a temple of Apollo and an early Christian basilica, carries within it every layer of the site's history. The view from the ramparts over the Gulf of Messenia with the snow-capped peaks of Mount Taygetus behind is magnificent.

activities.text: Methoni's beach, east of the castle, is a long strip of fine sand at the foot of the ramparts. The water is clear and shallow. The evening is ideal for a swim facing the illuminated fortress walls — one of the most photographed sunsets in the Peloponnese.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani

visits.text: It is better to take your time at the Averoff Art Gallery than to make lots of brief stops in Metsovo. Opened in 1988, it showcases Greek painting from the 19th and 20th centuries, including works by Gyzis and Lytras: here in the mountains, the collection reaches far beyond local folklore. Plan this museum for the morning, before the winery; check its usual Tuesday closure before arranging your day.

The dark wood and textiles at the Tositsa Museum make it feel like a home that is still lived in. In this family residence, which became a museum in 1955, utensils, looms, and traditional clothing remain displayed in the rooms used for domestic life; the reception rooms tell a different story from the storerooms. Visits are guided: arrive before a group departs and check the Thursday closure.

Metsovo invites you to look up, then watch where you step. Around the central square, sloping lanes connect houses, fountains, and shops; this town with a Vlach heritage is easier to understand on foot than through a windshield. The same benefactors’ names appear at the museum and the art gallery. Park before your walk and wear shoes with a good grip on the cobblestones.

activities.text: Book a time slot at the Katogi Averoff winery to move from paintings to bottles without leaving Metsovo. The guided tour combines winemaking facilities with videos and works of art, so there is more to the visit than a succession of barrels. A tasting may follow the tour, depending on the package you choose. Check what is included and taste only after parking the car for the night.

If you are looking for another way to get to know Metsovo, start with a plate of local products. Metsovone brings a smoky flavor, while herb pies and cheeses from the Tositsa Foundation offer more tangible points of reference than an extensive tourist map. Compare flavors rather than quantities and ask which products come from the village. Eat early enough to keep your evening free.

days_plan.itin_title: Metsovo and the Northern Pindus: 3 Days Among Villages and Forests

visits.text: Mikrolimni’s small harbor gives Lake Mikri Prespa an almost domestic scale. The houses meet the wetland landscape, with no large developed waterfront. The village also serves as a departure point for trips to Vidronisi Island. Stop along the accessible shore without entering the reed beds.

activities.text: If you enjoy observing more than taking long walks, Mikrolimni deserves a stop with binoculars. Around Lake Mikri Prespa, reed beds and shallow waters attract waterbirds; their presence varies with the season. Look for movement from the shore without approaching the colonies.

You will follow the first stretch of the trail from Mikrolimni toward Lapsista Bay to ease your way out of the village. This old path linked the villages of Prespa to the Korçë region; it was wide enough for pack animals to pass. This walk is optional: turn back according to the time you have available, without continuing as far as Kranies.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: Three successive gates defend Molyvos Castle, making the climb feel like a route through fortifications. The reddish-brown volcanic stone visually connects the ramparts to the houses of the town, also known as Mithymna. Since you are staying overnight in Molyvos, save the castle for the next morning when it opens at 8:30 a.m.; it closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

After visiting the ramparts, walk down into old Molyvos, following the narrow streets between the houses. Stone and wood shape the architecture of this town clinging to the slope; you feel the terrain more underfoot than you see it on a map. Wear shoes with good traction and leave your luggage at your accommodation.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Monemvasia makes an impression as soon as you see it from the road: a 300-metre-high rock rising from the Aegean Sea, joined to the mainland by a single 130-metre causeway. Its Greek name — moni emvasia, “single entrance” — says it all. Founded in 583 AD by Laconians fleeing Slavic invasions, it was successively Byzantine, Frankish (having resisted a 3-year siege), Venetian, Ottoman, Venetian again, then Ottoman. In 1821 it was one of the first fortresses liberated during the War of Independence. Pass through the main gate and let yourself be surprised by the cobbled lanes that unfold in the shadow of the walls.

The church of Christos Elkomenos (Christ in Chains) is the cathedral of the lower town, founded in the 13th century by the Byzantines, converted into a mosque under Ottoman rule, then restored to Orthodox worship after 1821. Its Venetian bell tower is characteristic of this mix of influences. Since 2011 it has housed one of the most important Byzantine icons in Greece: a 14th-century Crucifixion that had been stolen, recovered, and displayed for years at the Byzantine Museum in Athens.

Climb to the upper town via the paved path that winds along the cliff face — allow 30 to 45 minutes of walking. Take care: the cobblestones are slippery, especially on the way down. You'll pass the remains of a 17th-century Ottoman hammam before reaching the Church of Agia Sofia, built in the 12th century under Andronikos I Komnenos, at the cliff's edge. Successively Orthodox, a Venetian Catholic convent, then Orthodox again, it embodies the layers of history of the rock. The view from its forecourt over the Aegean Sea and the Peloponnese is probably the most beautiful panorama in the whole of the southern Peloponnese.

The archaeological museum, housed in a former 16th-century Ottoman mosque in the lower town, displays artefacts that trace the city's history: mosaics, sculpted fragments and everyday objects from the different occupations. The building itself — one of the few surviving mosques in the Peloponnese — is worth a look.

activities.text: Lose yourself in the lanes of the lower town without a map — there's only one main commercial street (Mesi Odos) and a tangle of alleys that all lead either to the sea or to the cliff. Pick up local olive oil, Malvasia wine or mead from the small shops. At dusk, once the day-trippers have left, Monemvasia reveals its most authentic self.

Pori beach lies outside the old town, on the coast north of the rock: it is a few minutes' drive away. Nearly two kilometres long, it offers clear water and an open view of the rock of Monemvasia. Ideal for a swim in the middle of the day, before or after the climb to the upper town.

Malvasia wine is one of the great wine stories of the Mediterranean. The Malvasia grape takes its name from Monemvasia itself — it was through this fortress port that the Venetians shipped the sweet, fragrant wine to the rest of Europe throughout the Middle Ages. Legend has it that George Plantagenet, sentenced to death in 1478 by his brother Edward IV, chose to be drowned in a barrel of Malvasia — Shakespeare immortalised the scene in Richard III. Local winemakers have revived production on its original terroir. You can taste the wines in the old town's shops.
Gonguès, home-made pasta similar to gnocchi but made with flour, and saïtia - fried cheese pies with fresh herbs - are the local specialities. Enjoy dinner in one of the tavernas of Monemvasia.

visits.text: Monodendri perches at 1,060 meters altitude at the southern entrance to the Vikos Gorge. The Agia Paraskevi monastery, clinging to the cliff face 800 m from the village via a paved path, was built in 1412 by local lord Michael Therianos in gratitude to the saint for curing his daughter. From its terraces, the gorge floor—900 meters below—stares straight back at you. Take care: there's no guardrail at the precipice edge.

The Oxia viewpoint, 7.5 km north of the village via a drivable track, offers the best view of the gorge from the Monodendri side. On the way, you pass through the 'stone forest'—a field of limestone columns eroded over millennia, some reaching several meters high. Once at the viewpoint, you gaze straight down into the vertiginous chasm: the narrowest point of the gorge is barely a few hundred meters wide and over 1,000 m deep.

Vikos Gorge is listed in the Guinness Book of Records as the world's deepest canyon relative to its width: 20 km long, with walls reaching 1,000 meters and a width sometimes reduced to a few hundred meters. The classic trail descends from Monodendri to the village of Vikos—allow 5 to 7 hours depending on your pace. Vikos-Aoos National Park, which encompasses it, is a UNESCO geopark home to more than 1,800 plant species and 186 bird species, including golden eagles and griffon vultures.

The Vradeto steps, starting from Kapesovo, are a masterpiece of engineering: roughly 1,100 steps carved into the cliff face of the Mezaria canyon over a 400-meter elevation gain. Until 1970, this was the only access to the village of Vradeto, perched at 1,340 meters—the highest village in Zagori. The ascent takes 45 minutes to an hour and offers increasingly spectacular views of the gorge.

activities.text: For a first look at the gorge without crossing it in full, follow the trail down from Monodendri to the floor of Vikos Gorge along the old kalderimi (paved path). The descent takes 1 hour 30 minutes and lets you see the limestone walls from the bottom of the canyon. Returning by the same path is more demanding: save some energy for the climb back to Monodendri. The turquoise Voidomatis springs are not halfway down this short descent, but toward the village of Vikos.

Late in the day, wander the lanes of Monodendri and neighboring villages Vitsa and Ano Pedina. All houses are built from local stone and roofed with stone slabs—Zagori's designation as a national historical monument prohibits any other materials. Tavernas serve pites (savory pies) with wild mountain mushrooms and grilled local lamb.

The full crossing of Vikos Gorge from Monodendri to the village of Vikos is one of Greece's great hikes. The O12 trail is marked but requires good physical fitness and hiking boots. Once on the gorge floor, you walk between forest-covered limestone walls. Stop at the karst springs of the Voidomatis: the water emerges from the limestone in an unreal shade of turquoise blue. A return transfer can be arranged from the village of Vikos.

visits.text: Silence accompanies you as you read the headstones at East Mudros Military Cemetery, near Moudros. This cemetery preserves the memory of soldiers of World War I, during which Lemnos served as an Allied base for the Dardanelles campaign. Take time to read the inscriptions, staying on the paths and respecting the solemn atmosphere.

activities.text: You can extend the day with a walk along Moudros harbor. Looking out over this now peaceful bay, remember that the town and its harbor served as an Allied base during World War I. Choose a short walk before dinner; you are staying here tonight before heading to the northeast of the island tomorrow.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 3 Days: Villages, Ancient Sites, and Dunes

visits.text: Chora, Mykonos's capital, is a whitewashed labyrinth said to have been designed to confuse pirates trying to find their way around. Wander its narrow lanes early in the morning before the cruise ship groups descend on the port—after 10 a.m., the town belongs to the crowds. The whitewashed houses with blue doors and balconies overflowing with bougainvillea set the quintessential Cycladic scene.

The seven windmills of Kato Mili overlook the port of Alefkandra—built in the 16th century by the Venetians to grind wheat brought from neighboring islands, they were powered by the Meltemi, the northerly wind that blows over Mykonos in summer. Go in the late afternoon: the orange light falling on their whitewashed walls makes for the island's signature photograph. Beware of gusts as you climb up to them—the wind can catch you by surprise.

Little Venice gets its name from the 18th-century sea captains' houses built right at the water's edge, their colorful balconies practically dipping into the Aegean. It's one of the few places in the Cyclades where you can have a pre-dinner drink with your feet almost in the waves. If you're here in the evening, book a table ahead in summer—the terraces fill up by 7 p.m.

Panagia Paraportiani stands apart in the entire archipelago: not one church but five, built between 1425 and the 17th century, stacked and melded together to form an absolutely unique asymmetrical white mass. Listed as a Greek historical monument since 1936, its interior is usually closed—but it's the exterior you come to see. Visit at different times of day: the rounded forms change completely with the light.

The Archaeological Museum of Mykonos holds a selection of the ceramics and sculptures recovered from the island of Delos during excavations—notably amphorae, red-figure vases, and some funerary stelae. If you're planning to visit Delos the next day, this museum provides a good preview to help you understand what you'll see on-site.

Delos, reachable in 30 minutes by boat from Mykonos's old port, is one of the Mediterranean's most important archaeological sites: the entire 3.5 km² island has been a UNESCO site since 1990, and no modern construction is permitted. According to Greek mythology, this is where Apollo and Artemis were born. The French School of Athens has been excavating here since 1873, and only a third of the site has been uncovered. Plan at least 3 hours on-site.

The Terrace of the Lions is Delos's most famous image: a row of lions carved from Naxos marble, offered by the Naxians in the 7th century BC to guard Apollo's sanctuary. There were originally 16 lions; only 5 replicas remain on-site—the originals, worn by erosion, are preserved in the island's museum. One of the lions taken to Venice still stands outside the Arsenal, where it's been since the 17th century.

The Hellenistic houses in the theater quarter preserve some of the finest floor mosaics in the Greek world, notably the famous mosaic of Dionysus on a panther. These mansions belonging to wealthy 2nd-century BC merchants give a concrete sense of Delos at the height of its glory—one of the most active cosmopolitan ports in the Mediterranean.

The ancient theater of Delos, built between 314 and 250 BC, could accommodate between 5,000 and 6,500 spectators. Imagine the festivals honoring Apollo that took place there—the Delia, a Panhellenic festival comparable to the Olympic Games, was held every four years.

Mount Kynthos rises to 113 meters—not a major climb, but the view from the summit sweeps across the entire island and the surrounding Cyclades on clear days. This, according to tradition, is where Apollo was born. A sanctuary dedicated to Zeus and Athena once stood at the top. Bring good shoes—the path is rocky.

activities.text: Stroll through Chora's lanes in the morning to catch the fish market near the old port—fishermen sell their dawn catch there at prices far more reasonable than in the tavernas. It's one of the last authentic moments of the town before mass tourism takes over.

The beaches of Paradise and Super Paradise, about ten kilometers south of Chora, are the island's party playgrounds: loud music, beach clubs, international vibe. Buses run there from Chora in summer. If you're after more peace, head to Agrari just next door—fine sand, fewer people, water just as clear.

In the evening, settle into Little Venice for a pre-dinner drink, then explore Chora on foot: luxury boutiques rub shoulders with jewelers and art galleries in a maze where it's easy to get lost—and that's intentional. Mykonos's nightlife is renowned across the Mediterranean; if that's your thing, the night here rarely starts before midnight.

Try kopanisti, Mykonos's sharp PDO cheese—a fermented soft cheese with an intense flavor, to spread on toasted bread with a drizzle of olive oil. You'll find it in local grocery stores and some tavernas.
Louza, Mykonos's spiced dried pork charcuterie, is eaten as mezze with cheese and olives. It's a Cycladic tradition you won't easily find elsewhere in Greece—ask for it in the old port tavernas.

Take the boat early in the morning from Mykonos's old port—first shuttles depart around 9 a.m. The site closes at 3 p.m. in low season, so check the hours before departing. There's no restaurant or water for sale on the island once the site opens: bring water and a snack, as the sun is merciless in summer.

The Archaeological Museum of Delos, built in 1904 by the Archaeological Society of Athens and expanded twice since, houses the originals of the terrace lions, a 6th-century BC kouros torso, and a collection of mosaics, jewelry, and inscriptions. Allow 45 minutes for the nine rooms.

Amygdalota, small almond cookies coated in powdered sugar, are Mykonos's signature sweet, made in the monastic tradition. You'll find them in artisan bakeries in Chora when you return from Delos—they keep for several days.

visits.text: Deserted, yet far from empty: Kato Chora preserves traces of old Milopotamos within its walls. Above the gate, the lion of Saint Mark recalls the Venetian presence; houses and churches survive inside. Explore the accessible passageways without entering the ruined buildings, whose condition means some areas cannot be freely explored.

Thirteenth-century frescoes await you before the stalactites in Agia Sofia Cave in Milopotamos. The entrance combines religious paintings and a chapel, before the route continues to the natural cave formations. Confirm opening times and visiting arrangements before leaving the village: this cave should not be confused with its namesake in Kalamos.

activities.text: Beneath the plane trees, the shade changes the atmosphere around Milopotamos and Fonissa Waterfall. The stop continues along the valley, past the remains of watermills and small bridges. Reach the waterfall by whichever trail is currently passable; abandon any plans to continue toward Kalami if the terrain becomes steep or slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 4 Days: Coves and Villages

visits.text: Ios has a dual identity that you will grasp as soon as you arrive: Chora, perched on its hill, is an authentic Cycladic maze of whitewashed lanes adorned with bougainvillea and 12 windmills - but after dark, the bars take over, and for more than 40 years the island has been a major party destination in the Aegean Sea. If you are looking for peace, go up to Chora early and come back down before noon. History lovers can visit the prehistoric site of Skarkos, 10 minutes from Chora. The hill where Homer's tomb is believed to stand can be reached via paths in the north of the island.

Mylopotas is Ios's largest beach—a crescent of sand over 1 km long facing due west, with Blue Flag status and crystal-clear water. It's also the liveliest: beach clubs, wakeboarding, diving, evening concerts. The eastern part of the beach is calmer than the western end, where nightlife is concentrated. The bay offers an anchorage with good holding on a sandy bottom, but it is very busy in July–August.

activities.text: Swimming and paddleboarding in Mylopotas bay—SUP and canoe rental on the beach. Waters stay shallow for 5 to 10 meters from shore.
Anchorage in the bay (good holding on sand, heavy seasonal traffic). In season, it's best to arrive early in the morning to drop anchor.

visits.text: The climb to Myrina Castle is worth the effort, both for the walls and for the scenery. The fortress follows the contours of a volcanic peninsula: the Byzantines built it on an ancient acropolis, and the Venetians and Ottomans later altered it. Here, the rock forms an extension of the defenses. Head up during the cooler hours, wear shoes with good traction, and leave enough daylight to walk back down without rushing.

Since August 2025, the Archaeological Museum of Lemnos in Myrina has offered a new permanent exhibition. The building once housed the Ottoman governor’s administration; it now brings together finds from Poliochni, Myrina, and Kabirion, among other sites on the island. It provides a good introduction to the remains you will later see at the sites themselves. Check opening hours with the museum before fitting this visit into your day.

activities.text: You can walk from Romeikos Gialos to Myrina’s small harbor through the market streets. The waterfront mansions give this walk a different character from the ramparts you saw earlier. Alternate between the waterfront and the narrow streets, then stop on the quay. Save this walk for late afternoon and leave your car parked to avoid having to find parking several times.

You can finish in Myrina with a tasting of Lemnos cheeses, kalathaki and melichloro. These island specialties let you continue your journey over a meal after the dunes and ancient sites. Ask for a small plate to share at a taverna and check where the products come from; leave the rest of the evening free.

visits.text: Mystras is one of the great revelations of the Peloponnese: an entire Byzantine city, built amphitheatre-like across the slopes of Taygetus at 620 metres above sea level, founded in 1249 by William II of Villehardouin and abandoned in 1832. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1989, it was at its peak the second city of the Byzantine Empire after Constantinople, home to 20,000 inhabitants. The philosopher George Gemistos Plethon, who taught here in the 15th century, directly influenced the Italian Renaissance. Get there early in the morning — the climb is tough in the heat.

The Metropolis (Cathedral of Agios Dimitrios), founded from 1264 onwards, is the first monumental building you'll encounter when entering through the lower gate. Its 13th- and 14th-century frescoes on the pillars and walls are remarkably refined. On the marble floor, a carved double-headed eagle marks the spot where Constantine XI Palaiologos — the last emperor of Byzantium — was crowned in 1449, two years before the fall of Constantinople.

The Monastery of Peribleptos, literally clinging to the rock inside a hollow in the cliff, is the site's most hidden treasure. Its 14th-century frescoes — particularly Christ Pantocrator surrounded by the Virgin and the apostles in the dome — possess a rare dramatic intensity and rank among the masterpieces of late Byzantine art. The atmosphere inside is almost mystical: darkness, colours that emerge gradually, and the smell of damp stone.

The Monastery of Pantanassa, inaugurated in September 1428, is the last building erected on the site and the only one still inhabited — a small community of Orthodox nuns lives here and maintains the site. Its intricately carved stone façade and 15th-century frescoes in vivid colours are strikingly beautiful. The nuns welcome visitors discreetly. Modest dress is required; cover your shoulders and legs.

The Palace of the Despots, in the upper town, is the most imposing palatial complex on the site. Its two recognisable wings — the Cantacuzene wing and the Palaiologos wing — speak to the power of the governors of the Morea. On the second floor of the Palaiologos wing stands the throne room known as the Chrysotriklinos. From the terraces, the view across the plain of Sparta and the Eurotas valley is stunning. Climb further to the Villehardouin fortress at the very top for a full 360° panorama.

activities.text: Plan to spend the entire day on the site: a complete visit of the lower town (Metropolis, Peribleptos, Brontochion) and the upper town (Palace, Pantanassa, fortress) involves roughly 3 to 4 hours of walking with changes in elevation. Wear closed-toe shoes — the cobblestones are uneven and can be slippery. Admission costs a few euros.

In the evening, the plain of Sparta and the peaks of Taygetus are magnificent when seen from the heights of Mystras. If you're staying nearby (a handful of guesthouses sit at the foot of the site), the early morning hours before the gates open offer a special atmosphere, as golden light begins to stream through the Byzantine windows and illuminate the frescoes.

Try beef kokkinisto for dinner — a meat stew simmered in a tomato sauce with onion and red wine, typical of the Peloponnese. Diples, thin ribbons of fried dough drizzled with honey and sprinkled with crushed walnuts, are Laconia's festive dessert. Pair it all with a glass of Xinomavro from Naoussa, the tannic red from northern Greece that holds its own against stewed meats.

days_plan.itin_title: Laconia Road Trip: Sparta, Mystras & Monemvasia

visits.text: To understand Mytilene, nothing beats its fortress. Between pine trees and the sea, Mytilene Castle preserves the coats of arms of the Palaiologos and Gattilusi families, along with buildings added under Ottoman rule: successive occupants left their signatures in stone. Start as soon as it opens; the site closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

The new Archaeological Museum of Mytilene brings theater to life in mosaics. Among the decorations from ancient residences, the House of Menander preserves a portrait of the author and a depiction of Orpheus charming the animals. Arrive before lunch to enjoy the galleries: the museum closes at 3:30 p.m., with last admission twenty minutes earlier, and is closed on Tuesdays.

activities.text: Save Ermou Street in Mytilene for last-minute shopping and a stroll. This shopping street runs through an area once occupied by a channel separating the peninsula from the rest of the city; today's storefronts conceal this ancient geography. Visit while the shops are open and have oil or fragile products packaged to suit your mode of transportation.

Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Nafpaktos's port is among Greece's most picturesque – a circular basin ringed by 15th-century Venetian ramparts, with a lighthouse, century-old plane trees and cafés spilling onto the quays. It was here, under its Venetian name of Lepanto, that the greatest naval battle between sailing ships in history took place on 7 October 1571: the Holy League (Spain, Venice, Rome) against the Ottoman fleet. 300 ships on one side, 330 on the other. The Ottoman fleet was destroyed – 187 of its 251 vessels sunk, over 20,000 dead. Among the Holy League soldiers was a young Spaniard of 23 named Miguel de Cervantes, who received two bullets in the chest and lost the use of his left hand. His statue now stands by the harbour.

The climb to the Venetian citadel is steep but rewarding: walls descend from the hill in several concentric enclosures to the sea, a defensive system among Greece's best preserved. From the summit, views encompass the Gulf of Corinth, the cable-stayed Rio–Antirrio Bridge (2004, one of the world's longest with its 2,252 m suspended span (2,880 m in total)) and, on clear days, the mountains of the Peloponnese. The Botsaris Tower on the ascent is a 15th-century structure housing a museum dedicated to the Battle of Lepanto.

activities.text: The coastal road from Galaxidi to Nafpaktos follows the Gulf of Corinth for 70 km – one of mainland Greece's most beautiful roads, between the sea and wooded cliffs. Psani and Gribovo beaches in Nafpaktos have Blue Flag status and the water is excellent. In the evening, the harbour terraces beneath the plane trees are ideal for a seafood dinner – octopuses drying on washing lines above fishing boats are the harbour's emblematic image.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

visits.text: The Palamidi Fortress towers over Nafplio from 216 metres above sea level. The Venetians built it between 1711 and 1714 under the direction of French engineers Lasalle and Levasseur — but the Ottomans under Ali Douad Pasha captured it as early as 1715, before it was even finished, slaughtering the entire garrison. Climb the stairs from the old town: legend says 999 steps, though actual counts range from 857 to 913. Bring water and avoid midday in summer. The view from the ramparts over the Argolic Gulf, the town and the islet of Bourtzi is the finest panorama in the eastern Peloponnese.

The Bourtzi is the small fortress on the islet at the harbour entrance, built by the Venetians in 1473 under the name Castello dello Soglio. Its history is worth a closer look: a chain stretching from Akronafplia to the islet blocked enemy ships from entering the port — hence its Venetian nickname Porto Cadena. The Ottomans renamed it Bourtzi (“fortress”). Later, it served as the residence of the executioner of Palamidi prison, a figure the town kept isolated for obvious reasons. A small boat leaves from the harbour roughly every 30 minutes in season.

Nafplio's old town may be compact, but its Venetian alleyways, stone staircases and cascading bougainvillea make it one of the loveliest towns in the Peloponnese. Nafplio was the first capital of independent Greece in 1828 — it was here that Ioannis Kapodistrias, the country's first governor, was assassinated on the steps of the Church of Agios Spyridon in 1831. The commemorative plaque is still visible. Don't miss Syntagma (Constitution) Square with its cafés under the arcades: this is where the first legislators of modern Greece held their sessions.

The Nafplio Archaeological Museum, housed in an 18th-century Venetian building on Syntagma Square, holds Mycenaean, Geometric and Classical collections from across the Argolid. Its star exhibit is a nearly complete Mycenaean bronze suit of armour dated to the 14th century BC, discovered at Dendra near Midea — one of the few surviving Bronze Age suits of armour in the world. Allow 45 minutes.

Mycenae lies 25 km from Nafplio — an easy half-day trip from your base. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999, it is the heart of the Mycenaean civilisation that dominated the eastern Mediterranean from the 15th to the 12th century BC. Right at the entrance, the Lion Gate greets you: built around 1250 BC, this monumental doorway is topped by an 18-tonne lintel and a relief of two lionesses in heraldic pose flanking a column. It is the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe, and the original bronze heads vanished in antiquity. Wear sturdy shoes — the site is steep and the rocks, polished by centuries of wear, are slippery.

Inside the Cyclopean walls, Grave Circle A is where the self-taught archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann discovered royal tombs in 1876 containing gold funerary masks, inlaid swords and jewellery of staggering richness. It was in Grave V that he found the famous mask known as “Agamemnon's” — actually predating the Homeric king by three centuries, as we now know, but no matter: the original is in the Archaeological Museum in Athens, and the replica in the Mycenae museum is worth a detour.

The Treasury of Atreus, a few hundred metres from the citadel, is one of the most audacious structures of the ancient world. This tholos (beehive-shaped) tomb dates to around 1250 BC — its entrance dromos measures 36 metres long and 6 metres wide. Once past the threshold (the lower lintel weighs 120 tonnes), you enter a circular chamber 14.6 metres in diameter and 13.5 metres high, built by corbelling. This dome was the largest in the world until the construction of the Pantheon in Rome in the 2nd century AD. It had already been looted in antiquity — but the space itself is striking.

The Mycenae Museum, opened in 2007, stands at the entrance to the site. Modern and well-documented, it displays painted Mycenaean pottery, bronze weapons, jewellery and terracotta idols recovered from local excavations. Look out in particular for the Linear B tablets — this syllabic script, the earliest form of written Greek, was only deciphered in 1952 by the British architect Michael Ventris.

activities.text: Climb to the Palamidi Fortress on foot from the gate on Arvanitia Street in the old town. Start early in the morning (before 9 am in summer) to avoid the heat and enjoy the low-angle light over the gulf. If you'd rather spare your knees, the eastern access road (3.6 km by car) drops you right at the entrance.

Stroll along Arvanitia Beach, a 10-minute walk from the old town along the coastal path beneath the Akronafplia fortress. It's a small pebble beach popular with Nafplio residents, with crystal-clear water and a direct view of the cliffs and ramparts. Ideal for a late-afternoon swim after sightseeing.

Dinner in the old town with youvetsi on the menu: lamb braised slowly with orzo pasta in a thick tomato sauce, baked in an earthenware dish. It's the quintessential festive dish of the Argolid. Pair it with a red agiorgitiko from Nemea — the leading grape variety of the Peloponnese, velvety and fruity, produced 40 km away.

Explore the Mycenaean acropolis: climb to the royal palace at the top of the hill. The megaron (large central hall) is recognisable by its four column bases. From there, the view across the Plain of Argos and, on a clear day, as far as the Argolic Gulf recalls why this site was chosen: an unrivalled strategic position controlling the entire plain. The Cyclopean walls, up to 8 metres thick in places, are built of blocks that the ancient Greeks of the Classical period attributed to the Cyclopes — the only beings strong enough to lift them.

Return to Nafplio via Tiryns, the other UNESCO-listed Mycenaean city (just 5 km from the centre of Nafplio). It is less spectacular than Mycenae but has even better-preserved Cyclopean walls, up to 8 metres thick. The interior vaulted galleries — carved entirely from blocks without mortar — are among the most astonishing examples of prehistoric Greek architecture.

Try homemade tzatziki in a taverna in Nafplio's old town: thick Greek yoghurt, grated and drained cucumber, garlic and dill — fresher and less fatty than the tourist versions. Ordered as a mezze with pita bread and Kalamata olives, it's the ritual at the start of a meal that promises a good evening.
