visits.text: Naoussa brings together Paros's charm in one village. The fishing harbor is ringed by whitewashed lanes climbing toward the Kastro—a partially submerged 15th-century Venetian fortification whose round tower still stands at the harbor entrance. The old Venetian warehouses have become elegant restaurants serving the morning catch. Naoussa actually boasts the largest fishing fleet in all the Cyclades: watch fishermen mending their nets early in the morning before the terraces fill. Come evening, the Kastro lanes turn into an open-air lounge.

Kolymbithres, 4 km northwest of Naoussa, is Paros's most photographed spot. Giant granite boulders, polished by millennia of wind and sea waves, have formed natural basins filled with translucent saltwater—somewhere between swimming pools and stone sculptures. The water is often less than a meter deep and takes on milky-blue reflections against the pearl-gray stone. In July–August, the pools fill with people as early as 11 a.m.: arrive before 10 a.m. to be among the first or come late in the day. Caiques make the trip from Naoussa harbor.

activities.text: Anchorage at Naoussa marina or Ormos Plastira depending on conditions—good holding on sandy bottom, sheltered from the north.
Snorkeling in the coves of Kolymbithres: the granite formations create tunnels and underwater cavities accessible with just a mask. Colorful fish guaranteed.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The name promises a school, while the setting offers caves: the School of Aristotle at Mieza corresponds to the nymphaeum of Isvoria. This sanctuary is traditionally associated with the lessons given to Alexander, but recent research instead places the school in the ancient gymnasium. The remains therefore invite you to distinguish tradition from archaeological identification. Read the signs on site and check access before continuing to the other sites at Mieza.

Painted as a tribunal of the dead, the facade of the Tomb of Judgment at Lefkadia is more intriguing than a simple monumental entrance. Hermes leads the deceased toward Aeacus and Rhadamanthus, the judges of the Underworld. The monument dates to the late 4th century BCE and combines Doric and Ionic elements. Confirm that it is open before visiting and take time to look at the paintings rather than just the architecture.

Palmettes and colorful flowers enliven the Tomb of the Palmettes at Lefkadia, far from the image of an entirely white ancient world. This monument from the early 3rd century BCE takes its name from its decoration; plant motifs also cover the ceiling of the antechamber. Here, color is part of the funerary architecture. Ask which areas are accessible and follow the lighting and photography guidelines provided at the entrance.

This is worth an extra stop: the ancient theater of Mieza complements the tombs with a place intended for the living. Built in the 4th century BCE, it retains a form extensively remodeled during the Roman period, particularly in the 2nd century CE. The archaeological landscape thus brings together several periods. Include this visit in your journey between the sites of Mieza and Lefkadia, and bring water and sun protection.

activities.text: Head to the shaded paths of Agios Nikolaos Park, near Naoussa, for a change of pace after the ancient remains. About 3 kilometers from town, the springs of the Arapitsa River feed a landscape of large plane trees and walking paths. The water is as much heard as seen. Choose a loop that suits the time you have available and shoes that will not slip on wet sections.

If you would like to meet a winemaker, book a tasting at a winery in Naoussa. Xinomavro is the signature grape variety of this wine region, whose vineyards cover the foothills of Vermio; visits connect the landscape with what is in your glass. Ask for an introduction to the winery’s work and confirm your appointment in advance. Designate a driver before starting the tasting.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: Naxos' Portara is visible from the ferry long before docking: a massive marble doorway perched on Palatia islet at the port entrance. Its four blocks each weigh 20 tons - too heavy for the Venetians to move, which explains why it's the only standing remnant of Apollo's temple begun around 530 BC under tyrant Lygdamis and never completed. According to mythology, this islet is where Theseus abandoned Ariadne. Go at sunset: the sun descends exactly through the doorway's axis.

Chora Naxos' Kastro, founded in 1207 by Marco Sanudo, first Duke of Naxos, dominates the port from a hill. Its outer walls are formed by the backs of Venetian palaces, many retaining their coats of arms. Inside: the 13th-century Catholic cathedral, an archaeological museum housed in the former 1627 Jesuit lyceum - where Nikos Kazantzakis, author of Zorba the Greek, was a student - and a Venetian museum.

The Temple of Demeter at Sangri, 15 km south of Chora, is a 6th-century BC Doric temple partially reconstructed with its original materials. Small site museum with carved fragments found. The place is quiet and non-touristy - worth seeing if you have a vehicle.

Chalki, the island's former capital, is a marble village in the heart of the Traghéa plain, surrounded by olive trees and vineyards. Its main square is enlivened by a few tavernas and the Vallindras distillery, which has produced kitron, a local liqueur, since 1896. The village is approximately 11 km from Chora, a 15-minute drive.

Apiranthos is one of the best-preserved villages on Naxos, with lanes entirely paved in marble, Cycladic stone houses and four small museums. Most residents are descended from Cretan refugees who arrived in the 17th century. Do not leave without visiting the café on the main square, where local life unfolds naturally. The village is approximately 14 km from Chora, a 20-minute drive.

The Kouros of Apollonas, at the northern tip of the island, is a giant 11-meter, 80-ton statue abandoned in its quarry in the 7th century BC, probably because of a crack in the marble. It has lain on its back in the rock for more than 2,700 years. Access is free, beside the road. The site is approximately 18 km from Chora, a 25-minute drive.

activities.text: The beaches on Naxos' southwest coast - Agios Prokopios, Agia Anna, Plaka - are among the Cyclades' finest: fine, pale sand, shallow turquoise water. Agios Prokopios is the most equipped; Plaka stretches 5 km and is wilder. All are accessible by bus from Chora.

Arseniko (Naxos graviera), a hard aged cheese with powerful flavor, is produced under PDO on the island. Taste it with local honey at Chora cheese shops. Naxos potatoes - small, flavorful, PDO - are renowned throughout Greece: roasted with olive oil and lemon, they accompany all taverna dishes.

The route between Chora, Chalki, Apiranthos and Apollonas crosses the mountainous heart of Naxos - olive trees, vineyards, marble villages and Aegean Sea views. It's the best way to see the island in its reality. Allow half a day with stops.

Aliko Beach, in the south-west of the island, is one of the most secluded and unspoilt on Naxos, with fine sand, cedar-covered dunes, clear water and very few people. A sandy path leads through the dunes to the water's edge. Bring provisions, as there is nothing on site. The beach is approximately 14 km from Chora, a 15-minute drive.

Late afternoon, return to Chora for the Portara at sunset - it's even more beautiful than on arrival, from the pedestrian causeway crossing the port. Then settle into a waterfront taverna for your last evening in Naxos.

Cyclades Journey: Athens, Santorini, Mykonos & Naxos
Cyclades Journey: Athens, Santorini, Mykonos & Naxos
Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: If you arrive before the morning is over, Nea Moni gives you time to view its mosaics with gold backgrounds. This 11th-century monastery has been a World Heritage Site since 1990, along with Daphni and Hosios Loukas. Aim to enter around 11 AM: official opening hours are 9 AM–1 PM, except on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: To understand Nemea, a visit to the Sanctuary of Zeus offers more than a quick photo from the road. The temple places the ancient athletic contests in their religious setting, amid a landscape now shaped by vineyards. Keep the combined ticket for the site, museum, and stadium, and check seasonal opening hours.

Next, head to the ancient stadium of Nemea to get a tangible sense of the athletic contests described at the sanctuary. The track is in a separate area from the temple; the museum also shows a video explaining how the starting mechanism worked. Allow time for this second site and check access with your combined ticket.

Long before the ancient athletic contests, gold was already circulating around Nemea. At the Archaeological Museum of Nemea, gold jewelry from the 15th century BCE broadens the story beyond the Temple of Zeus. Admire its delicate workmanship, then the objects from nearby excavations; this stop complements the two outdoor sites.

activities.text: If you enjoy red wines, Nemea’s vineyards add another dimension to the landscape you have been traveling through. Agiorgitiko is the region’s signature grape variety, and wineries welcome visitors to explain their work and offer tastings. Book an appointment before setting out and arrange for a designated driver who will not drink.

days_plan.itin_title: Corinthia in 3 Days: Temples, Vineyards, and Lakes

visits.text: Lake Plastiras — a 25 km² artificial lake created in the 1950s by damming the Tavropos river — has every appearance of a natural Alpine lake: clear blue water, fir and oak forests along the banks, the Agrafa mountains as a backdrop. The 70 km loop road around the lake connects villages perched between 850 and 1,000 m altitude. Neochori, the largest (500 inhabitants), offers a spectacular lake view from its belvedere — and a few decent tavernas.

The Monastery of Panagia Pelekiti is one of the strangest attractions in the area: it's literally carved into the vertical cliff face overlooking the lake. Construction began in the late 15th century and was completed in 1529. Its vertiginous position is comparable to the Meteora monasteries — only much smaller and far less visited. The access path winds along the rocks above the lake.

Morfovouni, a mountain village built like an amphitheatre north of the lake, is home to a small museum dedicated to General Nikolaos Plastiras - the man who commissioned the construction of the dam in the 1950s and after whom the lake is named. Plastiras was born in this village in 1883 and wanted to protect his native region from seasonal floods.

activities.text: The lake is ideal for kayaking and canoeing — calm waters and wooded banks. Local operators rent out boats from the lakeside villages, particularly Kalyvia Pezoula. The atmosphere is a world away from the coastal beaches: quiet, uncrowded, with nothing but wind in the fir trees for company. If you're here in spring, the seasonal waterfalls in the Megalo Rema gorge are worth a detour.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

activities.text: 55.8 °C at the source: at the Nigrita thermal baths, the water emerging from underground is far from lukewarm. The center is in Therma, near the town. A short session can provide a break on the road to Amphipolis. Call before taking the detour to confirm that the center is open, check booking arrangements, and verify access to the baths.

days_plan.itin_title: Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

visits.text: Stefanos Crater, at the center of Nisyros's caldera, is one of the Aegean's most striking geological experiences. The caldera measures 4 km in diameter and Stefanos itself spans 300 meters across and 30 meters deep. The last phreatic eruption occurred in 1888, but hydrothermal activity is very present: sulfur fumaroles, ground hot and yellow underfoot, bubbling mud pots—all with a frank rotten-egg odor. Arrive before 9 am: in peak season, up to 1,000 day-trippers from Kos land in the morning. Closed shoes mandatory—the ground burns in places.

Mandraki, Nisyros's capital, is a compact village with white houses and lanes paved with pebble mosaics—a technique you'll find in squares and even private courtyards. The archaeological museum covers more than 3,000 years of island history, from the Neolithic to the Byzantine era. The waterfront with its tavernas comes alive in the evening, when the day-trippers have departed and the island regains its calm.

The Monastery of Panagia Spiliani—'Our Lady of the Cave'—is built directly inside the ruins of the Knights of Saint John castle, on a 30-meter rock above Mandraki. Access is via a staircase of more than 130 steps. The monastery is partly carved into natural rock: the atmosphere inside the cave-sanctuary, cool and dark, contrasts with the blinding whiteness of the Aegean. The 1725 iconostasis and library preserve manuscripts and liturgical objects of great value. From August 6-15, celebrations for the Dormition of the Virgin draw pilgrims from across the Dodecanese.

Nikia, perched on the caldera's rim, is one of Greece's most photogenic villages. Its central square is entirely paved with pebble mosaics, bordered by colorful-shuttered houses. From here, the plunging view onto Stefanos Crater below is vertiginous—this is the ideal spot to grasp the volcano's scale. Two small tavernas serve on the square.

Paleokastro, Mandraki's ancient acropolis, is remarkably well-preserved from the Classical era (6th-4th century BC). Its black volcanic stone walls run nearly 2 km in perimeter and some blocks weigh several tons. From the ramparts, the view embraces the port, the sea and neighboring islands. The climb takes about twenty minutes from Mandraki.

activities.text: Hike between Nikia and the caldera on the trail that descends from the village rim to the crater floor—about 45 minutes down on a marked path that crosses landscapes of yellow sulfur and black rock. You transition from a white village with colored shutters to a near-lunar landscape in under an hour. The ascent is strenuous: count on 1 hour and bring water.

From Mandraki, walk to Chochlaki Beach, very close to the village. Its name comes from the large, smooth, black volcanic pebbles that also cover the entrance to the water. Follow the shore to the cavity carved into the rocks at one end, then return along the same beach. Bring water shoes: entering the sea is awkward over the large pebbles. Swim only when the sea is calm; if it is rough, stay ashore to observe the rocks and the coast of Nisyros.

'Soumada,' a beverage made from bitter almond extract mixed with cold water, is Nisyros's signature non-alcoholic specialty—refreshing and fragrant. 'Pitia,' focaccia topped with tomatoes, onions, olives and herbs, is sold in Mandraki bakeries from morning. For a heartier meal, 'Bogana' (lamb braised with garlic and potatoes) and 'Kapamas' (goat stuffed with rice and cooked in tomato sauce) are the island's two traditional main dishes.

Emborios, semi-abandoned on the caldera rim, has been reinventing itself in recent years: ruined houses are being restored one by one by artists and Athenians. A small café terrace overlooks the volcano directly—it's one of the island's most dramatic viewpoints. Come in the evening when raking light makes the fumaroles smoke.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Circuit: Patmos, Leros & Karpathos

visits.text: The ARCTUROS bear sanctuary in Nymfaio is above all an invitation to slow down in a beech forest. The bears housed here live in a protected area at an elevation of 1,350 meters; whether you see them depends on their movements. Take the guided tour in suitable shoes and plan this stop for a day other than Wednesday.

You can extend your visit at the Nikeios School in Nymfaio, where ARCTUROS provides information about the life and protection of the brown bear. The building houses an information center, separate from the forest sanctuary: observing an animal and understanding its needs call for different perspectives. Include this stop only on a weekend, after confirming opening hours.

A walk through Nymfaio is worth the detour, even when the bears keep a low profile. The stone houses and metal roofs give the village a profile different from Kastoria’s waterfront; these roofs help snow slide off. Explore the lanes on foot, wearing shoes with good traction.

activities.text: You will step away from Nymfaio to hear the forest rather than village conversations. The E4 European long-distance trail crosses this mountain area, but a short walk is enough for this itinerary. Ask locally for a suitable marked section; avoid setting out without a plan if fog obscures the landmarks.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

places.name: Oia

visits.text: Oia - pronounced “i-a”, not “oya” - deserves a full morning before the tourists arrive. What you are walking through is not a medieval village: it is a reconstructed merchant town. In 1890, Oia had 130 ships and its own shipyard, trading between Russia and Alexandria. The 1956 earthquake destroyed everything and emptied the village, whose inhabitants left for Piraeus. Its revival dates only from the 1980s. Walk through the lanes before 9 a.m.: the atmosphere is completely different from what you will find later.

The Castle of Agios Nikolaos, also called the Kastro, is the 15th-century Venetian ruin perched at Oia's north-western tip. Built by the Dargent family, descendants of Byzantine emperor Romanos Argyros, it served as an observation point over the caldeira. The 1956 earthquake toppled most of it, but the remaining wall panels are enough to offer Greece's most famous sunset. Arrive at least an hour before sunset for a good spot - crowds gather here every summer evening. Access is free.

Step into Oia's Maritime Museum, housed in an old captain's mansion tucked down an alley. Ground floor: navigation instruments and maritime equipment; upstairs: uniforms, shipowner portraits and impressive ship models. It's modest, but it explains better than any guide why Oia was a commercial powerhouse in the eastern Mediterranean - and gives meaning to the “captains' houses” you'll see throughout the village.
Enter Panagia Platsani Church if it is open - according to tradition, it houses a miraculous icon of the Virgin found in the caldera.

Descend the 300 steep steps to Ammoudi port - it's a walk not to be missed, even if the return climb is warm work. At the bottom you'll find a tiny fishing haven with red cliffs, coloured boats and tavernas serving this morning's catch. You can also swim from the rocks at the port entrance: the water is absolutely clear. For the climb back, donkeys await you at the foot of the steps if your knees have a say.

activities.text: Oia's sunset is a mass phenomenon: every summer evening, hundreds of people crowd the Kastro with selfie sticks. If you want the spectacle without the battle, opt for a taverna terrace set back from the main street, or head down to Ammoudi - the view is almost as fine and the atmosphere far more serene. Outside high season, the Kastro remains the best spot.

The Fira-Oia hike edges the caldeira for roughly 10 km. It crosses Firostefani and Imerovigli before reaching Oia, with permanent views of the volcanoes and white villages clinging to the cliffs. Allow 3 to 4 hours depending on pace. Start early, bring water and sunscreen - there's virtually no shade on the trail.

Venture into Oia's secondary lanes, far from the main street and its generic souvenir shops. You'll find open artist studios and art galleries where local painters display watercolours of the caldeira - a more personal souvenir than a fridge magnet. Take your time: these lanes are far more photogenic than the high street, and almost empty before 10am.

If you dine at Ammoudi, order the grilled octopus: sun-dried on a line in the morning, charred over coals in the evening, it's rarely as good anywhere else on the island. Pair it with a salad of Santorini's wild capers - their piquant, vegetal taste bears no resemblance to the brined capers you know, and their production is also PDO-protected. Avoid tables on the front row of Oia's main street where prices are indexed to the view, not quality.

End the evening with a glass of Vinsanto, Santorini's grand sweet wine. It's produced from Assyrtiko and Aidani grapes dried in the sun for 12 to 14 days after harvest - the sugar concentration is such that fermentation yields an amber, honeyed wine, sometimes aged several decades in barrel. Ask for a vintage of at least 5 years to appreciate its depth. It pairs naturally with honey-based desserts or a fresh cheese board.

days_plan.itin_title: Santorini Road Trip: Caldeira, White Villages and Minoan Sites

visits.text: Designed to defend the houses, Olympi’s vaults now form a covered route through the narrow streets. The central tower and the Trapeza, a medieval building with two levels, tell the story of this collective organization. Also look for Agia Paraskevi near the square; park outside the village and keep the passageways clear for residents.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: The archaeological site of Olympia, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989, is the birthplace of the Olympic Games, which were held here without interruption from 776 BC to 393 AD — 1,169 years. The River Alpheios flows alongside, and the pines and olive trees give the site an atmosphere unique among the great Greek sanctuaries. Set aside at least two hours for a full visit. Enter from the east and walk through the Altis (the sacred grove), heading towards the Temple of Zeus.

The Temple of Zeus, built around 460 BC by the architect Libon of Elis, measured 64 metres long by 28 metres wide — one of the largest Doric temples in Greece. All that remains are the columns lying where they fell, toppled by earthquakes in the 6th century AD. Inside once stood the chryselephantine statue of Zeus by Pheidias (c. 435 BC): 12 to 13 metres tall, made of gold and ivory over a wooden frame, and ranked as the third Wonder of the Ancient World. It was taken to Constantinople in the 5th century and destroyed in a fire.

The ancient Olympic Stadium is reached through the vaulted tunnel that athletes used to enter the track — slip through this passage and picture the 40,000 spectators waiting for you on the other side. The track measures 212 metres long by 28 metres wide. The marble starting line is still visible. Try the stadion by running the length of the track: this was the premier event of the earliest Games.

The Workshop of Pheidias, west of the site, was definitively identified in 1958 thanks to a wine jug bearing the Greek inscription “I belong to Pheidias”. The workshop's dimensions match those of the cella of the Temple of Zeus exactly — the statue was first assembled here from separate pieces before being installed in the temple. A Byzantine church was established there in the 5th century, then abandoned after the 6th-century earthquakes.

The Archaeological Museum of Olympia ranks among the finest in Greece — some place it on a par with the National Archaeological Museum in Athens for the quality of its collection. It holds the world's largest collection of ancient bronzes. Its star exhibits: Hermes Carrying the Infant Dionysos by Praxiteles (4th century BC), the Nike of Paionios in Parian marble (2.11 metres, the first monumental Nike depicted in flight in history, dated to 421 BC), and the pediments of the Temple of Zeus. Allow at least 1 hour 15 minutes.

activities.text: Run the full length of the Olympic Stadium (212 metres) on the ancient track from the marble starting line: it's the symbolic gesture every visitor makes, and it's all the more moving because it is exactly the same as that of the athletes of the 8th century BC.

Try stifado in the evening in a taverna in the modern village of Olympia: a stew of rabbit (or beef) simmered in a red wine sauce with small pearl onions, cinnamon and cloves. It's one of the finest slow-cooked dishes in Greek cuisine, and the Elis region has a particularly fragrant version. Pair it with a glass of mavrodaphne from Patras — this sweet red wine, produced 90 km away, is reminiscent of a light port.

Evening walk along the banks of the Alpheios downstream from the site: the river winds between plane trees and reeds through a landscape free of cars and tourists. This is where ancient athletes came to purify themselves before the Games.

visits.text: Handfuls of earth can tell a story of exile. At the Historical and Folklore Museum of Orestiada, they accompany belongings that refugees brought from their places of origin, along with costumes and family documents. Aim to arrive before noon and confirm the hours: tourist information lists morning opening hours and a Monday closure.

activities.text: You will finish with a walk around Orestiada’s central square after viewing the museum’s collections. Founded in 1923 to welcome refugees, this city tells a much more recent story than the fortresses seen in the morning. Sit out on a terrace, then keep the afternoon free; you will spend your final night here before departing the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Kolona is one of the Cyclades' great surprises. A narrow sand tombolo—a natural spit barely a few meters wide—connects the main island to the islet of Agios Loukas, creating two back-to-back beaches with different water temperatures: the one on the right is slightly warmer because hot springs emerge nearby. It's rare to find such a formation in the Mediterranean. Access is via a dirt track (the water taxi from Merichas is preferable, 15 min)—there's no shade on the beach, so bring sun protection.

Dryopida, Kythnos's second village, deserves a 20-minute detour from Kolona. Its red-tiled lanes break from the usual Cycladic white—this is where the island's characteristic tiles have been made for centuries. Katafyki cave, beneath the village, sheltered residents during World War II. It's open in season.

activities.text: Swimming between two seas: swim on one side then the other of the tombolo to feel the temperature difference. Snorkeling possible around the islet's rocks.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The Prosphorion Tower dominates the entrance to Ouranoupoli's harbour — a 14th-century Byzantine fortification built to protect the metochion of Vatopedi Monastery, and one of the best-preserved medieval monuments in the region. It houses a small museum on the history of the Athos peninsula. It's also the rallying point for every cruise to Mount Athos: you'll recognise it by the quay packed with pilgrims and tourists in the morning.

Ouranoupoli — 'City of Heaven' in Greek — is the last town before the border of the Monastic Republic of Mount Athos, an autonomous theocratic state home to some 1,500 monks in 20 monasteries. Women and non-Orthodox laypeople are not permitted to enter (10 non-Orthodox per day, men only, by special permit). From the harbour, though, you can see the foothills of the peninsula rising from the sea.

activities.text: Take the coastal cruise departing from the harbour — boats leave daily at 10:30am to sail along the western coast of the Mount Athos peninsula and observe the monasteries clinging to the cliffs from the sea. The cruise lasts about 3 hours 45 minutes and passes monasteries such as Xenophontos and Simonos Petras. It's open to everyone, men and women, and is the only way for the vast majority of visitors to get close to the site. Book ahead in summer.

In the late afternoon, catch the small ferry to Ammouliani Island, 10 minutes from Ouranoupoli. This island, largely untouched by mass tourism, has crystal-clear waters and secluded beaches — notably Alikes beach, a spectacular crescent of golden sand. The return trip in the late afternoon leaves time for sunset over the harbour.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece
Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

activities.text: “Pachies Ammoudies,” meaning “thick sands,” is the local name for the Gomati dunes, near Katalakkos. The fine sand forms ridges among scattered shrubs, far removed from the image of a beach lined with umbrellas. Leave your car in the parking area and continue on foot without trampling the vegetation; avoid the hottest hours and bring your own water.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 3 Days: Villages, Ancient Sites, and Dunes

visits.text: Once neglected, Palaios Agios Athanasios has seen renewed activity thanks to tourism on Kaimaktsalan. At about 1,200 meters, the old village retains its stone and wood architecture, with cobblestone streets that invite you to slow down. Park at the entrance if the narrow streets are congested, then explore the village on foot.

activities.text: Settle into a taverna in Palaios Agios Athanasios before heading up into the heights of Voras. The old village, known as Tsegani, made its living partly from producing cheese, meat, and wine: a rural history behind this mountain stop. Ask about the daily specials and plan to eat early enough to prepare for your excursion afterward.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

visits.text: Take the ferry back to Hora Sfakion in the morning, collect your car and drive west through the White Mountains, with striking views of barren plateaus and gorges. In Paleochora, climb to the ruins of Castel Selino, the Venetian fortress built in 1282 by Duke Marino Gradonico. The castle was destroyed in 1539 by the pirate Barbarossa. Only sections of wall remain at the end of the peninsula, but the view over the two beaches on either side of the headland rewards the climb.

Northeast of Paleochora, the Monastery of the Holy Fathers of Azogires stands near the village, while the cave associated with the monks is a separate site higher up. Built in the 19th century, the monastery stands near a large plane tree linked to local traditions. Stop in the village to see the monastery and its church in the Cretan hinterland.

activities.text: Pachia Ammos Beach, west of the Paleochora peninsula, is the town's main beach: fine sand stretching several hundred meters, relatively calm waters on the east side. The town closes its alleys to traffic in the evening and restaurants spill out onto the cobblestones—it's the best time to stroll and dine on a terrace.

For the curious, the archaeological site of Lissos lies in a wild cove accessible by water taxi from Paleochora harbor (10 minutes). This ancient Roman city from the 1st–3rd centuries AD has left ruins scattered under centuries-old olive trees: temple, tombs, Roman baths, and 4th-century mosaics. Few visitors, a pebble beach for swimming after the visit.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: Hidden in the ravines, yet not spared from attack: Paleochora preserves the ruins of the former capital, Agios Dimitrios. The town was destroyed by Barbarossa’s men in 1537. Access includes an unpaved road; check its condition and stay on stable paths without descending into the gorges.

days_plan.itin_title: Kythira and Elafonisos in 4 Days: Coves and Villages

visits.text: Megalo Papigo and Mikro Papigo are the two most photographed villages in Zagori, separated by 3 km along a hiking trail. Their cobbled lanes, houses built of stone and roofed with stone slabs, and century-old plane trees on the central square are perfect examples of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Epirote architecture. Look up and you'll see the Astraka Towers dominating the landscape—vertical limestone columns connecting the summit of Mount Tymfi (2,497 m) to Vikos Gorge.

Near Kipi, the Kalogeriko (or Plakidas) Bridge is Zagori's emblematic three-arched bridge; plan a day trip from Papigo. Built in 1814 by Abbot Seraphim of the local monastery to replace a wooden bridge, it spans the watercourse over a length of 56 meters and a height of 6.7 meters. Seen from the surrounding hills, its three successive arches resemble a moving caterpillar—a nickname that has stuck. A few minutes away, Kokkoris Bridge, built in 1750, is framed by two sheer rock faces: the region's most spectacular setting.

activities.text: Between Megalo and Mikro Papigo, the trail connecting the two villages passes by the Ovires (or Kolymbithres)—natural pools carved into the limestone rock by the Rogovo River. Legend has it that Ali Pasha himself came here to bathe. In summer, the water is cool and the cascading pools offer a unique swim. The trail makes an easy loop through both villages in 2 hours.

For this excursion, plan a day trip there and back from Papigo to Kipi, then walk the bridge circuit (10 km, 3 hours) to discover six arched bridges in a single outing. The Kipi and Koukouli area has the highest concentration of stone bridges in all of Zagori - every configuration is represented: one, two and three arches. These bridges were the only connection between the villages until the first paved roads arrived in the 1950s.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld

visits.text: A worthwhile detour to better understand the forest, the Natural History Museum of Paranesti puts the scale of the Rhodope Mountains into perspective. Its large relief map helps you locate the valleys, while taxidermy specimens introduce wildlife rarely seen on a simple walk. Visit Tuesday through Saturday from 8:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m., or Sunday from 11:00 a.m. to 2:30 p.m.; the museum is closed on Monday.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: The blue sea frames Parga’s Venetian castle, perched on a promontory between the town and Valtos. The winged lion of Saint Mark on the gate recalls the Venetian presence; Ali Pasha later altered the fortress after acquiring Parga in 1819. Look for these traces rather than furnished rooms: the visit is mostly about ruins and viewpoints. Head up early and wear shoes with good traction on the cobblestones.

Busy, but easy to enjoy on foot, Parga’s old town retains its sloping lanes above the harbor. Colorful facades face the islet of Panagia, whose chapel stands out in the bay. The terrain explains the town better than a list of monuments: climb through the lanes, then head back down to the quay. Leave your car outside the center and save this walk for late in the day.

Built in 1814 to besiege Parga, Ali Pasha’s castle in Anthousa seems to watch every movement along the coast. Yet its military role soon faded: Parga was handed over to Ali Pasha in 1819, five years after its construction. The western gate and towers help you understand this fortress designed for use against its neighbor. Stop here on your way in from Sivota to avoid a round trip from Parga, and save some water for the climb.

activities.text: Head down to Valtos to see Parga’s castle from the other side of the bay, then take some time to swim. The beach combines sand and small pebbles; its facilities and tavernas make it an easy place to relax after the climb to the fortress. For this short stay, choose this beach or Lichnos. Look for areas without rented loungers and ask about lounger prices before settling in.

Lichnos offers a different sense of scale from Parga’s lanes: an open bay bordered by hills and Mediterranean vegetation. The beach is a few kilometers from town, with facilities that make it easy to stay for a swim or a meal. It is a good place for a break on the way out toward Ammoudia. Arrive by road to keep control over your departure time, and check sea conditions before swimming.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: Parikia's old harbor greets you on arrival with its white windmills on the breakwater—a quintessential Cycladic postcard scene. Behind the ferries and bustling quays, the old town winds through pebble-paved lanes around a Venetian kastro built in 1260 from marble blocks taken from a nearby Temple of Athena: look carefully and you'll still spot ancient columns embedded in the walls. The old market follows the main street to the kastro and brims with tavernas, bakeries, and little boutiques. Get lost in this maze—the late afternoon light on the white facades is worth more than any guidebook.

The Panagia Ekatontapiliani basilica—“the church of a hundred doors”—ranks as Greece's third-largest early Christian sanctuary. Its foundation dates to the 4th century, traditionally attributed to Saint Helena, mother of Constantine the Great; the present building dates from the 6th century and was restored under Justinian. The complex is enclosed by a 252-meter wall and houses a main church measuring 40 by 25 meters, flanked by the oldest baptistery in the Christian East. Legend holds that the hundredth door is invisible and will open only when Constantinople is reconquered. Visit early in the morning—the filtered light in the nave, the Doric columns salvaged from a Roman gymnasium, and the 15th-century iconostasis are worth the stop. It's also a major pilgrimage site for the Assumption, almost on a par with Tinos.

Return along the west coast of Paros from Antiparos - a quiet passage between the two islands. Finding Parikia again feels almost like a relief after the wild stops of the past few days: Wi-Fi, fresh water, fresh provisions, and lively Chora for a final dinner facing the sea.

activities.text: Swim at Livadia Beach, the most accessible beach from the port - a 10-minute walk away. Fine sand and shallow water, ideal for a first dip after the crossing.
Sheltered anchorage available at Krios Beach depending on conditions, just across from Parikia harbor—dinghy shuttle, good holding on sandy bottom.
Final quick swim depending on timing and weather—Krios beach, dinghy-accessible from anchorage, is perfect for a farewell plunge in still-turquoise water.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves
Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Panagia Ekatontapiliani—“the church of a hundred doors”—is the Cyclades' largest early Christian sanctuary and Greece's third largest. According to tradition, Saint Helen, mother of Emperor Constantine, vowed to build one during her stop at Paros in the 4th century. The current structure dates to the 6th century under Justinian. Its name comes from a legend: the church is said to have 99 visible doors, and the hundredth will open the day Constantinople becomes Greek again. Don't miss the 4th-century baptistery attached to the church—it's the oldest and best-preserved in the Christian East.

Parikia's Kastro, built in the 13th century by Marco Sanudo, perches on the hill overlooking the port. Its walls are made from blocks of columns and lintels salvaged from ancient temples on the site—look carefully climbing the steps and you'll still see the column drums. The view from the top sweeps across the entire bay of Parikia.

Naoussa, in the island's north, is Paros's most charming fishing port: its white houses cascade down to the water, its tavernas spill onto the quay, and fishermen's caiques bob in the bay. A small 14th-century Venetian kastro guards the harbor entrance—it's half in the water, giving it a singular appearance.

Lefkes, the largest inland village, was Paros's capital during the Ottoman era. Its white marble lanes, blue-shuttered houses, and two large churches make it one of the Cyclades' most beautiful villages. An 8th-century Byzantine marble path, partially restored, links Lefkes to neighboring villages.

The Valley of the Butterflies (Petaloudes), in the island's center, is a nature reserve where thousands of moths (Callimorpha quadripunctaria) gather each summer on the valley's damp trees. It's an unusual spectacle for the typically arid Cyclades.

activities.text: Kolymbithres beach, north of Naoussa, owes its charm to granite rock formations carved by erosion into coves and natural pools. The water is calm and deep blue, and the rocks create underwater terrain ideal for snorkeling. Plan a day trip from Parikia for this visit. Accessible by water taxi from Naoussa or by car.

Revythada is a signature Paros dish: chickpeas cooked very slowly in a potter's oven for hours, with no seasoning beyond olive oil and salt. The result is creamy, tender. Ask for it in Parikia or Naoussa tavernas—some only serve it on Sundays.

Gouna is a fishermen's specialty: mackerel split in half and sun-dried for several days, then grilled over charcoal. It's a typical Paros mezze, eaten with a glass of ouzo while gazing at the sea. Look for it in the port tavernas of Naoussa or Parikia.

Paros is one of the world's top kitesurfing destinations, with Golden Beach (Chryssi Akti) leading the way—the wind is consistent and predictable thanks to the Meltemi. Rental centers offer equipment and lessons for all levels.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Road Trip: Athens and the Cyclades
Greece Road Trip: Athens and the Cyclades
Cyclades Island Hopping: Mykonos, Delos, Naxos, Paros & Antiparos

places.name: Patmos

visits.text: The Monastery of Saint John the Theologian has commanded the heights above Chora since 1088—the year monk Christodoulos, commissioned by Byzantine Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, laid the first stones atop the ruins of an Artemis temple. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999, the complex resembles a fortress from the outside—high grey walls, corner towers—but the interior holds a revelation: a library housing 4,000 documents including the celebrated Codex Purpureus, Saint Mark's Gospel inscribed in silver letters on purple-dyed parchment, one of the world's oldest illuminated manuscripts. Allow at least 90 minutes to explore the museum and central courtyard. In high season, arrive at opening to beat the tour groups.

Halfway between Skala port and Chora, the Cave of the Apocalypse is carved into living rock—this is where Saint John, exiled to the island by Emperor Domitian around AD 95, supposedly dictated Revelation to his disciple Prochoros. Look closely at the wall: a three-lobed fissure in the stone symbolizes, according to tradition, the voice of the Trinity. The atmosphere is otherworldly—cool and silent even in peak crowds—contrasting sharply with the island's blazing white sunlight. Plan for 45 minutes on site.

Chora, the medieval village that grew around the monastery starting in 1138, is one of the rare Greek settlements to have evolved continuously since the 12th century—UNESCO cites this unbroken lineage as a criterion for World Heritage status in its own right. Lose yourself in its cobbled lanes between whitewashed houses with wooden balconies: several mansions once belonged to wealthy Aegean sea captains and bear witness to past prosperity. In the evening, this is one of the island's finest spots to watch golden light settle over the rooftops.

Skala, Patmos's main port, is the island's beating heart: fishing boats, inter-island catamarans, waterfront tavernas and colorful shops. This is where you'll take the pulse of daily life—far removed from the monastery's contemplative atmosphere. If you're here on a Sunday, you'll often encounter pilgrims in traditional dress disembarking for Holy Thursday Mass, when the abbot reenacts the washing of the feet in the monastery courtyard.

In Chora's lanes, push open the doors to the Zoodochos Pigi monastery, founded in 1607, and the Annunciation (Evangelismos), founded in 1937—two active convents of nuns that prove Patmos remains a living religious center, extending well beyond the main monastery alone. The sisters receive visitors discreetly but genuinely: dress respectfully.

activities.text: Walk from Skala to Chora on the flagstone path that winds between fig trees and dry-stone walls—about 40 minutes. It's the same route pilgrims have followed for centuries. The panorama over the island's bays widens at every turn. If you prefer to drive, note that Chora's parking is tiny and fills quickly in July-August.

Take a day trip to Patmos's southern beaches—Psili Ammos is accessible only by boat or via a 45-minute hiking trail from Diakofti. The sand is fine and the bay sheltered, yielding water of rare calm. Water taxis depart from Skala throughout the morning.

'Pouggia,' small cakes filled with almonds and cinnamon, are Patmos's signature sweet, tied to monastic tradition. Look for them in Skala bakeries—available year-round, but especially tender when they emerge from the oven in the morning. 'Revithia fournou,' chickpeas baked slowly overnight with olive oil and herbs, appear on most Chora taverna menus on weekends.

In Skala, stop at Sarampelou Café Wine Bar, which stocks wines from the Patoinos estate. Ask which local bottles are available, then examine the three styles produced on the island: white Assyrtiko, red Mavrothiriko and orange Assyrtiko. As production is limited, choose the wine with the staff rather than relying on a specific label. This half-hour stop allows you to buy wine genuinely made on Patmos. A visit to the Patoinos estate itself requires advance booking.
