places.name: Patras

visits.text: Kastria Cave, nicknamed the “Cave of the Lakes”, is one of the Peloponnese's most surprising natural curiosities. It extends for a total of 1,890 meters and contains a succession of 13 terraced underground lakes—3 of which are accessible during the guided tour (a 500 m route). The blue-green water reflects stalactite and stalagmite formations in very soft light, and 10 species of bats quietly coexist on the ceiling. The adjoining museum displays fossils found on site, including bones of European hippopotamuses—yes, hippopotamuses once lived in Greece. Preferably arrive in the morning: the cave stays at 14°C throughout the year, which is pleasant in summer. The guided tour lasts about 30 minutes. From Patras, allow for a drive of approximately 71 km and 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the cave.

Patras, Greece's third-largest city and the Peloponnese's largest, is known mainly as the departure port for Italy—but it deserves a stop. From the Aghiou Nikolaou pedestrian street, 192 steps climb to the old town and its colorful neoclassical mansions. At the top, Patras' medieval castle, built in the 6th century AD on the ruins of the ancient Acropolis, offers sweeping views across the gulf and the Rio-Antirrio bridge—the cable-stayed suspension bridge completed in 2004 that links the Peloponnese to mainland Greece over 2.8 km. It's one of the world's longest cable-stayed bridges. As you descend toward the port, the seafront promenade invites one last Mediterranean pause before boarding.

activities.text: In late afternoon, catch the ferry from Patras port to Bari in Italy—the crossing takes approximately 16 hours 30 minutes, with berth or seat options depending on budget. Companies serving the route operate regular departures. Book well in advance for July–August. Onboard: bar, restaurant, and usually an outdoor area. It's an elegant way to close this road trip, watching the Greek coast recede in the sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South
Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani
Road Trip Greece: Epirus, Peloponnese and Athens

map_keywords: Cave of the Lakes Kastria Kalavryta

visits.text: Gaios, the capital of Paxos, stretches along a natural channel sheltered by two islets: Agios Nikolaos, which bears the ruins of a Venetian fortress built between 1424 and 1510, and Panagia, home to a small monastery. The pastel-coloured waterfront with its Venetian-influenced buildings is one of the most charming in the Ionian Islands. According to Greek mythology, Poseidon struck off the tip of Corfu with his trident to create Paxos as a love retreat for himself and Amphitrite. Standing here, you can believe it.

The blue caves along Paxos' west coast are accessible only by sea — no road, no stairway. Local boats depart from Gaios or Lakka to cruise along the limestone cliffs, where sunlight filtered through the water casts blue and green reflections inside the cavities. Set aside half a day for the excursion and book ahead in July–August.

Lakka, at the northern tip of the island, nestles at the head of a horseshoe-shaped bay with perfectly still waters — sailing boats moor here by the dozen in summer. The village is tiny (a handful of tavernas, flower-lined lanes) but the waterfront atmosphere at sunset is hard to beat. If you have access to a small boat, rent one and explore the pebble beaches along the north coast, unreachable any other way.

Loggos is the most discreet of Paxos' three villages — a fishing port of a few dozen houses, with tavernas right on the water. It's the best address for a lunch of grilled fish in an authentic setting, well away from the organised excursions that flood Lakka in high season.

The Tripitos arch, on the west coast of Paxos, is a natural limestone arch several metres high rising sheer above the sea. It can be reached on a short walk from the village of Ozias. Few tourists make this detour - it is one of the most spectacular landscapes on the island.

activities.text: Book a boat trip to Antipaxos as soon as you arrive — the little sister island sits just 15 minutes to the south. Its beaches of Vrika and Voutoumi regularly rank among the finest in the Mediterranean — fine white sand and turquoise water that could pass for the Caribbean. The excursion typically takes a full day and includes a stop at the blue caves.

Set off on the footpaths that wind through the centuries-old olive groves in the island's interior. The Republic of Venice actively promoted olive cultivation on Paxos from the 15th century to secure its oil supply — the gnarled trees you'll see are often several hundred years old. The coastal trail from Loggos to Lakka (roughly 2 hours) offers magnificent views.

Paxos' bourdeto is a local twist on the Corfu classic: fish (scorpionfish or gurnard) simmered in a spicy tomato sauce, with a more pronounced kick than the Corfu version. Enjoy it at a harbour-side taverna in Gaios with a glass of tsipouro, the anise-scented grape marc spirit of the Ionians, served ice-cold.

Amygdalota from Paxos are small, soft almond-and-icing-sugar biscuits traditionally baked in the island's monasteries for religious feast days. You'll find them in the artisanal grocery shops of Gaios — pick up a box for the ferry ride the next day.

days_plan.itin_title: Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada

visits.text: At Agios Georgios, the woodwork deserves as much attention as Perivoli’s stone walls. This 18th-century church has a carved iconostasis that brings the visit down to the scale of fine detail: it rewards a close look, provided the interior is accessible. The pulpit, also carved, deserves the same attention. Ask in the village whether the church can be opened, then adjust your stop to accommodate services and access conditions.

Stop in Perivoli’s square before turning your attention to the forest. This Vlach village in the Grevena area follows the rhythms of the mountains, with visitor numbers varying greatly between winter and summer; its restored houses make this a lived-in stop, rather than a hiking backdrop. Locate your meeting point with the guide as soon as you arrive and confirm your evening meal, especially outside peak season.

activities.text: If you want to reach the heart of Valia Kalda, take a guide’s 4×4 from Perivoli. Black pines, Bosnian pines, and beeches fill this “warm valley,” whose name comes from Vlach; Arkoudorema supplies its flowing water. The outing combines authorized tracks with walking and returns to the village. Ask for a short walk so you can keep the stop in Samarina.

days_plan.itin_title: Metsovo and the Northern Pindus: 3 Days Among Villages and Forests

visits.text: 114 steps: in Petra, reaching Panagia Glykofiloussa takes effort from the very start of the climb. The church crowns a rock about 40 meters high and preserves, among other features, a carved wooden bishop’s throne. Climb before the hottest part of the day, taking water with you, then descend the same staircase without rushing visitors coming up.

More than a facade to photograph, the Vareltzidaina House offers a view of Petra from the inside. This late-18th-century residence preserves wall paintings and a domestic layout that contrasts with the village’s sanctuaries. Check its opening hours before climbing to the church, and leave your car in the same parking spot for both visits.

If you enjoy small sanctuaries, stop at Agios Nikolaos, the Church of Saint Nicholas in Petra. Near the large plane tree, this 17th-century church preserves frescoes, including an unusual scene depicting the death of Judas. Enter only if it is open and no service is taking place; the visit is brief.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Stone draperies replace the sky inside Petralona Cave. Mineral formations sit alongside traces of fossil fauna, including bears and hyenas; the setting tells the story of animals as much as humans. Wear shoes with good traction and bring a light layer so you can explore the galleries at a leisurely pace.

Set aside time for the Petralona Museum: understanding the cave adds to the experience after exploring it. Paleontological discoveries place the fossils in their environmental context, beyond the famous human skull that brought the site to prominence. Plan on two separate tickets, one for the cave and one for the museum.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

activities.text: You’ll walk along Mikrolimano before heading toward Eleusis. This small harbor in Piraeus brings together boats, cafés, and restaurants along a pedestrian promenade: here, you take in the port from the quayside. Save this walk for early morning to leave time for visits with more restrictive opening hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion
Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion
Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses
Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses

visits.text: Rebuilt after the flood of 2015, the Plaka bridge nevertheless looks as though it was built to last. The original structure dates to 1866, and its arch spans the Arachthos without a pier in the middle of the current. Photograph it from the riverbank before getting closer; stay away from the river’s edge when the water rises.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

visits.text: Preveli Monastery perches on a rocky spur overlooking the Libyan Sea—take time to stop on the terraces and contemplate the view. Founded in the 16th century, it played a heroic role during World War II: in 1941, the monks hid hundreds of Allied Australian and British soldiers after the Battle of Crete, helping evacuate them by submarine to Egypt. In retaliation, the Germans vandalized the monastery and tried to carry off the golden Holy Cross—legend says three failed attempts convinced them of a miracle. A memorial at the entrance depicts an armed abbot alongside a British soldier. Modest dress required.

Preveli Beach is one of Crete's most surprising: the Megalopotamos River descends from the Kourtaliotiko Gorge to flow into the sea amid a palm grove. You'll think you're in West Africa rather than the Mediterranean. The palm grove had been entirely destroyed by fire in 2010 and has since regrown. Access is via a path from the monastery parking lot (20-minute walk) or by boat from Plakias.

activities.text: On the road between Koxare and Asomatos, descend a few steps to the bottom of Kourtaliotiko Gorge to see the small church of Agios Nikolaos seemingly embedded in the rock. The vertical walls reach 600 meters high at this point. The road itself is already spectacular—pull over at the roadside to photograph the canyon plunging toward the Libyan Sea.

Plakias is a quiet little beach resort at the back of a beautiful bay. The main beach is long and breezy—perfect for swimming after a day on the road. For more tranquility, the coves of Ammoudi and Damnoni lie 5–6 km to the east and are much wilder. Dive centers offer outings on the clear southern coast seabeds.

days_plan.itin_title: Grand Traverse of Crete
Wild Southern Crete: Gorges, Deserted Beaches & End-of-the-World Villages

visits.text: The detour is worthwhile mainly for the scenery: at Platamonas Castle, the ramparts overlook the sea and the passage between Macedonia and Thessaly. The defensive walls, citadel, and keep make the strategic importance of this position easy to understand. Visit early, then head to Palaios Panteleimonas; wear closed-toe shoes for the stones and uneven paths.

Cobblestones underfoot, roof tiles above the facades: Palaios Panteleimonas preserves the stone architecture of a mountain village. Here, with the coast below, the stroll matters more than a collection of monuments. Park at the entrance and continue on foot; keep your visit short so you can reach Ampelakia before the Schwartz House closes.

activities.text: If the morning is getting late, have an early lunch in Palaios Panteleimonas to keep the afternoon free. Savory pies and goat dishes are among the specialties served in the village tavernas. Choose a simple meal and explain your time constraint before ordering: the Schwartz House closes at 3 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: Sifnos is the Cyclades' island of ceramics and gastronomy. Since at least the 9th century BC, the island has exported utilitarian pottery throughout the Mediterranean—Sifnos clay is rich in feldspars that speed vitrification. In the 18th and 19th centuries, about a hundred workshops ran at full tilt. Today a handful of potters perpetuate the tradition: at Platys Gialos and Vathy, you'll still see the old pottery buildings recognizable by their curved roof and elongated shape. Several workshops welcome visitors.

Platys Gialos is Sifnos's largest sandy beach - a long, well-exposed bay with a Blue Flag, waterfront tavernas and a convenient anchorage on the left side of the bay. The White Tower stands 1.5 km to the northeast. A 2 km walk takes you to Chryssopigi beach, the island's most iconic, with its small white monastery perched on a rocky spur - one of the most photographed sights on Sifnos.

activities.text: Swimming and paddleboarding at Platys Gialos: wide sheltered bay, shallow water, fine sand. SUP rental on the beach.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: A still at the Barbayanni Ouzo Museum offers a useful introduction to Plomari’s history. Displayed among the family’s earliest equipment, it was built in Constantinople in 1858; bottling machines complete the story. Save this visit for the following morning, before Mytilene, and confirm the opening day with the distillery.

activities.text: Follow Plomari’s quays, then the streets that climb behind the harbor. Ouzo shares the town’s economic history with soap, olive oil, and shipbuilding: maritime activities explain the town as much as its distilleries do. Take this walk when you arrive, then save the museum visit for the following morning.

If the sea is calm, Agios Isidoros Beach offers a break near Plomari. About two kilometers from town, this seaside area lets you stay on the coast without adding an overnight stop; it is also on the distillery side of town. Bring water shoes and skip swimming if the waves grow stronger.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: There is no columned temple at Poliochni: its appeal lies in the traces of a Bronze Age town. The building known as the “Bouleuterion” has tiered seating and may have hosted meetings; its function remains an archaeological interpretation. Locate it using the site map, and bring water and a hat to explore the exposed remains.

days_plan.itin_title: Lemnos in 3 Days: Villages, Ancient Sites, and Dunes

visits.text: At the Archaeological Museum of Polygyros, faces and objects bring to life the ruins you will see later. Its permanent exhibition, inaugurated in 2022, brings together discoveries from across Halkidiki rather than a single city. Schedule this visit before lunch: the published closing time is 3:30 p.m., and the museum is closed on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

visits.text: Koufonissia—actually two islands, Ano and Kato Koufonissi—is the rising star of the Lesser Cyclades. Ano Koufonissi's Chora, the only inhabited village, sprawls around a colorful harbor dominated by the church of Agios Georgios. But what makes the island unique is its southeastern coast: a 45-minute coastal path from Chora links the beaches of Finikas, Fanos, and Italida—surreal turquoise waters on golden sand—before reaching Pori, the archipelago's finest beach. At Pori's northern tip, the Ksilobatis caves offer limestone arches bathed in emerald water. Budget 3 hours round trip for the full circuit from Chora, no shade along the way: leave early and pack water.
Gala Beach is a hidden cove whose Greek name means 'milk' - the foam of the waves in the cave does indeed give the water a distinctive milky hue.

activities.text: Sea kayaking from Ammos beach toward the cliffs of Kato Koufonissi: paddling along the sheer walls reveals arches and coves invisible from land. Kayaks are for rent at the main beach. Check the wind (meltemi) before setting out.
Anchorage in Pori bay: sandy bottom, good holding depending on conditions. Water taxis from Chora make 4 runs per day—handy for alternating between swimming and exploring Chora.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: The Poros Clock Tower rewards the climb with views over the rooftops and the channel. From this vantage point, the mainland seems almost within reach: Galatas lies on the opposite shore. Head up before lunch and allow enough time to walk back down to the dock without rushing.

Land donated by the Koryzis family made it possible to establish the Archaeological Museum of Poros on the square bearing the family’s name. A visit adds a cultural break to your stopover, right in the town rather than at the end of an excursion. Check that day’s opening hours before climbing to the Clock Tower, as your next boat sets your time limit.

activities.text: You will follow the Poros waterfront to Pounta, staying along the docks. Fishing boats sit alongside sailboats, while neoclassical facades face the passage toward the Peloponnese. Take this walk after your sightseeing and return to the boarding point before your ferry arrives.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses

visits.text: Standing on the water yet accessible on foot, Agios Nikolaos Monastery in Porto Lagos connects its islets with wooden footbridges. This complex is under the authority of Vatopedi Monastery and sits in the lagoon at the outlet of Lake Vistonida. The monastery welcomes visitors from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m.: arrive before 12:20 p.m.; otherwise, start with Lake Vistonida.

activities.text: You can keep your binoculars handy along the accessible shores of Lake Vistonida, near Porto Lagos. This wetland hosts flamingos, herons, and pelicans, among other birds, though sightings are not guaranteed on every visit. Observe from public access points with your engine off, and keep your distance from both the birds and fishing facilities.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: Entering the Kassandra peninsula, stop at Nea Fokea to see the Byzantine tower by the harbour. This 28-metre stone tower, built in 1407 to protect the metochion of the Saint Paul Monastery on Mount Athos, is the best preserved in all of Halkidiki — intact right up to the battlements. In 1821, it served as the headquarters of Emmanouil Papas, leader of the Greek uprising in Halkidiki. At its base lies the cave sanctuary of Saint Paul, a chapel hewn into the rock.

Cape Possidi, at the south-western tip of Kassandra, is a shifting tongue of sand that juts into the sea — its shape changes with the tides and the seasons. The 19th-century lighthouse at its end is one of the most photographed sunset spots in Halkidiki. The village of Afitos, perched on the ancient acropolis a few kilometres away, is worth a detour for its stone houses, cobbled lanes and views over the Toroneos Gulf.

activities.text: The beaches of Kassandra are among the most accessible in Halkidiki — several hold the Blue Flag, the sand is fine and the shallow waters are ideal for families. The coast around Possidi alternates between organised beaches with sunbeds and wild coves fringed with pines. Swim in the morning, before the buses from Thessaloniki arrive.

days_plan.itin_title: The Most Beautiful Places in Northern Greece

visits.text: The rumble of water accompanies a visit to Anemotrypa Cave, near Pramanta: you can hear the underground stream deep below. Mineral formations and pools line the developed visitor route, three kilometers from the village. Guided tours last 20 to 25 minutes and run daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.; bring an extra layer.

Pramanta offers a breather between the bridges and mountainside villages. In its central square, an old plane tree stands beside the historic Arapis fountain and Agia Paraskevi Church. The town is the seat of the municipality of North Tzoumerka. Park nearby and explore the square on foot before heading to your accommodations.

activities.text: Take time for lunch in Pramanta instead of snacking between bends in the road. The town is known for its grilled meat restaurants, making it a convenient stop before the narrow roads to the north. Ask about portion sizes before ordering and bring water for your next visits.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

visits.text: The Acheron is one of the five rivers of the Underworld in Greek mythology and actually rises in Epirus. For the ancient Greeks, this river, which plunged into karst chasms before reappearing near the Ionian Sea, could only be the boundary between the world of the living and that of the dead. In the Odyssey, Homer sends Odysseus to consult it and question the seer Tiresias. The village of Glyki is the starting point for activities on the river; plan a day trip from Preveza.

At Mesopotamos, the ruins of the Necromanteion of Ephyra stand on a hill; plan a day trip from Preveza. Since 1958, the site has been identified as the oracle of the dead described by Homer in the Odyssey, although this identification remains disputed among archaeologists. According to this interpretation of the site, pilgrims descended into an underground labyrinth after purification rituals and sacrifices to “receive” the souls of their dead. The ruins from the 4th century BC are worth a visit, whatever interpretation is given to them.

Nikopolis—“the city of victory”—was founded in 31 BC by Octavian Augustus on the very hill where he had pitched his camp during the naval Battle of Actium against Mark Antony and Cleopatra. It's the largest ancient city in Greece, covering 900 hectares. Its Victory Monument still bears anchor-shaped notches where bronze rams from ships captured from the enemy were set—it is said to have had 36 in all. This is also where Epictetus, the slave-philosopher founder of Stoicism, taught until AD 125.

The Archaeological Museum of Nikopolis, inaugurated in 2009, is an essential introduction before exploring the site. It presents collections chronologically: from the Battle of Actium to the city's abandonment. Don't miss the early Christian mosaics from the basilicas—some are of exceptional quality and exceptionally well preserved—and fragments of Augustus's votive inscription, 54 meters long.

activities.text: The hike through the Acheron Gorge starting from Glyki is one of Greece's most beautiful river hikes; plan a day trip from Preveza to reach Glyki. The trail follows the river for an 8 km round trip between limestone walls covered with plane trees and oleanders. The water is clear and cool—swimming is possible in the natural pools along the way. Operators also offer canoe descents from Glyki, which are less physically demanding and just as spectacular.

Preveza, 7 km south of Nikopolis, is a quietly charming Ionian port town. In the evening, the pedestrian Spiliadou street comes alive around its fish and seafood tavernas—the Ambracian Gulf before you is the same one where the fate of the Roman world was decided on September 2, 31 BC. Aktion airport is 20 km away, across the strait.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld
Epirus & Zagori: Gorges, Stone Villages and the River of the Underworld
Road Trip Greece: Epirus, Peloponnese and Athens
Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: Water laps against the boats in front of Psarades, a village facing Great Prespa Lake. Houses and tavernas line this small bay on the shores of a lake shared by Greece, Albania, and North Macedonia. Locate the boarding point before your meal, then confirm the departure directly with a boat operator.

Agios Georgios offers a shaded stop before the descent to Psarades. Around this chapel, an old stand of junipers forms a protected area within the park: the trees make the detour as worthwhile as the building itself. Park only in an authorized space and stay on existing paths, without collecting branches or plants.

activities.text: You will board a boat in Psarades to read the cliffs of Great Prespa Lake like a painted facade. The hermitages of Panagia Eleousa, Metamorphosis, and Mikri Analipsi occupy cavities above the water; religious images survive on the rock. Book locally, confirm the price and any stops ashore, and accept a postponement if the wind prevents the outing.

A plate of food sometimes explains Psarades better than a long description. The tavernas serve lake fish, particularly carp, as well as tsironia, small dried and salted fish with a stronger flavor than a simple grilled fillet. Ask what is available that day and confirm the portion size and price before ordering.

days_plan.itin_title: Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in 4 Days: Lakes, Bears, and Frescoes

visits.text: The fortress of Niokastro commands Pylos from a headland overlooking the Bay of Navarino. Built by the Ottomans from 1573 — two years after their defeat at Lepanto — to secure the entrance to the bay, it forms an irregular triangle with a perimeter of 1,566 metres. Inside you'll find a star-shaped citadel with five bastions built by the Venetians, a mosque converted into a church, ramparts with magnificent views over the bay and the island of Sphacteria, and four museums including one devoted to underwater archaeology with headless Hellenistic statues recovered from the sea.

Voidokilia beach is one of the most perfect in the Mediterranean: an almost geometric omega (Ω) shape drawn by nature, fine sand, turquoise water, and the ruins of the Frankish Paleokastro perched on the cliff behind. The Gialova lagoon alongside it is home to 254 bird species — including flamingos depending on the season. To get there, drive around the lagoon from Gialova (5 km), leave the car and walk down to the beach.

activities.text: The Bay of Navarino is where, on 20 October 1827, 27 Allied warships (British, French and Russian) trapped and destroyed an Ottoman fleet of 80 to 90 vessels without losing a single ship. This victory forced Ibrahim Pasha to withdraw from the Peloponnese and made Greek independence inevitable. Local operators run boat trips around the bay to see the memorials on the island of Sphacteria and the wooden wrecks of Ottoman ships, still visible in calm weather.

Three Admirals Square in the heart of Pylos, shaded by centuries-old plane trees, is the centre of local life. The marble stele and period cannons honour the faces of Codrington, De Rigny and Hayden — the three Allied commanders at the battle. It's the perfect spot for an outdoor dinner with views of the lit-up harbour and the silhouette of Niokastro.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Peloponnese: Olympia, Three Venetian Fortresses and the Wild Mani

visits.text: Pyrgi turns its facades into pages of black-and-white patterns. These geometric decorations, called xysta, cover the houses of a medieval village tied to mastic cultivation. Move closer to examine the details, then step back into the square to compare the facades; avoid blocking the doors of residents’ homes.

A short detour to Agioi Apostoloi, behind Pyrgi’s facades, is worthwhile. This Byzantine church follows the architectural model of Nea Moni, a connection that adds meaning to your later visit to the monastery. Look for the access alley near the square and check the opening hours before planning to visit the interior.

You’ll understand the villages better after visiting the Chios Mastic Museum near Pyrgi. The exhibits connect the techniques used to cultivate the mastic tree, its resin, and the organization of the Mastichochoria; the trees extend the visit outdoors. A single tree thus sheds light on an entire landscape. Allow 1 hour for the museum, which is closed on Tuesdays.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

places.name: Pyrgos

visits.text: Pyrgos - its full name is Pyrgos Kallistis, 'the most beautiful tower' - is Santorini's former capital, the island's chief town in the 18th century. Perched at 365 metres altitude on a hill at the island's centre, it offers 360° views over the caldeira, vineyards and the Aegean. It's one of Santorini's least touristy villages, which makes it one of the most pleasant. Built around a Venetian Kasteli in a defensive labyrinth against pirates, its narrow lanes are designed to disorient the enemy - you'll get lost too, and that's the charm. Allow 2 hours for a leisurely tour.

Climb to the monastery of Profitis Ilias, which crowns Santorini's highest point at 567 metres. Founded in 1711 by the brothers Gabriel and Joachim Belonias, it served as a refuge for revolutionaries during the Greek War of Independence in 1821. From the terrace, on a clear day, you will see Crete to the south and the islands of Ios, Anafi and Amorgos. Inside, a small museum displays icons, relics and ancient manuscripts. Ignore the antennas and military installations occupying part of the summit: they do not spoil the view.

The Church Theotokaki, at the Kasteli's heart, is one of Santorini's oldest, dating from the 10th century. The Museum of Icons and Ecclesiastical Artifacts, installed in the former Agia Triada chapel, displays remarkable religious relics. Pyrgos counts over 40 churches and chapels for a village of just hundreds of residents - some Catholic, the majority Orthodox. Feel free to step inside wherever the doors are open.

Tour the vineyards encircling Pyrgos to understand something unique worldwide: Assyrtiko vines are pruned into low baskets called kouloura, woven close to the ground to resist the island's violent winds and capture nocturnal moisture. The oldest vines are over 200 years old and ungrafted - phylloxera never reached Santorini thanks to its volcanic soil. Several nearby estates offer tastings with caldeira views: allow at least an hour.

activities.text: The climb to Profitis Ilias Monastery from Pyrgos takes roughly 30 to 40 minutes on foot. The road winds through vineyards and Mediterranean scrub. If you drive, parking is available nearby. Go late afternoon for the light - and to avoid the few tourist coaches that pass in the morning.

When tasting at a winery, ask to compare a classic dry Assyrtiko, a Nykteri and a Vinsanto side by side: these are three radically different expressions of the same base grape, and the contrast is striking. Specify that you want to understand the differences in method - most estates have guides or explanatory sheets. Allow at least 1h30 to avoid being rushed.

Dine in Pyrgos rather than heading back down to Fira or Oia: the central square's tavernas serve slow-cooked dishes - sfougato (courgette and cheese omelette), moussaka, stifado - at prices significantly lower than the caldeira. If you keep your eyes open, you'll find a few cafes run by year-round residents, where Greek coffee is served as it is everywhere in Greece except Santorini.

Orthodox Easter in Pyrgos is the most spectacular event in the local calendar: the village illuminates with thousands of candles arranged on walls and roofs to create a luminous procession. It's one of Greece's most beautiful Easter celebrations. If your trip coincides with this date, book accommodation months in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Santorini Road Trip: Caldeira, White Villages and Minoan Sites

map_keywords: Museum Santorini of the Past Pyrgos

visits.text: The cool air comes as a surprise as soon as you step into the Tunnel of Eupalinos, above Pythagoreio. This 1,036 m aqueduct was dug in the 6th century BCE by two teams starting from opposite sides of the mountain. Their meeting underground is the detail to remember. Reserve your time slot at +30 22730 62813: only partial routes are currently available, as the full crossing is closed; the tunnel is closed on Tuesdays and in winter.

An immense temple, yet almost no columns left standing: at the Heraion of Samos, the contrast helps you imagine what has disappeared. Part of a column remains in its ancient position, amid the foundations of the sanctuary dedicated to Hera. The site shares its 1992 UNESCO inscription with Pythagoreio. Visit before the museum, and bring a hat and water: the announced closing time is 3:30 p.m., with last admission at 3:10 p.m.; the site is closed on Tuesdays.

It is worth setting aside time for the Archaeological Museum of Pythagoreio, even after the tunnel and the Heraion. Sculptures, coins, and everyday objects bring the ruins you have seen outside to life. Look especially for the inscription describing wheat distributed free to citizens through a public fund: a very concrete detail about community life. Arrive before 2:15 p.m. to enjoy the galleries without rushing; the museum closes at 3:30 p.m. and is closed on Tuesdays.

activities.text: You can end the day with a walk around Pythagoreio harbor once your archaeological visits are behind you. The present-day town occupies the site of ancient Samos, around a harbor basin still in use. Look for the statue of Pythagoras on the quay, then leave the waterfront to explore the nearby narrow streets. Save this walk for late afternoon and leave your car parked: the center is easier to explore on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls
Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls

visits.text: At Pythio Castle, two towers served different purposes: one was a residence, the other a defensive structure. John VI Kantakouzenos had this refuge built in the 14th century; the staircases are built into the thickness of the walls. Stop here on your way to Orestiada, exploring the exterior if the towers are closed.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Kimolos takes its name from the Greek 'kimolia'—chalk—and its houses are indeed whiter than white. The island covers just 36 km² and is easily explored on foot or by scooter from Psathi port. The village of Chorio, perched on a hill 2 km from the port, is dominated by a 14th-century Venetian kastro, some of whose houses are still inhabited. The metropolitan church of Panagia Odigitria (1592) is its religious heart. Wandering Chorio, look for the syrmata at tiny Goupa beach: these are former boat garages carved into rock, intact maritime heritage.

Prassa beach (also called Agios Georgios) is unanimously considered Kimolos's finest—some even say the finest in all the Cyclades. Almost surreal white sand, turquoise water of exceptional clarity. A beach bar, sun loungers, and sea caves within swimming distance with fins. Near Prassa, natural hot springs with reddish waters are said by locals to have healing properties. It's not uncommon to spot a monk seal in the neighboring waters.
The Skiadi rock is worth the 20-30-minute walk from the main road: erosion has sculpted a formation shaped like a giant mushroom. Look for the marked path between Chorio and the west coast.

activities.text: Swimming at Prassa and snorkeling around the rock formations: corals, sea urchins, and colorful reef fish in remarkably clear water. The nearby Vromolini sea caves will please freedivers.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Climb to the Fortezza late in the day rather than mid-afternoon—the light on the sea from the western bastions is far more beautiful, and the heat less brutal. This Venetian fortress, whose construction began on 13 September 1573, was designed to shelter Rethymnon's entire population in case of Ottoman attack—but for lack of budget, only the military section was completed. Result in 1645: 8,500 people crammed into a space planned for far fewer, and the governor had to capitulate after only 23 days of siege. Spot the mosque of Sultan Ibrahim inside the walls—its massive dome is the direct legacy of the Ottoman period.

Wander through the lanes of the old town without a precise plan - it is the best way to explore Réthymnon. Look for the Rimondi Fountain (1626), whose lions' heads spout water in the heart of a shaded little square. Look up: the minarets rising above the rooftops recall two centuries of Ottoman presence, including the Grand Minaret of the Neratze Mosque, now used as a concert hall.

In the evening, head down to Rethymnon's Venetian harbour—smaller and far less crowded than Heraklion's, making it one of the island's most pleasant. The lighthouse at the jetty's end dates from the 19th-century Egyptian occupation. Settle into a sea-facing taverna for grilled fish: the menu is often simple, the produce fresh and the atmosphere, as night falls, worth lingering for.

Twenty-three kilometres south-east of Rethymnon, Arkadi monastery is the most emotionally charged historical site in all Crete. Its current fortress-like structure dates from the 16th century, with a church (katholikon) completed in 1587—a jewel of the Cretan Renaissance. But what made Arkadi famous throughout Europe is the drama of 8 November 1866: surrounded by the Ottoman army, superior Gabriel Marinakis ordered the powder magazine blown up rather than surrender. Of the 964 people sheltering there—fighters but mostly women and children—most perished. Plan to have shoulders and knees covered to enter.

activities.text: Start with the Fortezza in the morning before the heat, then descend into the old town lanes to wander. Cretan craft shops—embroidery, ceramics, silver jewellery—are concentrated around Arkadiou and Souliou streets. Rethymnon is less touristy than Heraklion or Chania, giving it a more relaxed pace.

The excursion to Arkadi monastery takes about half a day (1 hour's round-trip drive + visit). Return via the road through the inland villages – Episkopi with its springs, or Margarites, known for its pottery workshops, are worth a 20-minute stop.

In the evening at the harbour, taste gamopilafo—literally 'wedding rice'. This traditional Cretan festive dish is prepared with lamb simmered long in its broth, in which rice then cooks until creamy, bound with butter and lemon juice. You'll find it in old town tavernas, often as the daily special.

For dessert, ask for mizithra with local honey. This fresh sheep's or goat's cheese, with a texture close to ricotta, is eaten on the spot in cheese shops or as dessert in most tavernas—drizzled with Cretan thyme honey and scattered with walnuts.

visits.text: If you’re looking for a sanctuary facing the sea, Rhamnous adds a new dimension to the trip. Nemesis and Themis were worshiped here near a fortified city that watched over the passage to Euboea. Focus your visit on the temple terrace, starting at 8:30 AM; ask the caretaker which areas are accessible before venturing farther.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

places.name: Rhodes

visits.text: Rhodes Old Town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988, and it thoroughly deserves that recognition. The Knights of St. John occupied it from 1309 to 1522 and set about transforming it into an impregnable fortress—the 4 kilometers of ramparts you'll walk along bear witness to this. What makes the site exceptional is the layering: behind Gothic walls hide Ottoman mosques, Turkish baths, and Byzantine alleyways. Enter through the d'Amboise Gate late morning, before tour buses flood the narrow streets.

The Palace of the Grand Masters dominates the old town from the highest point of the citadel. Built in the 14th century, it contains 150 rooms, of which 24 are open to the public. What you absolutely can't miss inside: the mosaic floors, brought from Kos by the Italians during their controversial 1930s restoration. Worth knowing: in 1856, a gunpowder magazine explosion nearly destroyed the entire palace—what you see today is largely a Fascist reconstruction, intended to welcome Mussolini, who ultimately never visited. Look for the commemorative stele bearing his name near the ticket office.

The Street of the Knights (Odós Ippotón) is one of the best-preserved Gothic monuments in Europe. The Knights of the Order were organized into seven “tongues”—France, Italy, Spain, Provence, Auvergne, England, Germany—and each had its inn along this main thoroughfare. You'll see their facades at every turn. Take time to read the coats of arms carved above the doors: the Auvergne inn bears those of Guy de Blanchefort, Grand Master from 1512 to 1513.

The Archaeological Museum of Rhodes is housed in the former Great Hospital of the Knights, built between 1440 and 1489. The star of the collection? The Crouching Aphrodite, a Hellenistic marble statue of remarkable finesse. Allow 45 minutes to an hour for a complete tour. The combined ticket (valid 3 days) includes this museum, the Palace of the Grand Masters, and the church of Panagia tou Kastrou—a smart way to optimize your visits.

The Suleiman the Magnificent Mosque, built in 1522 just after the Ottoman conquest of Rhodes, visually marks the transition between two civilizations. Its pink minaret is visible from afar within the old town. It's closed to regular visits, but the exterior and surrounding square are worth seeing in the evening, when the light is soft and crowds thinner.

The acropolis of Lindos stands on a cliff 116 meters above the sea. Allow about an hour's drive from Rhodes town to Lindos, then walk up to the acropolis. The temple of Athena Lindia, in its present form, dates from around 300 BC (it replaced an older temple destroyed by fire in 392 BC). At the entrance, look for a rare detail: the stern of a warship carved into the rock in the 2nd century BC, once the pedestal for a bronze statue that has disappeared. Arrive before 9 a.m.; after that, the climb becomes a procession.

The village of Lindos, entirely pedestrian, is built in an amphitheater on a hillside. Its lanes paved with black-and-white pebble mosaics lead to the “captains' houses” from the 16th century, built by shipowners who had made fortunes in maritime trade. Push open the door of the Church of the Virgin (Panagia), founded in the 14th century and restored in 1489 by Grand Master d'Aubusson: its interior frescoes date from 1779 and are among the best-preserved on the island. Skip lunch on a terrace here—prices are noticeably higher than elsewhere on Rhodes.

St. Paul's Bay (Paralia Agios Pavlos), below Lindos, takes its name from the apostle Paul, who supposedly landed here during his journey to Rhodes. The water is a striking turquoise, enclosed on three sides by cliffs and the acropolis. It's also a popular wedding venue—if you're there on a weekday, you'll have better chances of finding the peace needed to enjoy it.

In the west of the island, Kamiros is nicknamed the “Greek Pompeii” of Rhodes: a Dorian city founded in the 5th century BC, abandoned after an earthquake and rediscovered in 1852. Allow about 33 km from Rhodes town and 35 minutes by road. You will see a sophisticated water system of cisterns, pipes and fountains that supplied the whole city. The stoa, terraced houses and temple of Athena are sufficiently well preserved to give you a clear idea of ancient town planning. Allow an hour for the visit.

On the way back from Kamiros, the Valley of the Butterflies (Petaloudes) is worth a quick stop between June and September, when thousands of Panaxia quadripunctaria butterflies settle there in the coolness of plane trees and waterfalls. Off-season, the site remains pretty but the butterflies aren't there—check the timing before making the detour.

activities.text: Wander through the lanes of the lower town (Chora) as you please: craft shops, workshops making painted ceramics and small tavernas tucked away in courtyards.

Stroll along Mandraki harbor late in the day. At the harbor entrance stand two columns topped with bronze stag and doe—tradition claims the Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, stood at this spot (nothing proves it, but visitors love the story). Three Ottoman windmills and Fort Saint Nicholas complete the panorama. A café terrace facing the harbor at sunset—that's the best moment of the day.

Try pitaroudia, chickpea fritters typical of Rhodes, fried in olive oil with onion and dill. You'll find them in all the old town's tavernas, often served hot as an appetizer. Pair them with a glass of Athiri, the local white varietal: dry, light, slightly citrusy, perfect with mezze and fresh fish.

If you have the energy, climb onto the ramparts from the entrance to the Palace of the Grand Masters during opening hours (which differ from the palace's; check before setting off). The walk offers sweeping views over the old town and the harbor that you will not find anywhere else.

The climb to Lindos acropolis is on foot from the village—bring good shoes and water, the slope is steep under the sun. Mules offer rides up, but several local sources discourage this option out of concern for the animals. The reward at the top: a 360° view over Lindos' two bays, the Aegean Sea, and on clear days, the Turkish coast.

After the acropolis, head down to swim in the main bay of Lindos (Main Beach). The water is clear, the beach organized with sunbeds and umbrellas. To avoid summer crowds, opt for neighboring St. Paul's Bay: smaller, less known, and just as beautiful.

Try souma before leaving: it's a traditional Rhodes fig eau-de-vie, sweet and fragrant, found in small grocers in Lindos village. Pair it with takakia, these little bites of fried octopus with lemon served by most waterfront tavernas. For wine, the local Mandilaria—fruity and light red—is perfect with grilled meats.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos
Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos

map_keywords: Palace of the Grand Master Rhodes

visits.text: You've arrived in Greece. The coastal road from Igoumenitsa to Riza Beach, about an hour south, sets the tone: long stretches of sand following one after another, translucent waters, and eucalyptus trees lining the road. Riza Beach is a fairly unspoiled sandy beach, still frequented mainly by motorhome travelers and Greeks. There's no major tourist infrastructure, which is precisely what gives it its charm for your first evening. If you've just arrived on the ferry at Igoumenitsa, allow at least 30 minutes to get out of the port before hitting the road.

On the way from the port, make a detour to the village of Plataria, 12 km from Igoumenitsa, which beautifully combines green mountains with the blue Ionian Sea. And if you still have time before dropping off your bags, continue to Sivota Bay—about fifteen kilometers south of Plataria—where small green islands stand out against unbelievably blue water. It is one of the most beautiful natural anchorages in Epirus. If you are already settled in Riza, allow for a round trip by car during the day for these visits.

activities.text: Swimming and unwinding at Riza Beach—you have time to catch your breath after arriving. The taverna at Acrogiali campground, a few meters from the beach, is a good option for dinner: Greek specialties made with fresh ingredients in a simple but pleasant setting. Time to order your first tzatziki and skewers in peace.

days_plan.itin_title: Road Trip Greece: Epirus, Peloponnese and Athens

visits.text: Megali Panagia’s most surprising feature is in its apse: a pine tree has grown there. The church in Samarina also has frescoes painted by village artists and carved wood decorations. Look at the exterior first, then ask whether the interior is accessible; do not assume it is always open.

activities.text: Finish with a walk around Samarina that connects its stone fountains. The fountains of Megali Panagia and Mikri Panagia mark the route, complementing the facades and narrow streets without requiring an additional hike. Keep this stroll short if you need to get back on the road, and check locally whether the water is safe to drink.

days_plan.itin_title: Metsovo and the Northern Pindus: 3 Days Among Villages and Forests

visits.text: Melissani Cave — also known as the 'Cave of the Nymphs' — is a limestone cenote whose ceiling collapsed during the 1953 earthquake, allowing sunlight to pour directly onto the underground lake. The lake stretches roughly 160 metres long and reaches depths of 30 to 40 metres; its surface sits one metre above sea level, fed by water that has travelled 15 km underground from the Katavothres in Argostoli. Archaeological excavations in 1962 uncovered a sanctuary dedicated to the god Pan on a small central islet, along with clay figurines and oil lamps dating from the 3rd–4th centuries BC. Plan your visit between 11 am and 1 pm: that's when the sun strikes the opening directly and transforms the water into a kaleidoscope of blues and violets. The tour is by rowboat and lasts 10 to 15 minutes.

Drogarati Cave, 5 km from Sami, was discovered around 300 years ago when an earthquake caused its entrance to collapse. It measures 65 metres long, 45 metres wide and 20 metres high, with a steady temperature of 18°C — a relief in summer. The stalactites and stalagmites, some of which resemble dolphins according to speleologists, have formed over roughly 100 million years. The main chamber, known as the “Hall of Apotheosis”, has such remarkable acoustics that it has hosted concerts — including, in 2014, a performance by the Bavarian Philharmonic, which arrived on a cruise ship docked at Argostoli. Bring a jumper even in summer, and wear sturdy shoes for the slippery steps.

Sami's harbour is Kefalonia's main ferry port, with connections to Patras and Ithaca. The town itself is modest but pleasant, with a handful of tavernas and cafés along the waterfront. Just next door lies Karavomylos, the village where the resurgent springs from the Katavothres emerge — the seawater that entered the ground in Argostoli reappears here, slightly brackish, after its 14-day underground journey.

Antisamos Beach, 4 km from Sami, is one of the most beautiful on Kefalonia: a long sweep of white pebbles framed by pine forest that tumbles down to the shore, with deep turquoise water. Several scenes from the 2001 film 'Captain Corelli's Mandolin' were shot right here. The beach is lifeguarded in summer but never overcrowded — the winding access road from the main highway puts off the lazier crowd. Bring your snorkelling mask: the seabed is rich.

activities.text: A combined visit to both caves (Melissani + Drogarati) works best as a half-day outing. Start early in the morning with Drogarati to beat the cruise-ship coaches, then head to Melissani around 11:30 am to catch the peak sunlight. Allow about an hour at each cave, including queuing time in high season.

After the caves, head to Antisamos for a swim. The water is crystal-clear and less crowded than at the southern beaches. If you have a mask, dip your head below the surface and look around — the visibility is exceptional.

Riganada is dried bread (a rustic rusk) rubbed with fresh tomato, drizzled with olive oil, topped with feta and sprinkled with dried oregano — a Greek summer classic across the Ionian Islands. Very simple, very good. Order some with a well-chilled glass of white Robola at a taverna by Sami harbour at the end of the day.

days_plan.itin_title: Greece Grand Tour: 21 Days from North to South
Kefalonia and Zakynthos Tour: Caves and Beaches

visits.text: Ferry Paros → Santorini, about 3 hours. Stay on deck as you approach the island: you'll sail along the caldera cliffs, streaked in black basalt, red, brown, and white pumice—the successive layers of a colossal eruption around 1600 BC that likely destroyed Minoan civilization. These cliffs plunge from 300 meters above you and continue underwater to a depth of 400 meters. Book ahead in summer.

Settle in and set out to explore Fira, Santorini's capital. The clifftop promenade follows the caldera's edge for several hundred meters, with constant views of the Nea Kameni volcano at the center of the old crater. Don't miss the Three Bells of Fira—the small Orthodox church with its blue-and-white bell tower clinging to the cliff is one of Greece's most reproduced images. The Orthodox cathedral with its Venetian influences also merits a stop.

Before setting out to hike, head up to Imerovigli for the most unobstructed view of the caldera—this village perched at 300 meters is the island's natural lookout. Make the detour to Skaros Rock: this isolated promontory housed Santorini's fortified capital under the Venetians. Only a rocky spur jutting out above a sheer drop remains, but the 360° view across the caldera, volcano, and Oia in the distance is dizzying.

Use the morning to visit the archaeological site of Akrotiri, the Greek Pompeii. Allow for the round trip from Fira when planning this visit. This Minoan city was buried under ash during the eruption of 1600 BC and rediscovered in the 1960s. Excavations have uncovered entire streets, frescoes and everyday utensils in perfect condition—no bodies, unlike Pompeii, as the inhabitants had time to flee. The site is covered and open all year round.

activities.text: In the evening, take the KTEL bus to reach Oia, at the island's northern tip. This village perched on the caldera's ridge is world-famous for its sunsets. Winding lanes between cave houses and purple bougainvillea lead to Oia Castle, where the view across the caldera and the sun plunging into the Aegean is simply extraordinary. Arrive at least 45 minutes before sunset to secure a good spot—in high season, hundreds of people crowd onto the ramparts.

The Fira → Oia hike is the island's must-do activity. The ridge trail follows the caldera for 10.3 km - allow 3 to 4 hours, with an elevation gain of 328 meters. Throughout the walk, you look down over the cliffs from a height of 250-350 meters, passing through Firostefani and Imerovigli. Set off before 8 a.m. to avoid the heat and crowds. Bring at least 1.5 liters of water per person. Return from Oia by KTEL bus.

Upon arriving in Oia, rest at one of the cafés on the central square before descending to Amoudi port, on foot via the 214 steps that plunge beneath the village. This miniature fishing port, wedged into the cliff, is the ideal spot for a fresh-fish lunch with direct views across the caldera. Return to Fira by bus in early evening.

Book the catamaran before you even arrive in Santorini—in summer, they sell out several days ahead. Departures are from the port of Vlychada or the old port of Fira. First stop: the red beach of Akrotiri, whose sand gets its color from a layer of solidified lava—jump into the water, the contrast is striking. Then head toward the volcanic islet of Nea Kameni, formed by several eruptions between the 16th and 20th centuries. Next, a dip in the hot springs of Palea Kameni: the sulfurous water reaches 30 to 35°C, and you need to swim around thirty meters from the boat to reach them. Allow a full day, 5 to 7 hours in total.

Last evening in Fira: climb from the old port on foot via the 588 steps of the mule track or by cable car, and treat yourself to dinner on the caldera clifftop. Fira's atmosphere is more accessible than Oia's, with more varied and less touristy spots—this is where locals live year-round.

Greece Road Trip: Athens and the Cyclades

visits.text: To get a sense of Serres, Koulas offers a view that tells you more than a map. This hill preserves traces of the Byzantine acropolis and overlooks the Strymon plain; the church of Agios Nikolaos is also part of this historic complex. Plan a short climb in the late afternoon and wear supportive shoes for the uneven stretches.

Once a covered market, the Bezesteni provides an unexpected setting for the collections of the Serres Archaeological Museum. The Ottoman building has housed the museum since 1970, taking you from a place of trade into the region’s history. Check opening hours before visiting, and also take a look at the exterior from Eleftherias Square.

Timiou Prodromou Monastery offers a break away from Serres, in a ravine on Mount Menoikio. Founded in the 13th century, it preserves buildings and paintings from several periods. Allow time for the round trip from the city, confirm visiting hours, and wear clothing that provides appropriate coverage for a working monastery.

activities.text: Set aside some time for the pedestrian streets of Serres around Eleftherias Square. The shops and outdoor seating areas offer a break between the Bezesteni and the climb to Koulas. Park once and continue on foot: this walk lets you see the center without moving your car from street to street.

If you’re torn between savory and sweet, bougatsa in Serres makes for an easy snack break. This flaky pastry is one of the specialties associated with the city and comes with various fillings. Ask which version is available and share a portion: you can then continue your walk without extending your food stop.

days_plan.itin_title: Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

visits.text: Head uphill to Servia’s Byzantine castle, where the ramparts trace the contours of the hill. The site preserves the different parts of a former fortified town, including the remains of homes and churches: it was more than just a fortress. Wear shoes with good traction for the climb and avoid wet stones.

Neraida offers the right vantage point to take in Lake Polyfytos and the large Servia Bridge. Its 1,372 meters span an artificial lake created on the Aliakmonas River, yet the landscape looks like a vast natural expanse of water. Stop in the village to view the bridge, rather than on its roadway.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

activities.text: A tropical name, but hiking shoes are needed: reaching Seychelles Beach takes some effort. Its sand, pale pebbles, and rocks line a cove formed by a landslide associated with cutting through the terrain for the road to Magganitis. Bring water for the descent and save some energy for the climb back up; skip swimming if the sea turns rough.

days_plan.itin_title: Ikaria in 3 Days: Hot Springs, Beaches, and Villages

visits.text: Color extends even to the woodwork at the Poulko mansion in Siatista, where the main attractions lie behind its walls. This 18th-century merchant’s residence in the Gerania neighborhood preserves painted decorations that reveal the tastes of its former owners. According to the regional website, it is open daily from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m.: visit in the morning.

A carved watermelon is an unexpected feature at the Nerantzopoulou mansion in Siatista. Dating to 1754, the house bears verses dedicated to Ioannis by scholars from Siatista; its ceiling also features a melon, so the motifs are far from exclusively religious. Confirm interior access before visiting and, if no opening hours are announced, plan to view the exterior.

Agia Paraskevi in Siatista looks understated beside the mansions, but its paintings deserve a stop. The church in the Gerania neighborhood preserves post-Byzantine decoration that reflects the history of this merchant town; its imagery and woodwork offer more to see than the facade. Check opening hours and wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees.

activities.text: Walk between Gerania and Chora to get a feel for Siatista at street level. These two neighborhoods contain the homes of merchant families whose prosperity depended on trade with Central Europe. Look at the projecting upper stories and window frames; leave your car away from the narrow streets.

If you enjoy sweet wines, ask for liasto in Siatista instead of choosing a bottle at random. It is made with sun-dried grapes, which concentrate the aromas before winemaking. The sun thus plays a part in the winemaker’s work. Book any winery tasting in advance and designate a driver who will not drink.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

visits.text: An iron castle without metal walls: Issari Castle gave Sidirokastro its name. Its ruined fortifications overlook the town and the Serres plain; the panorama remains the main attraction. Wear shoes with good traction and bring water for the climb, then limit your exploration to clearly accessible paths.

An understated facade, then rock: Agios Dimitrios holds a surprise in Sidirokastro. This church is partly carved into the rock, giving it an interior unlike those of neighboring places of worship. Check that it is open before heading up, and ask permission before taking any photographs inside.

activities.text: Head back down toward the Krousovitis to walk through Sidirokastro. The river divides the town in two, with the Stavrou and Kalkani bridges among the crossings connecting them: a short walk is enough to offer a different perspective after the castle. Keep this loop easy and choose a shaded path during the hottest hours.

days_plan.itin_title: Serres and Kerkini: 3 Days of Pelicans and History

places.name: Sigri

visits.text: Trees turned to stone: this is the central theme of the Natural History Museum of the Lesbos Petrified Forest in Sigri. Established in 1994, it places the fossils within the geological evolution of the Aegean, going well beyond a collection of trunks. Start with the galleries before visiting the park; the museum lists daily opening hours of 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The Sigri Petrified Forest Park preserves standing trees, but their wood has fossilized. Some root systems remain in their original locations; other trunks were moved here for conservation. Follow the signs to distinguish between the two and stay on the paths, with a hat and a supply of water.

places.name: Sitia

visits.text: Sitia is the easternmost town in Crete, and the least touristy—it moves at its own rhythm. Built in an amphitheater facing the Aegean Sea, it was destroyed then abandoned in the 16th century before being repopulated from the mid-19th century onward, giving it a half-historic, half-living character. Climb to the Venetian fortress of Kazarma late in the afternoon for a panoramic view over the bay—the walk from the harbor takes barely 10 minutes and the coastal panorama is worth the effort. Below, the harbor hosts fishing boats and ferries to the Dodecanese.

Toplou Monastery sits about ten kilometers east of Sitia, in the middle of an arid, lunar landscape. It's one of Crete's most important and most fortified monasteries—its Turkish name 'Toplou' means 'with a cannon,' which sums up its character nicely: pillaged by the Knights of Malta in 1530, destroyed by earthquake, rebuilt in the 17th century. Its icon museum houses the masterpiece of Ioannis Kornaros: the icon 'Megas ei Kyrie' (Great art Thou, O Lord), dated 1770, a composition in 57 zones with hundreds of faces illustrating the Great Blessing of the Waters. The monastery also produces renowned organic wine and quality olive oil, sold at the entrance. Open in summer 9 AM to 1 PM and 2 to 6 PM, entrance €3.

The Vai palm forest, 24 kilometers east of Sitia, is Europe's largest natural palm forest, classified as a nature reserve. It shelters thousands of specimens of Phoenix theophrasti, the palm endemic to Crete and Turkey's southern coast—a species that grows nowhere else in Europe. The beach bordering the palm forest has earned the Blue Flag. According to legend, the palms grew from date pits tossed by Egyptian sailors, Saracen pirates, or Mithridates' army... Arrive early: in summer the beach is overrun from early morning.

Three kilometers north of Vai, take time to climb up to the site of Itanos: an ancient Phoenician city whose ruins—temples, basilicas, cisterns—sprawl across a sandy hill that's almost deserted. The city was famous in antiquity for its trade in purple dye, the red color extracted from murex shells. You'll very likely have the site to yourself. Below lie two wild beaches in isolated coves—ideal for snorkeling in crystalline waters, far from any infrastructure.

If you have a full day to devote to Minoan Crete, head down to Kato Zakros (45 kilometers from Sitia) for the Palace of Zakros—the fourth-largest Minoan palace in Crete after Knossos, Malia, and Phaistos. Built around 1900 BC, it faced eastward: excavations have yielded elephant tusks, ivory, stone vases, and exotic objects from Egypt and the Near East. You can reach it directly by car, or through the Gorge of the Dead (8-kilometer hike from the village of Zakros). Excavations, begun in the 1960s, still regularly reveal new rooms.

activities.text: Explore Sitia's harbor in the evening: tavernas come alive around 8 PM, locals play cards in traditional cafés, and the promenade runs along the sea to Sitia Beach, a long strip of fine sand. The people of Sitia are renowned in Crete for their warmth and musical culture—you might stumble upon an impromptu terrace concert. Local raki (tsikoudia) automatically accompanies the welcome meze at authentic tavernas.

To reach Zakros Palace on foot, take the Gorge of the Dead starting from the village of Zakros: 8 kilometers descending through a limestone canyon with vertiginous walls, dotted with caves that served as burial sites in the Minoan era—hence the name. It's one of the most beautiful hikes in eastern Crete, shaded and cool even in summer. Allow 3 hours, wear closed shoes, and arrange to have a car waiting at Kato Zakros below—otherwise you'll climb back up those 8 kilometers on foot.

At the end of a meal in a Sitia taverna, order xerotigana: ribbons of dough fried in oil, drizzled with honey, and sprinkled with sesame or crushed walnuts. It's the traditional festive dessert of eastern Crete, served at weddings and baptisms—and at good tavernas in summer. Pair them with a red Liatiko, the indigenous grape of the region, sweet and fragrant with notes of dried grapes.

visits.text: Sivota harbor feels like an archipelago, even though you are still on the mainland. Small neighboring islets break up the bay and serve as destinations for boats leaving the village. From the quay, you can check departures without rushing between beaches. Compare trip lengths before booking.

activities.text: To reach an island at Bella Vraka, you can leave the boat at the dock. A sandy passage through the water connects the mainland to the islet of Megalo Mourtemeno. This walk through the water is what makes the beach appealing, but how easy it is depends on conditions. Check the depth and abandon the crossing if the sea is rough; protect your belongings from the water.

If the sea is calm, set out from Sivota harbor toward Pisina, nicknamed Blue Lagoon. This bay is part of the small cluster of islets off the village; the trip lets you see the coves from the water. Choose a short outing that fits into this half-day. Ask about the return time and how much time you will actually have to swim before paying.

days_plan.itin_title: Epirus Coast in 3 Days: Beaches, Parga, and Preveza

visits.text: Panagia Gorgona seems perched at the water’s edge on its rock in Skala Sykamias. Beneath the chapel, the volcanic formations trace back to an eruption of Lepetymnos 17 million years ago: the little harbor also tells the geological story of Lesbos. Observe the rocks from public areas without climbing them.

activities.text: Colorful hulls bob in the harbor of Skala Sykamias. This fishing hamlet belongs to the same village community as Sykamia, which sits higher up the slopes; here, the walk follows the quays and outdoor terraces. Explore on foot, keeping access to boats and fishing equipment clear.

days_plan.itin_title: Lesbos in 4 Days: Villages, Fossils, and the Aegean Sea

visits.text: Skiathos town is a lively little capital whose cobbled lanes wind their way down to the double harbour. It's the most tourist-oriented island in the Sporades — in summer the atmosphere is cosmopolitan and the nightlife is intense, with bars open until dawn on Papadiamanti Street. If you prefer peace and quiet, avoid July–August or arrive in the morning to see the sights before the influx of cruise ships.

The Bourtzi peninsula, linked to the old harbour by a short footbridge, holds a 13th-century Venetian fortification built by the Ghisi brothers to defend the island from pirates. Century-old trees cover the headland, making it a pleasant spot in the evening — concerts are sometimes held here in summer. The view across both harbours of Skiathos from the tip of the peninsula is one of the most photogenic on the island.

Evangelistria Monastery, founded in the 18th century on a hillside 4 km above town, is the most historically charged site on Skiathos. It was here, in September 1807, that the first Greek flag — a white cross on a blue field — was designed, woven, blessed and raised in the presence of the revolutionary hero Theodoros Kolokotronis. The monks who still live in the monastery produce wine, olive oil and honey. The museum housed in the old olive press displays the loom that, according to tradition, was used to weave that first flag. Take the marked trail from town rather than the road — it's more enjoyable and shorter.

Kastro is the former fortified capital of Skiathos, perched on a rocky headland in the north of the island. The inhabitants took refuge here in the 14th century to escape pirate raids and only moved back down to the coast after Greek independence, in 1829. A few churches still cling to the cliffs, including the chapel of the Nativity of Christ, along with a striking view over the Aegean Sea. It can be reached on foot (3 km of track, then a path) or by boat from the port. By car from the overnight stop, the road ends before the site: the last stretch is done on foot.

The Papadiamantis Museum, at number 12 on the street of the same name near the port, occupies the birthplace of Alexandros Papadiamantis, Greece's greatest 19th-century novelist, born on Skiathos in 1851. The two-storey house retains its period interior virtually intact: original furniture, personal library, everyday objects. The cave known as the 'Murderess's Cave' near Lalaria takes its name from one of Papadiamantis's short stories. Open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:30 am to 1:30 pm and 5:15 pm to 8 pm.

Koukounaries, around twenty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, is the picture-postcard beach of Skiathos - ranked among the most beautiful in Greece, with 1,200 metres of fine golden sand edged by an Aleppo pine forest protected under Greek law. Behind the beach lies the wetland of Lake Strofilia, a refuge for rare migratory bird species such as swans and herons. In high season, sunbeds are snapped up early in the morning - arrive before 9am or come in the late afternoon.

Lalaria is Skiathos's show-stopping beach: reachable only by boat from the old harbour, it curves in a half-moon of round white pebbles beneath sheer limestone cliffs that plunge into water of an almost unreal blue-green. A natural arch carved into the rock is the focal point of every photograph of the island. Boats run daily from the port, but if the northerly winds pick up the crossing is cancelled. Bring water and food — there's nothing on site.

The sea caves near Lalaria are every bit as worthwhile as the beach itself. The Blue Cave (Galazia) owes its name to the extraordinary colour of the water inside when the sun hits — reflections off the limestone walls produce an almost supernatural blue glow. The Dark Cave (Skotini), roughly 20 metres long, can only be entered by small boat because the opening is so narrow. Most excursions to Lalaria include a visit to these caves.

Troulos, 8 km west of town, is a family-friendly beach with shallow water and a quiet atmosphere. Pines reach down to the sand, and a few tavernas serve grilled fish. Facing it is the cluster of Troulonisia islets. It's the ideal beach with children if Koukounaries feels too crowded.

activities.text: Papadiamanti Street, the main artery of Skiathos town, is the hub of local life in the evening: craft shops, tavernas with outdoor tables, and ouzo bars. Stroll along it from 7 pm when the locals start to come out — the summer crowds don't descend until after 9 pm. It's also the best spot to order a mezze platter: taramosalata, tyrokafteri, grilled octopus.

Astakomakaronada, the signature dish of the Sporades, is spaghetti with fresh lobster in a lightly spiced tomato sauce. You'll find it at almost every taverna along Skiathos's old harbour — ask whether the lobster was caught that day, as the fishermen deliver directly in the morning. It's one of the island's best combinations of quality and freshness.

Tsipouro, a Greek spirit distilled from grape pomace, is the Sporades' drink of choice. On Skiathos it's served cold, in small glasses, alongside mezze — grilled octopus, feta, marinated olives. The monks at Evangelistria produce an artisanal version available from the monastery shop.

Book a half-day boat trip from Skiathos old harbour to Lalaria and the sea caves — it's the simplest and most enjoyable way to get there. Departures are usually at 9 am or 10 am. In July–August, book the day before: places sell out fast. Options include swimming and snorkelling stops in coves that are impossible to reach on foot.

Revithada, a thick soup of chickpeas slow-baked with olive oil, onion and herbs, is a vegetarian dish from the Sporades often served on Sundays in tavernas. It's a reheated winter dish, though some inns keep it on the menu year-round. With country bread and olives on the side, it makes a complete and very inexpensive lunch.

Retsina is a Greek white wine infused with resin, made according to a tradition stretching back millennia — pine resin once prevented oxidation in amphorae. Its distinctive, slightly terpenic taste pairs perfectly with grilled fish and mezze. It's the cheapest and most authentic bottle you'll be served in the tavernas of the Sporades.

days_plan.itin_title: Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos
Sporades Trip: Skiathos, Skopelos and Alonissos

visits.text: Skopelos town is built amphitheatre-style around a deep bay — white houses with red-brown tile roofs tumble down toward the harbour in a setting the filming of Mamma Mia made famous worldwide. The town alone counts 123 Orthodox churches and chapels — nearly as many as days in the year — some dating back to the Byzantine era. Wander the cobbled alleys of the upper town: no two facades are alike.

The Kastro of Skopelos, on the hill above the harbour, is the highest point in town. The Venetian and Byzantine ruins here offer the best panoramic view over the bay, the ferries coming and going, and, on a clear day, the outline of Alonissos on the horizon. Head up towards the end of the day: the light is ideal and the atmosphere calmer than at midday.

The chapel of Agios Ioannis Kastri is perched on top of a sheer rock that drops into the sea, in the north of the island of Skopelos, near the village of Glossa, around 30 km from the overnight stop, a 45-minute drive. To reach it from the car park below, you have to climb 106 steps cut into the rock. This is where the outdoor wedding scenes of the film Mamma Mia were shot in 2007. Arrive early in the morning or after 5pm to avoid the groups of fans who turn up all day long in summer. The view over the Aegean Sea and Alonissos is worth the detour even if you have never seen the film.

The village of Glossa, perched in the hills of Skopelos, around 24 km from the overnight stop, a 40-minute drive, is one of the best-preserved mountain villages in the Sporades. Its Macedonian architecture - overhanging roofs, stone houses, a square shaded by plane trees - contrasts with the white Cycladic houses of the rest of the island. The inhabitants still grow olive and plum trees here. The central square with its cafés is an ideal place to stop on the way to the chapel of Agios Ioannis.

Panormos is a sheltered seaside village tucked into a natural bay, with a fine-sand beach fringed by pines. It's a very pleasant stop for recreational boaters, and its waterfront tavernas serve fresh fish in a peaceful setting. Less crowded than the beaches in the south of the island, it's the perfect spot for lunch by the water.

The beaches of Kastani and Milia are two of the most recognisable Mamma Mia filming locations. Kastani, in particular, hosted the longest scene in the film. These two coves - pebbles or sand depending on the spot, turquoise water, a pine forest running down to the shore - are among the most beautiful on Skopelos, quite apart from their cinematic fame. Milia is windier and ideal for snorkelling. Kastani lies around 15 km from the overnight stop, a 25-minute drive, and Milia just before it on the same road.

The Sendoukia are an archaeological mystery in the hills of Skopelos: four large sarcophagi cut straight into the rock at the top of a hill, linked by local legend to the Greek pirate Glaucus, who is said to have ruled these seas. Their dating and exact purpose are still debated by archaeologists. You drive up from the overnight stop, the last part on a dirt track, to the start of the path, then it is around a 15-minute walk along a waymarked trail. The view from the site alone is worth the effort.

activities.text: The kalderimi trails — old paved paths that once linked Skopelos's monasteries — are the best way to explore the island's wooded interior. The route to the 18th-century Evangelismos Monastery on Mount Palouki passes through a pine forest with panoramic sea views. Set off in the morning to avoid the heat and bring water.

The tyropita on Skopelos is different from the one you know: here, local cheese — a fresh, lightly salted sheep's-milk cheese — is wrapped in homemade puff pastry, not industrially produced filo. It's the island's breakfast speciality, sold in bakeries from 7 am. Don't leave without eating one hot, straight from the oven.

Skopelos plums are recognised for their geographical origin and are the island's agricultural pride. Family orchards produce plums preserved in syrup, sun-dried, or turned into liqueur. You'll find these products in the shops around town — they're the best edible souvenir to bring home from Skopelos.

The ideal day on the west coast of Skopelos: set off by car in the morning for Panormos and a coffee by the sea, head down to Milia for a swim, then on to Kastani for the afternoon. Finish at the small cove of Hovolo, around thirty minutes' drive from the overnight stop, which is less crowded, with flat rocks perfect for snorkelling. Boat hire companies in Skopelos town also offer small motorboats for exploring these coves on your own.

Astakos — lobster simply grilled with lemon and olive oil — is served at the fishermen's tavernas in Panormos and at small harbours like Agnontas. Ask whether it was caught that morning: Skopelos fishermen have a reputation for delivering straight to the local tavernas. Pair it with garlic-rubbed toasted bread.

Loukoumades — small, light doughnuts fried to order, drizzled with honey and sprinkled with walnuts and cinnamon — are the street dessert of the Sporades. You'll find them at the kiosks on Skopelos town's harbour from 6 pm. They're hot, crisp on the outside and airy inside. Eat them standing up with sticky fingers, the way the locals do.
