visits.text: From cocoon to fabric, materials transform before your eyes at the Soufli Silk Museum. Housed in the Kourtidis house, built in 1883, and a building associated with cocoons, the exhibition traces silkworm rearing and then silk thread production. Plan this visit for the afternoon after Dadia, except on Tuesdays, when the museum is closed.

activities.text: You’ll continue your visit along Soufli’s shopping streets, browsing the fabrics offered in the stores. Silk production shaped the economy of this town in Evros, yet the fabrics on sale do not all share the same origin. Before buying, ask where the piece was woven and check its fiber content.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Kavokolones, the “cape of columns”: this was the name sailors gave Sounion. The Temple of Poseidon served as their landmark while overlooking a strategic outpost linked to the nearby mines. Come in the late afternoon if you’d like light at a lower angle; last admission is twenty minutes before sunset.

At the Temple of Athena at Sounion, focus your attention on the ground. On the neighboring hill, its foundations reveal a building with colonnades along only two sides, an unusual layout described by Vitruvius. View the remains from the open paths before visiting the Temple of Poseidon; do not cross any fences to find a better angle.

days_plan.itin_title: Attica Beyond Athens: 3 Days from Piraeus to Sounion

visits.text: The Archaeological Museum of Sparta, housed since 1875 in a neoclassical building — Greece's first purpose-built provincial museum — holds most of the objects discovered in Laconia, from the Neolithic to the Roman era. Its centrepiece is the marble bust of King Leonidas (5th century BC), wearing the crested helmet of the hoplites. The other treasure is unique in Greece: a collection of votive terracotta masks worn during initiation rites at the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia — old women, bearded warriors, satyrs, gorgons. Allow 45 minutes.

The statue of Leonidas, erected in 1968 at the entrance to the modern city's stadium, depicts the king at a height of 3 metres, helmeted and with a shield on his arm. The pedestal bears the reply ΜΟΛΩΝ ΛΑΒΕ — “come and take them” — which Leonidas is said to have given the Persian king Xerxes when he asked him to surrender his weapons at Thermopylae in 480 BC. It's the quintessential Sparta photo: take it, then continue to the archaeological site just behind.

The archaeological site of Sparta sometimes disappoints those expecting an Acropolis like that of Athens — and that's understandable. The Spartans believed their courage was their best defence and never built fortresses or grand monuments. You'll wander through a park of olive trees among scattered remains: fragments of the theatre, remains of a 10th-century Byzantine basilica, and an Archaic circular building 41 metres in diameter whose purpose remains a mystery.

The Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia lies 800 metres north-east of the stadium, near the River Eurotas, and is free to visit. This is where, from the 9th century BC onwards, Spartan initiation rites took place — notably the ritual flogging of young men before the citizens to prove their endurance. The Romans even had an amphitheatre built in the 3rd century AD to accommodate tourists coming to watch the spectacle.

The Eurotas valley stretches below Sparta, green and fertile, lined with orange and olive trees. This mythological river of Laconia, on whose banks Leda was seduced by Zeus transformed into a swan, flows peacefully between Taygetus and Parnon. An hour's drive south through the valley offers mountain panoramas that help explain why Sparta, without defensive walls, was so difficult to capture.

activities.text: Modern Sparta was re-founded in 1834 by order of King Otto, two years after Greek independence, on a grid plan with wide avenues and citrus trees. This clean, quiet town, far from tourist crowds, is pleasant to explore on foot for its cafés on the squares and its unpretentious tavernas. In the evening, the atmosphere of the central square, with its bars beneath the orange trees, is typical of provincial Greece.

The Mani's orange sausages are the Laconian region's charcuterie speciality: minced pork, orange zest, spices and slow smoking over myrtle wood. You'll find them in local delicatessens and tavernas in Sparta. Pair them with ladera — seasonal vegetables simmered in olive oil and tomato, without meat, which Greeks love to eat at lunchtime.

visits.text: You will start at the Bouboulina Museum to put a face to the maritime history of Spetses. The house preserves weapons, letters, and furniture associated with the heroine of Greek independence; the carved ceiling of the main drawing room draws as much attention as the collections. Confirm the visiting time before planning the rest of your stopover.

Underfoot, the courtyards of Spetses display pebble patterns between the neoclassical houses. Balconies, flowers, and facades form an ensemble that tells the story of the town’s maritime prosperity, which developed in the 18th century. View the courtyards from public spaces and favor lanes near the center to keep detours to a minimum.

activities.text: The Old Harbor of Spetses offers a longer stroll than the lanes in the center. Follow the waterfront to the boats, with traditional houses in the background: maritime activity remains the island’s common thread. Walk there and back, then return to your departure dock with plenty of time before the ferry to Piraeus.

days_plan.itin_title: Saronic Islands: 3 Days from Aegina to Hydra and Spetses

visits.text: Beneath the walkways in the Cave of the Lakes, pools rise in tiers like steps on a staircase. The cave system contains thirteen lakes, but the visitor route reveals only some of them. Do not expect to see them all; wear shoes with good traction and come in the morning, on a day other than Tuesday.

A useful addition after exploring the walkways is the Cave of the Lakes interpretation center. Its permanent exhibition combines geology, archaeology, and paleontology, with screenings that explain the site in its environmental setting. You will better understand what the walkways do not reveal; check at reception whether your ticket includes access.

days_plan.itin_title: Achaea in 3 days: gorges, Cave of the Lakes, and Helmos

activities.text: If philosophy seems abstract to you, Aristotle’s Park in Stagira makes it hands-on. Twelve devices, from a prism to a pendulum, illustrate physical phenomena; the parabolic reflectors even invite you to play with sound. Try the available installations before heading to the ancient city, which is in a different location, near Olympiada.

days_plan.itin_title: Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos

visits.text: Evangelistria Church in Stavroupoli is worth looking up at before you get back on the road. Its architecture combines Byzantine and neoclassical elements; inside, the carved iconostasis draws more attention than the building’s size. Visit outside service times to view the iconostasis without disturbing worshippers.

If you enjoy everyday objects, the Folklore Museum of Stavroupoli is a good addition to your exploration of the village. Costumes, tools, and furniture tell the story of local life on a domestic scale that contrasts with the sweeping landscapes of the Nestos.

activities.text: You’ll walk to Stavroupoli’s central square to see the houses along the nearby streets. The tobacco trade contributed to the town’s prosperity, traces of which remain in its homes and narrow streets. Then take a seat on a terrace on the central square.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: Walk up through Stemnitsa’s lanes before heading to your accommodations: the facades are better appreciated on foot than from behind the wheel. Several houses were built by craftspeople from Lagkadia, renowned for their stonework. After walking through the gorge, stick to a short tour of the village and adjust your stroll to your energy level.

It is hard to look at Prodromou Monastery without raising your eyes to the cliff that shelters it. The sanctuary developed from earlier hermitages, and its balconies overlook the Lousios Gorge. Wear clothing that provides adequate coverage, respect religious services, and confirm visiting hours before setting out: this visit is part of a day of walking.

Two foundations, two distinct atmospheres on the same slope: Philosophou is more than a single building. Philosophou Monastery comprises an older establishment in the cliff and a more recent one, connected to the Lousios trail network. Head to the new monastery for this short visit, without adding the detour to the old ruins.

activities.text: The sound of water accompanies the descent into the Lousios Gorge. Between Prodromou and the new Philosophou Monastery, the trail crosses the river and climbs the opposite slope: the short distance conceals changes in elevation. Return along the same trail, carry water, and skip the hike after heavy rain.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Entering Gialos harbor, the spectacle hits you all at once: hundreds of neoclassical houses in shades of ochre, pink, blue, and yellow rising in tiers up the hillside, reflected in the harbor water. One hour by ferry from Rhodes, Symi owes this architecture to its 19th-century prosperity, when the island was a major shipbuilding center producing up to 500 vessels a year. The village of Gialos is a classified historic monument—facades are protected in their original state. Give yourself time on the waterfront before climbing toward Chorio.

Chorio, the upper village, is reached from Gialos via the Kali Strata—literally “the beautiful stairs”—500 steps lined with the island's finest manor houses. The climb is worth it as much for the sculpted facades as for the views over the harbor that open at each landing. At the top, the ruins of the 15th-century Knights' castle dominate everything, and Chorio's quiet lanes contrast with the bustle of Gialos below.

Panormitis Monastery, in the island's south, is one of the Dodecanese's most important pilgrimage sites. Founded in the 18th century, it's dedicated to the Archangel Michael, patron saint of sailors. Its baroque bell tower rises above a sheltered bay accessible only by sea or by winding road. Inside, the walls are covered with ex-votos offered by grateful sailors—bells, silver boats, objects recovered after shipwrecks. Several boat excursions from Gialos stop here.

The Maritime Museum of Symi, near Kampos Square, recounts the history of this island of sailors and sponge divers. Diving suits, archive photographs and nineteenth-century diving equipment show how dangerous the trade was: decompression accidents were frequent and left many men disabled. It is a short visit (30 to 45 minutes), but it gives valuable context to what you see around you.

Symi's beaches are mostly pebbles rather than sand, accessible mainly by taxi-boat from Gialos. Agios Georgios Dyssalonas, Nanou, and Agia Marina are among the island's most beautiful coves—turquoise waters, cliff backdrops, no roads leading to them. Check at the harbor in the morning for departures and the last return boat.

activities.text: Position yourself on the ferry deck as you approach Symi—the entrance to Gialos harbor with its amphitheater of houses is one of the Dodecanese's most photographed moments. If you're spending the night on the island, enjoy the evening calm when day-trippers from Rhodes have caught their boat back: tavernas empty by half and lanes regain their silence.

Take a taxi-boat from Gialos to reach one of the isolated coves on the island's south or east coast—Nanou or Agia Marina are best for swimming. It's the only way to access these bays unreachable by road. Ask at the harbor about the last return boat before departing.

Symi's specialty is tiny local shrimp (garides Symis)—minuscule, caught in the deep waters around the island, crispy and delicious eaten whole. They're served fried with a squeeze of lemon and a glass of ouzo. Every harbor taverna offers them—quality varies, but it's the dish you can't miss. Finish with galaktoboureko, that pastry of semolina cream wrapped in phyllo, soaked in lemon syrup.

days_plan.itin_title: Dodecanese Journey: Rhodes, Symi & Kos

visits.text: Sãracu in Aromanian: Syrrako also has a name that sounds different from the one on Greek signs. The village preserves its traditional buildings on a steep slope and remains associated with the poet Kostas Krystallis. Cars are prohibited in the center, so you explore on foot along the cobblestones.

activities.text: Follow the start of the Syrrako-Kalarrytes trail to see the villages from their outskirts, taking a short walk rather than completing the full crossing. The path connects the two villages through the gorges; it requires more effort than strolling from square to square. Check the condition of the trail markers and turn back early enough to leave yourself extra time for the drive.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

visits.text: The appeal of the Temple of Athena Alea in Tegea lies as much in its marble fragments as in the vanished building. The sanctuary linked Athena with the local deity Alea: a double name, not two temples. Start with the ruins, then head to the nearby museum to better understand what you are looking at.

Save the Archaeological Museum of Tegea for after the temple: the fragments will then make sense in context. The collections shed light on the ancient city and the sanctuary of Athena Alea, whose architecture is associated with Scopas. Check opening hours before leaving Kalamata and focus on this visit to leave time for Mantinea.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: Do not assume you can cross: at Agia Paraskevi, in the Vale of Tempe, access depends on the footbridge reopening. The church carved into the rock stands beside the Pinios. Check with the local tourist office to see whether access is open; if it is closed, stay within the permitted areas of the valley.

days_plan.itin_title: Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: To reach Thasos, take the ferry from Keramoti, 35 km south-east of Kavala — the crossing takes just 35 minutes and departures run every 30 minutes in season. It's by far the quickest and cheapest option. Once in Limenas, the capital, head down to the ancient agora: it sits right in the heart of the modern town, surrounded by the ruins of sanctuaries dedicated to Heracles, Dionysus, Artemis and Poseidon, with a medieval tower occupying one corner. Information panels at the entrance show a reconstruction of what the square once looked like — helpful for grasping the scale.

The ancient theatre of Thasos, built into a natural hollow in the hillside north-east of town, dates in its earliest phases from the late 4th century BC. In the 1st century AD it was converted into an arena for gladiatorial combat. It has been fully restored in recent years using white marble from Thasos — the same stone used in antiquity, quarried on the island. The view from the upper tiers over the harbour of Limenas and the Aegean is one of the finest on the island.

The Archaeological Museum of Thasos, founded in 1935 and renovated between 1989 and 2000, is the oldest museum in the Eastern Macedonia and Thrace region. Its centrepiece is the Kouros of Thasos: an archaic statue standing 3.5 metres tall, depicting a young man carrying a ram — a masterpiece of the 6th century BC discovered in 1911 in five pieces inside a Byzantine wall, where it had been reused as building material. The museum also holds a fine head of Alexander the Great and an Aphrodite with a Dolphin regularly lent to major international exhibitions.

The acropolis of Thasos dominates the town from its rocky spur. Climb up from the theatre along the signposted path: you'll pass the sanctuaries of Apollo and Athena, then the Sanctuary of Pan carved directly into the rock face. Along the way, look for the Cyclopean ramparts of white marble — some blocks are fitted so precisely that you still can't slide a credit card between them. The view from the top sweeps across the entire northern coastline of the island.

The village of Panagia, perched in the mountains 10 km south of Limenas, is one of the most beautiful on the island: stone fountains, century-old plane trees, tile-roofed houses and cobbled lanes on the hillside. It's the birthplace of the local dance and one of the best-preserved villages in Eastern Macedonia. Arrive on a Sunday morning to see the locals in traditional dress after Mass.

The village of Theologos, which calls for a day trip from Limenas, was the island's medieval capital under Genoese and Turkish rule. This is where the population took refuge to escape pirates. Its narrow lanes, stone houses with enclosed gardens and old fountains distinguish it from the modernised coastal villages. Allow 45 minutes to walk around the whole village.

The marble quarries of Alyki, on the cape of the same name 32 km south-east of Limenas, are an exceptional archaeological site: the extraction of Thasian white marble — one of the most prized in antiquity — is documented here from the Archaic period through to Byzantine times. Half-cut blocks have been waiting in the rock for twenty centuries. This white marble with its glittering crystals was used, among other things, to build the Arch of Galerius in Thessaloniki. From the beach at Alyki, submerged blocks are visible beneath the water.

activities.text: Swim at Makryammos, 2 km east of Limenas: a crescent-shaped cove with fine sand, emerald-green waters and maritime pines reaching down to the sea. This is the picture-postcard image of Thasos - the blend of dense vegetation and clear sea that earned the island its nickname, “the Emerald Island”.

In the evening, settle into a café on the harbour at Limenas and order a local retsina — the resinated white wine produced on the island, slightly bitter, served chilled with olives and goat's cheese. It's here that you understand why ancient Greece regulated its wine production by law: Thasian amphorae bearing inspection seals have been found across the entire Mediterranean basin.

Drive around the island: the coastal road covers 95 km and can be comfortably done in a day with stops. Don't miss Golden Beach (Chrisi Amoudia) on the east coast — a long beach of golden sand with deep-blue water, considered one of the most beautiful in the northern Aegean. Behind the beach, archaeologists uncovered a well dating from the 3rd century BC, and on the headland above, the ruins of a 4th-century BC lighthouse.

Sample roast goat with mountain herbs at a taverna in Theologos or Panagia: it's the island's traditional festive dish, oven-roasted or spit-roasted with wild herbs gathered from the slopes of Mount Ipsarion. The mountain-village tavernas are cheaper and more authentic than those on the beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi
Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi

visits.text: The modern city is built directly over the ancient Cadmée - the acropolis of the mythical city - which explains why ruins appear among ordinary streets. According to mythology, Héraclès and Dionysos were born here, OEdipe ruled here, and Antigone was sentenced to death here. In 335 BC, Alexander the Great destroyed the city following a rebellion, killing or enslaving its 30,000 inhabitants. The renovated Archaeological Museum is remarkable: the painted funerary stelae from ancient Démétrias are an absolute rarity in Greece, and the Linear B tablets (Mycenaean writing from the 15th century BC) attest to the site's antiquity. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

500 m east of the museum, Megalo Kastelli Park contains Mycenaean burial chambers from the 14th–13th centuries BC, dubbed the “tomb of Oedipus's children” by local tradition – a legendary attribution, but the architecture is real. Along Pindarou Street (named after the Theban poet Pindar, 518–438 BC), remnants of ancient Cadmea emerge between houses. The medieval tower visible at the museum entrance dates from the 13th-century Frankish occupation.

activities.text: Thebes attracts few tourists – precisely what makes it an authentic stop. The cafés on the central square are frequented exclusively by locals. Have lunch in a taverna in the centre before continuing towards Distomo in the afternoon: for Osios Loukas, allow for a same-day round trip from Thebes.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Greece & Gulf Coast

visits.text: A welcome break after the winding drive: in Theodoriana, water sets the agenda for what comes next. The village provides access to the Souda waterfalls and the trails along Marks Stream, in a wooded setting. Use this stop to find your trailhead and check the weather before continuing to the waterfalls.

activities.text: Follow the trail to the Souda waterfalls through the cool forest instead of adding more kilometers behind the wheel. Near Theodoriana, the water splits into two falls about 25 meters high. Park near the marked trailhead and wear shoes with good traction: wet rocks are slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: Tzoumerka in 3 Days: Arta, Kipina, and Mountainside Villages

activities.text: If the road has left you feeling shaken up, the renovated Thermes hydrotherapy center awaits in the village square. The hot springs are in the valley and should be distinguished from the various hamlets named Thermes. Outdoor pools are a few minutes’ walk from the center; bring a swimsuit and towel.

days_plan.itin_title: Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: A fortress on the outside, a prison within: the Heptapyrgion tells a less peaceful story than its panoramic views suggest. Under its Ottoman name, Yedi Kule, this citadel housed prisoners from 1890 to 1989; the prison buildings completely change how you see the city walls. Take time to look at the courtyards as well as the walls, then head to the surrounding grounds overlooking the city. Check opening hours before heading up: the site is closed on Tuesdays.

Follow the Byzantine city walls to Trigonion Tower, where Thessaloniki spreads out all the way to the Thermaic Gulf. The tower is Ottoman, although it stands alongside fortifications generally described as Byzantine; the city walls form part of the heritage ensemble inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1988. Look for changes in the masonry as you walk downhill along the walls. Stick to public access routes: in winter, the interior of Trigonion Tower can be visited on Fridays by appointment.

Vlatadon Monastery deserves a stop for more than its views: this is still a place of active religious life. Founded in the 14th century, this Byzantine monastery remains active, although its church has changed considerably through successive alterations. From the surrounding grounds, you can take in the contours of Ano Poli and the neighborhoods descending toward the sea at a glance. Wear clothing that provides adequate coverage and respect areas reserved for the community.

In the dim light of Hosios David, the tesserae draw more attention than the sanctuary’s size. This 5th-century church, a remnant of Latomou Monastery, preserves a mosaic depicting Ezekiel’s vision with a beardless Christ, a detail that can be surprising if you expect a bearded figure. Medieval frescoes round out the visit. Keep your phone on silent.

Born in Thessaloniki before founding modern Turkey, Mustafa Kemal gives Atatürk’s birthplace an unexpected significance. The house next to the Turkish consulate tells the story of a childhood in what was then an Ottoman city; the museum reopened on November 9, 2025, following restoration. Pay as much attention to the domestic architecture as to the documents on display to maintain a connection with the neighborhood. Contact the consulate before your visit to confirm access requirements and opening hours.

Rebuilt, yet with its past still very much in evidence: Agios Dimitrios preserves traces of its history both below and above ground. The basilica was devastated by the fire of 1917 and later restored; its crypt occupies part of former Roman baths and houses an archaeological display. Look for the surviving mosaics before heading downstairs, as the two levels tell complementary stories. Wait until a service has ended before walking around the church.

Stop at Bey Hamam to look at the domes before continuing toward the markets. Built in 1444 under Murad II, these Ottoman baths had separate sections for men and women, along with cold, warm, and hot rooms. Small openings in the domes illuminated the architecture, which was designed around the body and steam. If the rooms are closed, use this stop to study the building’s forms from the street.

The Bezesteni deserves more than a quick glance between purchases: its roof already reveals its purpose. Six domes cover this former Ottoman market, devoted particularly to textiles and valuable objects, which remains a place of commerce. Here, the monument and the shops share the same space, with no prescribed museum route. First observe the building’s forms from outside, then step beneath the domes during shop opening hours, keeping access routes clear.

Behind its understated exterior, Panagia Acheiropoietos hides decoration you might pass by too quickly. This 5th-century basilica preserves mosaics in its arches, while an inscription on a column recalls its conversion into a mosque after the Ottoman conquest. The contrast between the marble, plant motifs, and this political trace adds depth to a short visit. Come outside service times and take time to look up beneath the arcades.

Gold catches the light inside Agia Sofia, but the decoration above all draws your gaze upward. The dome bears a mosaic of the Ascension dating from the late 9th century, while the apse shows a Virgin and Child from a different period. These layers of imagery let you compare several periods of Byzantine art within a single building. Wear clothing that provides adequate coverage and avoid visiting during a service.

Its original purpose is uncertain, but its impact is immediate: the Rotunda places you beneath a vast dome adorned with mosaics. Built under Galerius, it later served as a church and then a mosque; its initial use remains debated, so the same space has accommodated successive forms of worship. Step back to compare the Roman architecture with the Christian decoration. Avoid Tuesdays, the stated closing day, and check seasonal opening hours before buying your ticket.

Kamara: this common name for the Arch of Galerius makes it easy to overlook the propaganda carved above passersby. Its reliefs celebrate the emperor’s victories over the Persians, while the remains of the Palace of Galerius, near Navarinou Square, place the monument within a Roman residential complex. Walk from the arch to the ruins to understand this connection.

If you want to understand what the facades no longer tell you, start at the Jewish Museum of Thessaloniki. The collections explore daily life, synagogues, the necropolis, and the Holocaust, rather than reducing the Jewish presence to a single period. Documents, photographs, and objects give a human scale to this history, which a sightseeing itinerary can easily overlook. Plan a morning visit: published opening hours are limited, and the museum does not list Saturday hours.

Gold draws you in, but bronze holds your attention: at the Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki, the Derveni krater deserves a proper pause. This vessel depicts the wedding of Dionysus and Ariadne amid figures in motion; the Derveni papyrus is also among the items displayed in the collections. You can explore the section devoted to precious metals to compare jewelry, wreaths, and funerary tableware. Focus on a selection if you are also visiting the Museum of Byzantine Culture.

Head to the Museum of Byzantine Culture to discover the objects behind the churches you visited the day before. Its eleven galleries display mosaics, icons, funerary paintings, and everyday objects, among other items; the layout lets you choose a gallery without walking through the entire museum. This flexibility helps you avoid fatigue after visiting the neighboring Archaeological Museum while connecting the works to their uses. Choose your themes as you enter.

From bastion to museum, the White Tower has changed roles without leaving the waterfront. Its name recalls its whitewashing in 1883, after the building had served as a prison; the current exhibition tells the story of Thessaloniki, and the terrace offers views over the gulf. Save some energy for the stairs. Full-price admission costs €8.

activities.text: Walk back down through Ano Poli along its cobblestone lanes. Low houses, gardens, and Macedonian architecture give the upper town a different scale from the commercial center; some stretches of the route are interesting mainly for their everyday surroundings. Use this walk to observe the facades and take a break at a neighborhood café. Wear shoes with good traction: the slopes and stairs require extra care after rain.

If you feel like leaving the stonework behind, Seich Sou Forest extends your morning in the hills. Also known as Kedrinos Lofos, this forest on the city’s outskirts consists mainly of pines mixed with other tree species and offers paths with views of Thessaloniki. A short loop is enough for a change of scenery without turning the outing into a mountain hike. Start from a clearly identified access point near the Heptapyrgion, bring water, and check fire restrictions before setting out.

Go from the stalls of Kapani to the Modiano market hall to compare two ways of shopping at a market. The former offers fish, meat, and spices, among other goods; the latter, designed by Eli Modiano, returned to active use after its renovation and reopening in 2022. Make this detour a food break between the Bezesteni and the churches in the city center. Come in the morning and ask about prices before choosing what to sample.

Follow Thessaloniki’s waterfront to Nea Paralia to end the day with an unobstructed horizon. George Zongolopoulos’s umbrellas, installed here in 1997, transform an ordinary object into a sculpture open to the sky; gardens and a promenade extend the walk along the Thermaic Gulf. Turn back whenever you feel ready. Aim for late afternoon, bring water, and watch for cyclists when crossing.

As evening begins in Ladadika, voices from outdoor seating areas gradually drown out the sound of footsteps. This former commercial district now brings together tavernas, restaurants, and bars on pedestrian streets near the port, with restored buildings that retain their low-rise scale. Settle in to share a few meze dishes and observe the neighborhood’s rhythm. Check the menu and prices before sitting down, especially if music is offered.

Halkidiki in 3 Days: Villages and Shores of Athos
Mount Olympus and Pieria in 3 Days: From Dion to Larissa

visits.text: First stop on the road: the Corinth Canal. Dug between 1882 and 1893 (plans date back to antiquity — Nero himself launched construction in 67 AD before giving up), it connects the Gulf of Corinth to the Aegean Sea over a length of 6.4 km. What really strikes you are the sheer vertical walls: 79 meters of limestone sliced clean. The width is only 21 meters — enough for small cruise ships, but not for supertankers. Park on the road bridge and look straight down: vertigo guaranteed.

The Theatre of Epidaurus is often described as the most perfect in antiquity, and for once, that's not an exaggeration. Built around 330 BC by the Argive architect Polykleitos the Younger, it originally had 34 rows of seats (6,200 capacity), with 21 additional rows added in Roman times to bring the total to 12,000 spectators. Climb to the very top row and ask someone at the bottom to whisper or crumple a sheet of paper: you'll hear it perfectly from 22 meters above. Researchers still debate the exact acoustic explanation — the limestone may filter out low frequencies while letting high ones through. Arrive early in the morning to beat the cruise ship coaches from Athens.

The Sanctuary of Asclepius, god of medicine, is considered the first major healing center of antiquity — the "Lourdes" of the ancient Greek world. The sick traveled from across Greece to practice incubation: they slept in the abaton (a 70-meter-long portico) hoping that Asclepius would appear in their dreams to reveal a cure. The complex also included a gymnasium, baths, a 180-meter stadium and a library — embodying the idea that body and soul heal together. A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1988.

The small Archaeological Museum of Epidaurus, at the entrance to the site, displays ancient medical instruments, stelae carved with accounts of miraculous healings, and a remarkable statue of Hygieia dating from the 4th century BC. The inscriptions on the stelae are particularly gripping: they describe cures, visions and resurrections — a blend of real medicine and faith. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.

End the day in Nafplio, the first capital of independent Greece in 1829, nestled at the head of a sheltered gulf. Its Venetian center is one of the most beautiful in the Peloponnese: cobblestone lanes, ochre and burgundy façades, cafés lining the local Syntagma Square. If you still have energy, climb up to Palamidi Fortress — 999 steps according to some, 216 according to others. The view over the bay and the floating fort of Bourtzi is worth every step.

Tiryns is often overlooked in favor of Mycenae — unfairly so. This Mycenaean citadel from the 14th century BC boasts the best-preserved Cyclopean walls in the ancient world: up to 14 meters thick, with vaulted galleries carved into the walls themselves. The ancient Greeks believed only the Cyclopes could have assembled such massive blocks. Homer called it "Tiryns of the mighty walls." It's a UNESCO site and far less crowded than Mycenae: chances are you'll have the place to yourself.

From Tolo, allow about 29 km and 35 minutes on the road to reach the site. Mycenae was the city of Agamemnon, the king who led the Greeks against Troy. Founded, according to legend, by Perseus, it reached its height between 1400 and 1200 BC and influenced the whole eastern Mediterranean. Entering through the Lion Gate, erected around 1250 BC, you pass beneath the oldest monumental relief in Europe: two lionesses (their metal heads long gone) flank a Minoan-style column. The cyclopean blocks of the ramparts weigh several tonnes each and are fitted together without mortar. Arrive early - in high season the car park fills up by 9am.

Don't miss the Treasury of Atreus, 300 meters from the main gate — it's actually a royal tholos tomb dating from 1250 BC. You enter through a 36-meter open-air corridor (the dromos), flanked by walls 6 meters high. The circular chamber measures 14.50 meters in diameter and 13.20 meters in height: it was the largest dome in the Western world until the Pantheon in Rome was built five centuries later. The acoustics inside are eerie and mesmerizing — try clapping your hands.

Head back down to Nafplio to explore its Venetian old town. Palamidi Fortress, perched 216 meters above the harbor, was built by the Venetians between 1711 and 1714 in a record time of three years. From its upper bastion, the view sweeps across the entire Gulf of Argolis. If you're only going to climb one fortress at sunset on this trip, make it this one: the golden light on the gulf is stunning.

activities.text: In summer, the Athens & Epidaurus Festival programs performances of ancient tragedies and comedies on Friday and Saturday evenings at the Theatre of Epidaurus. Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides performed in their original setting, under the open sky, with the Argolid mountains as a backdrop — an experience unlike anything else. Check the program before your trip and book well in advance.

The bay of Tolo, a small seaside resort a few kilometers from Nafplio, makes the ideal base for the night. The waterfront tavernas serve grilled fish straight off the morning boats. Order some psarosoupa (fish soup) and saganaki (fried cheese) with a glass of local white wine.

Nafplio deserves real time on foot. Cross Syntagma Square, ringed by Venetian and Ottoman houses, pass the Trianon, a former mosque now a theatre and exhibition hall, then follow the harbour to the Bourtzi fort, built on an islet in the middle of the bay. Water taxis get you there in a few minutes.

Argolid cuisine is generous: lamb kleftiko (slow-braised lamb), crispy spanakopita, local cheeses drizzled with Peloponnesian honey. The tavernas along Nafplio's harbor are among the best in the region — look for the ones without a laminated menu posted by the door.

days_plan.itin_title: Classical Greece Road Trip: Athens To Olympia
Classical Greece Road Trip: Athens To Olympia

activities.text: The cliffs draw closer and the Nestos fills your view along the gorge trail, accessible from Toxotes via Galani. The path follows the river through the same corridor as the railroad. Set out early, bring water, and choose a short out-and-back walk; never extend your walk along the railroad tracks.

days_plan.itin_title: Drama and Nestos in 5 Days: Caves, Forest, and Delta

visits.text: Water at 51 °C, but no bathing planned: in Traianoupoli, the thermal spa is listed as out of service by its operator. The stop still holds historical interest thanks to the Hana, a former travelers’ inn, and the remains of the Ottoman baths. Limit your visit to the accessible parts of the site and don’t count on a thermal spa session.

activities.text: You’ll arrange your outing in the Evros Delta with the Loutra information center before you arrive. This wetland along the border combines freshwater areas and lagoons; the birds you see vary with the season. Book a guided outing and clarify which permits are required: foreign visitors need to arrange access to the monitored area in advance.

days_plan.itin_title: Evros in 4 Days: Delta, Raptors, and Castles of Thrace

visits.text: Trikala is little known to foreign travellers — which makes it one of the best "real" towns in Thessaly. The Byzantine fortress on the hill above the city has ancient origins: this is the site of the Sanctuary of Asclepius, the Greek god of medicine whose mythical birthplace was Trikala. The current fortress dates from the 4th century, with later Byzantine and Ottoman modifications. The Ottoman clock tower, still standing at the eastern corner, has become the symbol of the city.

The Varousi quarter, at the foot of the fortress, is the old Ottoman neighbourhood with its narrow lanes, overhanging houses, and old churches. The Asclepieion of Trikala — the remains of the ancient healing sanctuary dedicated to Asclepius — is visible in the park below the fortress. The Koursoum Mosque (16th c.), one of the best preserved in Greece, stands in the lower town — it's no longer active but its Ottoman architecture is remarkable.

On the banks of the Litheos river, the Matsopoulos mill (19th century) is a singular industrial monument: built of imposing stone, it is still standing. The footbridge across the Litheos opposite the mill is the locals' favourite meeting place in the evening - with views of the water and the lights of the old town.

activities.text: Trikala is known for its spiced sausage (loukaniko Trikalinon) seasoned with herbs from nearby Mount Koziakas, its mountain feta cheese, and its tsipouro. The tavernas in the centre are affordable and packed with locals — a welcome break after the tourist prices of Kalambaka. The Tuesday morning market in the lower town draws producers from across the region.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Massive yet full of curves, Aziz Aga Bridge towers over the Venetikos near Trikomo. Built in 1727, it has three arches; a bell suspended beneath the large arch once warned travelers about the wind. Walk to the site if the access road is in poor condition, and stay away from the banks when the river is in flood.

Spanos Bridge looks broad and calm after Aziz Aga’s large arch. Near the road from Grevena to Krania, it crosses the Venetikos on five arches and recalls the movement of herds between the mountains and the plain. Park off the roadway and approach on foot without obstructing vehicles.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

visits.text: Tripoli, the capital of Arcadia at 650 metres above sea level, deserves a brief stop for its Areos Square: a large neoclassical square with fountains, cafés with terraces and the archaeological museum building designed by architect Ernst Ziller, who also designed the Royal Palace in Athens. Tripoli may not look like much at first glance, but it makes an ideal base for exploring the surrounding mountains of Arcadia.

The Tripoli Archaeological Museum houses collections from ancient Arcadia: sculptures, inscriptions, ceramics and mosaics from local sites such as Tegea and Mantinea. The Mycenaean collections from Arcadia are displayed here, offering an insight into a region often overlooked on classical itineraries. Allow 40 to 50 minutes.

Dimitsana, a mountain village 50 km from Tripoli, is perched on a rocky spur above the Lousios Gorge. Its cobbled lanes, stone tower houses and numerous churches make it one of the most beautiful villages in Arcadia. The library founded in 1764 held 5,000 volumes before the 1821 revolution — according to the memoirs of Kolokotronis, their pages were used to make cartridges with local gunpowder.

The Open-Air Water Power Museum of Dimitsana, opened in 1997, is the only one of its kind in Greece. It showcases the restored buildings of a flour mill, a tannery, a gunpowder mill (which supplied the 1821 revolutionaries with ammunition) and a still. The working hydraulic mechanisms, explained with scale models, paint a vivid picture of pre-industrial life in Arcadia.

activities.text: Hike in the Lousios gorge between the monasteries of Prodromos and Philosophos: a trail of 45 minutes to 1 hour between two limestone walls blackened by damp, above a river that Pausanias said had the coldest waters in Greece. The Prodromos monastery (16th century), still inhabited by monks, literally clings to the cliff - its wooden balconies overhang a drop of several dozen metres. The Philosophos monastery (rebuilt in 1691) is the easiest starting point. Allow for a day trip there and back from your overnight stop.

Tasting in Dimitsana or Stemnitsa: hilopites, egg pasta cut into small squares and dried in the sun, and trachanas, a dried preparation made from flour and fermented milk — the two mountain specialities of Arcadia most often cooked as winter soups. In summer, tavernas serve them in a lighter form with grated cheese. Arcadian fir honey, dark and thick, is among the best in Greece.

days_plan.itin_title: Peloponnese Road Trip: Mycenae, Epidaurus & Olympia

visits.text: Tsagarada, on Pelion's east side facing the Aegean, is one of the most beautiful villages on the peninsula. Its central square is dominated by a plane tree that locals say is over 1,000 years old — its circumference exceeds 14 m and its shade covers half the square. It was under this tree that villagers gathered for centuries to hold the agora, settle village affairs, and debate politics. Have your morning coffee here, facing the Aegean Sea glimpsed between the trees — it's one of the finest terraces in Greece.

Damouchari, below Tsagarada, is one of those tiny Pelion harbours that look like a postcard of the ideal Mediterranean: a bay split in two by a headland topped with the ruins of a medieval castle, fish tavernas right on the jetty, water so clear you can see the bottom at 5 metres. Several scenes from the film "Mamma Mia" were shot here — the producers didn't have to look far.

activities.text: Mylopotamos beach, reached from Tsagarada via 7 km of side road followed by a 15–20 minute walk along a forest trail, is one of the most beautiful on the Greek mainland: white sand, rocks splitting the beach into two coves, turquoise water, and pine trees reaching down to the shore. The walk through Pelion's dense forest is as good as the beach itself. Plan on spending the afternoon — the descent is easy, the climb back takes a good 30 minutes of effort.

The inter-village trails of Pelion (monopatia) are paved with grey schist slabs and date largely from the Ottoman period — they connected villages when there were no roads. The Damouchari–Tsagarada section (roughly 45 minutes one way) is one of the finest: dense forest, waterfalls, and sea views. The trail is waymarked and manageable for everyone.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Schinoussa is even smaller than Iraklia—8 km², fewer than 300 residents. Its main village, Chora (or Panagia), perches 1.5 km from Mersini port: a single street you can walk down in 5 minutes, lined with family tavernas and geranium-draped houses. Here, everyone knows everyone and newcomers quickly blend in. Come evening, Chora comes alive on the central square: locals and the Greek vacationers who make up most of the island's clientele gather over a warm rakomelo. Push open the door of kafeneio Xara—an institution.

Tsigouri beach is Schinoussa's most accessible beach, 600 m from Chora along a paved road. Golden sand, shallow water and tamarisk trees for shade. A beach bar serves drinks and mezedes. For a wilder experience, Psili Ammos beach is worth the 45-minute walk from Chora: an unspoiled bay with water of unreal clarity and no facilities. Arrive early in summer.

activities.text: Swimming and lounging at Tsigouri—or swim out to the small islet 200 meters offshore for absolute solitude.
A short coastal hike to Livadi or Aligaria beach: Schinoussa's paths connect the beaches, all less than a 40-minute walk from Chora.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Porto Katsiki ('Goat Port') is one of the most photographed beaches in the Mediterranean. A concave limestone cliff drops sheer onto a strip of white pebbles and sand, lapped by water of an almost unreal blue-turquoise hue — locals attribute the colour to the geological composition of the seabed. From the car park at the top of the cliff, roughly a hundred steps cut into the rock lead down to the beach. Arrive before 10am in July–August: after that, the beach fills quickly and the staircase becomes a queue.

Egremni, a few kilometres north of Porto Katsiki, stretches for almost 2.5 km of golden pebbles at the foot of 150-metre-high cliffs. The earthquake of 17 November 2015 destroyed the old staircase of 347 steps and buried part of the beach under a landslide. A new staircase was built in 2021, but the municipality closed land access in 2025 because of ground instability, and the February 2026 storms damaged the steps: the beach is reached by boat from Vassiliki, which keeps it wilder and less crowded than Porto Katsiki. The waves can be powerful: take care with children.

Vassiliki is a world-class windsurfing destination — the reliable afternoon thermals that blow across the bay from the open sea draw competitors and enthusiasts from around the globe. In the morning, the bay is a mirror-flat playground for beginners; from 2pm, the wind picks up and sails multiply. Dozens of windsurf and kitesurf schools cater to all levels.

Karya, a mountain village in the centre of the island at 550 metres above sea level, is famous throughout Greece for its handmade embroidery - the village women carry on a tradition dating from the 19th century with intricate floral patterns. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. The local folklore museum traces this history. In summer, an artisans' market livens up the central square. The view from the heights takes in both coasts of the island.

Kathisma beach, halfway between the capital and Porto Katsiki on the west coast, is the largest organised beach on the island: golden sand, sun loungers, beach bars and sometimes paragliding sessions from the nearby hill. Plan a day trip from Vassiliki. If Porto Katsiki feels too chaotic, Kathisma offers the same turquoise water with a little more comfort.

activities.text: Take a windsurfing lesson in Vassiliki — it's one of Europe's most renowned spots to learn or improve. Conditions are close to ideal: calm mornings for the basics, steady thermal winds in the afternoon for practice. Book your slot the day before — schools fill up fast in high season.

Head out early by boat from Vassiliki to Egremni and Porto Katsiki — the perspective from the sea on those white cliffs plunging straight down is completely different from the view at the top. Water taxis and small excursion boats leave from the harbour from 9am.

Savoro is a traditional preservation dish of Corfiot and Lefkadian fishermen: fish (sardines, mackerel) is fried, then marinated in vinegar, raisins and rosemary. The result is a surprisingly tangy-sweet preparation served cold — perfect for a light lunch after the beach.

Pasteli, a sesame-and-honey bar, is the traditional beach snack of the Ionian Islands — people have been eating it since ancient Greece. Simple, energising and utterly unprocessed. Pick up a few from a grocery shop in Vassiliki before heading down to Porto Katsiki: you'll need the fuel for the climb back up.

Ionian Islands Road Trip: Corfu, Paxos & Lefkada

visits.text: Ormos Vathy is one of the Cyclades' finest anchorages—a perfectly sheltered horseshoe bay with a small fishing village at the back. On nearby Tsopos beach, the Atsonios pottery has operated for 4 generations: it's one of the last workshops set up the old way, right on the beach, with wood-fired kilns and drying tables. Watch the potter work before choosing from the utilitarian ceramics and artisan pieces on display.

Apollonia, Sifnos's capital, perches in the hills at the island's center. It's a maze of paved lanes where you'll happily get lost among artisan shops, traditional tavernas, and small flower-filled squares. It was founded in the 6th century BC and bears the god Apollo's name. Come evening, it's the island's liveliest spot—open terraces, Greek music, warm ambiance without Mykonos excess.

activities.text: From Vathy, travel to Faros by road for this walk: the fishing hamlet borders a small sheltered beach. Walk along the waterfront, then follow the coastal path toward Glyfo beach; it follows the shoreline and lets you explore the coves on foot.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves
Samos in 3 Days: Temples, Hilltop Villages, and Waterfalls

visits.text: To understand Velvendos, the folklore museum offers more than a simple photograph of its houses. Housed in the 19th-century Kosta mansion, it recreates domestic rooms and showcases local trades and clothing. The objects come from residents: arrange an appointment with the municipality before arriving.

activities.text: Follow the Skepasmeno trail near Velvendos for a walk beneath the trees. The ravine brings together waterfalls, natural pools, and shaded vegetation at the foot of the Pieria Mountains; choose the short walk to the falls rather than the full route through the valley. Wear shoes with good traction and skip the walk after heavy rain.

If you are traveling during harvest season, it is worth stopping at a fruit seller in Velvendos. Peaches help define the agricultural identity of this irrigated plain, alongside apples and strawberries. Buy ripe fruit to eat that day and avoid leaving it in the car in the sun.

days_plan.itin_title: Kozani, Siatista, and Grevena: 3 days in Northern Greece

places.name: Vergina

visits.text: Gold gleams in the dim light of the Museum of the Royal Tombs of Aigai in Vergina. The grave goods from the tomb attributed to Philip II include a gold larnax weighing 11 kilograms; the exhibition also protects the funerary monuments in their original locations. The museum is concealed beneath a tumulus-shaped covering. Let your eyes adjust to the lighting before examining the details, then check the terms of the combined ticket.

Much more than an annex, the central building of the Polycentric Museum of Aigai deserves a separate visit from the royal tombs. Inaugurated in 2022, it broadens the focus to the inhabitants, queens, and daily life of the ancient Macedonian capital. The objects tell the story of a city, not just a dynasty. Plan this visit after the tombs to better connect the collections, and check the opening times for each part of the site.

Designed for public life, the Palace of Aigai looks less like a royal residence than a gathering place. Its peristyle courtyard and mosaic decoration help you imagine how the Macedonian capital functioned in the 4th century BCE. Architecture made power visible. Visit the accessible areas in the morning, bring water, and wear shoes suitable for the ground at archaeological sites.

Peaceful today, the Theater of Aigai nevertheless preserves the memory of an assassination that changed Macedonian history. Philip II was killed here in 336 BCE during the celebrations for his daughter’s wedding; Alexander succeeded him. The remains add context to the neighboring palace. Make this stop after visiting the palace and check the permitted route rather than trying to cross excavation areas.

activities.text: Next, walk through the Royal Necropolis of the Temenids at Aigai to place the treasures in their funerary landscape. This complex belongs to the Polycentric Museum and reveals another part of the royal cemetery, separate from the tombs displayed beneath the tumulus. Here, the visit takes place outdoors. Check whether it is included in your ticket and bring a hat: this walk complements the museums, with a different level of sun exposure.

places.name: Veria

visits.text: The colors are the first thing to catch your eye in the Church of the Resurrection of Christ in Veria. Dating to 1314–1315, this small church preserves frescoes by Georgios Kalliergis; the richness of its decoration contrasts with the simplicity of the building. Check opening times with the Byzantine Museum before heading there, as access to the churches depends on visiting hours.

A peaceful place for a walk, but also a place of remembrance: the Jewish quarter of Barbouta borders the Tripotamos River in Veria. Its traditional houses surround a synagogue dating to 1850, a reminder of the city’s Jewish community. Explore the narrow streets on foot and inquire before your visit if you would like to see inside the synagogue.

A pleasant surprise: the Byzantine Museum of Veria offers as much to see in its building as in its collections. Housed in an industrial building from the early 20th century, it presents the city’s Christian heritage, from the early centuries through the post-Byzantine periods. Save this visit for the hot hours of the day and check the official opening times.

activities.text: Follow the narrow streets of Panagia Dexia in Veria to find the Tripotamos River between the old houses. This traditional neighborhood combines homes and passageways near the river; the urban landscape becomes less dominated by stone as you walk. Wear shoes with good grip on the cobblestones and save this walk for late afternoon.

If you enjoy syrup-soaked desserts, try Veria’s revani at a pastry shop downtown. This local specialty is served plain or with a scoop of ice cream; the contrast makes a noticeable difference to the tasting experience. Ask for a small portion to start and enjoy this break before resuming your walk.

days_plan.itin_title: Vermio and Imathia: 5 Days from Aigai to the Mountains of Pella

map_keywords: Church of the Resurrection of Christ Veria

visits.text: Santorini—the caldera and its hilltop villages seen from the sea offer one of the Mediterranean's most spectacular arrivals by sea. Vlychada harbor on the south coast is calmer than the crowded caldera and ringed by white cliffs with lunar shapes. It's the best overnight anchorage. The volcanic sand beach of Perissa and Perivolos stretches 7 km: burning-hot black sand (bring sandals), crystal-clear water, and a gently sloping sandy bottom. In high season, it's one of the island's liveliest.

The Akrotiri archaeological site is Santorini's equivalent of Pompeii—a Minoan city buried under meters of volcanic ash during the catastrophic eruption around 1500 BC. Excavations began in 1967 under Spyridon Marinatos. Beneath a massive protective dome, you wander the ancient city streets: two-story houses with sewer systems, murals depicting daily life, pottery, tools. No bodies were found, suggesting inhabitants fled before the eruption.

At Red Beach, a blood-red cliff plunges vertically into the sea, creating a striking contrast with the blue water. The beach is narrow and busy; access is restricted because of rockfall risks. Enjoy it from the sea.

activities.text: Swimming on the volcanic beach of Perissa or Perivolos—the black sand absorbs heat, consider water shoes. Water is deep and clear.

Wine tasting in Santorini—the island's vineyards produce assyrtiko, a mineral white wine unique in the world, with vines trained into baskets (kouloura) on volcanic soil. Several estates are accessible from the anchorage or by road.

days_plan.itin_title: Cyclades Cruise: Islands and Coves

visits.text: Footsteps echo through the sloping lanes of Volissos, between Christos and Pythonas squares. The village rises in tiers beneath its fortress, with houses facing the western coast. After the drive from Mesta, save this walk for late afternoon and leave the climb to the castle for the following morning.

Volissos Castle gives you a reason to climb before breakfast. Its six round towers outline an enclosure remodeled by the Genoese in the 15th century, above the houses and the coast. Set out early, wear closed-toe shoes, and stay on permitted access routes; exploring the ruins is unlike strolling through a landscaped garden.

days_plan.itin_title: Chios in 3 days: the mastic villages and Nea Moni

visits.text: Volos stretches between the sea and the first slopes of Pelion - a setting that gives it a character of its own in Greece. Start with the Athanasakeion Archaeological Museum, built in 1909 thanks to the fortune of Alexios Athanasakis, a Pelion merchant who made his money in Egypt. The collection will surprise you: the painted funerary stelae of ancient Demetrias, their colours still vivid, are an absolute rarity in Greece - the pigments survived because the stelae were buried. You will also see Neolithic pieces from the sites of Dimini and Sesklo, located less than 15 km from the town.

The old Palia quarter, a former Byzantine fortress fortified in the 4th century, grew around the port from the 19th century onwards. The Ottomans held it from 1423 until the liberation of Volos in 1881 — nearly 460 years. Behind the train station, the Volos City Museum occupies the former Papantou tobacco warehouse (1920), restored in 2014: the glass floor on the first level reveals 6th–7th-century water channels beneath your feet. The building alone is worth a visit for its industrial architecture.

activities.text: In the evening, Volos reveals its true self through its tsipouradika — tsipouro bars, named after the local grape spirit, where you eat mezze while sipping slowly. It's an institution here: Volos is widely regarded as the Greek capital of tsipouro. The waterfront (Argonauts' promenade) is packed with these places, at their best around aperitif hour. The city owes its mythological name to Iolcos, from where Jason and the Argonauts are said to have set sail in search of the Golden Fleece — a myth that looms over the entire region.

days_plan.itin_title: Thessaly & Meteora

visits.text: Since 1748, the Vovousa bridge has connected the two banks of the Aoos with a single stone arch. The crossing fits the scale of the village: just a few steps take you to the other bank and give you a different perspective on the houses. Cross slowly and find your angle from an accessible riverbank, without climbing down onto wet stones.

A detour through Vovousa’s lanes is more rewarding than simply taking a photo of the bridge. This village in Zagori preserves an Aromanian heritage; Băiasa is its name in that language, revealing another side of the region. Look at the houses on both banks and respect the peace of residential areas by staying on public paths.

activities.text: The sound of the Aoos accompanies your walk in Vovousa long before you look at the water. The village provides access to much longer forest routes, but the walk at this stop remains short and close to the river. Stay on passable paths and return to the village if rain makes the banks slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: Metsovo and the Northern Pindus: 3 Days Among Villages and Forests

activities.text: The scent of fir trees accompanies your approach to Vytina, on the slopes of Mainalo. In the village, stone houses and shops give your stroll a different pace from the morning’s ancient sites. Leave your car at the entrance to the center and keep your walk to the lanes so you can reach Dimitsana before evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Arcadia and Bassae in 3 Days: Villages and Monasteries

visits.text: The old town of Xanthi (Palia Poli) is one of the largest preserved traditional settlements in Greece: 380,000 m² declared a protected zone in 1976, with over 1,200 buildings listed as monuments. It was rebuilt after two devastating earthquakes in 1829 and reached its zenith between 1880 and 1925 thanks to basma tobacco — an exceptional aromatic variety that supplied imperial courts and European markets. The Epirote and Macedonian craftsmen who built it blended Baroque, Neoclassical, Romanesque and Ottoman elements into a result the Greeks then nicknamed “Little Paris”.

Walk up the main street to Demokratias Square to see the clock tower, erected in 1870 by the Pomak Hadji Emin Aga. The Greek authorities wanted to demolish it in 1972 — protests by Muslim residents forced a reversal. It stands as a symbol of Xanthi's particular brand of coexistence, where Greek Orthodox Christians, Turks and Pomaks have shared the same streets for centuries.

The History and Folklore Museum of Xanthi occupies the Kougioumtzoglou House, a former double residence built in the 1860s by the Kougioumtzoglou brothers, major tobacco merchants. It's a rare example of a three-storey semi-detached house in the local style. The collections feature traditional costumes, embroidered textiles, craft tools and archives from the tobacco era. Allow an hour to do it justice.

At the entrance to the train station, the former tobacco warehouses (the Mandra) bear witness to Xanthi's economic might at the turn of the 20th century. The most notable, shaped like the Greek letter Pi (Π), housed the Ottoman tobacco monopoly's operations until 1912. It's currently being converted into a cultural venue. If you travel through the neighbourhood by car or bus, their imposing red-brick silhouettes are visible from the road.

activities.text: Walk through the lanes around Antika Square in Xanthi: this is where terrace cafés, grocery shops fragrant with eastern spices, leatherworking workshops and Turkish coffee shopfronts cluster. The morning atmosphere is particularly authentic - residents meet here before going to work. A thick Greek coffee, served with a glass of cool water, is the customary ritual.

Excursion into the Rhodope Mountains to the Pomak villages, an hour's drive north: Sminthi with its white mosque and stone lanes, Echinos set amid deep forests, Ottoman bridges over mountain torrents. These villages, isolated in the folds of the Rhodopes, have preserved architecture and traditions virtually unchanged since the 19th century. The road itself is spectacular — wooded gorges, crystal-clear rivers, not a tourist in sight.

Try soutzouk loukoum, Xanthi's signature sweet: Turkish delight flavoured with walnuts or rose, sometimes coated in a layer of toasted hazelnuts. It's the Thracian version of a widespread Ottoman confection, but Xanthi's sweet shops have a well-established regional reputation. Pair it with a lightly anise-flavoured Thracian tsipouro — milder than ouzo.

days_plan.itin_title: Thrace Road Trip: Kavala, Thasos & Philippi
Xanthi, Vistonida, and Komotini: 4 Days in Greek Thrace

visits.text: Xerokampos tells a story of cold even when the snow is gone. This valley on Mount Helmos retains moraines and a glacier-carved basin, described in the park’s geological guide. Observe these landforms from accessible roadside areas, without using closed facilities.

activities.text: Set off from Xerokampos for a short walk toward Livadi tou Louka, in the Helmos massif. The route described by local guides continues to Souvardo and Vrachni; here, you will walk only the first section. Turn back after forty-five minutes and skip the walk if snow, fog, or a thunderstorm makes navigation uncertain.

days_plan.itin_title: Achaea in 3 days: gorges, Cave of the Lakes, and Helmos

visits.text: Zakynthos Town — dubbed “the Flower of the East” (Il Fiore di Levante) by the Venetians — was completely destroyed in the 1953 earthquake and rebuilt in a neo-Venetian style with arcades and colonnaded façades. Solomos Square, the largest in town, opens directly onto the Ionian Sea. Here you'll find the Byzantine Museum, a statue of the poet Dionysios Solomos (who penned the Greek national anthem in 1823), and the town hall. This is where the action is in the morning; in the evening, head up to Bohali.

The Church of Agios Dionysios is dedicated to the island's patron saint. Founded in 1708, it houses his relics in a silver reliquary and features a gilded carved iconostasis along with fine Byzantine frescoes restored after 1953. The bell tower overlooking the harbour is one of the defining landmarks of Zakynthos. Every year on 24 August and 17 December, thousands of worshippers gather here for the saint's feast days.

The Byzantine Museum of Zakynthos, on Solomos Square, is one of the richest in the Ionians. It brings together carved wooden Byzantine icons, original frescoes from the 15th to 17th centuries rescued from churches destroyed in 1953, and 18th-century paintings by artists of the Ionian School such as Doxaras, Koutouzis and Kandounis. Some canvases depict the town before the earthquake — a striking comparison with what it looks like today. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

The Venetian Castle of Bohali, perched on the hill above the town, was built in the 15th century by the Venetians on even older foundations. The enclosure among the pines overlooks the harbour from 150 metres — from the ruined ramparts you can take in the entire bay, the port and the mountains of the hinterland in a single glance. Drive up or walk (25 minutes from Solomos Square). At sunset, locals from the village of Bohali settle on terraces with a drink — join them.

Zakynthos National Marine Park (NMPZ), created to protect Caretta caretta turtles, encompasses Laganas Bay and the nesting beaches in the south of the island. The turtles lay their eggs on these beaches between May and August - access is regulated, but glass-bottom boat excursions allow you to observe them in their natural habitat without disturbing them. If you visit in summer, do not miss a trip out to sea.

Navagio Bay - also known as “Smugglers' Bay” - is the most photographed image in all of Greece. It takes its name from the wreck of the cargo ship Panagiotis, which ran aground here on the night of 2 October 1980 after being chased by the Greek navy during a storm. The ship had left Argostoli carrying contraband goods. The white limestone cliffs rise more than 200 metres above the white-sand beach and turquoise water. Warning: landing on the beach and swimming in the bay are prohibited because of rockfall risks. Viewing from a boat remains subject to access restrictions. For the view from above, allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town, via Anafonitria or Volimes, to the clifftop viewpoint, subject to permitted access conditions.

The Blue Caves are a series of arches and tunnels carved by the sea into white limestone cliffs in the north of the island, between Agios Nikolaos harbour and Cape Skinari. Their name comes from the electric colour of the water inside, caused by sunlight reflecting off submerged limestone - a phenomenon very similar to the Blue Grotto on Capri. The walls and even your body underwater take on a vivid blue hue. They can only be reached by small boat (maximum 50 passengers to enter the arches). From Zakynthos town, allow for a return road trip to Agios Nikolaos harbour or Cape Skinari, followed by the boat visit.

Cape Skinari is the northern tip of Zakynthos, facing Kefalonia - on clear days, Mount Ainos on the neighbouring island is clearly visible. The lighthouse dates from 1897 and stands 9.5 metres tall. This is a departure point for boat excursions to the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach the cape. The cape's characteristic windmills have become one of the island's symbols.

Anafonitria Monastery, inland in the northwest, dates from the 15th century. It is one of the island's oldest and is famous for having welcomed Saint Dionysios as a monk before he became the patron saint of Zakynthos. It is surrounded by groves of century-old olive trees and a medieval defensive tower that still stands. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town for this visit. The atmosphere is peaceful, far from the beaches.

Xigia Beach is a natural curiosity: sulphur springs emerge directly into the sea from the rocks, giving the water a milky hue and a faint characteristic smell. The therapeutic properties of these sulphurous waters have long been known locally. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Xigia. The beach is small, wild and lightly visited - a good alternative to Navagio for those who want a different bathing experience.

activities.text: Roma Street, the main pedestrian thoroughfare leading off Saint Mark's Square, is lined with local shops where you can pick up mandolato nougat (almonds, honey, egg white — the island's signature sweet), ladotyri (a hard cheese aged in olive oil, Zakynthos PDO) and olive-oil products. It's also the place for evening outings — the tavernas come alive from 8 pm.

Facing Saint Mark's Square stands the Solomos and Kalvos Museum, housed in the island's former casino and open since 1968. On the ground floor lie the tombs of the two poets — Dionysios Solomos, author of the national anthem, and Andreas Kalvos. Upstairs: manuscripts, personal belongings and period documents. A must for anyone interested in Greek literature.

Fritoura is a traditional sweet from Zakynthos: a thick mixture of semolina and water, cooled, cut into pieces, fried and sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon. You can taste it from vendors who prepare it, especially during the island's festivals. In Zakynthos, look for the kiosk in front of Saint Dionysios Church to discover this speciality, served warm and crisp on the outside, with a soft centre.

Verdea is Zakynthos's AOC white wine, made from local grape varieties (pavlos, goustolidi). Dry, with lively acidity and a slightly bitter finish - it contrasts with the rounded whites of most islands. Ask for it at the taverna with local cheeses.

The ideal plan for this last day: leave early in the morning for Cape Skinari and board a small boat to the Blue Caves (allow 2 hours). Then head inland to Volimes and Anafonitria, passing through olive groves and mountain villages. In the afternoon, make the detour to the Navagio viewpoint for the photo, then finish at Xigia Beach for a dip in the sulphurous waters before returning to Zakynthos Town.

The hill village of Volimes is known for its textile artisans - rugs, embroidery and lace are displayed in the small shops along the main street. Allow for a return drive from Zakynthos town to reach Volimes. This is also where the best local products are sold: mountain honey, olive oil and handmade mandolato. The sellers are often the producers themselves.

The boat excursion combining the Blue Caves and Navagio Bay (viewed from offshore) lasts between 3 and 4 hours, depending on the option chosen. Boats depart from Agios Nikolaos harbour or Zakynthos's main port. For a departure from Agios Nikolaos, allow for a return road trip from Zakynthos town to this harbour in the north of the island. Book the day before in summer - places sell out quickly. Small boats carrying 12 to 50 passengers can enter the caves; larger ones can only pass around them.

Ladotyri is the AOC cheese of Zakynthos: a hard cheese made from sheep's and goat's milk, aged in olive oil — hence the name (lado = oil, tyri = cheese). It has a firm texture, a dark rind and a powerful, slightly fruity flavour. It is eaten at the end of a meal with local honey, or diced with an aperitif.
